CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Aphra Behn (1640–1689)

Behn was one of the first Englishwomen to earn her living by writing — in a century when a married woman had no legal identity separate from her husband. Baptised in Kent in 1640, she probably visited the English colony of Surinam in 1663–64 (the setting of her novel Oroonoko, 1688). She may have married a merchant, Johan Behn, who died or left soon after 1664. In 1666 Charles II's government sent her to Antwerp as a spy (code name "Astrea"); she went unpaid, borrowed to get home, and was threatened with arrest for debt — whether she was ever jailed is unproven. By 1670 she was writing for the stage, for money, and went on to write around nineteen plays, second in output only to Dryden.

She knew her sex was the charge against her. Defending a play attacked as indecent, she wrote: 'I am not content to write for a Third day only. I value Fame as much as if I had been born a Hero' — the "third day" being the night whose takings went to the author. Virginia Woolf, in A Room of One's Own (1929): 'All women together ought to let flowers fall upon the tomb of Aphra Behn… for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds.' She is buried in Westminster Abbey.

Restoration England

The Restoration (1660) brought Charles II back to the throne after the Civil War, the execution of his father Charles I (1649) and the Puritan Commonwealth, during which the theatres had been closed (1642–60). The new court prized wit, theatre and sexual frankness; love was spoken of as a game, a hunt or a battle, rarely as gentle sentiment. Politics had not gone away: within living memory a king had been tried as a "tyrant". When Behn calls Love Tyrannic, she borrows the language of political oppression for private feeling.

The Play: *Abdelazer, or The Moor's Revenge* (1676)

The song opens Behn's revenge tragedy (staged 1676, printed 1677), set at the Spanish court. As the curtain rises, music plays to Abdelazer, a Moorish prince sitting in gloom; the song is the Queen's entertainment — she is in love with him, and has helped poison her husband the King. Abdelazer answers it with contempt: 'On me this music lost?' So the first thing the audience hears is a song about love as cruel conquest, sung into a court where desire will lead to murder. Behn reprinted it on its own as 'Love Arm'd' in Poems upon Several Occasions (1684).

The Tradition: Cupid at War

Two old conventions meet here. Ovid's Amores declared that 'every lover is a soldier' (militia amoris) — love as warfare. Petrarch's Triumph of Love pictured Cupid as a Roman general in a victory parade, with captive lovers chained to his chariot. Petrarchan love poetry added the cruel, indifferent beloved, the suffering lover's sighs and tears, and the beloved's eyes as weapons.

Behn uses all of it — Triumph, sighs and tears, Languishments, Bright Eyes, Killing Dart — but changes the logic. Love has no weapons of his own: he takes them from the lovers, so both lovers are to blame for the god's tyranny, though only one suffers. And the lover's voice — usually a man's lament — is written by a woman, who claims a desire Enough to undo the Amorous World. (The text never states either lover's sex, which leaves the poem open; in the play it is sung to a man by the Queen's command.)

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Song: Love Armed
TSong: Love Armed
1Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,
2Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,
3For whom Fresh pains he did Create,
4And strange Tyrannic power he showed;
5From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire,
6Which round about, in sport he hurled;
7But 'twas from mine he took desire
8Enough to undo the Amorous World.
9From me he took his sighs and tears,
10From thee his Pride and Cruelty;
11From me his Languishments and Fears,
12And every Killing Dart from thee;
13Thus thou and I, the God have armed,
14And set him up a Deity;
15But my poor Heart alone is harmed,
16Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Song: Love Armed
Language & devices

Genre label: Song — this was written to be sung, as the opening number of Behn's tragedy Abdelazer (1676). Past participle: Armed is passive — Love does not arm himself; someone arms him. Love is personified as Cupid, the boy-god with bow and arrows, here turned soldier.

Meaning & effect

The title poses the question the poem answers: who armed Love? By line 13 the answer is the lovers themselves — thou and I. A song is meant to be sweet and light; this one is an indictment, so the form itself works as an irony: the audience hums along to an account of cruelty.

Line 1
Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,
Language & devices

Personification: Love as a conqueror enthroned. Triumph recalls the Roman triumph — a victorious general's parade with captives in chains — and Petrarch's Triumph of Love, where Cupid rides in a chariot followed by captive lovers. Diction: Fantastic in 1676 meant imaginary, born of fantasy. Trochaic inversion: LOVE in puts the stress on Love first.

Meaning & effect

Love is static and idle — he simply sat — while everything around him suffers. Fantastic plants the poem's suspicion: this triumph is a fantasy the lovers have made real by believing in it. The god takes the first beat of the poem as he takes everything else.

Line 2
Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,
Language & devices

Synecdoche: the lovers are reduced to Bleeding Hearts — organs, not people. Literalised cliché: the conventional "bleeding heart" of lovesickness becomes an actual wound. Verb: flowed suggests both blood flowing and a crowd streaming around a throne. Conjunction: Whilst — at the same time as.

Meaning & effect

The image sets the poem's basic arrangement: one figure enthroned, many bleeding, and both happening at once. Love's ease and the lovers' agony are simultaneous and unconnected — he does not even look at them. Remember this Whilst: it returns in the last line.

Line 3
For whom Fresh pains he did Create,
Language & devices

Oxymoron: Fresh pains — "fresh" is normally a positive word. Spondee: FRESH PAINS lands two heavy stresses together, so the phrase hits hard. Diction: Create (capitalised) is God's verb; the emphatic did Create stresses the deliberateness.

Meaning & effect

Love does not merely allow suffering — he manufactures new pain for those already bleeding (For whom). He is a parody of a creator-god: what he creates is injury. The suffering is renewed, never dulled by familiarity.

Line 4
And strange Tyrannic power he showed;
Language & devices

Political diction: Tyrannic power — the language of a ruler who governs by force, not law. Adjective: strange — unnatural, alien. Verb: showed — power put on display, as spectacle.

Meaning & effect

The first quatrain ends by naming Love a tyrant. In 1676, with the Civil War and the execution of Charles I (1649) in living memory, "tyrannic" was a charged political word, not a cliché. Love's power is arbitrary, unanswerable and performed — fitting, for a song sung on a stage.

Line 5
From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire,
Language & devices

Apostrophe: the first thy — the speaker now addresses the beloved directly. Petrarchan convention: the beloved's eyes as a source of fire. Spondee: BRIGHT EYES. Verb: took — Love takes; he owns nothing of his own.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from spectacle to accusation: Love's weapons came from the beloved. The beloved's beauty supplies the fire that burns others. Love is exposed as a borrower — his power is only what lovers lend him.

Line 6
Which round about, in sport he hurled;
Language & devices

Juxtaposition: in sport (play) against hurled (violence). Adverbial phrase: round about — in every direction, without aim.

Meaning & effect

The fire is thrown carelessly, for fun — the damage is indiscriminate and nobody is targeted, which makes it worse. Suffering is the god's game. The beloved's beauty hurts people without the beloved having to do anything at all.

Lines 7–8
But 'twas from mine he took desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World.
Language & devices

Conjunction: But sets the speaker's contribution against the beloved's. Ellipsis: mine = my eyes. Enjambment: 7→8 is the poem's only true run-on line — the desire spills over the line-end. Hyperbole: Enough to undo the Amorous World; undo = destroy, and also "ruin" in the sexual sense (an "undone" woman).

Meaning & effect

The beloved's eyes give fire; the speaker's eyes give desire — the beloved is looked at, the speaker does the looking and the wanting. The speaker claims a desire vast enough to wreck the whole world of lovers: a strikingly bold claim for a woman's voice in 1676. The first stanza ends with the speaker's power — the second will show what it cost her.

Lines 9–10
From me he took his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty;
Language & devices

Anaphora and Antithesis: From me… / From thee…. Ellipsis: line 10 drops the verb — "From thee [he took] his Pride and Cruelty". Semantic contrast: the speaker gives sighs and tears (suffering, inward); the beloved gives Pride and Cruelty (aggression, outward).

Meaning & effect

Stanza 2 becomes a ledger, an itemised account of who supplied what. The alternation looks fair, like a balanced exchange — but the items are not equal. The speaker's gifts are symptoms of suffering; the beloved's are the qualities that cause it.

Lines 11–12
From me his Languishments and Fears, / And every Killing Dart from thee;
Language & devices

Anaphora continues: From me his Languishments and Fears. Languishments is standard love-poetry diction — the wasting, pining state of the lover. Inversion: line 12 moves from thee to the end of the line. Totalising adjective: every Killing Dart.

Meaning & effect

The speaker supplies weakness and anxiety; the beloved supplies every lethal weapon — not some, all. Moving from thee to the line's end gives the beloved the last and strongest position, just as the beloved will have the last word in the poem. The ledger is complete, and wholly one-sided.

Line 13
Thus thou and I, the God have armed,
Language & devices

Logical connective: Thus — the turn from evidence to verdict. Joint subject: thou and I — the only time the two are united, and it is in guilt. Rhyme: armed will rhyme with harmed (line 15). The line answers the title.

Meaning & effect

The conclusion: Love has no power of his own — both lovers armed him. This is the poem's most radical idea: the tyranny of love is something lovers build themselves. Responsibility is shared; the next lines show the damage is not.

Line 14
And set him up a Deity;
Language & devices

Religious metaphor: set him up a Deity — to set up an idol, a made god (idolatry). Also political: to "set up" a ruler. Rhyme: Deity continues the long /ee/ rhyme of Cruelty… thee.

Meaning & effect

The god is manufactured — worshipped into existence. The lovers have handed away their own power and then bowed to it. The /ee/ sound of thee keeps returning (Cruelty, thee, Deity, free): the beloved's sound takes over the whole stanza.

Line 15
But my poor Heart alone is harmed,
Language & devices

Volta: But — the final turn. Adverb: alone — isolated, singular. Pathos: my poor Heart. Rhyme: harmed clinches armed — cause and effect bound by sound.

Meaning & effect

Two people armed the god; only one is hurt. After all the careful balance of me and thee, the outcome is entirely lopsided. The speaker's heart now joins the Bleeding Hearts of line 2 — she has become one of the god's casualties.

Line 16
Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.
Language & devices

Ellipsis: thine = thy heart. Structural echo: Whilst repeats line 2 — again someone triumphs while someone bleeds. Military diction: Victor. End-focus: the poem ends on free.

Meaning & effect

The beloved now sits where Love sat in line 1: triumphant and untouched. The final word free — unbound, uncommitted — is everything the captive speaker is not. The poem closes its frame: the opening spectacle of a god among bleeding hearts was the story of this relationship all along.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Song: Love Armed' is usually described as a complaint about the cruelty of love. That description is not wrong, but it undersells the poem and mistakes its direction of travel. Read from first line to last, this is an anatomy of how power is manufactured: a demonstration, conducted in two eight-line sentences, that the tyrant-god of love has no resources of his own — that every instrument of his rule was transferred to him by the two people he rules — and that the transfer, once made, cannot be recalled. The complaint is real, but it is the evidence in a larger argument, not the argument itself. The clearest way to see this is to track the poem's grammatical subject, because the poem passes it from hand to hand like a crown.

In lines 1–4, Love owns every verb: he 'sat', he 'did Create', he 'showed'. The speaker is nowhere — there is no 'I', no 'me', not even an implied vantage point, only the tableau itself, staged with the impersonality of a state occasion. This is the Petrarchan Triumph of Love — Cupid as Roman victor amid his captives — but Behn has removed the observer that tradition supplies. Petrarch watches the procession and eventually joins it; Behn's opening has no witness position at all, which is the first quiet hint that the spectacle may be internal, a pageant of someone's imagining. The diction says so too, for those reading with period ears: 'Fantastic' meant of fantasy — the triumph is announced as imagination before it is revealed as construction.

Lines 5–8 turn the public pageant intimate, and the speaker enters her own poem — but only obliquely, in the object case. 'From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire': suddenly there is a 'thy', an addressee, and the god's arsenal acquires a supplier. Then 'But 'twas from mine he took desire': the speaker's first appearance is as a possessive from which something has been extracted. She exists, grammatically, as a site of theft. This is the poem's method in miniature — agency is revealed retrospectively, through the audit of what was taken — and the stanza's one enjambment ('desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World') lets her single donation overflow the line, the largest item in the inventory and the only one that will not fit its container.

Lines 9–12 formalise the audit into double-entry book-keeping: 'From me… From thee… From me… from thee'. The frames are perfectly symmetrical; the contents are not. Her entries are inward and self-consuming (sighs, tears, 'Languishments and Fears'); his are outward and lethal ('Pride and Cruelty', 'every Killing Dart'). And the verb of theft, having appeared three times, is now gapped — 'From thee his Pride and Cruelty' has no 'took' at all — so that expropriation reads as routine, an administration too established to need stating. The parallelism does something to the reader as well: it trains an expectation of parity, entry for entry, which the ending will deliberately betray.

Line 13 is the poem's hinge, and its grammar is the argument. 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed': for the first and only time, both humans occupy the subject position — and they occupy it jointly, in the sentence that convicts them. Each party is a grammatical subject exactly once in the poem, and only here, in the act of arming their own oppressor. The tense matters as much as the pronouns: 'have armed' is perfect — completed action, present consequence, no undoing. 'And set him up a Deity' names the mechanism with theological bluntness: this is idol-making, worship as manufacture. The god who monopolised the verbs of stanza one is now the object of human verbs; the apparent apotheosis is, syntactically, a demotion.

Then the poem does its cruellest thing. Having dissolved the god — he never appears again after line 14 — it does not liberate his subjects. 'But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free': the final couplet contains no Love at all, only two human hearts, one wounded, one triumphant. The 'Whilst' of line 16 restages the 'Whilst' of line 2 — someone enthroned, someone bleeding — with the beloved now seated where the god sat. The audit succeeded; the tyrant was exposed as a fiction; and the fiction's dividends were paid anyway, to the party who felt less. Even the rhyme concedes it: 'free' chimes with 'thee', the beloved's own pronoun, so the last sound of the poem belongs to him.

The strongest objection to this reading is tonal, and it should be faced squarely. This is a song, written to open a tragedy of erotic obsession; its texture in stanza two is anguished, not analytic — 'my poor Heart' is the phrase of a sufferer, not an auditor; and the speaker goes on capitalising 'the God', 'Deity', as if belief survived the exposure. On this view the "anatomy" reading over-intellectualises a lament: the poem does not demystify love, it demonstrates helplessness before it, and the ledger is just the obsessive circling of a wounded mind. The theatrical frame seems to agree — the Queen whose serenade this is knows precisely what Abdelazer is, and desires him anyway.

But that objection, followed through, strengthens the thesis rather than defeating it, because the poem's most unsettling claim is exactly that disenchantment does not cure. The perfect tense of 'have armed' means the god cannot be un-made by being seen through; 'set him up a Deity' is knowledge, and the knowledge changes nothing — line 15 still begins with 'But'. The pain and the analysis are not rivals for the poem's centre; they need each other. The anguish authenticates the audit (this is not a philosopher's thought-experiment but a casualty's testimony), and the audit dignifies the anguish (this sufferer understands her suffering completely, names its mechanism, and is destroyed by it anyway). Notice, finally, what the poem never does: it never petitions. Petrarchan complaint begs — for pity, for reciprocity, for the god's mercy. This poem asks for nothing, prophesies nothing, curses nobody. Its speech-act is a verdict, delivered in a court the speaker has built herself, in the full knowledge that the verdict carries no sentence. That is the poem's whole movement: from a fantasy of someone else's absolute power to the fact of one's own unrecoverable donation — from 'Love… sat' to 'thine the Victor is', with the terrible discovery in between that we were the armourers. What begins as mythology ends as arithmetic; and the arithmetic hurts more.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & Genre

The poem is a SONG — a lyric composed to be sung on stage in Behn's play Abdelazer (1676). It is therefore a dramatic lyric, intended to be performed, not merely read. Songs embedded in Restoration drama were expected to crystallise the emotional or thematic content of the scene they precede or accompany. This song opens the play, establishing its dominant themes of love, power, and suffering before a single scene is enacted.

Stanzas

Two octaves (2 stanzas of 8 lines each) = 16 lines total. The quatrain is the underlying rhyming unit, but the printed stanza is an eight-line one in the 1677 playbook, the 1684 collection and the anthology alike. The regularity of the stanzas mirrors the relentless, systematic nature of Love's power — there is no escape from its symmetrical cruelty.

Rhyme Scheme

ababcdcd efefgfgf. Stanza 1: sat/Create (a), flowed/showed (b), fire/desire (c), hurled/World (d). Stanza 2: tears/Fears (e), armed/harmed (g), and one dominant f-rhyme — Cruelty / thee / Deity / free — which takes over every second line to the end. The alternating rhyme rather than AABB couplets is significant: it mirrors the me/thee oscillation throughout the poem — the two speakers are interlocked but never unified, never finishing each other's rhymes.

Metre

Predominantly iambic tetrameter (4 iambic feet per line: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM = 8 syllables). Occasional trochaic inversions (DUM-da at line openings) for emphasis — e.g. LOVE in Fantastic Triumph SAT — the opening stress on Love announces the tyrant immediately. The bouncy, marching iambic rhythm creates a song-like quality — appropriate, but also ironic. The cheerful form carries anguished content.

Volta / Structural Turn

The turn occurs at line 15: But my poor Heart alone is harmed. The conjunction But is the pivotal word of the entire poem. The first 14 lines have been building — describing Love's armoury, cataloguing the me/thee exchange. Line 15 delivers the blow: after all this shared creation, only the speaker suffers. The final couplet (ll.15–16) is the emotional destination of everything that preceded it.

Anaphora

Lines 9–12 use strict anaphora: From me… / From thee… / From me… / And every [Killing Dart] from thee. This liturgical repetition accumulates evidence for the asymmetry of the relationship. It has the quality of a legal case being made — exhibit by exhibit.

Capitalisation

The printed text capitalises major nouns throughout: Love, Fantastic, Bleeding, Fresh, Tyrannic, Bright, Amorous, Pride, Cruelty, Languishments, Fears, Killing Dart, God, Deity, Victor. This was a 17th-century typographic convention but also works poetically: these abstractions are elevated to near-mythological status, suggesting how overwhelming these forces feel to the speaker.

Epistle/epistrophe

Lines 9–12 use anaphora (repetition at line starts: From me… From thee…) and a positional inversion: line 10 begins From thee, while line 12 ends from thee. This is not epistrophe — the phrase migrates rather than repeating in place. The grammatical symmetry enacts the poem's structural argument: me and thee produce the same Love, yet the effects are entirely asymmetrical.

2.1 Scansion (stress in CAPITALS; feet marked |)

LScansionSubstitution and what it does
1LOVE in | fan-TAS-tic | TRI-umph | SAT — i.e. / x | x / | x / | x /Initial trochaic inversion. The god seizes the first stress before the iambic contract is even established — a metrical coup d'état; the line then settles into iambs as Love 'sits', the rhythm itself taking the throne. Stress frames the line: LOVE … SAT.
2whilst BLEED-ing | HEARTS a- | ROUND him | FLOWED (x / x / x / x /)Perfectly regular. The gore is processional: the metre flows as smoothly as the hearts, normalising atrocity into music — regularity here is the horror, not relief from it.
3for WHOM | FRESH PAINS | he did | cre-ATESpondee in foot 2, pyrrhic-leaning foot 3. The paired stresses land the blow ('FRESH PAINS'), then the auxiliary 'he did' hurries past — pain is emphatic, agency almost casual. The period filler 'did' also isolates 'Create' at line-end as a bare, God-like act.
5from THY | BRIGHT EYES | he TOOK | his FIRESpondee on the blazon. The beloved's eyes are literally the heaviest thing in the line — the gaze given double metrical force at the moment it is expropriated.
7but 'TWAS | from MINE | he TOOK | de-SIRERegular — but the ictus falls on the contrastive pronoun 'MINE': the metre does the pointing. Throughout the poem thy/mine/me/thee land on beats; the me/thee war is fought on the strong syllables.
8e-NOUGH | t'un-DO | th'AM-'rous | WORLDOnly tetrameter if elided as the 1677 playbook prints it ('Enough t' undo'). Read in full ('to undo the Amorous') the line swells past the measure — desire 'Enough' to exceed the very line that contains it. Either performance choice is expressive: compression or overspill.
11from ME | his LAN | -guish-ments | and FEARSPyrrhic third foot. 'LANguishments' drapes its two unstressed syllables across the middle of the line: the metre goes limp exactly at the word for going limp — prosodic languor.
13THUS THOU | and I | the GOD | have ARMEDSpondaic opening + medial comma. The verdict is hammered in ('THUS THOU'), and the caesura after 'I' splits the line into the couple on one side, the armed god on the other.
15but MY | POOR HEART | a-LONE | is HARMEDRhetorical promotion of 'poor' crowds stresses into 'POOR HEART'; the long open vowels (poor–heart–alone–harmed) slow the line into a wail. 'aLONE' takes the central beat — isolation at the line's core.
16whilst THINE | the VIC | -tor IS | and FREEWeak promoted ictus on 'is' makes the metre hesitate at the comma — a suspension before the door shuts — then the poem's final beat lands on 'free': the last stress in the poem belongs to the beloved's liberty.

Every line ends on a stress (masculine endings throughout): the song never lets a line die away — even 'Cruelty' and 'Deity' are forced up onto a promoted final beat, which is the point (see below).

2.2 The exact rhyme scheme — and the takeover

ababcdcd efefgfgf.

Stanza 1: sat/Create (a) — flowed/showed (b) — fire/desire (c) — hurled/World (d). Stanza 2: tears/Fears (e) — Cruelty/thee/Deity/free (f) — armed/harmed (g).

  • sat/Create — a half-rhyme (imperfect even in period pronunciation): the poem opens on a rhyme that doesn't quite close, a hairline crack in the pageantry.
  • fire/desire — a full rhyme that welds the two contributions together: his fire, her desire, chiming as one sound — the couple's only perfect union is acoustic.
  • hurled/World — violence rhymed with totality: the throw and its target.
  • The f-rhyme takeover is the poem's masterstroke. Stanza 2 should, by the pattern of stanza 1, run efefghgh. Instead the f-sound — the long /iː/ of 'thee' — returns in lines 10, 12, 14 and 16 (Cruelty, thee, Deity, free), colonising every second line to the end. The beloved's pronoun becomes the stanza's dominant sound; the speaker's rhymes (tears/Fears, armed/harmed) each sound twice and are displaced. The poem's final word, 'free', rhymes with 'thee': the beloved wins the argument at the level of pure sound. Form enacts verdict.
  • armed/harmed — a minimal pair differing by a single aspirate: add one /h/ — one exhaled breath, a sigh — and arming becomes harming. The poem's entire causal argument is audible in one phoneme.
  • The two polysyllabic f-rhymes (Cruelty, Deity) rhyme on an unstressed, metrically promoted -y — conventional in the period, faint to the ear; the monosyllables (thee, free) ring clean. The abstractions chime weakly; the beloved himself, and his freedom, chime strongly.

2.3 Line 13: 'Thus' — and the two-stage turn

Readers hunt for a single volta; the poem has two turns with different functions:

  • Line 13, 'Thus' — the logical turn. The lyric has been conducting a forensic audit ('From… From… From…'), and 'Thus' is its QED: inventory becomes verdict. Three further signals converge here: (i) 'thou and I' is the poem's first and only compound subject — the couple achieve grammatical union only in culpability, in the sentence that convicts them; (ii) the tense shifts to the perfect, 'have armed' — a completed act whose consequence is still present; (iii) hyperbaton delays the verb — 'the God have armed' — so that the god physically stands between the couple and their own deed on the line.
  • Line 15, 'But' — the adversative turn: joint cause, single casualty. Note that the poem's only two 'But's (7, 15) both introduce the speaker's side of the account (her desire; her harm) — the grammar of objection is hers alone.
  • The 'Whilst' frame (2 ↔ 16) — the strongest structural observation available. Line 2: 'Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed' — Love triumphant, others bleeding. Line 16: 'Whilst thine the Victor is, and free' — the tableau restaged, with the beloved now occupying Love's position and the speaker among the bleeding hearts. The poem ends by revealing that its opening spectacle was a prophecy: deify desire, and the person you desire becomes the tyrant.

2.4 The syntax of lines 5–12 enacts the argument

  • One clause template, obsessively repeated: 'From X he took Y'. The poem's middle is a deposition — exhibit by exhibit — and the pronouns alternate on the beats (2.1).
  • Chiasmus of donors. The four central donations run thee (fire) – me (desire) – me (sighs/tears) – thee (Pride/Cruelty): an ABBA arrangement across the stanza break that encloses the speaker's two inward gifts inside the beloved's two outward ones — the syntax stages a siege. Lines 11–12 then re-run the pair in miniature (me–thee), like a refrain tightening.
  • Positional inversion, not epistrophe. Line 10 begins 'From thee'; line 12 ends 'from thee'. The beloved's prepositional phrase migrates from line-head to line-tail — syntactically mobile where the speaker's 'From me' is anaphorically fixed (9, 11). Freedom of position previews 'thine the Victor is, and free'; the inversion also reserves 'thee' for the rhyme, feeding the f-takeover.
  • The vanishing verb. 'He took' appears in 5, 7 and 9 — then is gapped by ellipsis in 10, 11 and 12 ('From thee, his Pride and Cruelty'). The thefts accelerate into bare book-keeping: by the end of the ledger, appropriation is so systematic it no longer needs stating. Expropriation has become routine administration.
  • Result: lines 5–12 are one long balanced sentence-machine whose symmetry of contribution sets up the asymmetry of outcome — the reader is trained by parallelism to expect parity, so that 'alone' (15) lands as a betrayal of the poem's own grammar.

2.5 Capitalised abstractions: convention and meaning

Frame it precisely: seventeenth-century printers routinely capitalised substantives, so "Behn capitalises X for emphasis" is naive — say "the printed text capitalises". But in the anthology text the capitals are selective and patterned, and the pattern is readable:

  • Stanza 1 keeps the speaker's raw feelings lower-case — 'fire', 'desire', and in stanza 2 'sighs and tears' — while the capitals cluster on the allegorical pageant ('Fantastic Triumph', 'Bleeding Hearts', 'Tyrannic', 'Bright Eyes', 'Amorous World') and, in stanza 2, on the completed armoury: 'Pride', 'Cruelty', 'Languishments', 'Fears', 'Killing Dart', 'God', 'Deity', 'Victor'.
  • Reading: what enters the poem as private feeling (lower-case desire) is returned by Love as official, reified equipment (upper-case Killing Dart). Capitalisation is the typographic equivalent of 'set him up a Deity' — the promotion of emotion into institution. It is a reading of the printed page, not a claim about Behn's intention.
SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Alliteration

Fantastic Triumph (f-t): the two adjectives share the fricative 'f' and the plosive 't', giving Love's triumph a quality of force. Fresh… Fears… free: the recurrent 'f' sounds create a thread connecting the newness of pain, the anxiety of the speaker, and the freedom of the beloved. Bright… Bleeding: hard 'b' plosives give these images physical impact.

Sibilance

sat… showed… sport… sighs: the repeated 's' sounds create a hissing undercurrent, suggesting something slippery, dangerous, and seductive. Love's power has the quality of a serpent — beautiful but lethal.

Plosives

The hard plosive sounds in Tyrannic, Killing, Cruelty, took, Dart give physical weight to the instruments of Love's violence. These sounds hit the ear hard — enacting the impact of Love's weapons.

Rhythm

Iambic tetrameter creates a song-like, almost dance-like rhythm. This rhythmic regularity is ironic: the lightest form carries the heaviest content. The listener is drawn into the poem's music before registering its pain.

Rhyme

ABAB rhyme: the alternating rhyme pattern enacts the me/thee oscillation. Tears (speaker) rhymes with Fears (speaker); Cruelty (beloved) rhymes imperfectly with thee (beloved). Even the rhyme scheme refuses to let the two parties touch.

Onomatopoeia

flowed (l.2): the word sounds like movement, like liquid running. hurled (l.6): a sharp, explosive sound mimicking the act of throwing. These sound-effects make the poem viscerally physical.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something beyond itself. This poem is built from a small kit of both, each introduced in stanza one and transformed by stanza two — traceable in order on the printed page.

The armoury (motif — announced in the title, withheld in the text)

'Armed' stands over the poem as a past participle with a missing agent: armed by whom? The text delays the answer for thirteen lines. The weapons appear first as spectacle — the 'fire… hurled' in lines 5–6, ballistic and incendiary — then as itemised stock ('every Killing Dart', 12), and at each appearance they come with a supplier attached: thy eyes, from thee. What changes across the poem is the weapons' ownership history: conventional Cupid arrives pre-armed by mythology; Behn's Cupid is progressively revealed as carrying only donated equipment, until line 13 supplies the title's missing agent — 'thou and I, the God have armed' — and the rhyme immediately converts armament into its consequence, 'harmed'. The motif's trajectory: from decoration, to inventory, to indictment.

The heart (symbol, then possession)

The heart is the poem's one conventional symbol — seat of love, emblem of feeling — and Behn re-literalises it into a casualty. It enters plural, anonymous and liquefied: 'Bleeding Hearts around him flowed' (2), persons reduced by synecdoche to their woundable organ, the crowd of love's dead. It returns at the end singular and owned: 'my poor Heart alone is harmed' (15) — the speaker discovers herself inside the opening tableau, one of the hearts she had watched from apparent safety. And the final line adds a second, unbleeding heart: 'thine' (elliptical for thy heart) 'the Victor is, and free'. The symbol's movement is from generic spectacle to personal possession to antithesis — two hearts left on the field, distinguished not by what they gave (both gave) but by what they felt.

Fire and eyes (paired motif — the elemental split)

'From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire' (5) compresses the entire Petrarchan optics of love — the beloved's gaze as the channel of passion — into a single act of asset-stripping. 'Bright Eyes' is the only physical detail of any body in the poem: the sole blazon item, instantly weaponised. The fire then behaves like ordnance ('round about, in sport he hurled'), damaging at a distance, costing its owner nothing. Against it the speaker's contributions form the opposing elements: water and air — 'sighs and tears' (9) — self-consuming where fire is other-consuming; she burns inward, he outward. The play confirms the motif's currency: the Queen enters bidding music play 'whilst we from eyes — thus — dying, fan the fire', and Abdelazer complains of 'killing looks' — eye-fire is the scene's shared language of desire as harm.

The language of sovereignty (motif rising to symbol)

Trace the sequence of titles: 'Triumph' (1) — the Roman ceremony of victory, legitimate but performative; 'Tyrannic power' (4) — rule without right or limit; 'the God… a Deity' (13–14) — power theologised, beyond appeal; 'the Victor' (16) — and here the crown leaves the god entirely and lands on a human head. Each term escalates the register (military honour → political illegitimacy → divinity), and then the whole structure collapses onto the beloved, whose only qualification is that he felt less. 'Set him up' is the idiom of installation — of idols, and of usurpers. This is where motif crystallises into symbol: the manufactured Deity stands for every power — romantic, political, religious — that exists because its subjects resource and worship it. In a poem written by a Tory royalist to open a tragedy of usurpation, the resonance is deliberate; the play immediately literalises it ('This many-headed beast your lust has armed').

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Love as power

Love is a conqueror, a tyrant and a god, ruling through spectacle and pain. Desire is presented not as gentle feeling but as a relationship of domination.

02

Unequal suffering

The balanced ledger of From me… From thee promises fairness; line 15 delivers the opposite: my poor Heart alone is harmed. Equal contributions do not bring equal costs.

03

Shared responsibility

Thus thou and I, the God have armed: Love has no weapons of his own. The lovers build the tyranny they suffer under — which means it is human-made, and could be unmade.

04

Love as false religion

The lovers set him up a Deity, an idol worshipped into existence. Like a false religion, it demands sacrifice from the faithful and rewards only the powerful.

05

Gender and desire

The speaker gives sighs, tears and longing; the beloved gives pride, cruelty and weapons — a pattern that maps onto the double standards of Restoration society. A woman claiming a desire Enough to undo the Amorous World was itself a bold act.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

Four places where meaning is genuinely contestable — in each, the skill is to hold the ambiguity and argue what it does, not to resolve it.

1. Who is 'thou'? The ungendered addressee

The difficulty: nothing in sixteen lines genders either party. The "female speaker / cruel man" reading is imported — from Behn's biography, from the inverted-Petrarchan template, and from the play (the Queen's serenade to Abdelazer). Competing readings: (a) woman to man — supported by the frame, by the gendered feel of the inventories (her tears, his pride), and by Behn's polemical career; (b) genuinely open address — supported by the text's silence, by the unspecified stage singer (any voice the company supplied re-gendered it nightly), and by Behn's own 'To the Fair Clarinda', which shows her deliberately engineering ambiguous address elsewhere. What a strong answer does: treats the indeterminacy as functional, not accidental — the pronouns are roles, not persons; whoever desires more occupies 'me', whoever feels less occupies 'thee'; the poem analyses a structure of unequal desire that any two people can instantiate, which is exactly why it detached so easily from its play and survived it.

2. What is 'thine' in line 16?

The difficulty: 'Whilst thine the Victor is, and free' — 'thine' needs an antecedent. Competing readings: (a) elliptical for thy heart, in strict parallel with 'my poor Heart' — supported by the poem's habit of exact antithesis and by the frame it completes (bleeding hearts at the start, two hearts at the end); (b) loose deixis for you/yours, as song grammar tolerates — supported by naturalness: 'Victor' and 'free' suit a person more readily than an organ. The evidence favours (a) — 'Heart' is the only available antecedent, one line above — but the strong answer notices what the ellipsis does: it makes the beloved's heart victorious as a heart, i.e. the organ of feeling wins the war by refusing to feel; and because 'thine' gestures at both the heart and its owner, the last line indicts both at once. Misread it as plain 'you' and the couplet loses its terrible symmetry: this was heart against heart, and one of them fought unarmed.

3. Victim or superior rhetorician?

The difficulty: tonal. 'My poor Heart' is the diction of naive pathos; the poem containing it is a machine of forensic control — balanced ledger, logical 'Thus', epigrammatic close, and the covert boast that her desire alone was 'Enough to undo the Amorous World'. Competing readings: (a) the sufferer speaks, and the formal poise is convention (songs are neat; neatness proves nothing); (b) the account is a counter-triumph — the beloved wins the affair, the speaker wins the record of it, fixing him forever as 'Pride and Cruelty' in a song that outlived him by three centuries. Evidence: (a) rests on the unguarded possessive 'my poor', the only self-description in the poem; (b) rests on everything structural — she controls all the naming, and he never gets a verb of his own. What a strong answer does: refuses the either/or and states the relation: the form performs the mastery the content denies; whether that is compensation, revenge, or just the only dignity available is the genuinely open question — and the poem is more interesting for not settling it.

4. Whose fantasy is 'Fantastic'?

The difficulty: the period sense — of fantasy, imaginary, capricious — makes line 1 unstable. Is the fantasy Love's (a god staging his own extravagant pageant), the lovers' (a projection they mistake for a god), or merely the observer's register for 'grotesque, extravagant'? Competing readings and evidence: the objective-spectacle reading suits stanza one's impersonal staging; the projection reading is retro-activated by lines 13–14 — 'set him up a Deity' assigns the manufacture, and therefore the fantasy, to 'thou and I'. What a strong answer does: reads the word proleptically — on first pass it is decor, after line 14 it is the poem's first confession, planted where no first-time reader can understand it. The poem teaches its reader to re-read: its opening spectacle was hindsight all along.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Six close readings

Card 1 — 'Love in Fantastic Triumph sat,' Techniques: allegorical personification; trochaic inversion; period diction; classical allusion. Analysis: The inverted first foot lets 'Love' seize the stress before the iambic pattern can establish itself, so the god's coup happens rhythmically before it happens semantically. 'Fantastic' in 1676 meant 'belonging to fantasy, imagination, caprice' — not 'wonderful' — so the triumph is announced from the outset as a mental pageant, a staged illusion; the poem will end by telling us exactly who staged it ('Thus thou and I…'). Behind the tableau stands Petrarch's Triumph of Love — Cupid as Roman victor parading captive lovers — compressed into a single line and made sinister by the flat, settled verb 'sat': not conquest in progress but occupation accomplished. Intention/effect: Behn plants the poem's sceptical thesis in its first word-pair — this god's grandeur is fantasy — while the reader, lulled by the pageantry, only feels the trap close at line 13.

Card 2 — 'Whilst Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,' Techniques: synecdoche; grotesque imagery; regular metre against violent content; dramatic irony (frame). Analysis: The victims appear only as their wounded parts — a battlefield synecdoche in which persons have already been reduced to trophies — and 'flowed' liquefies even those, hearts dissolving into the blood they shed, circulating round the throne like tribute. The line's perfectly regular iambs make the gore processional: suffering set to a dance-beat, horror normalised into entertainment — which is literally what it was, sung to a paying Restoration audience. The idiom 'bleeding heart' lets Behn pun conventional lovesickness into open wound: the metaphor lovers use decoratively is here taken at its word. Intention/effect: Behn makes the reader complicit — we consume the spectacle as pleasantly as Love does — so the poem's later accusation of cruelty-as-'sport' quietly includes its own audience.

Card 3 — 'From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire, / Which round about, in sport he hurled;' Techniques: weaponised blazon; theft diction; register clash; medial caesura. Analysis: The Petrarchan blazon is stripped to one item, the beloved's eyes, and immediately expropriated: 'took' — the poem's obsessive verb — turns praise into requisition, beauty into ordnance. The comma-isolated 'in sport' sits between 'round about' and 'hurled' like a shrug between two violences: 'sport' in Restoration usage covers both game and erotic dalliance, so cruelty and flirtation become the same gesture. The clash between the casual adverbial ('in sport') and the ballistic verb ('hurled') is the poem's tonal signature — atrocity performed with perfect insouciance. Intention/effect: Behn indicts the fashionable libertine style of loving — desire thrown about as recreation — and the reader feels the specific chill of harm done lightly.

Card 4 — 'But 'twas from mine he took desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World.' Techniques: the poem's only enjambment; hyperbole; period pun on 'undo'; contrastive 'But'. Analysis: Uniquely in a poem of end-stopped ledger-lines, the syntax here overruns the line-break: 'desire / Enough' spills over exactly as the desire it names exceeds containment — read unelided, the second line even swells past the tetrameter. 'Undo' carries the Restoration sense of sexual ruin (a woman 'undone' is one seduced and discarded), so the speaker's desire could, in the god's hands, ruin the whole 'Amorous World' the way one woman is ruined. The hyperbole cuts two ways: it is a lament, and it is a boast — her contribution outscales everything else in the arsenal; the beloved donated a spark, she donated the apocalypse. Intention/effect: Behn insists on the world-sized magnitude of female desire — precisely what her culture minimised — and makes the reader admire the speaker at the very moment she reports her ruin.

Card 5 — 'From me his Languishments and Fears, / And every Killing Dart from thee;' Techniques: anaphoric ledger; verb ellipsis (gapping); pyrrhic sag; positional chiasmus; reifying capitals. Analysis: By this point the audit no longer bothers with its verb — 'took' is gapped, leaving bare double-entry lines — so expropriation reads as routine administration, theft become book-keeping. The metre goes slack inside 'Languishments' (two unstressed syllables mid-line): prosody performing the debility the word names, while 'every Killing Dart' answers it with hard plosives — her entries drain, his detonate. The beloved's phrase has also migrated from line-head (10: 'From thee…') to line-tail (12: '…from thee'), enclosing the stanza's gifts and seizing the rhyme position, so that even syntactic mobility belongs to him. Intention/effect: Behn converts complaint into evidence — a legal deposition rather than a sob — and the reader is manoeuvred into the jury box, obliged to convict before the verdict is announced.

Card 6 — 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity; / But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the Victor is, and free.' Techniques: logical volta ('Thus') then adversative volta ('But'); minimal-pair rhyme; idolatry diction; structural echo of line 2; ellipsis in 'thine'. Analysis: 'Thus' delivers the QED of the whole ledger, and the poem's grammar convicts as it concludes: 'thou and I' is the lovers' only compound subject — union achieved solely in culpability — while 'set him up a Deity' is the vocabulary of idol-making, an almost blasphemous admission that this god is manufactured. The rhyme then executes the sentence: 'armed' becomes 'harmed' by the addition of a single breathed /h/ — cause and consequence one aspirate apart — and the final 'free' chimes with 'thee', handing the beloved the poem's last sound as well as its victory. 'Thine' is elliptical for thy heart: the closing contrast is heart against heart, hers harmed, his 'the Victor… and free', restaging line 2's tableau with the beloved now enthroned where Love sat. Intention/effect: Behn ends not with the god but with the man who has replaced him, so the reader grasps the poem's real target: not Cupid, but the human beloved whom worshipped desire licenses to tyrannise.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

Makes visible: that the poem's meaning is executed by its form — 'armed'/'harmed' as a minimal pair one aspirate apart; the f-rhyme (/iː/ of 'thee') annexing every even line of stanza two until 'free' hands the beloved the final sound; the gapped 'took' turning theft into book-keeping. On this view the poem is its machinery, and the machinery argues. Flattens: everything the machine was built into — the theatre, the Queen, the gender politics of a woman publishing desire. A purely formalist account cannot say why the same sixteen lines scandalised anybody, or what it meant that they were sung.

Feminist

Makes visible: the gendered economy of emotional labour: 'From me he took his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty' — feeling extracted from one party, licence from the other, and the products returned as weapons against the one who felt. It also restores the scandal of scale: a female-voiced claim to 'desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World' in a culture that pathologised female wanting. Flattens: the text's actual genderlessness (crux 1) — the reading must be imported and should say so; and it risks reducing the speaker to victim, when the poem's rhetorical mastery (crux 3) is half the evidence.

Marxist / materialist

Makes visible: an economy of extraction and alienation in the strict sense: the lovers' inner resources are appropriated ('took', three times, then silently), converted into capital — an armoury — and returned as a hostile power that dominates the producers: 'Thus thou and I, the God have armed'. The god is accumulated surplus. The lens also catches the poem's own material life: love-suffering written as a saleable song by the first Englishwoman to live by her pen — feeling literally monetised, twice (stage 1676, print 1684). Flattens: intimacy; tone; the fact that the poem's wound is betrayal by a person, not exploitation by a system — pressed too hard, the reading makes the beloved a class and loses the couplet's privacy.

Psychoanalytic

Makes visible: projection and splitting: two people disown parts of themselves — her longing, his aggression — and install them in an idealised external figure ('set him up a Deity') who can then be blamed, worshipped and obeyed; the god is a defence against the unbearable plain fact the last two lines state without him (he does not love her). The ending withdraws the projection, and what remains is exactly the reality the fantasy was built to avoid. Flattens: history and convention — it treats Petrarchan stock properties (darts, fire, sighs) as symptoms of a psyche when they are also simply the period's shared vocabulary; anachronism must be conceded, and 'the speaker' kept distinct from Behn.

Historicist

Makes visible: why 'strange Tyrannic power' is not a dead metaphor in 1676: written within living memory of a king's execution (1649) and a restoration, for a court culture that spoke of love as campaign and conquest, as the overture to a tragedy in which a queen's desire genuinely does arm a usurper ('your lust has armed', Act I). Love-language and state-language interpenetrate because the culture's power-anxieties ran through both. Flattens: the poem's portability — it reads the lyric as document and cannot explain why it works on readers who know none of this; the structure of unequal desire is not period-bound, and the poem knows it ('the Amorous World', not the Restoration one).

Reader-response

Makes visible: that the poem engineers its reader as deliberately as its god: the parallel ledger trains an expectation of parity that 'alone' (15) betrays — the reader feels the injustice as a broken formal promise before understanding it; 'Fantastic' only becomes legible on re-reading (crux 4); and the theatrical frame implicates the audience, who enjoy — 'in sport' — a song its onstage addressee orders silenced. Flattens: authorial design and historical situation; unanchored, it collapses into "I feel that…" — the discipline is to name the textual trigger for every response claimed.

(Postcolonial note, offered as a caution rather than a lens-application: the frame — a racialised Moor, a Spanish court, a source play trading in the period's stereotypes — rewards postcolonial attention, but the sixteen lines themselves contain none of it. Importing the play's racial politics into the lyric as if they were its content is a marked error; the honest formulation is that the lens illuminates the poem's staging, not its text.)

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative and contested readings

5.1 Proto-feminist reading (the default — state it precisely). The speaker's donations (desire, sighs, tears, languishments, fears) map onto the culturally 'feminine' position of exposed feeling; the beloved's (fire, pride, cruelty, killing darts) onto masculine display and licensed indifference; the poem anatomises a structural, gendered asymmetry — who may desire safely, and who pays. Evidence: the gendered inventories; the economy of ruin in 'undo'; Behn's own position and polemics (3.1). Weakness: it must be imported — nothing in the sixteen lines genders either party; 'the speaker is a woman' rests on biography and on the play's frame, not the text. Strongest when framed as "the poem maps onto gendered experience", not "the woman speaker".

5.2 Queer / ungendered-address reading. Both pronouns are unmarked; the poem is an 'I–thou–god' triangle open to any configuration, and the intimate 'thou/thee/thy' register works for any beloved. Behn demonstrably wrote beyond heterosexual convention — 'To the Fair Clarinda, Who Made Love to Me, Imagined More than Woman' (printed 1688) eroticises a deliberately double-gendered addressee — so indeterminacy here can be read as licence rather than accident: a lyric of desire engineered to be singable by anyone, to anyone. Evidence: total absence of gender markers; the unspecified stage singer (3.5), meaning the first audiences heard it in whatever voice the company supplied; Behn's Clarinda poem as canon-internal precedent. Weakness: the theatrical frame immediately heterosexualises it (the Queen's serenade to Abdelazer), and its 1684 placement among heteroerotic pastorals does the same; the openness is real but contingent.

5.3 Political-allegory reading. 'Tyrannic power', 'the God have armed', 'set him up' — the lexicon of usurpation and investiture. The lovers behave like subjects who authorise a sovereign (cf. Hobbes's covenant, 1651 — analogy, not allusion) and then discover he rules them absolutely; in the play this is literal: the Queen's desire arms Abdelazer's rise, and the scene re-uses the song's verb for politics ('This many-headed beast your lust has armed'). The song thus opens a tragedy about how private appetite manufactures public tyranny. Evidence: the political diction; the Act I echoes (3.5); Restoration memory of civil war and anxiety about arbitrary power. Weakness: Behn was a committed Tory royalist — reading her as attacking monarchy misfires; the target is arbitrary passion as usurper, and the allegory works through the play, not as free-standing political comment. Date-discipline needed: 1676 precedes the Exclusion Crisis.

5.4 Against the victim-reading: the speaker as rhetorical victor. The poem says she lost; it performs mastery. She controls the ledger, the logic ('Thus'), the balanced antitheses, the god's biography; her single donation is world-scale ('undo the Amorous World') while his are itemised trinkets; and she gets the last word about him. On this reading the complaint is also a counter-triumph: the beloved wins the affair, the speaker wins the account of it — and since the account is all we have, her defeat arrives already avenged in form. Evidence: the forensic architecture (2.3–2.4); the covert boast of line 8; the poised, epigrammatic close. Weakness: 'my poor Heart' is tonally unguarded — self-pity that resists the triumphant-rhetorician frame; and formal control can be read as defence mechanism rather than victory.

5.5 Metapoetic-sceptical reading. 'Fantastic' (fantasy), 'Create', 'set him up a Deity': the poem watches love being manufactured — out of stock Petrarchan parts, no less ('sighs and tears', darts, fire) — and says so. Cupid is a fiction assembled by lovers and by poets; the lyric deconstructs its own tradition even while singing it. Evidence: the idol-making diction; the arsenal composed entirely of literary conventions; the frame of a professional dramatist opening a play with a manufactured song. Weakness: the final couplet insists the harm is not fictional — 'my poor Heart alone is harmed' — so the poem's scepticism stops at the god, not at the suffering; a purely metapoetic reading under-reads the pain.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS

Analysis
  • The entire poem is written mainly in Iambic Tetrameter instead of sounding like a romantic heartbeat, it sound like the relentless march of an army (de-DUM, -deDUM)
  • Comprised of two stanza of 8 lines
  • Two quatrains in each stanza: ababcdcd / efefgfgf — in stanza 2 the thee sound (f-rhyme) returns and takes over
  • Single (masculine) rhyme, falling on the stressed syllable
  • The rhymes Harmed/armed, Cruelty/Deity are accentuated with dental T and D sounds dominating the poem and ensign each line on an empathic upbeat
  • The rhythm portrays the Tyrant’s cruel eagerness: he may be sat in lordly fashion, but his eyes are ever restless, his cruel gaze ever hunting for new victims
  • All lines but line 7 are end-stopped
  • Lack of enjambment shows restriction, lack of freedom, delivering a deliberate pace, offering a sense of finality and control in Love’s dominance over the speaker
  • Tone of restrained despair, with each line stands as a self-contained reflection of Love’s power and the speaker’s defeat
  • Predominantly end-stopped lines create a rhythmic regularity, mirroring the inevitability of the speaker’s emotional suffering as if each line marks the closing of an argument of painful truth
  • Manipulation of syntax to emphasis particular words and raises dramatic and elevated tone
  • Anastrophe (deliberate inversion of the usual order of words or clauses): Love in Fantastic Triumph sat rather than Love sat in Fantastic Triumph
  • Fronted Adverbial (adverbial word/phrase moved to the front of sentence): From me he took his sighs and tears, rather than He took his sighs and tears from me
  • Capitalisation in ad hoc manner (when necessary/needed): Fantastic Triumph and Bleeding Hearts
  • Capitalisation not strictly governed by rules as it is today
  • Used for emphasis to give words significance, key ideas, concepts, or personifications
  • Verb took explicitly repeated three times and implicitly repeated three times
  • Characterise Love as a parasitic creature which feeds and grows off emotions of other, giving nothing back but pain and sorrow
  • Anaphora of from enhances the one-sided, destructive and debilitating nature of love

Love Armed

Analysis
  • Love is personified and alludes to Cupid, the god of desire, erotic ove, attraction and affection (Son of Venus, Goddess of Love, and Mars, God of war)
  • A youth armed with a bow and arrow (Historically)
  • Behn portrays a more dangerous, militaristic force, rather than a charming figure inspiring mutual affection, almost as if Cupid has taken on more characteristics of his father, Mars, The God of War through the adjective of Armed
  • Equipped with weapons, ready for battle and capable of inflicting harm
  • Emphasises emotional conquest and suffering, Love as an aggressor or tyrant
  • Transforms love as a symbol of power and oppression exploiting and draining the emotions of both the speaker and the beloved
  • Ready to inflict damage underscoring the one-sided, destructive nature of love in the poem, as the speaker suffers emotional wounds without reciprocation or relief
  • Portrayed as a conqueror who leaves behind vulnerability, and pain in its wake
Effect, style & response
  • Sets up the Reader’s relief to imagine it as a Love song, about beauty, romanticism or even Desire
  • Makes them feel calm, concern-free (possibly slight concern with armed but possibly physically having one in your arm[s] rather than being militarily armed
1 / 2

Love in Fantastic Triumph sat, / While Bleeding Hearts around him flowed,

Analysis
  • The capital ‘L’ in Love implies proper noun and as the first word of the poem and being in the title it signals its centrality in the poem
  • Sets up and foreshadows the theme and idea of love (but subverted to an idea of evil and malevolence)
  • The very beginning breaks the rhythm with a Trochaic reversal immediately asserting the warlord (Love)’s dominance and violence before ending the first line, while revealing the all-encompassing power that Love posses
  • The diction Fantastic Triumph which presents Love in the posture of a ruling conqueror or victor surrounded by opulence and wealth
  • The term Fantastic can mean extravagant and imagined, not so much amazing but surreal, as if the poem is gazing into the speaker’s nightmare
  • The diction triumph also refers to Roman military parade celebrating victory, displaying captive and spoils of war framing Love as subjugation and Conquest (Splendid Parade)
  • Capitalisation and use of anastrophe shows Love’s self-satisfaction and self-congratulation at destructive power
  • The diction “Fantastic implies that is surpasses even the imperial grandeur of Ancient Rome; It’s so resplendent and grisly that it defies imagination
  • The aural pronunciation of FanTasTic Triumph saT and later BuT ‘Twas from mine he Took Desire all have dental sounds creating a cold, crisp, martial footstep that perfectly suits the malicious character of Love, and implies how warm emotions are cast aside struck down, and trampled upon
  • The personification of Love having sat allows for the imagery of Love being enthroned in a state of grandeur as he sits in relaxation and authority
  • The anthropomorphism merged with juxtaposition allows for a powerful contrast to Love’s relaxed state to the tormented condition of the assembled party in his court encircling him
  • The diction and anthropomorphism him also humanises Love and presents him as a callous male figure
  • The graphic visual imagery flowed and bleeding shows the broken hearts haemorrhaging blood that forms a larger blood pool, which so casually and is able to flow, as well as the pain of a broken hart
  • Anastrophe of sat and flowed contrasts Love’s serenity with carnage that surrounds him and highlights his position of unassailable power
Effect, style & response

<- The Depiction of Love as a Roman Warlord

<- Cupid

3 / 4

For whom Fresh pains he did Create, / And strange Tyrannic power he showed;

Analysis
  • The personified Love is inflicting new injuries on the already bleeding group which presents him as a psychopath because he is making their already bad condition worse.
  • Fresh Pains also provides tactile imagery of the extreme sensitivity of their wounds
  • The adjective Fresh to describe the pains of unrequited love carries the meaning of new, strong, and sharp, revealing a continuously renewing torment and the intense and acuteness of them
  • Emphasises the sharpness of the speaker’s emotional suffering
  • The perpetuity of love creating new wounds which are immediate and overwhelming, despite the old ones haven’t been healed shows the theme of relentless emotional suffering
  • Create in 1676 would have been pronounced as if there was no ‘e’ shortening the vowel to rhyme perfectly with sat which carries out the martial feel
  • The anthropomorphised and personified Love carried out other fearful actions that presented him as a Tyrant and oppressive ruler
  • The adjective strange and tyrannic to describe Love’s power evoke the notion of love as an oppressive, alien, and cruel force which dominates the speaker’s emotional love
  • Heavily contrasts to the classical, idealised, romantic version of love celebrated in poetry
  • Diction of strange highlights emotional alienation experienced by the speaker, showing the love she feels being isolating as it drives a wedge between her and any potential for emotional fulfilment
  • Hints at disempowerment of loving someone who does not return her affection, making love itself feel alien
  • Diction of tyrannic shows a dominating, cruel and oppressive force, evoking the image of a tyrant who exercises power arbitrarily and mercilessly, exploiting its victims while subjecting them to its will without care or compassion
5 / 6

From thy Bright Eyes he took his fire, / Which round about, in sport he hurled;

Analysis
  • From thy uses the archaic second person pronoun that signals that the speaker is speaking directly to someone else from whom something was forcibly taken while bright eyes is an allusion to the vitality, health and excitement that Persona two has
  • He took his fire again anthropomorphise personified Love and presents it as a forceful raider
  • The imperious (arrogant and domineering) picture of a victorious Tyrant is amplified by imagery of fire having stolen the bright light from another’s eyes he forges this energy into arrows of fire that he hurls indiscriminately so anyone unlucky enough to get struck is guaranteed to get burned
  • The imagery of the eyes refers to the renaissance belief that the yes were powerful conduits of emotions and desire and that love could be caught through the gaze
  • The diction of his Bright eyes signifies an eager anticipation, as we imagine him to lean forward on the edge of his throne hunting for more victims at which he can hurl his fiery arrows
  • How causing pain is a fun distraction for him
  • The speaker silently addresses the object of her love (King Philip’s son through the apostrophe (where the speaker speaks directly to an absent person, thing or idea)
  • Love has taken the sparks of passion and transformed them into a weapon, to be hurled and thrown carelessly about with considerable force for entertainment and sport
  • His fire has struck her down, causing an ignition of her desire through the archaic possessive pronoun thy
  • Related with thou, thee, thine
  • Used in an informal and familiar manner (similar to ton, tuo or tu in French, Italian and Spanish)
  • Discusses more about her tender feelings for him rather than their relationship
  • As a mere lady-in-waiting it would be outrageous to thou a prince in conversation rather than you
  • Strikingly shows the disregard with which Love toyed with what he took from Persona Two
  • The diction of “hurled’ also provides vivid Visual Imagery that he threw it with enormous force and blatant disregard as if it was a game
7 / 8

But ‘twas from mine he took desire / Enough to undo the Amorous World.

Analysis
  • Shifts the focus to the speaker and reveals that she too was a victim of Love who again like a raider drained her of zest, deep affection and enthusiasm
  • Love has taken the desire that has been ignited in her eyes recognising the destructive potential that it could even annihilate the very world and concept of love itself
  • Further emphasised through the only line with enjambment emphasising how the speaker allows her meaning to spill over from one poetic line to the next through the sheer force of her emotion
  • The hyperbole gives the degree to which the speaker has been exploited, and suggests that what was taken from her was so much that it can cause everyone in the world to become disinterested in sex and engaging in sexual relations
  • This paradoxical phrase implies that despite the overwhelming feeling the speaker experiences, desire can’t survive if the feeling isn’t returned, and how Love itself can destroy the idea of Love
  • Reinforces the Janian Nature of love: Uniting people together, separating and causing destruction
  • There is a longstanding literary tension between the opposing forces of reason and emotion, between Apollonian and Dionysian (In Greek myth, they are half-brothers who couldn’t be more different in character: Apollo stands for rational, logic, and reason; his brother for instinct passion, irrationality, and chaos (God of wine for a reason lol))
  • Her “sighs and tears’ cast the speaker in Dionysian robes, as does the extreme of her emotional pain: she feels so strongly that the Amorous World is literally undone
9 / 10 / 11 / 12

“From me he took his sighs and tears, / From thee his Pride and Cruelty; / From me his Languishments and Fears, / And every Killing Dart from thee;”

Analysis
  • Use of pairing reveals two more things that Love took from the speaker and are allusion to her groans and weeping, which reinforces that she is experiencing heartbreak
  • Continues the characterisation of “Love’’ as a parasitic force, which grows in power and strength as it feeds off the speaker’s and the man’s emotions
  • The verb took governs the subsequent phrases in lines 10, 11, and 12 despite not being explicitly repeated each time
  • The implicit repetition reinforces the relentless, one-sided nature of love in the poem
  • How Love continually draws out and takes away sighs, tears, languishments and fears and the beloved Pride, cruelty and killing darts
  • The repetition across both stanzas emphasises the act of conquest, where Love seemingly conquerors and takes over the body of the speaker
  • The anaphoric lines From me… From thee… From me… and the final inverted from thee (moved to the end of line 12) show a constant back and forth between thee and me creating the impression that never the twain shall meet (too different to exist together)
  • Constant use of From reinforces the one-sided nature of love too
  • The rhyme scheme composed in alternate rhyme (ABAB not AABB) rather than rhyming couplets evokes the impression of two people remaining at a distance from one another
  • Alongside the subversion of romantic imagery is a subversion of poetic form as Behn defines it as a Song which was often set to music to entertain and to delight courtly listeners with musical rhythms and rhymes yet Love Armed is not a dreamy love song
  • The only song heard is the flourishing of trumpets and beating of drums that accompany the return of a victorious army as it is written in Iambic Tetrameter
  • In a more conventional love poem it might evoke the passionate beating of lovers’ hearts, but here it more readily associates with the iron-shod boots of a marching army, as those hearts are ruthlessly trampled upon
  • Shifts the attention to Persona Two and suggests that they are arrogant and sadistic and it is from them Love got both traits that he is displaying
  • The use of the anaphoric from in the fronted adverbials emphasises the multiple raids that Love engaged in, while her repetition of “took’ emphasises how forcefully he grabbed what he collected, and Love’s insatiable appetite creating a sense of exploitation and imbalance
  • Exposes two additional things that Love stripped from the speaker and are allusions to her weak physical state, sadness, and anxiety through the diction of languishments
  • The imbalance of power between the pair becomes clear as the speaker is debilitated, weak, physically and emotionally drained, overcome with misery and despair, while the man is aloof and unfeeling
  • Shifts the attention to Persona Two and presents them as the only source of the tool from which Love murders people
  • Dart is an allusion to Cupid’s arrow, not as an arrow shot playfully to inspire mutual affection but rather a lethal weapon designed to strike down and cause pain and suffering
  • The killing dart also symbolises a dark twist on the idea of being lovestruck having been physically struck with blood flow[ing] out in a grisly pool
  • The speaker is clearly prone to emotion and suffering from a depth of feel seen through the symbols of emotions “sighs and tears’
  • The softness of the sounds of the diction and long vowel sounds of the ea combination in fears/tears or the breathy onomatopoeia of the word sigh
  • Yet the speaker's beloved displays a certain heartlessness, characterised by words such as Cruelty, Pride, and Fire
  • It is the object of her affection from whom the Tyrant took his Killing Dart, words made of sharp stabbing sounds K/D/T suggesting that this person, is more than capable of inflicting wounds of his own
Effect, style & response
  • This allusion to Cupid is quite obvious In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of love, desire, attraction, and eroticism. Also known as Amor (meaning love) and Eros in Greece, commonly portrayed as a slender winged boy (as above)
  • Always represented and conflated with the cherubim, small, winged angels who interceded between Earth and Heaven, and images of Cupid as a small chubby boy carrying bow and arrow, which are the source of his power to fill others with uncontrollable love and desire, were entering the public consciousness
  • Behn faintly alludes to well-known iconography, by distorting Cupid’s kindly features with malice as he launches yet another Killing Dart at an unsuspecting victim
  • The general semantic field of war armed, Bleeding, pains, power, Tyrannic, hurled, Killing Dart, harmed, and Victor all link to Cupid, drawing out his father’s legacy as the words are not naturally suited to compose a romantic ditty (song)
  • Difficult to judge whether the speaker and this other person have had a past relationship that’s turned sour, or whether this is just a case of spurned affection
  • The diction Cruelty faintly implies the speaker has some experience of the other, and in stanza two, line 13 which is the only line of the poem to feature both thou and I briefly placing the two side by side (more so a conjecture, but interesting!)
13 / 14 / 15 / 16

“Thus thou and I, the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity; / But my poor Heart alone is harmed, / Whilst thine the victor is, and free.”

Analysis
  • Attributes supernatural power to Love and presents it as an instigator (a person that brings about and initiate) that has put weapons in the hands of the speaker and her lover, so that they can fight and harm each other while he watches
  • The speaker and her beloved have both provided Love with the weapons that have enabled him to become a deity and a god
  • How Love is no god by himself, but rather enthroned as a god through others supplying him with the ability to be so
  • Despite both of them being responsible, she is the sole victim
  • The final contrast emphasises the speaker’s suffering and emotional vulnerability as she acknowledged that while they both played a role in empowering Love, only she bears the painful consequences of them both
  • Her heart is wounded and enslaved by the very force they have armed while her beloved remains untouched being the Victor and free
  • This dynamic reinforces the inequity (lack of fairness or justice) in their relationship, where love is not mutual where the speaker is trapped in emotional turmoil, while her beloved escaped unscathed
  • Underscores the parasitic nature of love where one person gives and suffers while the other benefits without sacrifice
  • Enhances the poem’s portrayal of Love in a man’s world, as a cruel and one sided force
  • Turns the focus back on the speaker and is a very direct detail of her claiming to be broken hearted, feeling pity for herself and being wounded
  • Again returns the focus to the speaker’s lover and shows that to her he won and has become unencumbered (Free and not impeded) after their breakup
  • Returning the idea of Dionysian and Apollonian, in contrast, her beloved, cast as the Victor” in this tug-of-war, seems immune to extremes of feeling (possibly his Pride holds him in check, as if he considered himself above such tawdry (showy but poor and cheap) emotions)
  • This major clash between the two is symbolised through the eyes of the speaker and her beloved, and in their brief moment of eye-contact, the fire in the other’s eyes ignited desire in the speaker’s own
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks (Cambridge anthology pairings)

PoemSharp linking ideaShared technique
'A Different History' (Bhatt)The oppressed co-produce the power that rules them: Behn's lovers 'the God have armed, / And set him up a Deity'; Bhatt's colonised 'unborn grandchildren / grow to love that strange language'. Both interrogate worship of what wounds — and both hang the scandal on the same adjective, Behn's 'strange Tyrannic power' answering Bhatt's 'strange language'.Personified deity (Cupid enthroned / 'Great Pan… emigrated'); patterned rhetorical repetition (Behn's declarative ledger vs Bhatt's accusing questions).
'The Chimney Sweeper' (Blake)The song form as sugared delivery-system for cruelty: Blake's nursery lilt carries child-labour, Behn's dance-metre carries bleeding hearts — and in both, the powerless are taught to consent to their own harm (Tom's angelic bargain, 'if all do their duty, they need not fear harm'; the lovers' self-made god).Deceptively musical regular metre and rhyme against dark content; dramatic irony at the speaker/singer's expense.
'Where I Come From' (Brewster)Two poems about what beings are made of: Brewster's 'People are made of places' composes selves benignly from their sources; Behn runs the same logic malignly — a god assembled from donated feelings that return as another's weapons. Constitution as belonging vs constitution as expropriation.Anaphoric catalogue as structural spine; accumulation of concrete items building an abstract whole.
'Report to Wordsworth' (Boey Kim Cheng)Humans arm the force that overwhelms them: Boey's 'insatiate man' has ruined Nature until 'God is labouring to utter his last cry' — a deity dying of human agency, where Behn's is empowered by it; both make mankind author of its own cosmic catastrophe.Classical allusion repurposed (Neptune, Triton / Cupid's triumph); personification of a vast power; compressed formal frame (near-sonnet vs song) containing enormity.
'The Cockroach' (Halligan)Both poems stage a spectacle that turns into a mirror: Halligan watches the insect until 'I thought I recognised myself'; Behn watches the triumphant god until line 13 reveals the observers built him. The volta of self-implication — spectator discovered inside the spectacle.Extended conceit sustained then broken by a turn; final-line recognition that redirects the whole poem.
'Lament' (Clarke)Elegy as indictment by litany: Clarke's 'For the…' catalogue of war's casualties parallels Behn's 'From me… From thee…' ledger — repetition as mounting evidence of cost, with the guilty party (war / the beloved) convicted by accumulation. Both also beautify damage ('the cormorant in his funeral silk' / 'Bleeding Hearts… flowed') so that elegance itself feels complicit.Anaphora as structural engine; ironic gap between musical, ceremonial form ('Song', 'Lament') and violent content.

02Post-colonial

A Different History

Sujata Bhatt · 1988

A culture that treats a book as sacred is asked why its grandchildren now love the language that was used to erase it.

Lines

Form

Date
