Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
The Chimney-Sweeper
Language & devices

Occupational noun: The Chimney-Sweeper names the child only by his trade. Intertext: Blake gave the same title to a poem in Songs of Innocence (1789), whose sweep has a name, Tom Dacre.

Meaning & effect

The child has no name: he is his job, a function rather than a person. Repeating the title of the earlier poem invites comparison — the Innocence sweep is comforted by a dream of heaven; this Experience sweep sees through the comfort.

Line 1
A little black thing among the snow,
Language & devices

Dehumanising noun: thing. Adjectives: little (pity) and black (soot, and the darkness of death and sin). Visual contrast: a black figure among the snow.

Meaning & effect

The observer first sees not a child but an object. The word records how society sees him: small, dirty, barely human. The stark black-on-white image isolates him in a cold, pure world from which he is excluded — Blake the engraver composes it like a picture.

Line 2
Crying ‘weep, ‘weep, in notes of woe!
Language & devices

Pun: ‘weep, ‘weep — the sweep's street-cry ("sweep! sweep!") lisped by a small child, which becomes the word for crying. Metaphor: notes of woe — his cry as a song. Exclamation: the observer's shock.

Meaning & effect

The cry that advertises his labour is also a cry of grief. Passers-by hear a trade call; Blake makes us hear weeping. Notes of woe returns in line 8, where we learn the song was taught.

Line 3
Where are thy father and mother, say?
Language & devices

Question: Where are thy father and mother, say? Pronoun: thy — intimate, or talking down to a child. Imperative: say? — tell me. In the set text the question has no quotation marks.

Meaning & effect

The observer assumes, as anyone would, that a child alone in the snow must have lost his parents. The question exists to be answered — and the answer will be far worse than orphanhood. After this line, the child speaks for the rest of the poem.

Line 4
‘They are both gone up to the church to pray.
Language & devices

Child's voice: the speech begins. Verb phrase: are both gone up — up places the church above the street. Plain statement: no complaint, just fact.

Meaning & effect

Both parents are alive, together and respectable: they are at church. The child's flat, matter-of-fact report makes the indictment sharper — piety and the abandonment of a child sit side by side, and up puts the praying parents above the child in the cold below.

Lines 5–6
‘Because I was happy upon the heath / And smiled among the winter’s snow,
Language & devices

Conjunction: Because — the child's explanation. Setting: the heath — open, natural freedom. Echo: among the winter's snow repeats line 1's among the snow.

Meaning & effect

The child's happiness is given as the reason he was sold into work. The logic is shocking — perhaps a contented child seemed able to bear it — and Blake lets it stand unexplained. The same snow that now isolates him once framed his smile: the echo measures what has been lost.

Line 7
They clothed me in the clothes of death
Language & devices

Metaphor: the clothes of death — the sweep's black, sooty clothes. Polyptoton: clothed… clothes. Irony: clothing a child is an act of care.

Meaning & effect

The parents dressed him for death: a trade that killed through falls, suffocation and disease. The caring verb clothed turns into its opposite. Death half-rhymes with heath — the poem's only imperfect rhyme, as if the freedom of the heath has been knocked out of true.

Line 8
And taught me to sing the notes of woe.
Language & devices

Repetition: notes of woe from line 2. Verb: taught — deliberate instruction. Rhyme: the stanza recycles stanza 1's snow / woe.

Meaning & effect

What was a spontaneous cry is now a trained performance: his grief has been made into his work song. Oppression does not just cause suffering — it teaches the sufferer to perform it, profitably. The recycled rhyme traps the child in the same sounds.

Lines 9–10
‘And because I am happy and dance and sing, / They think they have done me no injury:
Language & devices

Polysyndeton: happy and dance and sing — a child's chatter, and the cadence of the Bible. Anapaestic rhythm: And be-CAUSE I am HAP-py and DANCE and SING — a dancing lilt. Verb: They think — belief, not knowledge.

Meaning & effect

The child still dances and sings, and his resilience becomes the parents' excuse: if he seems happy, surely no harm was done. They think exposes self-deception. The colon after injury sets up what they are doing instead.

Line 11
And are gone to praise God and his priest and king,
Language & devices

Polysyndeton: God and his priest and king. Tricolon: religion, Church and state as one chain. Rhythm: the same anapaestic lilt as line 9.

Meaning & effect

The parents have gone to praise the very powers that allow children to be sold. For Blake, God (as the Church presents Him), the priest and the king are a single system of authority. The child's dancing and the parents' praising are set to the same tune: both are performances the system demands.

Line 12
Who make up a heaven of our misery.’
Language & devices

Paradox: a heaven of our misery. Verb phrase: make up — to construct and to invent. Pronoun: our — all sweeps, all the exploited. Rhyme: injury / misery.

Meaning & effect

The final accusation: those in power build their heaven — their comfort, and their religious consolation — out of children's suffering, and the heaven they promise is invented. Blake's draft first read "Who wrap themselves up in our misery"; the revision makes the charge both more theological and more damning.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The easy account of this poem — small child, cruel parents, wicked Church, reader duly moved — mistakes it for a plea. It is not a plea. Nothing in the child's nine lines asks for anything: no appeal, no 'help me', no address to the adult at all after the first answering line. The poem's real subject is the machinery by which a society converts a child's suffering into everyone else's comfort, and its real scandal is not that the child suffers but that he understands — better than his parents, better than the questioner, and at least as well as the reader. I want to argue that the poem is built to disqualify, one by one, every adult position from which the child might be viewed comfortably — including the position of feeling sorry for him — until the only stance left standing is his own analysis.

Begin where the poem begins, in the wrong voice. 'A little black thing among the snow' is the adult world's perception rendered with terrible fidelity: not a boy but a 'thing', its size noted ('little'), its colour noted ('black'), its setting noted ('among the snow') — the grammar of an object in a landscape, almost a connoisseur's grammar. The line has been called compassionate; it is at best pre-compassionate, the seeing that precedes recognition. The cry in line 2 is what forces the upgrade from 'thing' to interlocutor: ''weep, 'weep' is the trade-cry 'sweep! sweep!' as a very young mouth actually delivers it, the /s/ not yet manageable, and the mangling turns advertisement into lament without the child intending either. London heard this cry daily and heard it as commerce. The observer at least hears 'notes of woe' — and responds with the poem's one question: 'Where are thy father and mother, say?' It is a kind question and a hopeless one. It assumes the child's condition is an anomaly with a local cause — lost parents, a family misfortune — when the poem is about to demonstrate that the cause is not local at all. Pity personalises; the child is about to structuralise.

His answer opens with the poem's quietest devastation: 'They are both gone up to the church to pray.' Not dead, not lost: at church. 'Both' closes the escape-route the question offered — this is no orphan, but a complete, functioning, respectable family, which has chosen. The rest of his speech is organised as an argument, and the conjunctions carry it: 'Because I was happy… They clothed me… And because I am happy… They think… And are gone.' Twice the child identifies his own happiness as the operative cause. The first time it is the pretext: his visible contentment on the heath made it possible to put him to work without the appearance of cruelty — you can sell a smiling child and call it providence. The second time it is the alibi: his persistent cheerfulness is now the evidence by which his parents acquit themselves — 'They think they have done me no injury.' The logic is airtight and monstrous: happiness before the harm licenses the harm; happiness after the harm proves there was none. The child's joy — the one thing that is authentically his — has been converted at both ends into an instrument of his exploitation. This is a subtler claim than 'his happiness is fake'. The poem never says it is fake. It says something worse: that its being real is no obstacle to its being used.

The form is running the same argument in parallel. The poem wears the metre of the nursery — couplet chime, four-beat lines, an anapaestic skip — and the skip intensifies precisely where the content darkens: 'And be-CAUSE I am HAP-py and DANCE and SING' is three anapaests running, the most dancing line in the poem, and 'And are GONE to praise GOD and his PRIEST and KING' moves to the identical tune. Praising and dancing, worship and performance, are metrically one activity: the parents at their devotions and the child at his compulsory cheerfulness are both keeping time to the same song, and the song is the system's. Blake could have broken the metre to signal outrage. He does the opposite — he lets the pretty music play on, because the horror he is diagnosing is exactly that everything continues to sound lovely.

Then the trap closes grammatically. 'God and his priest and king' looks like a list of the venerable; the line ends; and the sentence does not. 'Who make up a heaven of our misery' — the poem's only significant enjambment tips the objects of praise over the line-break into the dock. 'Make up' will not settle: they fabricate heaven (a consoling fiction, invented to keep the poor patient); they constitute heaven (their comfort is literally assembled from child-labour — warm rooms, swept flues); and, at a stretch, they make up for misery with heaven, the compensatory bargain the Church actually preached. The genius of the phrase is that the ideological reading and the economic reading are the same reading: the story told about heaven and the comfort extracted from the child are one manufacture. And 'our' — the child's only plural — silently reveals that he has never been speaking merely for himself. Behind the single black figure in the snow stands the class of children for whom he is spokesman.

Set the Innocence poem beside this and the pairing sharpens rather than softens it. There, the child-speaker consoles Tom Dacre with the angel's bargain — be a good boy, do your duty, and 'you need not fear harm', with God as father in exchange. The Experience child has seen through precisely that transaction: 'They think they have done me no injury' answers 'they need not fear harm' across the five-year gap, and 'make up a heaven' names the bargain as a fabrication. What changed between 1789 and 1794 is not the child's circumstances — both freeze, both climb — but his epistemology. Innocence believes the consolation; Experience has costed it and knows who profits.

The obvious objection: no real climbing boy talks like this; the poem puts a pamphleteer's analysis in an infant's mouth, and its portrait of the parents — punishing a child for happiness — is caricature. The objection fails twice. First, the implausible articulacy is the device, not a flaw: every plausible voice in the poem has been shown to be compromised — the parents by self-deception, the questioner by the smallness of his pity — so the truth is given to the one speaker with nothing to gain from illusion. Making the child the poem's best thinker is the point at which pathos becomes accusation. Second, the parents are not caricatured; they are exculpated into something more frightening. They are believers, not monsters — 'They think they have done me no injury' grants them sincerity, and the final line transfers the deepest guilt from them to the system that manufactures their sincerity for them. Blake's target was never two individuals; it was the alliance — God's Priest, God's King, joined by that single possessive 'his' — which arranges matters so that ordinary, pious, even loving people can sell a child and feel righteous on the way to church. The poem ends without the child finishing his argument aloud to anyone; the questioner has long since vanished from it. Whom, then, is the analysis for? The reader — the only adult left in the snow, holding a pity the poem has just demonstrated to be insufficient, and an understanding it has just made impossible to refuse.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form

Three quatrains (4-line stanzas) with AABB rhyme scheme: snow/woe; say/pray; heath/death; snow/woe (repeated); sing/injury; King/misery. This is a ballad form — the form of folk songs and nursery rhymes. Blake deliberately deploys the cheerful, popular form of working-class oral tradition to describe a working-class child's destruction. The irony is both formal and social.

Nursery rhyme quality

The AABB couplet rhymes and approximate iambic metre give the poem the quality of a nursery rhyme. This is profoundly ironic — nursery rhymes are associated with the safety and innocence of early childhood. To use this form for a child who has been deprived of that very innocence is a savage formal irony.

Three stanzas — three perspectives

Stanza 1: third-person observer describes the child (dehumanising view from outside). Stanza 2: the child speaks — explaining the parents' betrayal of his happiness. Stanza 3: the child's devastating social-religious critique — parents praise God and King while their child suffers. The move from external observation (St.1) to the child's own voice (St.2–3) is dramatically powerful.

Dramatic shift in speaker

Line 3–4: A question is addressed to the child. From line 4 to the end, the child answers. This move from reported observation to direct speech gives the child agency and voice — the poem ends with the child's own analysis rather than an adult's pity.

Repetition of notes of woe

The exact phrase appears twice: l.2 (crying in notes of woe) and l.8 (taught to sing the notes of woe). The first is involuntary (the child's cry of suffering); the second is learned (what the parents taught). The repetition shows how the child's natural suffering has been appropriated and converted into a trained performance.

Because construction

Lines 5–8 and 9–11 both begin with Because I was… and And because I am… — the causal logic of the poem's accusation. The structure of because X, they did Y is the syntax of reasoned blame. The child is being very precise about the mechanisms of his exploitation.

End word: misery

The poem ends with misery — a word of complete hopelessness. Compare with the Innocence version which ends with harm (manageable) and the implication of future salvation. Misery has no such consolation. It is the poem's final, ringing verdict.

Stanza logic. Three quatrains, twelve lines — half the length of the Innocence poem's twenty-four. The halving is expressive: the Experience child has less life left, and needs fewer words because he understands more. The stanzas step inward: stanza 1, the street — an adult sees a 'thing', hears a cry, asks a question; stanza 2, the past — the child's history, told as cause and effect; stanza 3, the present — the child's analysis of what his parents believe and whom that belief serves. Sighting, history, ideology. The camera work runs from outside (a black object in a white field) to the furthest inside possible (what 'they think').

Two voices, one handover. Lines 1–3 belong to an adult observer — passer-by, reader-surrogate, or Blake himself; all three are possible, and the indecision is functional, since whoever it is stands where we stand. Lines 4–12 are the child. The handover at line 4 is the poem's true turn: the object of line 1 ('thing') becomes the poem's only intelligence. Asked a small question — where are your parents? — he answers a much larger one: why am I here? From line 4 the adult never speaks again; there is no room to. A second, quieter turn comes at line 9, where 'Because I was' becomes 'because I am': history becomes diagnosis. The third is the enjambment into line 12 (below).

Rhyme. Scheme: AABB / CACA / DEDE — with two deliberate disturbances.

  • Stanza 1 rhymes in couplets: snow/woe, say/pray. Nursery-rhyme certainty; question chimes with prayer as if piety were the natural answer to everything.
  • When the child begins explaining, the couplets open into cross-rhyme — argument replaces jingle. And stanza 2's B-rhymes are stanza 1's A-rhymes again: snow/woe return as rhyme-words (lines 6, 8). The poem cannot get out of its own first sounds; the remembered happy snow is locked to the present woe by the very rhyme-engine of the verse. Sound as fate.
  • heath/death (5/7) is the poem's one imperfect rhyme: the final /θ/ matches, the vowels refuse (/iː/ against /ɛ/). The rhyme that binds the child's free past to his sentence of death is audibly wrong — the ear registers a forced join, which is exactly what the syntax claims ('Because I was happy… they clothed me in the clothes of death').
  • injury/misery (10/12) rhyme only on unstressed syllables — a weak, falling, three-syllable chime. After the firm masculine rhymes (snow, woe, say, pray, sing, King), the poem's final couplet-sound is enfeebled, a dying fall: the nursery music runs down like a clockwork toy exactly as the largest accusation is made.

Metre. The base is a loose four-beat line mixing iambs and anapaests — the metre of songs, hymns and nursery rhymes — but the substitutions are doing precise work. Scansion of all twelve lines (stressed syllables in capitals; feet marked with |):

LineScansionWhat the substitution does
1a LITtle black THINGa-MONGthe SNOWThe anapaest hurries over 'tle black' and lands the beat on THING — metre itself objectifies the child.
2CRY-ingWEEP, WEEPin NOTESof WOETrochaic inversion then a spondee: two adjacent full stresses stall the line. The cry cannot be absorbed into the lilt; it stops the music.
3WHERE are thyFA-ther andMO-ther?SAY?Falling triple rhythm — the adult's sing-song solicitude — snapped shut by the stranded stress 'say?': tenderness ending in command.
4They are BOTHgone UPto the CHURCHto PRAYThe child answers in anapaestic swing — his signature rhythm, the trained cadence of a singer.
5Be-CAUSEI was HAPpy u-PONthe HEATHTwo mid-line anapaests: the remembered happiness skips.
6And SMIL'Da-MONGthe WINter's SNOWThe poem's only strictly iambic line — the one unbroken thing in it is the memory of being whole.
7They CLOTHEDme inthe CLOTHESof DEATHRead iambically only by promoting 'in'; the speaking voice gives three heavy beats — CLOTHED, CLOTHES, DEATH — with a dead patch between. A beat has gone missing, like everything else.
8And TAUGHTme to SINGthe NOTESof WOEThe anapaest falls on 'to SING' — the taught skip, the drilled lightness.
9And be-CAUSEI am HAPpy and DANCEand SINGThree anapaests and an iamb: the most dancing line in the poem is the dance. The metre performs the performed happiness.
10They THINKthey have DONEme no INjur-yAnapaests continue, then the line falls off its last stress — 'injury' trails away unstressed, harm minimised even by the cadence.
11And are GONEto praise GODand his PRIESTand KINGIdentical triple swing to line 9. The parents' worship moves to the same jig as the child's dance — metrically, praising and performing are one activity. That equivalence is the poem's accusation made audible.
12Who MAKEup a HEAV'Nof our MISer-yAnapaests again, then the falling tail: the poem ends on two unstressed syllables. No ringing final beat; 'misery' dies away rather than closing.

The most important metrical fact: lines 9 and 11 share the anapaestic pull, so the child's dancing and the parents' praising are set to the same tune.

Syntax. Stanza 1 is short units: statement, cry, question. The child's answer is two long periodic sentences built on the same frame — 'Because I was… They clothed me… And taught me…' and 'And because I am… They think… And are gone… Who make up…'. This is the syntax of proof: premise, agent, consequence. A child in a protest poem might be given exclamation; this child is given subordination — the grammar of someone who has worked out the mechanism. Note also what the syntax withholds: no 'but', no 'yet', no plea. There is no adversative anywhere in his speech because, from where he stands, nothing contradicts anything: the system is working exactly as designed.

Punctuation and lineation. Every line is end-stopped or lightly paused except one: 'to praise God and his priest and king, / Who make up a heaven of our misery.' The poem's only consequential enjambment tips praise over the line-end into what praise conceals; the relative clause arrives like the exposure of a hidden mechanism — you think line 11 has finished (a list of the great and good), and the sentence keeps going and indicts them. The heavy end-stopping elsewhere belongs to the nursery-rhyme surface: closed lines, closed world. Caesurae cluster in the adult's lines (line 2's cry is twice interrupted; line 3 breaks twice, at the question mark and before 'say?'), while the child's lines run fluently — the drilled fluency of someone who has said, or sung, all this before.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The missing /s/. The cry ''weep, 'weep' is the street-cry 'sweep! sweep!' — the trade's advertisement, shouted through residential streets — as it actually sounded in the mouths of children too young to manage the initial cluster: /sw/ collapses to /w/. Two things follow, and both are better than the usual 'pun' point. First, Blake invented nothing: London had been hearing infants cry 'weep, weep' for decades and choosing to hear 'sweep'. The poem is a transcription with the self-deception removed — the pun was found in the street, and the finding is the indictment (that the mangling itself is proof of how young the child was when put to work). Second, the poem then keeps making the very sound the child cannot: snow, say, smiled, sing, snow, sing — sibilants everywhere, including in the title's 'Sweeper'. The trade-word itself never appears in the twelve lines; its only trace is the maimed cry. The poem's soundscape holds the /s/ just out of the child's reach.

The long vowels. 'Weep! 'weep!' is built on the thin, high /iː/ — a keening, reedy vowel, the pitch of a small child's voice. Against it the poem lays a spine of long /əʊ/: snow, woe, notes, clothed, snow, notes, woe, gone — the moan-vowel, recurring like a tolling. Read aloud, the poem alternates keening and moaning; its two registers of grief are phonetic before they are semantic.

The th-web. Soft dental fricatives knit the poem's agents together: thy father and mother → They clothed me in the clothes of death → They think they have done me no injury. The whisper-consonant links the parents, their act, and their belief in one hushed thread. The effect on the reading voice is a kind of gentleness — the poem never raises its voice about them, which is far more damning than if it did.

Plosives. 'A little black thing' — after the soft opening 'A little', 'black' is spat, and 'thing' clicks the line shut. The hard /k/ and /g/ return in 'King', binding the poem's first cruelty of diction to its last named authority by sound.

Aspiration. 'Happy upon the heath' — open-mouthed, breathy, warm; the /h/ is the sound of exhaled ease, and it never recurs after line 6 except in 'heaven' — where the breath has been requisitioned.

Polysyndeton as liturgy. 'And… And… and dance and sing… and his priest and king' — the chained 'and's are simultaneously a child's paratactic chatter and the cadence of the King James Bible. The poem mocks the Church in the Church's own rhythm — scripture's syntax turned against scripture's administrators. That doubleness (childish/biblical) is why the last stanza sounds at once naive and prophetic.

Cadence. The poem's music runs down as its argument completes: firm masculine rhymes early, the weak falling injury/misery pairing late; the last line ends on two unstressed syllables. The nursery tune decays in real time. A reading voice discovers it cannot end the poem with any emphasis — 'misery' can only be let fall — and that enforced quietness is the final effect.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs; a symbol stands for something. This poem's method is to take a motif, repeat it once, and let the repetition convert it into a symbol — the second occurrence always arrives bent.

1. Snow. Line 1: 'among the snow' — an environment, an engulfing white field with a black object in it ('among' does the engulfing — surrounded, hidden, invisible). Line 6: 'smiled among the winter's snow' — the identical phrase-shape, but now the snow is the medium of remembered happiness: real cold that a loved child could smile in. The repetition proves the snow did not change; the child's relation to it did. Only across the two occurrences does snow become a symbol — of a world whose whiteness (purity, respectability, the churchgoers' self-image) is indifferent rather than clean, and which now excludes the blackened child it once delighted. Any reading that fixes snow as 'false purity' from line 1 has to ignore line 6; the motif's movement is the meaning.

2. The cry that becomes a song. Line 2: 'Crying… notes of woe' — involuntary, animal, heard in the street. Line 8: 'taught me to sing the notes of woe' — the same phrase, now the object of instruction. Between the two occurrences stands the poem's whole theory of oppression: the child's spontaneous grief has been converted into a trained performance, his voice made into his product (the cry advertises his labour; his labour causes the cry). By line 9 the conversion is complete: 'dance and sing' — woe fully professionalised as visible cheerfulness. The motif traces a production line: cry → curriculum → performance. As symbol, the 'notes' stand for every form of suffering that a system teaches its victims to present acceptably.

3. Clothing and blackness. Line 1: 'black thing' — the child is his covering; soot has replaced skin as his surface. Line 7: 'clothed me in the clothes of death' — the polyptoton (clothed/clothes) folds the act and the object into one another: the dressing and the shroud are the same event. Clothing a child is the elementary parental act of care; here it is the transfer of death onto his body. The image inverts baptism — instead of white garments welcoming the child into the community of the saved, black ones induct him into the community of the condemned. Traced across the poem, blackness moves from description (line 1) to investiture (line 7): he is not merely dirty; he has been robed in his fate, formally, by his own family.

4. Going, and going up. Line 4: 'both gone up to the church'; line 11: 'And are gone to praise'. The parents are defined twice by absence, and the absence has a direction: upward. Church sits above street; heaven above church; the child at the bottom in the snow. By line 12 the vertical motif produces the poem's final symbol — 'a heaven' at the top of a structure whose foundation, the syntax insists, is 'our misery'. The geometry matters because it is also the trade's geometry: a sweep climbs upward, inside the flue, so that the household above may be warm. Every ascent in this poem is made on the child.

5. Happiness. 'I was happy' (5) → 'smiled' (6) → 'I am happy and dance and sing' (9). The strangest motif, because it survives. Past happiness was the pretext ('Because I was happy… They clothed me'); present happiness is the alibi ('because I am happy… They think they have done me no injury'). Happiness never belongs to the child as a private good; each time it appears, the adults convert it into a licence. That is the motif's terrible trajectory: joy as provocation, then joy as exoneration — the one thing the child cannot afford to display is the one thing he cannot stop doing.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Innocence destroyed

The child's natural joy — happy upon the heath — is not simply lost with age but taken from him by adults. In Experience, innocence is something society actively targets.

02

Hypocrisy of family, Church and state

The parents pray while their child works; they praise God and his priest and king, the powers that permit his sale. Piety and exploitation are not opposites here but partners.

03

Resilience used against the victim

The child still dance[s] and sing[s], and his parents take it as proof they have done no injury. His endurance becomes their excuse.

04

Religion as social control

Who make up a heaven of our misery: the comfort of the powerful, and the heaven they promise the poor, are built out of suffering. Half a century before Marx called religion "the opium of the people", Blake shows it numbing the conscience of the comfortable.

05

Black and white

The little black thing against the white snow: soot against purity, the excluded child against a clean world. The blackness is literal grime and a mark of what society has done to him.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. 'Because I was happy upon the heath… They clothed me in the clothes of death' — what causal claim is this? The difficulty: read literally, the parents punished the child for being happy, which seems psychologically absurd. Competing readings: (a) the child's bitter post-hoc logic — he knows only that happiness was followed by betrayal, and his 'because' is the reasoning of someone making sense of the senseless; (b) the economic reading — his evident contentment made the sale feel harmless (a thriving child will cope; a smiling child cannot be being wronged), so happiness genuinely was the enabling condition; (c) the doctrinal reading — to the Church's eye, untaught natural joy is suspect, something to be corrected into discipline and duty, so happiness attracted correction as heresy attracts orthodoxy. Evidence: (a) leans on the child's age and the naive parataxis ('And… And…'); (b) on the exact parallel with stanza 3, where happiness demonstrably functions as evidence ('because I am happy… They think they have done me no injury'); (c) on 'taught me to sing the notes of woe' — woe as curriculum implies an institution that considers woe instructive. A strong answer refuses to pick: the line is written so that the child's naive logic and the system's real logic coincide — that is its horror. The mistake is to soften 'because' into 'although'; the poem means its preposterous causality.

2. 'And because I am happy and dance and sing' — is the happiness real? The difficulty: the poem's alibi-structure tempts you to call the joy performed, trained, fake — but the child himself asserts it in the present tense, and Blake elsewhere treats child-joy as indestructible energy. Competing readings: performance (the dance and song are literally his trade — the sweep's public patter — so 'happy' names the professional surface the parents mistake for wellbeing); resilience (the joy is genuine and unkillable, which makes the parents' inference almost reasonable and therefore more terrible); dissociation (the learned cheerfulness of the habituated victim, who can no longer find the injury he knows exists). Evidence: performance — 'taught me to sing' makes song curricular two lines earlier; resilience — the was happy / am happy symmetry insists the same quality persists through the catastrophe; dissociation — 'They think they have done me no injury' is knowledge held at arm's length, stated without anger. What a strong answer does: notices that the poem needs the happiness to be real and used — if fake, the parents are merely fooled; if real, they have done something worse than deceive themselves: they have made the child's own vitality testify against him. Hold the line open and the parents' guilt deepens.

3. Who is accused — 'They', 'they', 'Who'? The difficulty: the pronouns' reach keeps shifting. 'They are both' (4) is unambiguously the parents. But by 'They clothed me' (7) the agent could be parents, masters, or the adult world; 'They think' (10) again reads parental; then 'Who make up a heaven' (12) grammatically attaches to the nearest antecedents — 'God and his priest and king' — transferring the final, largest charge away from the parents to the institutional trinity. Competing readings: tight grammar (the child ends by accusing the institutions, having half-excused his parents as their instruments); loose grammar (the relative clause gathers everyone — parents praising and powers praised — into one 'Who'); and the editorial complication that Blake's plate has no quotation marks, so even the boundary of the child's speech, and hence who says the last line, is an editor's decision rather than Blake's. Evidence: the possessive chain 'his priest and king' constructs the institutions as a single system, a natural antecedent; but the sentence's subject throughout has been the parents ('They think… And are gone…'), and 'Who' caps their sentence. A strong answer uses the wobble: the pronoun-drift is the analysis — responsibility in this poem is a chain along which guilt travels upward, from father and mother to priest and king to 'God', and the grammar refuses to let any link detach itself.

4. 'Who make up a heaven of our misery' — fabricate, constitute, or compensate? The difficulty: 'make up' is triple, and 'of' is double, and every combination yields a different theology. Readings: (i) invent: heaven is a made-up story, sold to the poor so that present suffering feels like an investment — religion as management of the exploited; (ii) assemble: their heaven — comfort, warmth, clean flues, moral self-satisfaction — is physically composed out of the children's misery, as a house is made of bricks; (iii) compensate: heaven is offered in exchange for misery, the actual homiletic bargain preached to the poor (endure now, be rewarded after). 'Of' as raw material supports (ii); 'of' as derivation supports (i). Evidence for (i): 'make up' as fabrication sits naturally with 'They think' — the stanza is about manufactured belief. For (ii): the poem's economics — everything the adults have, from warm church to easy conscience, has been extracted from the child. For (iii): the Innocence poem states the bargain openly ('if all do their duty, they need not fear harm'), and this line is its audit. What a strong answer does: shows the senses are not alternatives but a mechanism — the fiction (i) is what enables the extraction (ii), and the promised exchange (iii) is the fiction's selling price. Then note the last word: after 'heaven', 'misery' — the poem ends by placing the two nouns in the order the system prefers, heaven on top, misery underneath, load-bearing.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. 'A little black thing among the snow,' — dehumanising diction; visual antithesis; indefinite article. The line performs the perception it condemns: whoever speaks it sees size, colour and category, but not a child — 'thing' is not Blake's cruelty but the world's, transcribed. The indefinite article does quiet work: a thing, one of an unnumbered many, glimpsed and generalised in the same instant — against which the title's definite 'THE Chimney Sweeper' reads as the label on a social type rather than a person's name. 'Among the snow' sets the poem's palette (one black mark on a white field — the composition Blake actually etched below the text) and its politics: the child is in the whiteness but not of it, an inclusion the preposition makes feel like engulfment. The stress-pattern lands the beat on 'THING', so the metre itself objectifies him. Intention and effect: Blake opens inside the language of the passer-by so that the reader begins the poem complicit, using the very grammar the child will spend nine lines correcting.

2. 'Crying ''weep, 'weep' in notes of woe!' — found pun; spondee; auditory imagery. The cry is the trade's street-advertisement, 'sweep! sweep!', in a mouth too young for its initial cluster: the /s/ drops and what remains is, by phonetic accident, the truth — weep. The pun is found, not made; London had been hearing it for decades and electing to hear commerce rather than grief, so the line simply removes the city's earplugs. Metrically the two stressed monosyllables jam the nursery lilt — the cry will not scan, will not be carried by the song, and that resistance is its pathos. 'Notes of woe' converts the cry to music, and 'notes' is proleptic: within six lines we learn the music was taught, which retrospectively poisons even this spontaneous-seeming grief. Intention and effect: Blake makes the reader's ear repeat society's failure — you must mishear 'sweep' inside 'weep' to understand the line, performing the substitution the adult world refuses.

3. ''Where are thy father and mother, say?' — interrogative + imperative; archaic second person; dramatic framing. The question is kindness at its least useful: it assumes absence, misfortune, an anomaly — that a crying child alone in snow must have lost someone. 'Thy' cuts two ways, and readers split exactly here: it is the intimate/downward form (as to a child or social inferior), so it is either warmth or condescension, and the poem declines to disambiguate. The appended 'say?' — a bare imperative with its own stress — tips solicitude into demand: even compassion, addressed downward, arrives as an order to account for yourself. The child's answer will expose the question's scale-error: the parents are not missing but present elsewhere, at prayer, which no 'where' question can reach. Intention and effect: Blake plants the reader's proxy in the poem and gives him the wrong question, so that the child's oversized answer measures the distance between pity and understanding.

4. 'They are both gone up to the church to pray.' — matter-of-fact declarative; 'both'; directional irony. The line's flatness is its horror: no protest, a full stop, the tone of a child reporting a routine — because it is one. 'Both' quietly dismantles every mitigating narrative the question offered — not orphaned, not a broken home, but a complete and functioning family whose two adults have made the same choice. 'Gone up' gives the poem its vertical axis: the parents ascend (to church, towards heaven) while the child remains at street level in the snow, and the poem will spend its last stanza pricing that ascent. The church is where they are instead of here; piety is rendered as a location, and the location is 'away'. Intention and effect: Blake lets the most damning sentence in the poem sound the most ordinary, so the reader feels the normalisation before being told about it.

5. 'Because I was happy upon the heath,' — causal conjunction; pastoral setting; past tense. 'Because' is the poem's most audacious word: it asserts that happiness was not incidental to the child's fate but its cause. The claim works at every level the poem contains — psychological (a visibly thriving child can be sold without visible cruelty), doctrinal (untaught joy reads to the pious as idleness needing correction), and rhetorical (the child has learned that in his world consequences follow joy). The heath is everything the flue is not — open, horizontal, unowned — and 'was' seals it in the completed past; the grammar performs the irreversibility. Note the breath in the line: the aspirated 'happy… heath' opens the mouth, a phonetic memory of ease that the poem never allows again. Intention and effect: Blake forces the reader through a logic that should not parse but, in this society, does — the shock is not that the reasoning is alien but that it is recognisable.

6. 'They clothed me in the clothes of death,' — polyptoton; inverted investiture; metaphor. Clothing a child is elementary parental care; here the act of care is the transfer of death onto the body, and the polyptoton ('clothed… clothes') seals act and object into a single gesture — the dressing is the shroud. The metaphor is simultaneously literal (the sweep's soot-blacked garb, the uniform of a trade that killed by cancer, suffocation and fall) and sacramental: an anti-baptism, black garments in place of white, induction into the condemned rather than the saved. 'Of death' hangs genitive and ambiguous — clothes belonging to death, made of death, leading to death — and the line does not choose. The agents remain 'They': by now the pronoun has widened past two parents towards everyone whose comfort requires the uniform. Intention and effect: Blake corrupts the tenderest domestic verb in the language so that the reader cannot retrieve an innocent sense of 'clothed' afterwards — the poem's method in miniature.

7. 'And taught me to sing the notes of woe.' — repetition with variation; institutional verb; irony of song. The phrase 'notes of woe' returns from line 2 transformed: there it was heard in the street, involuntary; here it has a syllabus. 'Taught' is the poem's coldest verb — suffering not merely inflicted but instructed, drilled, examined — and it converts the child's grief into a skill that serves his owners: the cry advertises the trade; the trained voice is the product. This is the poem's theory of oppression in one line: systems do not only cause pain, they administrate its expression, licensing the forms in which the victim may be heard. The genuinely disquieting consequence: everything the child says to us, lines 4–12, is delivered by a voice we have just been told was trained — his testimony arrives in the enemy's medium. Intention and effect: Blake implicates expression itself, leaving the reader to wonder whether even this poem's song is one of the notes of woe the system taught.

8. 'And because I am happy and dance and sing,' — anapaestic metre; polysyndeton; present tense. The scansion is the analysis: 'And be-CAUSE I am HAP-py and DANCE and SING' — three anapaests at a run, the poem's most dancing line, so that the metre performs the compulsory lightness it describes. The polysyndeton is double-voiced: a child's breathless chatter ('and… and… and') and the cadence of the King James Bible, so the sentence sounds at once naive and liturgical — the church's own rhythm carrying the evidence against it. 'Am' insists the happiness is current and real; the line's grammar is the first premise of the parents' syllogism ('because happy, therefore uninjured'), and the child recites it knowing exactly what it will be used to prove. Two lines later the parents' worship ('And are gone to praise God and his priest and king') moves to the identical anapaestic tune: dance and devotion are one music. Intention and effect: Blake sets the alibi to the prettiest rhythm in the poem so that the reader is charmed by it in the act of seeing through it.

9. 'They think they have done me no injury:' — cognitive verb; litotes/understatement; falling rhyme. Everything rests on 'think': not lied, not pretended — believe. The parents are granted sincerity, which is far worse than hypocrisy, because sincere belief is what institutions manufacture; the line's target is the machinery that produces good conscience. 'No injury' is the vocabulary of the tribunal and the account-book — the minimising register in which harm is audited and found absent; the child borrows their language for his own case, deadpan. Metrically the line dies away on 'injury', unstressed, rhymed weakly with 'misery' — harm minimised even by the cadence. The th-alliteration ('They think they…') whispers; the poem never raises its voice where an accusation is largest. Intention and effect: Blake relocates evil from cruelty to self-exculpating belief, and the reader — also an adult who thinks well of themselves — is not permitted to stand outside the diagnosis.

10. 'Who make up a heaven of our misery.' — enjambed relative clause; polysemous verb; first-person plural. The sentence seems complete at 'King'; the relative clause tips over the line-break and arrests the objects of praise — the poem's only significant enjambment, timed for the exposure. 'Make up' refuses to settle among its three senses — fabricate (heaven as consoling fiction), constitute (their comfort literally assembled from child labour), compensate (heaven as the promised exchange for patience) — and the phrase's power is that the senses describe one mechanism: the story is the extraction. 'Our' is the child's only plural, and it detonates quietly: he has been speaking all along for a class, not a case — the single black figure in the snow was a synecdoche. The poem ends on 'misery' — unstressed, dying fall, the word physically underneath 'heaven' in the line as in the world. Intention and effect: Blake compresses his entire critique of institutional religion into one relative clause, and leaves the reader holding the only question that survives it — who is heaven for, and who pays.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Marxist / materialist. The lens makes visible that this is a poem about production: the child is a commodity ('a little black thing' — the grammar of goods, not persons), his voice is his advertising ('weep, 'weep' cries his availability through the streets), and 'heaven' is the surplus extracted from his labour — 'Who make up a heaven of our misery' describes, with complete economic precision, comfort assembled from the exploited — bluntly, sweeps died so that the better-off could have warm, unsmoking rooms. Religion appears as ideology in the strict sense: the belief-system ('They think they have done me no injury') that reconciles the exploiters to the exploitation, anticipating Marx's 1844 'opium of the people' by fifty years. What it flattens: Blake's own supernaturalism. The lens must call the child's visionary clarity 'class consciousness' and heaven a pure fiction, but Blake attacked the Priest's heaven on behalf of a real spiritual life, not against one — the poem's rage is that of a believer watching belief weaponised. It also has little to say about why the poem is beautiful — why the nursery music matters.

Historicist. The lens restores the poem's documentary edge. Climbing boys were apprenticed from as young as four or five, because small bodies fit narrow flues; the trade's occupational disease — scrotal cancer, 'soot-wart' — had been identified by the surgeon Percivall Pott in 1775 as the first cancer traced to an occupation; Jonas Hanway had campaigned and published on the boys' conditions (1773, 1785); and Parliament had legislated — the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1788, minimum age eight, its licensing clause stripped out in the Lords, and in practice unenforced. Blake etched this plate six years after that Act. Read historically, 'They think they have done me no injury' indicts not just two parents but a nation that had already passed its law, filed the problem under 'solved', and gone back to church; the poem is written in the tense of failed reform. What it flattens: the poem's designed timelessness — Blake strips every date, name and place so that the mechanism (joy converted to labour, misery converted to heaven) stays legible in any century; historicism, pressed hard, turns a diagnosis of ideology into a period piece.

Psychoanalytic. The lens illuminates both households of the poem's mind. In the parents: disavowal — 'They think they have done me no injury' is the structure of knowing-and-not-knowing, belief maintained against available evidence because the alternative (we have sold our child) is unbearable; the church visit is the ritual that launders the knowledge. In the child: the compliant cheerfulness of the habituated victim — 'I am happy and dance and sing' as the false self presented to keep the adult world manageable, while the true accounting ('clothes of death') is delivered flat, without affect, to a stranger. The cry itself is overdetermined: 'weep' is what his mouth makes of 'sweep', grief speaking through the very word that denies it — a slip institutionalised as a street-cry. What it flattens: agency and accuracy. The child of this poem is not a case study; he is the poem's best analyst, and his conclusions are presented as true, not symptomatic. A purely clinical reading also privatises what Blake insists is systemic — it treats as family pathology what the last line assigns to priest and king.

Formalist. The lens takes seriously what the poem is made of: a nursery quatrain carrying an indictment. Couplet chime ('snow/woe… say/pray'), four-beat lines, anapaestic lilt — the acoustic apparatus of childhood safety — is made to transport its opposite, and the mismatch is the meaning: the form performs the society it accuses, pretty on the surface, load-bearing misery underneath. Within that, the local effects organise themselves with unusual economy: the one strictly iambic line (6) is the unbroken past; the one spondee (''weep, 'weep') is the cry the lilt cannot absorb; the one enjambment (11–12) is the exposure; the one weak rhyme (injury/misery) is the dying fall. What it flattens: the referent. A wholly formalist account can describe the machine and miss that soot cancer is not a verbal effect; the poem's occasion — actual children actually dying — exerts a pressure on the language that form alone cannot register, and Blake built the poem to keep that pressure unignorable.

Reader-response. The lens notices that the poem contains a reader: the questioner of lines 1–3, who sees, pities, and asks — exactly what we are doing. His question is well-meant and structurally useless, and the child's answer overshoots it so far that the questioner never speaks again; the poem dramatises the obsolescence of sympathetic curiosity. By the end the only person left to receive the analysis is us, and the child's 'our misery' quietly redraws the boundary: he speaks for a class we are not in, from which our warmth is extracted. (The Innocence poem makes the implication explicit — 'So your chimneys I sweep' — and this poem inherits that pointed second person silently.) The poem is thus a trap for pity: it solicits the tear and then demonstrates the tear's insufficiency. What it flattens: determinacy. Read purely as an experience-machine, the poem becomes open-ended, a mirror for each reader — but Blake is not open-ended here; the poem has a verdict, and a response-centred account risks replacing the verdict with our feelings about it, which is precisely the parents' manoeuvre.

Ecocritical (briefly). The lens foregrounds the two environments: the heath — open, unowned, unproductive ground where a child can simply be — against the city street and the flue, nature converted to infrastructure. The child's trajectory (heath to chimney, green to black) is enclosure in miniature: a commons-creature captured into the economy of coal and smoke. Even the snow changes function, from play-medium to exposure. What it flattens: the poem's insistence that the agent is not 'industrialisation' as weather but named institutions with addresses — church and crown; the ecocritical frame can dissolve responsibility into process, which the final stanza exists to prevent.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. The poem as attack on religion itself. Evidence: the unbroken chain 'God and his priest and king'; prayer rendered as abandonment ('gone up to the church to pray'); heaven as fabrication ('make up'). Weakness: Blake's God is not the poem's God — 'his priest and king' describes a deity annexed by institutions, and Blake, a Christian visionary hostile to churches, is attacking the annexation. The reading also cannot explain why the child's own idiom (polysyndeton, biblical cadence) stays scriptural: the poem fights the church in the Bible's voice, which an atheist reading flattens into confusion.

2. The parents as fellow victims. Evidence: poverty sold children to sweeps as a survival economy; 'They think they have done me no injury' grants sincere belief; the final accusation transfers upward, to the trinity of power who 'make up' both heaven and the parents' good conscience. On this reading the poem indicts a system that manufactures its agents' innocence. Weakness: 'Because I was happy' — the child twice makes his parents' motive his happiness, which no economics requires; and the poem pointedly notes they are 'both' gone. Blake leaves the parents sincerity but not exculpation: the system-reading risks doing their 'thinking' for them a second time.

3. The child's joy as indestructible innocence. Evidence: 'I am happy and dance and sing' in the unforced present; the was/am symmetry insists the same vitality persists; elsewhere in Blake, child-energy is the divine thing institutions fail to kill. On this reading the poem is not about destroyed innocence but about innocence surviving and being harvested. Weakness: 'taught me to sing' has already made his performances curricular, so the dance may be trade patter, not joy; and the reading flirts with consolation — precisely what the Experience version exists to refuse.

4. The sweep as revenant. (A minority position.) Evidence: 'clothes of death' as literal cerements; the eerie composure of the analysis; a black figure in white snow addressing a passer-by has the iconography of apparition; 'our misery' as spoken for the dead sweeps collectively. Weakness: the poem's present tenses are stubbornly embodied (crying, dancing, singing in the street now), and the documentary force — this is happening, six years after Parliament pretended to stop it — drains away if the child is already past saving. The reading buys atmosphere at the cost of urgency.

5. The child as ventriloquist's dummy. Evidence: no infant analyses ideology in subordinate clauses; the diction of 'injury' and the tricolon of powers are pamphleteer's tools; Blake has manifestly lent the child his own conclusions. On this reading the poem's flaw (or device) is that Experience speaks through rather than as a child. Weakness: the poem anticipates this — it shows us the training ('taught me to sing') that produced this articulacy, and it needs the child's analysis to outstrip every adult's precisely to invert the hierarchy of who understands; implausibility is the engine of the accusation, not a leak in it.

6. The poem as trap for the reader's pity. Evidence: the questioner — the reader's proxy — asks a compassionate, useless question and is never heard again; the child's answer exceeds and thereby exposes it; Innocence's 'your chimneys' aims the finger outward, and this poem inherits the aim. On this reading the poem's subject is the insufficiency of sympathy — feeling sorry being the emotional wing of 'they think they have done me no injury'. Weakness: lines 1–2 are not satirised — their pity is rendered with real tenderness ('little', the grieved exclamation), and Blake plainly wants the tear as well as the verdict; a reading that treats compassion as the poem's dupe mistakes a starting-point for a target.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Structural + General Analysis

Analysis
  • Made up of three quatrains (four-line stanzas)
  • Masking the complexity of the ideas by the simplicity of the structure
  • Split up into two main sections:
  • Initial sighting of the little black thing (the chimney sweep) in the snow
  • And the child’s reply which demonstrates his knowledge of his position using his experience
  • Songs of Innocence and Songs of Experience shewing the two contrary states of the Human soul is the full title of his collection (illustrates Blake’s belief of dual nature of human condition
  • Coexistence of innocence and experience, light and dark, joy and suffering
  • Contrasts the joy, freedom, and happiness that are the natural state of childhood with the oppression and exploitation of contemporary society
  • Contrast in length with Songs of Innocence shows the deterioration and weakening life-force/death of the chimney sweep from one poem to the next
  • Songs of Innocence (1789) present idealised and optimistic view of life, focusing on purity, joy, and the innocence of childhood
  • Songs of Experience (1794) explore much darker and more cynical view of the world, exploring themes of corruption, suffering and the loss of innocence, often criticising social and religious institutions
  • This volume reflects Blake’s growing disillusionment with the world
  • Read the photo above to see Blake's original punctuation
  • Chimney-Sweeper in Songs of Innocence
  • Unnamed adult speaker chances upon a weeping chimney-sweep in the snow, he asks him where his parents are
  • Young boy takes over the narrative and explains his parents are in the church praying
  • A child once full of innocence and joy, is now full of despair, condemned to a short and brutal life
  • Parents are ignorant of their child’s real suffering believing that they have acted in his best interests as they went up to church to offer their praise
  • Poverty drove families to sell their children into chimney sweeping (Few options for survival + lacking stable income)
  • By selling them a master chimney sweep provided, financial benefit + alleviated the responsibility of child care
  • Started as young children due to small bodies needed to climb into narrow, soot-filled flues
  • Hazardous, causes respiratory illnesses, burns, and even deformities due to prolonged crawling in confined spaces
  • Harsh reality of child labour deeply troubled social reformers
  • Contrasts the innocence of children with the bleak reality of their exploitation
  • Church justified child labour through religious, economic, and moral reasoning which aligned with the broader societal norms of the 18th and 19th centuries
  • Everyone had a God-given place in society and poverty and hardship were apart of God’s plan
  • Suffering faithfully would lead to rewards in heaven while emphasising obedience to parents and employers being virtuous
  • Hard work was equated with moral goodness
  • Character-building and a way to instil discipline and responsibility in children since idleness was believed to be sinful
  • Non-regular rhyming couplets
  • 1st Quatrain: Rhyming couplets (A, A, B, B)
  • 2nd and 3rd Quatrain: alternate rhyme (A, B, A B)
  • Partial rhyme The heath/”death” rhyme suggests somethings not quite right, speaking to the way that the chimney sweep’s natural enjoyment of being outdoors has been replaced by a king of death–the death of his childhood
  • Mainly single/masculine rhyme (emphasis on the final stressed syllables) e.g., snow and woe
  • Double/feminine rhyme in last stanza (emphasis on the first stressed syllable) e.g., misery and injury
  • Line lengths vary between 8 and 11 syllables
  • Metrical/rhythmic structure is irregular
  • Combination of Iambs (de-DUM) and anapaests (de-de-DUM)
  • a LIT-| tle black THING | a-MONG | the SNOW,
  • Occasional spondee (DUM-DUM)
  • WEEP, WEEP (for emphasis) and uncontrolability
  • The poem develops a very sing-song feel to it, like a nursery rhyme, reflective of the chimney sweep being a child (making childish rhythms appropriate)
  • Also singing the notes of woe reflects the poem being the song of the child’s misery
  • Also appropriate as the main subject is the exploitation of childhood
  • Diction is characteristically quite plain and simple with highly symbolic and richness in meaning
  • Accessible to a wider audience
  • SImplicity used to communicate powerful messages in a direct way (resonant and impactful)
  • Speaker 1 (Lines 1-3) could be a stranger, the reader, or just Blake, aware of the child's neglect
  • Speaker 2 (Lines 4-12) is the chimney sweep telling its tales (most chimney sweeps were male, but there were still female sweeps too)
  • Contrasts to the first The Chimney Sweeper from Songs of Innocence, where the sweep comes across as indoctrinated by what the authorities tell him, this sweep talks from experience and thus has perspective and understanding on why he finds himself in such a dire situation
  • He acknowledges his parents and more widely, organised religion are to blame for his exploitation. He talks wisely, and is able to neatly sum up the hypocrisy of the age through the paradox in the final line: Who make up a heaven of our misery
  • That is the church and society who thrive of exploitation
  • This sweep could be a ghost or visitation as he states clothes of death, hinting that he may be speaking from beyond earthly experience, revealing that society has doomed him to a short and difficult existence

The Chimney Sweeper

Analysis
  • Title itself is relatively self-explanatory
  • When compared alongside its companion poem The Chimney Sweeper in Songs of Innocence, acting as a powerful commentary on Blake’s view of the human experience
  • Songs of innocence
  • Optimism, naive light, where suffering can be overcome through spiritual faith and innocence
  • Songs of Experience
  • Darker side of life where child’s suffering is more fully acknowledged and criticised
  • Harsh reality of exploitation and societal neglect
  • Black underscores stark contrast between the two states of being
  • Innocence (naivety, purity, and spiritual faith)
  • Experience (disillusionment, suffering, and societal critique)
  • Repetition of title creates sense of unity, while highlighting the profound shift in perspective between the two volumes
1 / 2

A little black thing among the snow, / Crying “weep! ‘weep! in notes of woe!”

Analysis
  • Literally it characterises the boy’s physical condition as a chimney sweep, being covered in soot to the point of being unrecognisable
  • Contrast between Child’s blackened appearance and the white snow, which shows the child’s degradation and isolation from the natural world, while dehumanising the child through the diction thing suggesting that he is viewed as a mere creature
  • He becomes unidentifiable as a mere black shape, a dark mark on the conscience of society
  • Metaphorically the contrasts between the black of the boy and the white of the snow becomes symbolic
  • Ironically describing as society sees him as a being besmirched, stained, and blackened by original sin (Adam and Eve) among the snowy white purity and idealised virtue of the Church and society
  • Using original sin, it justifies the suffering of the innocent child as a form of redemption/expiation (making amends for guilt) for humanity's inherent sinfulness
  • By opening the poem in this way it Immediately exposes the dissonance between the Church’s teachings of purity and salvation and the Grim reality of its complicity in human suffering
  • The child, which acts as an emblem/symbol of innocence is paradoxically branded as impure by the very system that should protect him
  • The sound patterning emphasises the child’s distress
  • The epizeuxis (repetition of words in immediate succession) weep! ‘weep!
  • Acts as an echo (allusion) to the other The Chimney Sweeper where it undoes the false moralising of the first poem where despite weep[ing] they find comfort in the idea that God will grant them happiness if they only work obediently and dutifully
  • Could imply that it is one of the same boys from the first poem with the main different between that he is wise to the lies and deceptions of organised religion
  • Alliteration of the semi-vowel (a speech sound intermediate between a vowel and a consonant like /w/ or /y/) through Weep! Weep! and Woe links the further action of crying to the sweep’s life of misery
  • Repetition of the long ee sound creates a high-pitched, reedy quality, aurally mimicking the thin weak voice of a young child crying for help
  • Youth, physical frailty and vulnerability is also emphasised through the assonance of nOtes of wOE! mimics a sound of despair and a depressing song
  • Delicate consonance of A little black thing among the snow, acts as a gentle reminder that despite the speaker is world-weary and experienced, he is still small and vulnerable
  • The apostrophe before the word ‘weep! ‘weep! to indicate a letter is missing, Chimney sweeps normally chant out sweep! Sweep! to advertise their services (Elision: Purposeful missing letter(s))
  • Thus the diction ‘weep! ‘weep! transforms a cry of labour by a young child with underdeveloped language skills which lead to him struggling to pronounce his words clearly into a cry of pain and despair
  • The pun reinforces the dehumanisation of the child as his voice is reduced to the very labour that defines his existence, creating a strong sense of pathos
Effect, style & response
  • Makes the reader feel distraught, uncomfortable, sad, empathetic and Blake intends to put the reader in that position as part of an argument that everyone bears some responsibility for the way society works (or doesn’t work) where the reader becomes a spectator to the small child’s suffering
3 / 4

Where are thy father and mother, say? / They are both gone up to the church to pray.

Analysis
  • The unidentified adult speaker addresses the child using the archaic possessive pronoun thy
  • Used to express familiarity and among people who were intimate or to people who were of a younger age or lower status (like ton/’tuo’/’tu’ in French/Italian/Spanish)
  • A sudden intimacy that contrasts with the earlier dehumanisation of the child,
  • The direct question subtly accuses the absent parents while drawing the readers attention to the broader systems that permits such suffering to persist
  • Sets up child’s response as devastating in its naivety and acceptance of his fate
  • The 4th line is the child’s voice which emerges to take over the narrative
  • Child’s voice contrasts between the adult’s perspective and the child’s innocent yet resigned explanation of his plight (unfortunate circumstance) makes the situation more poignant (emotional, bitter and regretful) through the naivety
  • Internalised his suffering as normal
  • Blake empowers a figure that society typically silences, using this as evidence against these systems of exploitation and hypocrisy
  • The juxtaposition between the parents’ spiritual pursuits with their neglect of their child’s physical and emotional needs
  • The abandonment is literal being physically absent and symbolic by relinquishing (giving up) their responsibility by entrusting the child to harsh labour where the parents believe they have fulfilled their duties by seeking divine approval for their choices
  • Pervasive influence of religious teachings that prioritised suffering as a path to salvation
  • The consonance (voiced and not) runs throughout both of the lines, where the gentleness of this sound suggest the physical weakness of the chimney sweep, while linking directly to the father and mother which helps highlight the fact they aren’t around due to the lack of sound and presence
  • Solidifies the rhyme scheme for the stanza as AABB, where they also continue the poem’s tetrameter in a mix of trochees (DUM-da), anapaests (da-da-DUM) and iambs (da-DUM)
  • Allows for a very intuitive sound for the poem making it flexible so that the rhythm of the first speaker’s voice contrasts with the rhythm of the child’s voice
  • The initial stress in the speakers question Where captures the forceful inquiry of a concerned adult
  • Meanwhile, the two unstressed syllables in the first anapaest of the child’s response captures both his weakness and his innocence and his inability to make out strong forceful words due to his dehumanised and malnourished state
Effect, style & response
  • More personal and heartbreaking for the reader as they imagine if this someone they were familiar with, submitted to this cruelty
5 / 6 / 7 / 8

“‘Because I was happy upon the heath, / And smil’d among the winter’s snow. / They clothed me in the clothes of death, / And taught me to sing the notes of woe.”

Analysis
  • Remembers a time of happiness, purity and innocence
  • Diction of Heath meaning a vast grassland suggesting a contrast between the open countryside in his earliest years to the claustrophobic and filthy urban conditions where he now lives and works
  • Breathy alliteration of of the aspirated /h/ in Heath and Happy and sibilance of smil’d and snow emphasises former contentment in the natural setting
  • Juxtaposition with the child’s previous smile[..] with his current weep[ing] revealing his loss of innocence
  • The snow symbolises his coldness and suffering, in contrast to the summer before which shows how he previously didn’t feel this, an indication of his prior emotional and spiritual warmth
  • The juxtaposition of him not smil[ing] in the snow when he was just crying ‘weep! ‘weep! in notes of woe. showing how he was once happy to be out in the snow but no longer
  • Whiteness of the snow, suggesting purity, contrasts with the way the sweep is now disfigured by his covering of soot and ash
  • The causal conjunction at the beginning of the line implies the child’s former state of happiness and ignorance of sin was intolerable to the Church’s doctrine like a problem that needed correcting
  • Subtly criticises a system that thrive on guilt and suffering rather than fostering natural joy and freedom
  • Boy’s punishment for his former happiness being lines 7 and 8
  • How he was put into labour because he was caught being happy
  • Ambiguity in the pronoun They which is deliberate and powerful in implicating both the parents and the church creating a web of blame
  • Parents are directly responsible for the child’s suffering even though they are unaware of it
  • Church is responsible for the ideological framework which justifies the idea
  • Lack of clarity forces the reader to see the child’s suffering as systemic, enabled by societal norms, parental actions, and religious teachings
  • Diction of clothes of death can be literally as the soot-covered rags that blacken the child or metaphorically allude to the inevitability of an early death due to the physical toll that chimney-sweeping had on very young, under-developed and often malnourished boys
  • Helps draw out competing forces at work in society: life and joy vs. death and misery. While the child wants to live joyfully, society forces him towards death and misery
  • Polyptoton (repetition of words derived from the same root) of clothed and “clothes intensifies the claustrophobic tone and underscore the oppression that these boys have suffered
  • Suggests that whoever put the sweep in the clothes of death did so intentionally. That people exploit children with full knowledge of what they are doing
  • The soft consonance in THey cloTHed me in THe cloTHes of deaTH, which recalls the unknown whereabouts of THy faTHer and moTHer in line 3
  • The diction taught shows how he had to be forced to learn to sing the notes of woe while smile[s] came to him naturally
  • Criticism of religious and societal institutions, where instead of fostering joy and freedom, they impose suffering as a moral and spiritual obligation
  • The child’s learnt sorrow contrasts to the innate happiness he once knew
  • Suffering is an artificial construct than a natural state (contrasts to Christian belief that suffering is natural after the original sin where Adam and Eve caused all generations after them to be cursed)
  • Repetition of notes of woe emphasises the enduring and cyclical nature of this suffering
  • Also acts as a kind of refrain like in a song, which is in keeping with the sweep’s act of singing the notes of woe where the assonance of this phrase also adds to the songlike quality
  • The poem’s companion in Songs of Innocence, the child is taught to believe that society is a certain way, and that its harshness and brutality is just a fact of life
  • The church persuades people that if they don’t complain in this life, they will be rewarded by God in the next (heaven) thus preventing people from striving for improvements in this world
  • Misery and suffering, then, are things that the child has to learn, and not innate characteristics of life itself, where the poem argues that some institutions like the Church actively suppress the more joyful elements of life
  • The polysyndeton in this stanza and the next subtly mimics the language and tone of the King James Version of the Bible, and thus by harnessing the Bible’s tone the poem seems to mock the Church, arguing that the Church has lost the true spirit and meaning of Christianity

“‘And because I am happy and dance and sing, They think they have done me no injury: / And are gone to praise God and his priest and king, / Who make up a heaven of our misery”

Analysis
  • The present tense of am offers a confusing contrast as we question how he can be happy and dancing is he is woeful in the snow
  • Past tense may have caused rhyming issues which don’t match up
  • Could also indicate an enduring hope of salvation, a temporary relief from despair, from clinging to religious promises, even if they are ultimately hollow
  • Links to the companion poem in Songs of Innocence as the children find genuine solace in religious belief, imagining angelic visions of freedom and warmth
  • Then down a green plain, leaping, laughing they run,
  • “Tom was happy & warm;
  • So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.”
  • Polysyndeton of and in the first line and the simplicity of the syntax reveals the child’s own simplicity and ingenuousness (innocent naive)
  • Also gives the line a playful, jumpy feel that feels fit with the image of a happy child
  • Also evoke the sound of the KJV bible (a version full of polysyndeton) pitting its own vision of Christianity against the corrupted version of the church
  • Lack of child sign of distress to parents, allows them to be in a state of possible of sign of blissful ignorance or wilful denial as they think they have done me no injury:
  • Rationalised their actions in being the child’s best interest (both spiritually and materially)
  • Turning a blind eye to the terrible conditions
  • The gentleness of the /th/ alliteration in THey THink THey echoes the consonance in line 3 linking the they to the faTHer and moTHer figures
  • The repeated pronoun They has an accusative tone, making it clear that the sweep, knowing from experience, who is to blame for his miserable existence
  • More polysyndeton between God and his priest and king which implies the connection religion and government in a unified system of exploitation
  • Both are complicit in perpetuating the suffering of the vulnerable and that Individual’s relationship with God and/or spirituality is mediated by more worldly concerns and that you can’t have one without the others
  • Alliteration between gone and God emphasises the link between societal neglect and organised religion, that people who praise God are gone from their responsibilities
  • Linking the Priest to King draws the full picture of blame
