It refuses to separate theology from politics saying these forces are not incidental to the child's suffering but rather that they are its authors
  • The verb make up suggesting fabrication or invention, implying that the promise of heavenly rewards is a constructed narrative designed to pacify and control the oppressed
  • Oxymoron of heaven of our misery is very ironic as it underscores the hypocrisy of the system
  • A true heaven cannot coexist with misery
  • Church and state claim to be working towards a moral and spiritual paradise, built on the suffering of the vulnerable
  • Literally the heaven could refer to the comfortable lives led by the wealthy who prospered as a result of the misery of the poor what was effectively slave labour
  • Forces the reader to confront the paradox of the system which purports (claims) to save souls while destroying lives
  • Chimney sweepers are an emblem of the way that the powerful in society create their comfort and luxury by exploiting others, in this case the young and the poor
  • How the chimney sweeps literally die so that the middle and upper classes can have warm cosy homes to live in
Effect, style & response
  • Implores the reader to also think about who this They might be
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Love Armed' (Aphra Behn). Linking idea: power assembles itself out of the powerless — Love's tyranny is built from the lover's own contributions ('From me he took his sighs and tears…') exactly as the trinity's heaven is made 'of our misery'; both poems are audits of an extraction. Shared technique: the couplet/quatrain chime used ironically — courtly song carrying harm; personified or institutional power given regal iconography. Genuine difference: Behn's speaker is an adult inside a reciprocal (if rigged) erotic game, and her wound is survivable, even relished as performance; Blake's victim is a child in an economy, and nothing in his poem is a game — where Behn's antithesis balances ('my poor heart… whilst thine…'), Blake's final line refuses balance: heaven on one side, misery on the other, and one is made of the other.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt). Linking idea: the oppressor's deepest conquest is pedagogy — Bhatt's 'unborn grandchildren' who 'grow to love that strange language' are the child 'taught… to sing the notes of woe': both poems locate oppression's triumph in what the young are trained to love and perform. Shared technique: the pivotal interrogative (Bhatt's 'Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?' beside 'Where are thy father and mother?'), and religious frames (Sarasvati, the sacredness of books; church, prayer, heaven) tested against actual cruelty. Genuine difference: Bhatt's history has no named culprit — conquest is recursive, every language once the oppressor's, and the poem ends in troubled wonder; Blake names his defendants in a single line and convicts them. Bhatt's is a poem of implication, Blake's of indictment.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster). Linking idea: 'People are made of places' is this poem's premise weaponised — the heath-child and the flue-child are different people, and the making is literal: soot is what the city deposits in a person. Shared technique: structuring antithesis of two environments (Brewster's museum-smelling city against berry-picking woods; Blake's heath against street and chimney), with sensory coding — her smells, his black/white. Genuine difference: Brewster's formation is neutral, even tender — nobody chose her chickens and battered schoolhouses for her, and her free verse drifts like memory; Blake's formation is a transitive verb with agents ('They clothed me'), and his nursery metre is a cage someone built. In Brewster place shapes; in Blake people use place — heath taken away, snow left.

With 'Report to Wordsworth' (Boey Kim Cheng). Linking idea: both are reports on a god who no longer functions — Boey's God 'labouring to utter his last cry', Blake's God privatised by 'his priest and king'; in both, the machinery of veneration (sonnet-homage, church-going) continues while the thing venerated is destroyed or captured. Shared technique: compressed traditional forms (sonnet; hymn-like quatrains) turned to protest; religious lexis inverted (prayer, heaven, God) so that devotion becomes evidence. Genuine difference: Boey's culprit is 'man' at large and the damage ecological — grief without a defendant, ending in 'beyond hope'; Blake's culprits are institutions with titles, the damage is one child's body, and the poem ends not in hopelessness but in a verdict — bleaker locally, less resigned globally.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan). Linking idea: a small dark creature, closely watched, turns out to be a mirror — but the mirrors face opposite ways: Halligan projects himself onto the insect ('I thought I recognised myself'), while Blake's 'little black thing' refuses to stay an object of projection and answers back with an analysis of the watcher's world. Shared technique: the observed creature as emblem; tight rhymed form containing unease; the pivot on recognition. Genuine difference: Halligan's poem is private — conscience auditing itself through an insect, no social claim; Blake's is public — the 'thing' is a person made thing-like by named institutions. Halligan ends in a question about himself; Blake's child ends with a conclusion about everyone.

With 'Lament' (Gillian Clarke). Linking idea: the blackened innocent — Clarke's cormorant 'in his funeral silk' is the sweep's 'clothes of death' transposed to war's ecology: in both, a covering (oil, soot) is at once costume, stain and shroud, put onto the innocent by the powerful. Shared technique: liturgical repetition (her anaphoric 'For…' — the cadence of intercessory prayer — beside his biblical polysyndeton); irony of consolation (her 'the boy fusilier who joined for the company', his heaven made of misery). Genuine difference: 'Lament' is a litany — many victims, no speech, the elegist's voice doing all the mourning; Blake gives the whole poem to one victim who does not mourn at all but explains. Clarke's form is grief organised; Blake's is grief analysed — and only his victim gets the last word.

Where I Come From

Elizabeth Brewster · 1977

Identity is not chosen but carried — place gets into the senses and stays there, and the mind keeps its own weather.

ContextThe PoemThe Whole PoemForm & StructureSoundMotifs & SymbolsThemesDifficult MomentsClose AnalysisCritical LensesOther ReadingsRevision NotesConnections
CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Elizabeth Brewster (1922–2012)

Brewster was born on 26 August 1922 in Chipman, a small logging community in New Brunswick, Canada, and grew up in rural New Brunswick. She studied at the University of New Brunswick, Radcliffe College (Harvard), Toronto and Indiana, worked as a librarian, and taught English at the University of Saskatchewan from 1972 until 1990. Her first collection, East Coast, appeared in 1951, and she published poetry for six decades. Her style is plain-spoken and exact — concrete details, little ornament — a quiet manner that hides careful craft.

Her own life followed the path the poem looks back across: out of a small rural community, through cities and universities, into a professional world that never erased the landscape she started from.

The Poem

'Where I Come From' was collected in Sometimes I Think of Moving (1977), though it was probably written much earlier, in the 1950s. It is spoken by someone who now knows cities — their offices, subways and parks — but whose mind still keeps the weather of a rural childhood. Printings of the text differ (see the note above the poem).

Place in Canadian Writing

New Brunswick is a Maritime province of forest, small farms, logging and long, hard winters. Canadian literature has long been preoccupied with land and climate: the critic Northrop Frye wrote that Canadian writers seem less perplexed by the question 'Who am I?' than by 'Where is here?'. Brewster answers with a place — but refuses to romanticise it. Her home is farmhouses in need of paint, hens clucking aimlessly, burned-out bush: loved, and seen clearly.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Where I Come From

Printings differ. This is the 19-line text (as in the Coastlines anthology). Some printings, such as PoetryProf and LitCharts, give line 6 as three lines — nature tidily plotted in little squares / with a fountain in the centre; museum smell, / art also tidily plotted with a guidebook; — so their line numbers after line 6 run two higher. Quote only what your paper prints.

TWhere I Come From
1People are made of places. They carry with them
2hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace
3or the cool eyes of sea gazers. Atmosphere of cities

5or the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring,
6nature tidily plotted with a guidebook;

9crowded at rush hours.

11carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;

14with yards where hens and chickens circle about,

18A door in the mind blows open, and there blows

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Where I Come From
Language & devices

Colloquial idiom: Where I Come From is everyday speech — the phrase you use about home when you are somewhere else. First person: the title promises a personal answer. Present tense: come — the origin is not past; it is still where she comes from.

Meaning & effect

The title is held back: the poem starts with everyone (People), and the phrase only arrives at line 10, where it becomes the poem's turning point. So the title frames the whole poem as a move from general claim to personal testimony — and the phrase itself already implies distance, since you only explain where you come from to people who do not.

Line 1
People are made of places. They carry with them
Language & devices

Aphorism: People are made of places — a universal statement, stopped dead by a mid-line full stop. Diction: made of = composed of, as a table is made of wood — material, not merely "shaped by". Enjambment: They carry with them runs on into line 2, so the carrying literally continues.

Meaning & effect

The thesis comes first, total and unhedged: place is not an influence on identity but its substance. The present-tense carry adds that we take our places with us wherever we go. The rest of the poem tests — and quietly revises — this confident opening sentence.

Line 2
hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace
Language & devices

Listing: jungles or mountains — landscapes strung together on or. Diction: hints — traces, not obvious marks. Metonymy: a tropic grace — a hot climate carried as a way of moving.

Meaning & effect

Place shows on the body: people from hot countries carry its ease. The image is affectionate but generalising — it reads strangers by their climate — and hints admits that this is guesswork. The speaker is observing from outside, sorting people by habitat.

Line 3
or the cool eyes of sea gazers. Atmosphere of cities
Language & devices

Transferred epithet: the cool eyes of sea gazers — the sea's coolness passes into the watcher's temperament. Spondee: COOL EYES slows the line to a stare. Caesura: a mid-line full stop, then a new sentence begins: Atmosphere of cities.

Meaning & effect

Coastal people are named by what they look at — gazers — so the landscape becomes a way of seeing: cold places make calm watchers. This is the first cold in the poem, admired as composure; the poem's last line will return to cold as something felt. Then the sentence switches abruptly to the city.

Lines 4–5
how different drops from them, like the smell of smog / or the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring,
Language & devices

Broken syntax: Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them does not quite parse — how different is like an exclamation dropped into the sentence. Simile: like the smell of smog. Olfactory imagery and Compound coinage: the almost-not-smell of tulips.

Meaning & effect

City people do not carry their place deep inside: its atmosphere drops from them, shed like a smell. Nature survives in the city only faintly — tulips you can barely smell, a single managed season. The grammar breaks as the city enters, as if the city cannot be described in a clean sentence.

Line 6
nature tidily plotted with a guidebook;
Language & devices

Pun: plotted — laid out in garden plots, mapped, and schemed. Adverb: tidily — over-ordered (it will be answered by aimlessly in line 15). Symbol: the guidebook — nature that has to be explained to visitors.

Meaning & effect

City nature is managed and mediated: you need instructions to find it. The poem's criticism falls on the way the city treats nature, not on the people who live there. (Longer printings expand this line into three — nature tidily plotted in little squares / with a fountain in the centre; museum smell, / art also tidily plotted with a guidebook; — so that nature and art are also filed by the same phrase.)

Lines 7–9
or the smell of work, glue factories maybe, / chromium-plated offices; smell of subways / crowded at rush hours.
Language & devices

Metonymy: the smell of work — labour known by its odour. Hedge: glue factories maybe. Imagery: chromium-plated offices — a shiny coating, all surface. Enjambment: smell of subways / crowded at rush hours pushes the crowd down a line, underground. Verbless list: no main verb after drops.

Meaning & effect

The city list runs from industry to offices to commuters — a life organised by work and timetables, ending on hours. Maybe is the outsider's shrug: she knows the smell, not the life behind it. Like the chrome, the city's mark on people is a surface finish rather than something carried within.

Lines 10–11
Where I come from, people / carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;
Language & devices

Volta: Where I come from — the title phrase arrives, and the poem's only I. Enjambment: people / carry echoes line 1's They carry with them. Metaphor: carry woods in their minds. Repetition: woods… pine woods.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from observing others to speaking from inside a community — and she still says people, not "I": identity here is shared. The city's atmosphere dropped from people; these people carry their woods inside, acres of them, a landscape larger in the mind than the head holding it.

Line 12
blueberry patches in the burned-out bush;
Language & devices

Plosive alliteration: blueberry patches in the burned-out bush — five /b/ and /p/ sounds. Imagery: blueberries growing on ground cleared by forest fire.

Meaning & effect

Sweetness grows out of damage: the burned bush regenerates as fruit. The image is exact and unsentimental — the home landscape is scarred but alive. The heavy plosives give it a solidity the city's hissing smells never had.

Lines 13–15
wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint, / with yards where hens and chickens circle about, / clucking aimlessly; battered schoolhouses
Language & devices

Listing: farmhouses, yards, hens, schoolhouses. Postponed adjectives: wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint — the commas make the qualifications arrive like a second look. Onomatopoeia: clucking. Adverb: aimlessly — the opposite of tidily plotted. Diction: battered.

Meaning & effect

Home is loved but not prettified: old, unpainted, worn, a little aimless. The honesty is the point — she knows it from inside, so she can admit its shabbiness. The hens' unplanned circling sets a free, unmanaged life against the city's tidy plots, though aimlessly also hints at a place running down.

Lines 16–17
behind which violets grow. Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice.
Language & devices

Imagery: violets growing behind the schoolhouses — hidden, unplanned beauty. Metaphor: Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons. Colon: the poem's one definition. Repetition: ice and the breaking of ice.

Meaning & effect

The catalogue ends on grow — life, not timetable. Then the landscape moves inside: the mind has a climate, defined by extremes and by change — the long freeze and the thaw that breaks it. The repeated ice makes the line enact freeze, thaw, freeze; the outer place has become the shape of an inner life.

Lines 18–19
A door in the mind blows open, and there blows / a frosty wind from fields of snow.
Language & devices

Extended metaphor: the mind as a house with a door. Repetition: blows open… there blows. Half-rhyme: blows / snow — the poem's only end-rhyme. Iambic tetrameter: a FROSTy WIND from FIELDS of SNOW — the only fully regular line.

Meaning & effect

Memory is involuntary: the door blows open on its own, and home arrives as weather — felt on the skin, not pictured. The poem began with people carrying places; it ends with the place carrying itself into her. Whether the frosty wind is a welcome inheritance or an uninvited chill is left open — and the sudden rhyme and regular metre give the ending the force of something that cannot be argued with.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

"Where I Come From" opens with the most confident sentence in it — "People are made of places." — and then spends eighteen lines appearing to illustrate that thesis while actually revising it. The revision, not the illustration, is the poem. Read as illustration, it is a tidy compare-and-contrast of city and country with a decorative flourish at the end. Read as revision, it is an epistemological drama: a poem about two different ways of knowing places and people — acquaintance from outside, constitution from inside — which stages the second overtaking the first, and which ends by discovering that its own opening aphorism was not quite right.

Start with how oddly the thesis is supported. "Made of" is total, passive and finished: manufacture completed at some point in the past. But the evidence offered is instantly hedged — "hints of jungles", "a tropic grace or the cool eyes", "glue factories maybe". The first stanza is written in the epistemology of the observer: someone reading strangers' surfaces in transit, guessing at origins from a posture or a stare, guessing at a city's life from what it smells of. And the guessing is done in the city's own idiom. The stanza's lexicon is the lexicon of curation — "tidily plotted", "guidebook", "chromium-plated" — and its speaker is doing to people precisely what the guidebook does to nature: sorting them into tidy plots. Jungle people are graceful; sea people are cool; city people smell of subways. The typology skirts the postcard and the stereotype, and the poem knows it: that is what "hints" and "maybe" are for. Grammar completes the demonstration. The city sentence sprawls across six and a half lines with a single finite verb — "drops" — before decaying into verbless inventory ("chromium-plated offices; smell of subways"): knowledge-about accumulates but cannot predicate, cannot make anything happen. This is not city-hatred. It is a self-demonstration of the poverty of external knowing, performed in the first person plural of all of us who have changed trains somewhere and thought we knew it.

The dropped line at "Where I come from, people" changes the ground of authority, and the economy of that pivot is extraordinary. The first person enters once — a single "I", buried mid-formula, never repeated — and immediately dissolves into "people". The restraint is the argument. A poem claiming that persons are made by places, communally and involuntarily, would refute itself with an insistent lyric "I": whatever an "I" makes of itself is exactly what it was not made of by anywhere. So the speaker claims origin without claiming ownership, testifies for a "people" she belongs to, and lets the certainty of the new catalogue do the self-revealing. And it is certain: no more "maybe". Acres, blueberries, the paint, the hens, the violets behind the schoolhouse — the exactness of memory rather than research, a knowledge that includes what is behind buildings because the knower has stood behind them.

Yet the inventory refuses the reward it seems to promise. Home is peeling, "battered", economically becalmed; its hens go nowhere, "clucking aimlessly"; its bush is "burned-out". The stanza's tenderness is real but it is positioned, not stated — carried by prepositions. Blueberries grow in the burn; violets behind the battered school. Sweetness and delicacy are not compensations placed beside damage; they are located inside it, inseparable from it. This is where the poem's honesty cuts deepest: what home gives is not beauty but constitution, and the constitution includes the damage. Then the epigram names the deepest layer of the endowment: "Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice." Not scenery at all now, but a shape of feeling — a calendar of two extremes, stasis and rupture, with the temperate seasons deleted. No summer: the mind this place makes has no season of ease. What you inherit from such a place is a rhythm — long freeze, violent thaw — and the sentence performs it, two stressed "ice"s flanking a loosened slack of syllables, freeze-melt-freeze.

Everything to this point, however vivid, is willed: catalogues composed by a speaker in full control of her material. And that is exactly why the poem cannot stop there. If places really make people, recitation proves nothing — a tourist can recite. The proof must be something that happens to the speaker, against her will, in the poem's present tense. Hence the couplet: "A door in the mind blows open, and there blows / a frosty wind from fields of snow." Agency has drained out of the human: people carried, hens circled, violets grew — now a door blows open, unlatched from the far side, and weather arrives. The form seals it. The poem's only rhyme and only metrically regular line (a strict iambic tetrameter) close the free verse like a mechanism engaging — or, better, like the mind falling at last into its native measure, the cadence of where it comes from, once it stops steering.

The obvious objection says the poem is rural chauvinism with a canvas tote: city rendered as smells and sterility, country as flowers and growth, with a dash of climatic stereotype ("tropic grace") in the set-up. Concede the tilt; the stanzas are not neutral. But the tilt is epistemic, not moral. The city passage indicts a way of knowing — mediated, curated, olfactory, guessed — and flags its own guesswork while doing so; its human specimens get the poem's most admiring nouns ("grace", "cool eyes"). City-dwellers are inside the opening thesis too: they also carry their place; it is just that what the observer can know of it is residue. Meanwhile the country is given poverty, aimlessness and burn scars, and its climactic gift is a cold draught through the skull. A chauvinist poem ends warm, at the hearth. This one ends "frosty", in an unheatable mind.

The second objection is formal: that the couplet is a bolt-on epiphany — a rhymed, faintly gothic flourish that betrays the catalogue's hard-won specificity (a "door in the mind" could be anyone's; a blueberry patch in a burn is Brewster's). The preparation answers most of this: the mind has been a container since line 11, had a climate by line 17; the long ō of the rhyme is banked three lines early; and the rhyme itself is left imperfect, "blows"/"snow", one consonant short of tidy — the poem declines full closure even while closing. But the generality of the last image should not be argued away, because it is doing the final piece of work: at the moment origin returns as force, it stops being itemisable. Contents can be catalogued; weather cannot. The couplet has no local nouns because possession has reversed — she is no longer holding the place up for inspection; it is moving through her.

So the opening aphorism gets its quiet correction. "Made of places" promised a finished product, identity as material. The poem ends in the present progressive of weather: not made once, but still being made; not composed of a place, but inhabited, visited, blown through by it. Where you come from, on this poem's evidence, is not your substance. It is your climate — and climate does not stay outside.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Stanza logic: 9 / 8 / 2

The three stanzas are a narrowing aperture. Stanza 1 (9 lines) is everyone and everywhere: a typology of humankind sorted by habitat — jungle, mountain, coast, city. Stanza 2 (8 lines) is one community: the speaker's own, inventoried. Stanza 3 (2 lines) is one instant inside one mind. The poem sheds lines as it approaches what it actually cares about, and the shrinking stanzas enact its argument that the vast general claim ("People are made of places") is only verifiable in the smallest possible unit — a single gust through a single head. Alternatively: world, memory, now.

The first stanza break is bridged by a shared line: "crowded at rush hours." occupies the left of one line-slot (5 syllables), and "Where I come from, people" is printed dropped and indented to complete it (6 syllables). Together they make one pentameter-weight line split across the gap. The device does two things at once, and both matter: it separates (new stanza, new grammatical person, new world) and it continues (same line, same argument — the home community is another instance of the opening thesis, not an exception to it). The second break, before the couplet, has no such bridge: the final two lines are cut adrift, because what they describe — the ambush of memory — is discontinuous with the willed cataloguing that precedes it.

Metre: free verse haunted by the pentameter

Full lines run 10–14 syllables, mostly carrying four to six stresses — blank-verse width without blank-verse regularity — until the last line, which is the poem's only strictly regular one. Scansion of ten lines (stressed syllables in capitals):

  • L1 PEOple are MADE of PLAces. || they CARry with THEM — trochaic fall on the poem's subject-word, then three evenly spaced beats landing the aphorism; after the mid-line stop the rhythm turns rising. The poem asserts in falling rhythm and explains in rising: statement, then motion.
  • L3 or the COOL EYES of SEA GAzers. || ATmosphere of CIties — the spondee "COOL EYES" plus the heavy compound piles five stresses into six syllables: the pace drops to a held stare. Then the new sentence skitters in on a dactylic run ("ATmosphere of") — the city arrives faster and lighter, all surface.
  • L5 or the ALmost-NOT-SMELL of TUlips in the SPRING — the coinage jams adjacent stresses ("NOT-SMELL") so the voice stumbles exactly at the point of perceptual failure, then relaxes into anapaests ("of TUlips in the SPRING") once the non-event is past.
  • L6 NAture TIdily PLOTted with a GUIDEbook — tidy falling rhythm, equal small parcels of sound marching to the guidebook: the metre itself is municipal planting, laid out in neat beds.
  • L9 CROWded at RUSH HOURS. — five syllables, the stanza's shortest line, ending on the spondee "RUSH HOURS": the stanza's longest sentence dies in its most compressed line — maximum humanity per syllable, the verse as crowded as the carriage.
  • L10 WHERE i COME from, || PEOple — scannable as iambic ("where I come FROM"), but sense throws the weight forward onto WHERE, the questioned category; "PEOple" hangs at the enjambment, held over the turn until "carry" catches it.
  • L11 CARry WOODS in their MINDS, || Acres of PINE WOODS — the trochee "CARry" repeats line 1's verb at line-head with the stress now on it; the closing spondee "PINE WOODS" answers "RUSH HOURS" — each world ends a key line on a double-stress, compression against expanse.
  • L15 CLUCKing AIMlessly; || BATtered SCHOOLhouses — wholly falling rhythm, not one rising foot: trochees and dactyls subsiding one after another, movement without direction. Aimlessness performed metrically.
  • L17 are the MIND'S CHIEF SEAsons: || ICE and the BREAKing of ICE — three consecutive stresses ("MIND'S CHIEF SEA-") bear down like the claim itself; after the colon, two stressed ICEs flank a loose anapaestic slack ("and the BREAKing of"): freeze, thaw, re-freeze in rhythm. At 13 syllables this is the poem's widest line — it dilates to hold the epigram.
  • L18–19 a DOOR in the MIND BLOWS Open, || and there BLOWS / a FROSty WIND from FIELDS of SNOW — the mid-line stress-cluster "MIND BLOWS O-" bursts like the door itself; the line ends on an unanchored "BLOWS", the verb hanging in the doorway across the enjambment; and then the final line is perfect iambic tetrameter, the only fully regular line in the poem. After eighteen lines of speech-rhythm the poem locks into hymn-measure to close. Two readings of that lock, both usable: the free verse finally "comes home" to the metre that was underneath it all along; or the involuntary memory arrives with a formal authority the willed catalogues never achieved — when the mind stops steering, it falls into measure.

Rhyme

No scheme; one end-rhyme, "blows"/"snow", closing the poem — and it is imperfect: the vowel is exact, but the /z/ of "blows" is unanswered. The poem that mocked the "tidily plotted" ends with a closure one consonant short of tidy. The rhyme is also pre-paid: "grow" (16) and "Open"/"blows" (18) lay down the long ō so the couplet chimes with what the ear already holds. Elsewhere the poem substitutes identical repetition where rhyme would be — "woods … woods" (11), "ice … ice" (17), "blows … blows" (18), "smell" four times — as if this speaker distrusts ornament but cannot stop things recurring; recurrence, not rhyme, is the poem's form of memory. Incidental chimes: "grace"/"gazers" (2–3) binding the two admiring portraits; "maybe"/"subways" (7–8) letting the shrug echo inside the machinery.

Syntax: six sentences, two of them enormous

#SentenceLinesCharacter
1"People are made of places."1aaphorism
2"They carry … sea gazers."1b–3athesis instanced
3"Atmosphere of cities … rush hours."3b–9city catalogue, 6½ lines
4"Where I come from … violets grow."10–16ahome catalogue, 6½ lines
5"Spring and winter … breaking of ice."16b–17epigram
6"A door … fields of snow."18–19event

Two facts that repay more pressure than anything else in the poem's grammar:

  • Every full stop inside a stanza falls mid-line (after "places.", "sea gazers.", "grow."); the only line-final full stops close stanzas (9, 17, 19). Sense-units and verse-units are kept deliberately out of phase inside each stanza — every ending immediately re-opens — and snap into phase only at the stanza edges. The poem therefore reads as continuous carrying: nothing is allowed to rest at a line-end until a whole world has been put down.
  • Sentence 3 contains one finite verb; sentence 4 contains four. The city sentence predicates once — "drops" — and then stops predicating altogether: "nature tidily plotted…" is a hanging absolute, "chromium-plated offices" a verbless noun phrase, "smell of subways" an item on a list that has forgotten its grammar. This is anacoluthon doing argument: the sentence about the tidily plotted city is the poem's untidiest, an inventory drifting free of syntax, because guidebook-knowledge accumulates without organising life. The home sentence, exactly as long in spirit, is paratactically clean — "come", "carry", "circle", "grow", each item a well-formed phrase in the same case — and it closes on a finite verb of growth. The city catalogue's last word is "hours" (schedule); the home catalogue's last word is "grow" (life). That is the poem's judgement, delivered entirely by grammar and never stated.

Sentence 3's opening is genuinely broken — "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" — and the break is functional: see Cruxes 1.

Punctuation

Five semicolons, two in the city catalogue and three at home (6, 8; 11, 12, 15): the two worlds are built by the same paratactic machine, which is why the difference between them registers as content, not form. One colon in the poem (17), reserved for the definitional gesture — "chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice" — the syntax of a dictionary entry, the poem's one moment of stating a meaning rather than accumulating instances. The commas of line 13 ("wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint,") postpose the adjectives as afterthoughts — the grammar of a second look, appraisal arriving after recognition, a farmer's eye rather than an estate agent's.

Lineation, caesura, enjambment

  • "They carry with them / hints" (1–2) and "people / carry woods" (10–11): both stanzas launch on the same verb delivered across a line-break — the carried thing arrives after the turn, made to be waited for. The parallel is structural rhyme, and the difference is the payload: city people carry "hints"; home people carry "acres".
  • "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops" (3–4): the atmosphere literally drops down a line.
  • "smell of subways / crowded at rush hours" (8–9): the crowd is pushed below the line, underground.
  • "battered schoolhouses / behind which violets grow" (15–16): the violets are hidden behind the line-break as behind the building — you must go round the line-end to find them.
  • "and there blows / a frosty wind" (18–19): the wind blows through the poem's last line-break; the final gap in the verse is the open door.
  • Caesurae: the three mid-line full stops above, plus the semicolon pauses; line 13's triple-comma stutter is the poem's most halting moment, the voice picking its way across a dilapidated thing.

The turns

Two, of different kinds. Line 10 is a volta of source: third person to first, hearsay to memory, "maybe" to certainty — marked typographically by the dropped line. Line 18 is a volta of mode: catalogue to event, metonymy to metaphor, habitual present ("carry", "grow") to punctual present ("blows open") — marked by the only unbridged white space in the poem. Notice the grammar of agency across the turns: people carry (active), then a door blows open and wind blows in (the mind acted upon). The poem's last discovery is that "where I come from" is not something you hold; it is something that arrives.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The city's signature: sm- and sibilance

Five sm- onsets in five lines — "smell of smog" (4), "almost-not-smell" (5), "smell of work" (7), "smell of subways" (8) — and then none for the rest of the poem. The cluster /sm/ closes the lips and pushes a small breath through the nose: the repetitions make the reader's face perform a series of little sniffs, the exact gesture of testing city air. And by the fourth "smell" the word has gone semantically numb — repetition wears it featureless, which is the point: the city's identity-marker is a word rubbed smooth by overuse, like its chromium surfaces. Around the sm- spine hisses a wider sibilance — "cities", "spring", "nature", "offices", "subways", "rush" — urban static, air that is never quite silent. The vowels of this stanza thud short and flat where the poem's attention is coldest: "smog", "plotted", "offices" — while the admired coast and tropics got long, opened vowels ("cool", "grace", "gazers"). Vowel-length is this poem's warmth of attention: what the voice lingers on, it values.

Home's signature: plosives and gutturals

The second stanza detonates rather than hisses. "Blueberry patches in the burned-out bush" pops four b/p plosives — small explosions of the lips, buds and berries bursting out of scorched ground; the energy of germination is in the consonants before it is in the image. Then the yard clatters in gutturals: "chickens circle about, / clucking … acres … carry … battered". The onomatopoeia of "clucking" is conventional; what is not conventional is how its consonant spreads into the neighbours — chiCKens, cirCle, cluCKing — so that the whole line clucks, not just the verb. The stanza's binding vowel is the long i: "minds", "pine" (11), "behind", "violets" (16), "ice … ice" (17) — a thin, bright, glassy sound, light off ice. Notice what the first pair does: "minds" and "pine" share their vowel exactly, so the claim "carry woods in their minds" is enacted inside the words — the pine is already lodged in the mind at the level of the phoneme.

The ending's acoustics

The final rhyme is laid down early: "grow" (16), "open" and "blows … blows" (18), "snow" (19) — five long ō sounds converging, with "door" adjacent in vowel-space. The ō is the blown vowel: the lips round into the shape of a draught, and each initial b ("blows") is a plosive released straight into it — a puff. Add the fricatives of "frosty … from … fields" and the w of "wind", and the couplet is not describing wind so much as requiring the mouth to make some: the reader performs the weather that the speaker suffers. Against this, "ice and the breaking of ice" is built of hard glass: two long-i monosyllables at either end, and in the middle the poem's one br- cluster — "breaking" — an audible crack between two panes.

Cadence

The mid-line full stops (after "places.", "sea gazers.", "grow.") force level, unemphatic closes: the voice cannot rise to a line-end climax inside a stanza, which is how Brewster's famous plainness is enforced, not just chosen. The fastest passage is "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" — a tumble of light syllables, the city rushing itself; the slowest are the held spondee of "cool eyes" and line 13's comma-hobbled appraisal ("wooden farmhouses, old, in need of paint,"), the voice picking its way across a dilapidated thing. "Aimlessly" is a dying fall in the middle of a line — the adverb itself trails off, doing what it says.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

A motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something beyond itself. This poem works mainly by motif — its method is accretion — and then converts its material into symbol only at the very end, which is one reason the ending feels like a change of key.

Motif 1: smell (and its disappearance)

Smell enters as the very mechanism of place-identity — atmosphere drops from people "like the smell of smog" (4) — then runs the whole register of the city: degraded to near-absence ("almost-not-smell", 5), industrial ("smell of work", 7), and massed ("smell of subways", 8). Then the decisive change: after line 9 the vocabulary of smell is banished. The home stanza names things — pine, blueberry, paint, violets — whose odours are strongly implied (resin, smoke, damp timber) but never claimed. The logic: smell is how you know a place you merely pass through; it is the residue a place leaves on you, the thing that "drops from" you. Home is not sensed from outside but constituted from inside, so it needs no olfactory proof; and when a sense-channel finally returns in the couplet it is touch — "a frosty wind" — the one sense that requires contact. Trajectory: detachable trace → owned contents → felt weather.

Motif 2: carrying and containment

"They carry with them" (1) — carriage as luggage, exterior and portable. "Carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods" (11) — the container is now interior, and impossibly larger inside than out: acres in a skull. "The mind's chief seasons" (17) — the container has its own climate. "A door in the mind" (18) — the container has become a dwelling. And then the reversal that completes the motif: the wind blows in (19). What was carried now arrives under its own power; possession runs backwards. You carry home until home starts carrying itself into you.

Motif 3: the plotted against the unplotted

"Nature tidily plotted" (6), the "guidebook" (6), "chromium-plated" (8) — a lexicon of imposed finish, and "plotted"/"plated" are near-homophones: mapped surfaces, coated surfaces, the same gesture. Against it the second stanza sets landscapes re-planned by no planner: the "burned-out bush" (12), redesigned by fire; hens that "circle about … aimlessly" (14–15) — motion with no plan and no centre; violets "behind which … grow" (15–16) — growth in unplanned placement, behind rather than on display. The motif accumulates into the poem's structural irony: its own final couplet is the one formally "plotted" object in it (rhymed, metrical) — the unplanned mind turns out to generate pattern of its own, a different order from the municipal kind (and see Cruxes 4 for the reading that finds this a contradiction rather than a triumph).

Motif 4: cold

"The cool eyes of sea gazers" (3): temperature as temperament, and admired — composure, distance, appraisal. Tulips "in the spring" (5): the city's one season, feeble and curated. Then "Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice" (16–17): cold promoted from style to structure, the mind's actual calendar. Finally "a frosty wind from fields of snow" (19): cold as the substance of the self's origin. The poem begins by admiring coolness in other people and ends by discovering an absolute cold in itself — the motif is a slow homecoming of temperature.

Symbols

  • The door (18) — the threshold between present consciousness and formative past; crucially it is not opened but blown open, from the far side. It stands for the involuntariness of origin: you do not choose to remember where you come from; it lets itself in.
  • The guidebook (6) — a whole epistemology in one object: experience prescribed, routed, and read about rather than had. Everything stanza 1 knows, it knows guidebook-fashion; everything stanza 2 knows, it knows by heart.
  • The violets (16) — unsponsored persistence: delicacy surviving behind an institution that is itself barely surviving. The poem's emblem for what neglect cannot prevent.
  • The fields of snow (19) — the origin as expanse without feature: plenitude or blankness, undecidable (Cruxes 4). What the speaker comes from may be a fullness (fields, space, light) or a white nothing.
  • Ice / the breaking of ice (17) — hovering between motif (literal Maritime climate) and symbol (the psyche's freeze and rupture); the poem's most economical double-exposure.
THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Place as identity

The opening claim is total: people are not just shaped by places but made of them. The poem tests the claim on others first, then proves it on the speaker's own community, whose woods are carried in their minds.

02

City and country

City places leave a surface trace that drops from people — smells, chrome, managed nature with a guidebook. Home is carried inside. The criticism falls on how the city mediates nature, not on city people, and home is not idealised: it is old, battered and aimless, but real.

03

Memory as involuntary

In the final couplet the speaker does not remember home; home arrives. The door blows open by itself and a frosty wind blows in — identity as weather that comes whether or not it is invited.

04

The mind's climate

The outer landscape becomes an inner one: Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons. A life shaped by long freezes and sudden thaws learns to think in extremes — endurance, and release.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" (3–4): the sentence that will not parse

The difficulty: there is no grammatical reading of this clause that does not require repair. Three candidates. (a) Exclamatory interpolation: "Atmosphere of cities — how different! — drops from them", with the punctuation withheld; supported by the poem's habit of unmarked appositives and by speech-rhythm. (b) Inverted manner adverb: "how different[ly the] atmosphere of cities drops from them"; supported by the logic of the paragraph — the previous sentence described how people carry places, this one describes how differently city people do. (c) Anacoluthon: the sentence genuinely breaks and restarts — grammar failing precisely as the city enters, before decaying into the verbless inventory ("smell of subways") it never recovers from. There is a second instability inside the first: "them" should mean city people, but its only grammatical antecedent is the "They" of line 1 — all people. So either city-dwellers shed their atmosphere, or everyone who has passed through a city sheds a little of it. Careless readers silently normalise the line and move on; better to refuse to repair it, to notice that the poem about tidiness places its untidiest syntax exactly here, and to let the loose "them" include us all in the city's effect.

2. "a tropic grace / or the cool eyes of sea gazers" (2–3): is the typology endorsed?

The difficulty: the opening reads character off climate — people sorted by habitat, with a whiff of the colonial postcard in "jungles" and "tropic". Is Brewster asserting this or exhibiting it? Reading A (endorsed): it flows directly from the thesis, the tone is unironic, and the poem never retracts it; a poem of its period can hold assumptions about climate and character without embarrassment. Reading B (exhibited): the hedges — "hints", the alternatives strung on "or", the later "maybe" — mark the whole register as guesswork; the stanza's instrument, the guidebook, is discredited by the second stanza's insider knowledge; the poem shows what shallow people-reading looks like before performing the deep kind. The evidence is genuinely split. The best response is to notice that the poem needs the typology to be half-true — people are marked by place (the thesis requires it) — and half-glib — the marks cannot really be read off surfaces by strangers (the structure demonstrates it); and notice that the speaker types her own people identically ("people / carry woods in their minds") — the difference is not procedure but position: testimony instead of tourism.

3. "clucking aimlessly", "in need of paint", "battered" (13–15): what is the tone of the home inventory?

The difficulty: the stanza's nouns are loved but its modifiers are an audit of decline. Three readings. (a) Unsentimental fidelity: love that refuses to prettify; the tenderness lives in prepositions (blueberries in the burn, violets behind the school), not adjectives. (b) Economic elegy: a region running down — outmigration, resource decline — with "aimlessly" the community's condition displaced onto its hens, and the "battered" schoolhouse a public institution wearing out. (c) Covert pride: the anti-guidebook — refusing the picturesque is the boast; our place does not need curating to be constitutive. Evidence for each is real, and they cannot be fully reconciled. The key is to see that "aimlessly" is the exact antonym of "tidily plotted" — the poem's two adverbs are its poles — so the same word carries re-valued freedom (unscheduled, unplanned life; the hens circle where the city's nature is plotted) and undeniable drift. The hens are liberty and futility at once; a reading that picks one has thrown half the poem away.

4. "A door in the mind blows open…" (18–19): gift or breach — and earned or bolted on?

Three layers of undecidability. (i) Welcome or invasion? The wind as vivid inheritance, identity confirmed at full sensory strength — or as the draught of a mind that cannot be insulated, origin as cold you never chose. The poem's momentum honours where she comes from; but nothing in the couplet is warm, the door is forced from the far side, and winter has already been named the mind's chief season. (ii) "Fields of snow": plenitude or blankness? Space, light, home ground — or a featureless white nothing; what she comes from may be fullness or emptiness, and the line will not say. (iii) Does the poem earn the metaphor? Everything before is metonymy — real adjacent things standing for the place; the ending is sudden full metaphor, mind as house. For "earned": the container-mind is built stepwise ("woods in their minds", 11; "the mind's chief seasons", 17 — contents, then climate, then architecture); the rhyme is banked early ("grow", "open"); and it is left imperfect ("blows"/"snow"), one consonant short of tidy. For "not earned": the couplet's image is generic where the catalogue was owned — a "door in the mind" could be anyone's; a blueberry patch in a burn is hers — and a poem that sneered at the plotted ends in the one plotted form it contains. The strongest reading holds the tension as meaning: at the moment origin returns as force rather than as detail, it stops being itemisable — and being made of a place means your proof of belonging and your exposure to it arrive as the same gust.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

(The famous couplet is deliberately not among the ten — it is worked at length in Form, Sound, Difficult Moments and The Whole Poem. These are the moments that repay pressure.)

  1. "People are made of places." — aphorism; passive with suppressed agent; metonymy; earliest possible full stop, mid-line. The passive hides a maker: not "places make people" (process, resistible) but "are made of" (material, done). If a place is your substance rather than your manufacturer, travel cannot subtract it — the claim quietly forecloses escape before the poem begins. The mid-line stop is the poem's first shut door (and its last line will be a door blown open: the frame is exact). It is also the only sentence in the poem stated as law; everything after is instance, hedge or event, so the poem is best read as an eighteen-line stress-test of its own first five words. Intention and effect: to win the reader's assent to an absolute before scrutiny arrives, then to spend the poem quietly correcting "made of" into something less finished.
  2. "the cool eyes of sea gazers" — coined compound; spondee; transferred epithet. "Cool" carries the sea's temperature into the watcher's temperament: metonymy become physiognomy. The coinage names a people not by labour (fishermen, sailors) but by direction of attention — gazers, defined by where they look — so that climate becomes epistemology: cold places make watchers. The spondee ("COOL EYES") slows the line to the pace of the stare it describes. And it opens the poem's thermal thread: the first cold in the poem is admired composure; the last ("frosty wind") is involuntary weather — coolness travels from style to substance across the whole poem. Intention and effect: to establish that place-marks are subtle, bodily and legible only as style — and to plant the temperature the ending will weaponise.
  3. "Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them" — anacoluthon; exclamatory interpolation; enjambment. The missing article ("Atmosphere", not "The atmosphere") makes the city's air an abstract substance, and "drops" hands the process to gravity: no one intends it, it simply sheds. The interpolation is the poem's one exclamatory gesture — feeling briefly surfacing — instantly muffled by the grammar going wrong around it. The enjambment performs the verb: the atmosphere drops down a line. Whatever repair you choose (see Cruxes 1), the sensation of disorder arrives before any statement about order — the reader experiences the city before being told about it. Intention and effect: to let syntax fail exactly at the city limits, so that the stanza's later tidiness-vocabulary ("plotted", "guidebook") reads as compensation for a real formlessness.
  4. "the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring" — hyphenated compound of negation; stress-jam; phenomenological precision. The poem's finest small coinage: a noun built out of a failure to be one. Not "faint smell" — a weak positive — but a presence measured by its distance from nothing, approached from the wrong side. It is exact about a real experience: leaning to municipal tulips, knowing scent should be there, and receiving a trace that may be memory of tulip rather than tulip. The hyphens do municipal work, boxing the vacancy into a tidy compound — language plotting a little square around an absence — so the word enacts the city it diagnoses. Metrically the jammed stresses ("-most-NOT-SMELL") make the voice stumble at the precise point of perceptual failure. Set it against line 16's "Spring", unmodified and "chief": the city's spring is a negative quantity; home's is half the calendar. Intention and effect: to render administered nature as sensory debt — the reader performs a sniff that comes back empty.
  5. "nature tidily plotted with a guidebook;" — adverb as accusation; triple pun; personification of the city as curator. "Plotted" holds garden-plot, map-plotting and scheming in one participle — cultivation, cartography, conspiracy — and "tidily" makes neatness itself the accusation. Nature in the city is laid out to be visited, and it needs a guidebook to be found at all: experience pre-routed, discovery replaced by confirmation. "Tidily" is also the exact antonym of the home stanza's "aimlessly" — the poem's two adverbs are its poles. (Longer printings run this as three lines — "nature tidily plotted in little squares / with a fountain in the centre; museum smell, / art also tidily plotted with a guidebook" — so that nature and art are processed by the same verb-phrase and "also" files them together.) Intention and effect: to indict mediation, not citizens.
  6. "or the smell of work, glue factories maybe," — metonymy; epistemic adverb; grim materiality. "The smell of work": labour perceived as odour, class known through the nose before the mind. Glue factories boil hide and bone — the city's economy rendering bodies into adhesive — the stanza's ugliest fact, delivered in passing and unprotested. But the load-bearing word is "maybe": the speaker knows the smell, not the world it comes from, and flags her own guesswork in one unstressed shrug. It is the outsider's watermark on the whole stanza — nothing in the home catalogue is hedged, because she knows what grows behind the schoolhouse. Even the syntax (appended, verbless) files work as one more exhibit in a museum she is visiting. Intention and effect: to mark the limit of acquaintance-knowledge; the reader retroactively distrusts the confidence of everything stanza 1 asserted.
  7. "Where I come from, people / carry woods in their minds, acres of pine woods;" — dropped line; the poem's only "I"; enjambment echo of lines 1–2; doubling with specification. The first person enters once, buried mid-formula, and dissolves into "people" — origin claimed, ownership declined; a communal thesis kept communal (an insistent lyric "I" would refute the poem's own claim that place, not self-fashioning, makes people). Typographically the phrase completes the city's line while opening its own stanza: continuation and departure at once. "People / carry" re-runs "carry with them / hints" across a line-break — a structural rhyme whose difference is the payload: hints against acres, residue against terrain. And "woods … pine woods" is memory's grammar — category first, then the exact species — while "acres" lays a surveyor's measure over inner space: the impossible arithmetic of a mind bigger inside than out. Intention and effect: authority changes source in six words — from observation to testimony — and the reader hears certainty arrive.
  8. "blueberry patches in the burned-out bush;" — plosive train; fire-succession ecology; idiom double-exposure. The image is fact before symbol — blueberries genuinely colonise burnt ground — and the accuracy licenses the symbolism: sweetness conditional on scorch, renewal that requires damage rather than surviving it. Four b/p plosives pop like buds out of char; the stanza's first colour arrives inside its worst injury. Behind the literal bush hovers the idiom: a burned-out person — the community's exhaustion and its fruitfulness held in one participle. Note what is absent: any causal claim. Just "in" — the preposition carries the whole theology, grace located inside ruin, not compensating beside it. Intention and effect: to found home's beauty on disturbance instead of the picturesque; the reader tastes sweetness and ash in one phrase.
  9. "battered schoolhouses / behind which violets grow." — enjambment as concealment; register-shift; institutional against wild. The building for making futures is the most worn object in the poem. The line-break hides the violets behind the line-end as behind the building: syntax as topography — you must turn the corner of the verse to find them, and readers who miss them have re-enacted the outsider's blindness. "Behind which" is a starchy, taught-grammar relative in a plain-spoken poem: for half a line the syntax puts on its school manners, while the violets ignore the lesson and grow where no plan placed them. They are shade-flowers, unplanted, findable only by those who already know where to look — insider knowledge in botanical form, the exact opposite of the guidebook. The sentence then ends mid-line on "grow": the home catalogue's last word is a verb of life (the city's was "hours"). Intention and effect: home defined as the place whose hidden delicacies need no instructions — and the reader is quietly tested.
  10. "Spring and winter / are the mind's chief seasons: ice and the breaking of ice." — colon as definition; epanaleptic fold (A : B-of-A); deliberate exclusion; gerund. The poem's only colon performs its only act of definition — a dictionary entry for a psyche. The fold matters more than the pairing: spring is given no content of its own, defined purely as violence done to winter — renewal exists only as rupture of stasis. What is deleted is as eloquent: no summer (no season of ease), no autumn (no ripeness, no gentle decline) — the temperate middle of feeling edited out of this mind entirely. "Breaking" is a gerund, not a completed event: perpetual process, a calendar of two states and a crack. The rhythm enacts it — two stressed ICEs flanking a loosened slack — freeze, thaw, re-freeze. This, not line 1, is the poem's deepest thesis: what a place installs is not imagery but a rhythm of feeling. Intention and effect: climate converted into psychology in thirteen syllables; the reader inherits the binary in the cadence itself.
CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Ecocritical

Makes visible: the poem literalises bioregional identity — the psyche as ecosystem, people who "carry woods in their minds" and whose emotional calendar is set by the actual freeze-thaw of their latitude ("ice and the breaking of ice"). It also produces one of the sharpest early images of administered nature: "nature tidily plotted with a guidebook", scent managed down to an "almost-not-smell" — nature present in the city only as exhibit and deficit. And it is ecologically literate: blueberries genuinely colonise burnt ground; "blueberry patches in the burned-out bush" is fire-succession before it is symbol, which is what licenses the symbol. Flattens: the poem is not conservationist — no protest, no loss-narrative; the burn is a neutral fact of home, not an indictment. An ecocritical reading that turns Brewster into an environmental campaigner has confused her with Boey Kim Cheng.

Postcolonial

Makes visible: the opening's taxonomy — "jungles", "a tropic grace" — is the imperial habit of reading bodies by climate zone, the exhibition-catalogue gaze; and the poem's discredited instrument, the guidebook, is the metropole's way of packaging nature for visitors. Against that centre, a poet from a "battered", unstoried margin writes her periphery into literature without exoticising it — a quietly Canadian assertion that the hinterland is constitutive, not merely scenic. The lens also reads against the poem: this is settler ground — farmhouses, schoolhouses, logging woods — and the Indigenous presence of New Brunswick (Wolastoqiyik and Mi'kmaq land) is nowhere in a poem titled "Where I Come From"; its "people" who carry the woods in their minds are not the people longest made by those woods. The silence is analysable. Flattens: the poem's scale is personal and communal, not national-allegorical; pressed into a parable of empire it simply breaks.

Marxist / materialist

Makes visible: the catalogue is class-legible end to end — "the smell of work, glue factories" (rendering plants boiling carcasses to adhesive: industry's rawest conversion of bodies into product), "chromium-plated offices" (white-collar work as surface finish), "subways / crowded at rush hours" (commuting as commodified time — the catalogue's last word is "hours"). Rural poverty is material fact, not mood: private dwellings "in need of paint", public institutions "battered" — underfunded margins of a resource economy whose raw materials leave for the metropole. Even leisure is administered consumption: nature with a guidebook. Flattens: the poem stages no antagonism and imagines no change; it converts economic decline into character ("aimlessly") — a materialist would say it aestheticises what it ought to historicise.

Feminist

Makes visible: the poem refuses the heroic frontier register of much North American place-writing — no axe, no conquest, no settlement epic. Its home is the maintained-and-unmaintained communal world historically kept by women: yards, hens, paint, the schoolhouse (rural teaching, a women's profession) with violets behind it. Authority is claimed through attention rather than assertion, and the lyric ego is all but erased — one "I", instantly dissolved into "people" — a counter-model to the proprietorial "I" that plants flags in landscapes. "Grace", the poem's first admiring noun, is a gendered aesthetic reclaimed as environmental inheritance. Flattens: the poem carefully ungenders its "people" — there is not one gendered pronoun in it — and reading it as women's testimony narrows a voice built to be communal.

Psychoanalytic

Makes visible: the final couplet is a textbook return of the repressed — a sealed room in the mind-house breached from the far side, contents arriving as force and cold rather than as narrative; memory not recalled but suffered. "Burned-out" and "battered" double as psychic scar-vocabulary; "ice and the breaking of ice" reads as defence and breach, frozen affect and its violent thaw, a personality organised around containment and rupture with the temperate states deleted. Strangest and most productive: the remembered home contains no people — no parent, no name, only buildings, plants and poultry; attachment has been displaced wholesale onto terrain. Flattens: the climate is also just climate — New Brunswick winters are literal, and a reading that makes all weather symptom loses the documentary ground the poem stands on.

Reader-response

Makes visible: the poem is an engine for self-application. Stanza 1's typology invites every reader to find their own slot among the jungles, mountains, coasts and cities; "Where I come from" is a formula each reader already owns; and the withheld explanations — "maybe", the unglossed final image — delegate completion to us, which is why the poem survives annotation so well. Flattens: treated purely as prompt-material, the poem's actual New Brunswick — its burn ecology, its battered institutions — becomes interchangeable wallpaper, which is precisely the guidebook relation to place the poem despises.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The loyal-pastoral reading — a tribute to rural origins with the city as foil. Depends on: the structural favouritism (home gets the finite verbs, the flowers, the colours, the closing couplet) and the tender exactness of the inventory. Weakness: it must euphemise "battered", "aimlessly" and "burned-out", and explain away an ending that is cold rather than warm; it also flattens stanza 1's genuine admiration ("grace", "cool eyes") into sneering it does not contain.
  2. The anti-urban satire — an attack on city artifice. Depends on: "tidily plotted", the guidebook, the "almost-not-smell", the numbing sm- repetitions. Weakness: satire needs a verdict, and the poem withholds one — it hedges ("maybe"), admires the marks city people carry, and its opening thesis covers them too. The "disdain" often read into the poem is largely imported by readers; the poem's contempt-objects are curation and mediation, never citizens.
  3. The exile reading — spoken from away: a speaker now living in the city, for whom home exists only as memory. Depends on: the intimacy of the city textures (chromium offices, rush hours — known, not researched); the emigrant's formula "Where I come from" (you only say it elsewhere); the couplet as memory striking at distance; and the biographical rhyme of Brewster's own decades of migration through cities and campuses. Weakness: the poem never states a present location; the city knowledge could be a visitor's ("maybe" says exactly that); and the reading leans on biography the text deliberately withholds.
  4. The determinist manifesto — the poem straightforwardly asserts that people are products of environment. Depends on: "made of", the opening typology, a mind whose "chief seasons" are set by latitude. Weakness: the hedges corrode the law even as it is stated — "hints", "maybe", "almost" — and the only determinism the poem verifies is first-personal and momentary: one gust through one mind. "Carry" (portable, ongoing) quietly contradicts "made of" (fixed, finished); the poem ends closer to haunting than to manufacture.
  5. The ars poetica — a poem about writing: the city's "tidily plotted" nature as curated, derivative culture (longer printings make it explicit: "art also tidily plotted"); the unplotted catalogue as Brewster's own plain style; "fields of snow" as the blank page from which the real poems blow in. Depends on: the guidebook line; the self-referential irony of a poem that scorns the plotted and then ends in its one rhymed, metrical couplet. Weakness: nothing in the text names writing; the snow-as-page equation is imported wholesale; and the reading converts a poem about belonging into a poem about poems — clever, unfalsifiable, and thinner than what it replaces.
  6. The mood-cycle reading — a portrait of a psyche given to cyclical shutdown and release: "ice" as depressive freeze, "the breaking of ice" as violent thaw, the couplet as intrusive mood rather than memory (nothing of the farmhouse returns at the end — only cold). Depends on: "the mind's chief seasons" being explicitly psychological; the deletion of the temperate seasons; "aimlessly" as anhedonia displaced onto hens. Weakness: it medicalises a metaphor, and the poem's frame is communal — "people carry", a whole region's inheritance — so the clinical reading keeps collapsing back into what the poem actually says: climate.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Structural + General Analysis

Analysis
  • Stanzas of irregular length, the structure is free.
  • Syllable counts vary but turn around 12.
  • Nine, eight, and two lines (couplet), respectively
  • The indentation in the second stanza is made to follow the first. She wants to show the description of a rural area is in continuation of an urban area, but is still a different idea. The passage from third to first person makes the change more abrupt.
  • The author makes this indentation to show that rural and urban areas depend on each other, need each other mutually. Rural areas give the raw materials and urban areas exploit them to form goods.
  • The change from third to first person is made softer by the fact the word “I” is only used once in the entire poem. The rest of the second stanza is just a description, so the change is really only notable in the first verse of the second stanza.
  • Bold metaphorical statement followed by concrete imagery detailing with contrasting material
  • There is a larger separation with the third stanza as it is not in continuation of the second, as the second is the first. So the third stanza is set apart, it has an entirely different subject, it is not a physical description, we enter the mind of the author, return to childhood.
  • No rhyme scheme, once again a free style of writing, the author does not respect the organisation that she notices in the city, tidily plotted.
  • The three stanzas also present three angles on the poem’s material, as it becomes narrower and more subjective as it goes on
  • First stanza describes people in general, all of whom are made of places
  • The second talks more specifically about people from rural environments, like the one where the speaker grew up
  • The third and shortest stanza presents a particular psychological experience that ties in with stanza two offering a glimpse of what is likely to come from their wintry region, how a frosty wind always seems to blow somewhere in the mind
  • Two lists serving different purposes
  • Catalogues the smells and sensations associated with cities: (Rapid success, busyness, monotony, superficiality overwhelming, chaotic, and fragmented nature of urban life)
  • Repetition of smell revealing how sensory experiences in the city are unappealing, even something as beautiful as tulips are diminished into a not smell reinforcing the idea that City life lacks vibrancy and authenticity
  • Second half shifts to much more descriptive, and nostalgic list of rural images woods, blueberry patches, yards where hens and chickens circle, and violets
  • Evokes a sense of permanence and deep connection, etched into the speaker’s identity
  • Rhythm is slower and more meditative, reflecting the peace and timelessness of rural life. Images are carefully chosen (almost sacred) contrasting with the rushed impersonal tone of the urban section.
  • Juxtaposition of these lists underscores the central theme of the poem, which is that there are fundamental differences between city and rural life
  • Urban life is fleeting, artificial, and disconnected
  • Rural life is enduring, organic, and deeply personal
  • Modulates the rhythm through the use of enjambment and caesura, mirroring the natural ebb and flow of thought
  • Lists of images, all demarcated (limited) by semicolons
  • A layered, cumulative quality
  • As if piecing together impressions to explore the relationship between people and the places they inhabit
  • Reflect and conversational tone
  • Ideas about place and identity seem to unfold organically and naturally
  • Natural rhythm reinforces central idea that identity is shaped by a blend of sensory impression, memories, and connections to place
  • Brewster’s diction is very straightforward to allow for a clear and concise communication
  • Metaphor, Simile, Figurative Language, Sound Patterning are all restrained and understated

Where I Come From

Analysis
  • First line of the second stanza
  • Stress is placed on where expecting the poem and the author to focus on the geographical aspect of her origins
  • Feels as if poem will describe the physical characteristics, landscapes, and details about its location
  • Yet, the stress subtly shifts to where I come from and not others becoming a sense of self, and how her rural upbringing has shaped her personality and worldview
1 / 2 / 3

“ People are made of places. They carry with them / hints of jungles or mountains, a tropic grace / or the cool eyes of sea gazers.

Analysis
  • Brewster sets out her stall (makes her position very clear) with the metaphor People are made of places, suggests our identities are fashioned by where we grow up, us being the sum of the places we’ve been, not just an incidental part of their history
  • Plosive alliteration “P” subtly suggests the way are inextricably linked, inseparable, while intermingling with one another
  • Short syntax shows the force of this assertion, where she will brook (tolerate) no opposition to her claim
  • The next few lines They carry with them… cool eyes of sea gazers shows her belief that the connection to place is so deeply ingrained that is physically manifests in people’s demeanour, behaviour and mannerisms
  • Phrase carry with them shows how it's not just memories, but integral, ever-present part of their being, shaping how they move and interact with the world
  • Imagery of tropic grace and cool eyes of sea gazers shows how these geographical influences are visible in a person’s very essence, making place an inseparable component of identity
  • Positive imagery, linking those who come from the tropics as being elegant, while sea gazers functions as a metaphor capturing their connection to the sea and the reflective, calm, and expansive qualities that such an environment might instill in them
  • Cool temperature of the sea and sea-breeze changes how coastal people view life, limiting the sunny optimism that warmer places encourage
  • The sea is also paradoxical, always changing yet always the same, thus staring at it gives coastal people a cool, detached wisdom about the nature of existence
  • The relaxed character or way of being in the sunny beautiful outdoors (tropic)
  • The diction hints Brewster imagines this as a subtle expression, not overt, nothing to do with clothing, skin, colour, or any physical feature like that.
  • She’s not suggesting an old sea hand will be a deep person, or a mountain dweller hard, nothing to direct but rather Brewster imagines something ineffable in the way a person might gaze outwards, holding their graceful posture as a sign of their history
  • It asks us to consider the layered complexities of nature which are reflected in people, the qualities of a person felt rather than seen, that one can faintly detect the marks of lived experience
  • The speaker doesn’t tell the reader precisely how such places make people but rather allows the poem to act as an invitation to consider the idea that people are shaped by their surroundings, and asking them to consider how it applies to them and people they know
3 / 4 / 5 / 6

“Atmosphere of cities / how different drops from them, like the smell of smog / or the almost-not-smell of tulips in the spring, / nature tidily plotted with a guidebook;”

Analysis
  • After the caesura following sea gazers in line 3, the poem changes tack building up on the built-up urban environment/society, showing a sense of reluctance.
  • Similar to that of the ocean or great forests, cities too leave an indelible impression but instead of penetrating deep inside, Cities cling to people more superficially, repeating smells until you wrinkle your nose in distaste
  • Her tone subtly shifts, and how their identity is also shaped by their environment yet implied that its not in a good way
  • Exclamatory interpolation (Sudden exclamation inserted into a sentence, breaking the flow to convey strong emotion or emphasis) of how different signals the contrast she finds
  • Plosive consonance of “d” hints at Brewster’s disdain for city life
  • Punctuation seems to reflect her dismissive attitude
  • Lack of commas to separate the parenthetical remark (Word, phrase, or clause inserted into a sentence (often in brackets, commas, or dashes) to add extra information/declaration) between how different
  • Enjambment flowing down onto the next line shows a sense of carelessness, mirroring the way the atmosphere of cities drops from them, without intentional delicacy, almost as if they are contaminated and it is being excreted from their pores
  • Structural looseness contrasts sharply the implied elegance of the tropic grace which is instead carried by its people, reinforcing that urban life lacks the refinement, purity and authenticity of more natural environments
  • The hissing sibilance like the Smell of Smog subtly linking to Brewster’s disdainful attitude which is strung throughout accentuates the moribund (lack of vitality or close to death) and greasy images, giving the sharp tang of sibilance like a sour note hanging in the air
  • Seems faintly overbearing and unpleasant, in contrast to the tulips in the spring, it is overpowered by the other odours (like smog) that the beauty of the tulips are undetectable
  • The act of only being just able to smell the flowers shapes people’s lives encouraging them to find and appreciate beauty in unlikely places
  • The use of olfactory imagery is used to describe how the city might stay with someone while describing the acrid and putrid stench
  • With sweat lingering in the smell of work, crowded subways reeking with commuters (diction)
  • Vague, dreamy terms, never exactly spelling out how a smell might make someone who they are, perhaps because the speaker believes they don't have all the answer
  • The lack of grace or cool calm in Brewster’s city citizens show the stiflingness and the inability to penetrate and leave no lasting mark on the quality of people’s character beyond a faint unpleasant odour that drops in their wake
  • The lack of a cities wildness and unpredictability loses the deep and daily connection man can have where its always regulated and monitored, and simply using nature as an escape
  • The compound adjective almost-not-smell evokes the band artificiality of the municipal (town council planting)
  • Fragrance is so faint that it might just as well not be there, too ordered
  • Plants only grow where they have been planned
  • Water is artificially pumped
  • Reeks of uniformity and a rigid geometry where art and creativity are also curated and constrained
  • By accentuating how unnatural cities have become, Brewster comments on the effects of urbanisation on the soul and psyche of our collective humanity.
  • Since 2008, more than 50% of the world have lived in cities
  • The conspicuous repetition of the phrase tidily plotted suggests how restrained and constraining city life can be with no way of self expression besides by what is permitted by city planners.
  • Natural features become symbols of artificiality: nature needs a guidebook
  • Drained of spontaneity, and all arranged in orderly fashion
  • Indicates Brewster’s contempt
Effect, style & response
  • Links well to Boey Kim Cheng’s Report to Wordsworth on the ruins of urbanisation
  • While Boey discusses the destruction of the natural world
  • Brewster argues the superficiality and the destruction of the human soul and attributes

Analysis
  • (Longer printing only) Olfactory imagery of museum smell evokes a sense of being shut away, mustiness, sterility, and the odour of polished floors
  • Tidi[ness] normally has positive associations

  • The lack of detail reflects the ineffable quality certain places have due to their artificialness unlike nature, being able to be described with an abundance of words and phrases
  • The smell of leisure in the cities are tainted but the smell of work are also similarly tainted

  • If people are made of places, such prescribed environments will lead to them finding themselves lacking in qualities of creativity, spontaneity, and imagination as might be gained they lived somewhere less constrained
  • This sets up the next stanza while juxtaposing the city with the speaker’s rural hometown, by simply presenting their observations without making direct critical statements about people or their ways of life
