Weakness: the poem universalises on purpose — no event, place or date appears in it; historicism explains where the images came from but not why the poem strips their labels off, and it risks shrinking a poem about the death of the sacred into a time-capsule of 1992 anxieties.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

"Report to Wordsworth"

Analysis
  • Report = official account filed upward, to someone with power to act
  • Bureaucratic genre → promises facts, neutral voice; delivers myth, lament, prophecy
  • to Wordsworth → Apostrophe to William Wordsworth (1770–1850), Romantic poet of sacred Nature
  • Irony: report to a dead man → can never be acted on → real recipient = living reader
Effect, style & response
  • Younger poet reporting back to the master of the tradition (as Wordsworth called on Milton)
  • Every image that follows = one of Wordsworth's images, returned damaged

Context

Analysis
  • Boey Kim Cheng — b. 1965, Singapore (year of independence); family name Boey → "Boey", not "Cheng"
  • Poem in his 2nd collection Another Place (1992)
  • Emigrated to Australia 1997 → later taught in Newcastle (NSW) and at NTU Singapore
  • Grew up as Singapore was rebuilt: kampongs cleared → HDB high-rises; coast pushed out by land reclamation
  • But poem names no place, date or event → speaks of the whole Earth
Effect, style & response
  • Wordsworth = founding voice of English nature poetry → the right authority to report to
  • Early-90s backdrop: ozone hole (1985), whaling moratorium (1986), smog

Wordsworth intertexts

Analysis
  • 3 Wordsworth sonnets inside the poem
  • 'London, 1802' → "Milton! thou should'st be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee" → line 1
  • 'The World Is Too Much with Us' → "we lay waste our powers" (l. 2); "Proteus rising from the sea" (l. 5); "old Triton blow his wreathèd horn" (ll. 7–8)
  • 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge' → "And all that mighty heart is lying still!" (l. 12)
  • Chain of inheritance: Milton → Wordsworth → Boey
Effect, style & response
  • Allusion as audit → Wordsworth's images checked and found destroyed
  • Wordsworth's consolation (pagan gods) becomes a casualty list

Form & structure

Analysis
  • Shakespearean sonnet: 14 lines, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, loose iambic pentameter
  • Wordsworth's 3 sonnets are Italian → Boey answers in the English pattern
  • Half-rhymes smog/clock, waste/dazed → rhyme "choked"; full rhymes from l. 9
  • Sea-god list runs ll. 5–10 → and Neptune at l. 9 = no volta; damage ignores the form's borders
  • Real turns: l. 11 (Nature → human spirit), l. 13 (report → prayer)
  • Continuous tenses: slowing, dying, widening, labouring → end still happening
Effect, style & response
  • Sonnet = Wordsworth's own form → report written on the tradition's letterhead
  • Couplet closes the form; sense stays open
1

You should be here, Nature has need of you.

Analysis
  • Apostrophe to the dead Wordsworth
  • should → obligation + impossible longing (he can't come)
  • Rewrites 'London, 1802': Milton → Wordsworth; England → Nature
  • has need of → archaic, Wordsworth's "hath need of"
  • Capital N → Nature as a being / near-divine presence
  • Comma splice → urgent, breathless; You … you frames the line
Effect, style & response
  • Summons + lament at once → grief from the first words
  • Can carry reproach: come and see the Nature you trusted
2

She has been laid waste. Smothered by the smog

Analysis
  • She → Nature personified as a woman (Mother Nature) → victim; Wordsworth cast as rescuer
  • Passive voice → agent hidden until we dump (l. 7)
  • laid waste → military idiom (conquered land)
  • Flips Wordsworth's "we lay waste our powers": active → passive; our inner powers → Nature's body
  • Full stop after 5 syllables → sentence killed mid-line
  • Sibilance sm–sm → smog welded to smothering; smother = kill by stopping breath
  • Smothered = the flowers grammatically, but sits right after She → drifts like smog
Effect, style & response
  • Damage that seems to happen by itself → everyone responsible, no one accountable
  • Reader's own breath hisses the line
3

the flowers are mute, and the birds are few

Analysis
  • mute → flowers once "spoke" (beauty, scent) → silence motif begins
  • few → survey count; decline still under way
  • Simple parallel clauses → childlike, final
  • Echo (association, not certain allusion): Keats "And no birds sing" — epigraph of Carson's Silent Spring (1962)
Effect, style & response
  • Flowers + birdsong = stock materials of nature poetry → the tradition's losses too
4

in a sky slowing like a dying clock

Analysis
  • Simile: sky running down like a clock → time running out
  • dying clock → machine given a living death (paradox)
  • Nature reimagined as mechanism → something to run and use
  • Stopped clock = sign of a death in the house → lying still (l. 12)
  • Rhythm stalls → pentameter falters
Effect, style & response
  • Apocalypse as slow winding-down, not explosion
5–6

All hopes of Proteus rising from the sea / have sunk

Analysis
  • Proteus = shape-shifting, prophetic sea-god (Homer, Odyssey 4)
  • Quotes Wordsworth's wish "Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea"
  • rising → sunk = antithesis; idiom made literal (hopes sink into the sea)
  • All hopes → whole Romantic hope that nature restores us
  • entombed → god of escape sealed in; tomb = no resurrection
Effect, style & response
  • Wordsworth's consolation drowned
6–7

the waste / we dump

Analysis
  • waste → l. 2's ruin becomes literal rubbish → bathos (myth under trash)
  • Enjambment holds back the agent → we dump = sudden confession
  • we → only first person in the poem → speaker + reader implicated
  • dump → blunt, colloquial monosyllable vs mythic vocabulary
Effect, style & response
  • Moral turn: culprit finally named — and it's us
7–8

Triton's notes struggle to be free, / his famous horns are choked

Analysis
  • Triton = sea's herald; conch calms or raises the waves
  • notes struggle, not the god → sound trapped in a blocked instrument
  • famous → made famous by poets (Spenser, Wordsworth's "wreathèd horn")
  • choked → instrument given a throat; eyes are dazed → sight gone too
  • free rhymes with sea → pair Wordsworth rhymed praising Milton's voice
Effect, style & response
  • Balanced clauses + regular metre → reads like a medical chart
9–10

helpless as a beached whale

Analysis
  • Neptune = Roman king of the sea → power itself
  • Order of defeat: Proteus (renewal) → Triton (voice) → Neptune (sovereignty)
  • Simile runs downward → god compared to a stranded animal (Bathos)
  • Beached whale = 1980s emblem (whaling moratorium 1986)
  • and at l. 9 → refuses the sonnet's turn
Effect, style & response
  • All-powerful made as weak as the creatures they ruled
10

while insatiate man moves in for the kill

Analysis
  • insatiate = never satisfied → archaic, sin of greed (Shakespeare's "insatiate cormorant")
  • moves in for the kill → predator / hunter idiom; attacks prey already down
  • while → as the gods lie helpless
  • man → the species, not a nation or industry
  • Archaic word + modern idiom → Register collision
Effect, style & response
  • Anger in the open: cause named = human greed
11

Poetry and piety have begun to fail

Analysis
  • Alliteration p–p → art and reverence sound like twins
  • Turn: Nature's body → human spirit
  • begun to fail → decline being watched, not finished
  • Wordsworth's 1802 sonnets: "pen", "altar" failing England
  • Paradox: says poetry fails inside a working sonnet; line's crowded rhythm sags
Effect, style & response
  • Cause open: dying nature kills reverence — or lost reverence let nature die?
12

as Nature's mighty heart is lying still

Analysis
  • Near-quotation: Westminster Bridge "And all that mighty heart is lying still!"
  • There: London asleep at dawn (peace) → here: Nature's heart stopped (death)
  • as = while + because
  • Regular iambs = heartbeat rhythm carrying news the heart has stopped
  • Wordsworth's ! → Boey's full stop
Effect, style & response
  • Wordsworth's serenest line → a death certificate
13

O see the wound widening in the sky

Analysis
  • O → vocative of prayer and ode; report becomes plea
  • see → only imperative; aimed at the living reader
  • wound → sky as an injured body; widening → still opening
  • Ozone hole (reported 1985; Montreal Protocol 1987) → a reading, not a decode
  • Answers Wordsworth's "Little we see in Nature that is ours"
Effect, style & response
  • Damage felt as violence against a sacred body, not measured as data
14

God is labouring to utter his last cry.

Analysis
  • Summit of the casualty list: flowers → gods → poetry → Nature → God
  • labouring → straining + childbirth inverted: first cry → last cry
  • to utter → cry not yet made; poem ends before it sounds
  • Crucifixion echo: Jesus "cried again with a loud voice" (Matthew 27:50)
  • Full rhyme sky/cry closes the form; sense left open
Effect, style & response
  • God dies with nature — or no one left with the piety to hear him
  • Unfinished cry = the space left for the reader

Motifs

Analysis
  • Voice failing: mute → notes → horns are choked → Poetry → utter his last cry
  • Downward: laid, sunk, entombed, lies, lying still
  • Body of Nature: smothered, choked, dazed, beached, heart, wound, labouring
  • Time: dying clock → begun → widening → last
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

  • Love Armed (Behn). Link: both poems personify an overwhelming power enthroned above its victims — Behn's Love "in Fantastic Triumph sat" amid "bleeding hearts", Boey's "insatiate man moves in for the kill" — and both use formal elegance to contain violence (Behn's poised lyric stanzas, Boey's sonnet). Shared technique: personification pushed to allegory, plus a closing redistribution of harm (Behn's couplet discovers the wound is "alone" hers; Boey's couplet discovers the wound is God's). Genuine difference: the speaker's position — Behn speaks as the victim, her suffering erotic, survivable and half-relished; Boey speaks as bystander-accomplice ("we dump") for a victim with no voice at all. Cruelty as courtship game versus cruelty as extinction.
  • A Different History (Bhatt). The closest pairing in the set. Link: two postcolonial poets writing in English, each measuring cultural-spiritual loss through transplanted gods — but Bhatt's Pan "emigrated to India", gods migrating and surviving translation, while Boey's sea-gods are "entombed" and beached: gods who die untranslated. Both ask what the English literary inheritance is worth to its non-English heirs — Bhatt accuses the language ("the oppressor's tongue") yet ends with grandchildren loving it; Boey never accuses, and mourns with the tradition as its loyal executor. Shared technique: classical/mythological allusion carrying the argument; direct rhetorical address. Genuine difference: trajectory — Bhatt's poem bends toward rebirth and "unborn grandchildren"; Boey's toward a "last cry". Migration versus funeral.
  • The Chimney Sweeper (Blake, Experience). Link: both are reports on a body destroyed by the machine of "getting and spending", filed in deceptively traditional forms, and both end by implicating God's household — Blake's child's parents "are gone to praise God & his Priest & King", religion as accomplice; Boey's God is himself the final casualty. Between them they bracket the industrial era: Blake at the soot's source (1794), Boey downstream where the same smoke has become planetary "smog". Shared technique: the innocent/sacred victim rendered in monosyllabic plainness; irony carried by juxtaposition rather than statement. Genuine difference: Blake's God-language is savage irony aimed at institutional religion; Boey's is grief for the sacred itself — Blake wants the reader angry at heaven's earthly agents, Boey wants the reader bereaved of heaven.
  • Where I Come From (Brewster). Link: both poems run on the same equation — minds are made by environments — but in opposite directions: Brewster's "People are made of places", nature carried inward as identity ("hints of jungles or mountains"), against Boey's inversion, where the death of place kills the inward faculties ("Poetry and piety have begun to fail"). Put them together and you get a complete argument: if people are made of places, laying waste the places lays waste the people. Shared technique: catalogue/list as structure; sensory inventory (Brewster's smells, Boey's sounds). Genuine difference: temperature — Brewster is meditative, even-handed (her city gets its own sensuous list; no villain), Boey is elegiac and accusatory. Description that trusts the world to persist versus report on its ending.
  • The Cockroach (Halligan). Link: both are modern fourteen-liners that put a creature at the centre and bend the sonnet around it — but the creatures point opposite ways: Halligan's cockroach becomes a mirror ("I thought I recognised myself"), nature as emblem of the restless human self, while Boey's whale-god is a casualty, nature as victim of the human self. Watching versus mourning; the gaze inward versus the gaze at damage. Shared technique: sonnet-form irony (formal order framing disorder); a single extended conceit sustained across the whole poem; a turn on which the observer's detachment fails. Genuine difference: scale and stakes — Halligan's crisis is private (one man's unease about his life), Boey's is cosmic (God's death); Halligan ends in queasy self-knowledge, Boey in prophecy.
  • Lament (Clarke). The set's twin elegy. Link: two near-contemporaneous eco-elegies (Clarke 1991, Gulf War; Boey 1992) that both borrow a genre of formal grief for environmental catastrophe — Clarke the funeral lament (each stanza "For the…", a dedication list, victims given elegiac dignity: "the green turtle with her pulsing burden"), Boey the report-turned-psalm. Both catalogue casualties in escalating order and both sacralise the destroyed (Clarke's "burnt earth", Boey's wounded sky). Shared technique: anaphoric/list structure; the specific creature made to carry species-scale grief; religious register imported into reportage. Genuine difference: specificity — Clarke names a war and stays with nameable creatures, oil, ashes; Boey names no event and routes everything through literature (gods, Wordsworth, "Poetry"). Clarke's is a lament for the world; Boey's is also a lament for the words for the world. And Clarke's title names the genre she fulfils; Boey's title names a genre ("report") his poem deliberately exceeds.
✧
06Contemporary

The Cockroach

Kevin Halligan · by 2005

A man watches an insect lose its purpose and, in the last four words, stops being able to watch from outside.
