CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

Kevin Halligan

Very little is documented about Halligan: he is a Canadian poet and writer, born in 1964, who published many poems in the Times Literary Supplement between the late 1990s and mid-2000s, and two collections, Blossom Street (2001) and Utopia (2009). 'The Cockroach' was in print by 2005, when it appeared in the Cambridge anthology Songs of Ourselves. Reports that he lived in Cambodia or studied Buddhism are unconfirmed — and the poem names no place, religion or history, so no reading should depend on them.

The sonnet it bends

'The Cockroach' is a sonnet: fourteen lines of iambic pentameter. Its octave rhymes like an English sonnet (ABAB CDCD), but its sestet rhymes like an Italian one (EFG EGF), so the English sonnet's clinching couplet never comes — and the sentence that runs across lines 8–9 refuses the Italian turn as well. Giving the form of love poetry and self-examination to a cockroach is mock-heroic; the joke becomes serious when the speaker sees himself in it.

Karma and A former life

In Hindu and Buddhist thought, karma ("action") is the principle that deeds bring consequences, which may ripen in a later life; rebirth as an animal is one outcome of bad conduct. Lines 12–13 picture it in Western terms, as a court and an account book — due payment for some vicious crime.

What cockroaches do

Real cockroaches keep their bodies against surfaces, running along walls and edges — so a path between the wainscot and the door is exactly a roach's route, and an open shelf exactly the exposed place a roach avoids. A cockroach on its back is usually in trouble: healthy ones right themselves; sick or poisoned ones are left stranded. The poem's circling, flipping and stopping fit a creature in distress as well as one exploring.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

The Cockroach
TThe Cockroach
1I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,
2Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.
3At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace
4A path between the wainscot and the door,
5But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings,
6Circling the rusty table leg and back,
7And flipping right over to scratch his wings –
8As if the victim of a mild attack
9Of restlessness that worsened over time.
10After a while, he climbed an open shelf
11And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go.
12Was this due payment for some vicious crime
13A former life had led to? I don't know,
14Except I thought I recognised myself.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
The Cockroach
Language & devices

Definite article + creature: The Cockroach follows the naming habit of fables and emblem poems ('The Fly', 'The Tyger'), where an animal is shown and then read for a moral. Connotation: the cockroach is vermin — dirty, despised, almost impossible to kill.

Meaning & effect

The title promises a lesson drawn from an animal, and a lowly one. Giving vermin a sonnet — the traditional form of love and self-scrutiny — is mock-heroic. The joke turns serious when the creature turns out to be a mirror.

Line 1
I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,
Language & devices

First person: I watched — a detached observer. Hyperbole: giant. Anthropomorphism: pace — what anxious people and caged animals do. Iambic pentameter: a calm, regular opening line.

Meaning & effect

The poem sets up a clear distance: I on one side, the insect on the other. Pace already gives the cockroach a human restlessness. The rest of the poem will close the gap the first line opens.

Line 2
Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.
Language & devices

Verb: Skirting — edging around, avoiding. Personification: a ball of dust that rode the floor. Domestic detail: dust, a neglected room.

Meaning & effect

The insect keeps to edges and avoids obstacles — real cockroach behaviour, and a cautious way of living. The dust sets the scene as a shabby, neglected room: a small, closed world.

Lines 3–4
At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace / A path between the wainscot and the door,
Language & devices

Pronoun: he, not "it" — the insect is personified. Hedge: seemed. Diction: quite satisfied to trace / A path — routine, contentment within limits. wainscot — wooden panelling, the traditional haunt of household vermin.

Meaning & effect

At first the cockroach lives contentedly within boundaries, running between wall and door. Seemed admits that the speaker is interpreting: he cannot see inside the insect — only, as it turns out, inside himself.

Lines 5–6
But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings, / Circling the rusty table leg and back,
Language & devices

Conjunction: But — the first change. Imagery: jog in crooked rings — circular, irregular movement. Adjective: rusty — decay. and back — a return that goes nowhere.

Meaning & effect

Purpose gives way to aimless circling. The crooked rings are restlessness made visible: movement for its own sake, around and back. The rusty table leg adds to the sense of a world running down.

Line 7
And flipping right over to scratch his wings –
Language & devices

Trochaic inversion: FLIPping right over — the rhythm flips over in the line describing the flip. Detail: to scratch his wings — wings he never uses. Dash: a pause before the speaker interprets.

Meaning & effect

The insect is upended, undignified and comic — but a cockroach on its back is often in trouble. It has wings, the power to escape, and only scratches them. The dash suspends the image, inviting us to wonder what it means.

Lines 8–9
As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness that worsened over time.
Language & devices

Simile: As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness. Medical diction: attack — restlessness as an illness. Enjambment: the sentence runs across the octave–sestet boundary. that worsened over time — progression.

Meaning & effect

The speaker diagnoses the insect with a human condition: an anxiety that starts mild and grows. Because the sentence spills over line 8, the sonnet's traditional turn at line 9 is refused — the restlessness carries on regardless of the form.

Lines 10–11
After a while, he climbed an open shelf / And stopped. He looked uncertain where to go.
Language & devices

Verb: climbed — ascent, but to an open shelf, an exposed place with no walls. Caesura: And stopped. — a mid-line full stop. Short sentence: He looked uncertain where to go.

Meaning & effect

The climb leads nowhere: on the open shelf, away from the walls that guided him, he freezes. The full stop halts the poem's movement as the insect halts. This is the most human line in the poem — paralysis from having no direction.

Lines 12–13
Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to? I don't know,
Language & devices

Rhetorical question: Was this due payment…? Legal/financial diction: due payment, vicious crime — punishment as debt. Allusion: A former life — karma and rebirth. Colloquial monosyllables: I don't know — and the first I since line 1.

Meaning & effect

The speaker half-seriously wonders whether the creature is being punished for a past life — imagining karma as a courtroom and an account book. Then he gives up: I don't know. The return of I brings the observer back into the poem, ready for the last line.

Line 14
Except I thought I recognised myself.
Language & devices

Conjunction: Except — the real conclusion. Hedge: thought. Rhyme: myself answers shelf. Withheld couplet: the sestet rhymes EFG EGF, so the sonnet never gives its clinching couplet.

Meaning & effect

The watcher sees himself in the watched: the distance set up in line 1 collapses. The restless circling, the unused wings, the paralysis on the open shelf were his condition all along. The poem refuses a neat moral or resolving couplet; it simply stops at the moment of recognition — and leaves the reader to wonder whether they recognise themselves too.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The standard account of this poem — insect as allegory of human aimlessness, sonnet subverted, volta delayed, moral delivered — is not wrong, but it files the poem under a grandness the poem itself spends fourteen lines declining. The better reading is this: "The Cockroach" is not an allegory so much as a live demonstration of how allegories get made. We do not receive a finished symbol; we watch a man manufacture one in real time, hedge by hedge, out of boredom, a dusty room and a passing insect — and the poem's distinction is that it knows this about itself, and confesses it in its final line. Its subject is the mind's incorrigible habit of planting meaning in whatever it watches, and the self-portrait that habit accidentally produces.

Track the manufacture. The poem opens in the grammar of pure observation — "I watched" — and immediately begins to cheat. "Giant" magnifies; by line 3 the insect is "he", not "it", gendered like a person before it has done anything human; "seemed quite satisfied" plants an inner life while flagging, in "seemed", that the planting is speculative. The realist furniture — dust, wainscot, rusty table leg — is doing alibi work: this is mere reportage, the details insist, while the verbs quietly anthropomorphise. "Satisfied", "jog", "restlessness", "uncertain": each is a human word smuggled across the species line under cover of description. The famous simile is the poem's one moment of open honesty about the method — "As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness" — as if conceding that the diagnosis is the watcher's invention. By line 11 the pretence has thinned to nothing: "He looked uncertain where to go" reports the interior of an insect as flat fact. And once the creature has been filled with human uncertainty, the metaphysics follows as if naturally — "Was this due payment for some vicious crime …?" — a question that only makes sense about a person. The final line then does the one thing left to do: it names the person. "Except I thought I recognised myself" is less a twist than an audit. Of course he recognised himself; he had been drawing his own portrait since "satisfied".

Read this way, the poem's structural behaviour falls into place. The sonnet machinery runs to time throughout — every rhyme full, the pentameter never once broken, even (especially) through "And stopped." — while every ordering system inside the poem fails in sequence: the traced path deteriorates into crooked rings, the climb tops out on an empty shelf, the karmic hypothesis dies in "I don't know", knowledge itself decays from "watched" to "thought". By the last line the verse-form is the only machine in the poem still working. That is the deep joke of writing this experience as a sonnet: form persists the way habit persists, the way the roach goes on grooming its wings upside down — a residual order that no longer connects to any purpose. The withheld couplet is the point of maximum tact. A couplet is the English sonnet's gesture of confidence, and confidence is the one thing this speaker cannot honestly perform; so the poem ends instead on a rhyme four lines distant, technically resolving, barely audible — closure for those who check, uncertainty for the ear.

The obvious objection to my reading is that it makes the poem cold: a clever machine about projection, meta-literature, the despair dissolved into technique. The answer is that projection is not an alternative to self-portraiture but its most reliable form. What a mind plants in a trivial object is diagnostic of that mind; nobody bored and well projects "a mild attack / Of restlessness that worsened over time" onto an insect. The poem's despair is real precisely because it is found — planted — in so small a thing. Ambient unhappiness colonises whatever is to hand; the triviality of the host measures the saturation of the mood. And the vigil itself testifies before a single interpretive word: only a man with nothing he can bear to do watches a cockroach for this long, this closely. The symptom is the watching. The interpretation merely catches up.

There is a second objection, from the other flank: that the poem is slight — a shaggy-dog sonnet, a joke with a mock-solemn punchline. The joke-structure is undeniably there. "Giant" is mock-heroic; the grandest lyric form in English is handed to vermin; the octave's climactic enjambment winds up "a mild attack / Of—" and pays off with restlessness, pure bathos; "Except I thought I recognised myself" has the timing of a deadpan curtain-line. But the comedy is load-bearing, not decorative. Deadpan is the only register in which this confession could be made without curdling into self-pity; the moment the poem said I am in despair it would become the kind of poem its speaker could no longer trust. Instead it says something much smaller — I thought I recognised myself — and the smallness is the credibility. This is also why inflating the poem is misreading it. A response that reaches for Kafka, Camus, the absurd condition of modern man, the trauma of Cambodia, converts understatement into the very grandiosity the poem was built to avoid. The poem's scale is one man, one room, one insect, a few minutes; its abstractions are lower-case; its biggest metaphysical question is asked and abandoned inside a line and a half. Smallness is not a limitation it fails to transcend; it is the argument. Despair here is not tragic, operatic, historical — it is domestic, ambient, mildly comic and chronic, a condition that "worsened over time" while nobody was watching except the sufferer, who was watching an insect.

So the movement from first line to last is best described not as observation-then-revelation but as a closing loop. The poem begins "I watched" and ends "myself": first word the watcher, last word the watched, and the fourteen lines between them are the discovery that these were the same thing. The sonnet — historically the form in which a self addresses its beloved — is here the form in which a self, by way of a cockroach, finally addresses itself; and what it finds to say is four hedges deep, past tense, subordinate to "I don't know". The creature, meanwhile, is left where it stopped, on its shelf, unaware of having been used. That, too, is part of the poem's honesty: the roach never was the subject. It was the mirror — and the poem, unlike its many solemn paraphrases, never once pretends otherwise.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

The block. On the page the poem is a single unbroken fourteen-line block — no stanza breaks. The sonnet's architecture (octave, sestet) exists only in the rhymes, audible but invisible: a structured interior under a featureless surface, which is also a fair description of the speaker. The title runs the emblem-book convention — definite article plus creature, like a bestiary entry — and so promises a moral. The poem then declines to draw one; that gap between the fable-shaped title and the hedged non-moral of line 14 is the form's first joke.

Rhyme, worked letter by letter. Assign a letter to each new end-sound:

LineEnd wordLetter
1paceA
2floorB
3traceA
4doorB
5ringsC
6backD
7wingsC
8attackD
9timeE
10shelfF
11goG
12crimeE (rhymes time)
13knowG (rhymes go)
14myselfF (rhymes shelf)

Scheme: ABAB CDCD EFGEGF. Two things follow. First, the opening eight lines are pure Shakespearean procedure, which trains the reader to expect a third cross-rhymed quatrain and a clinching couplet (EFEF GG). Instead the poem swerves into an Italian-style sestet — and then warps even that: the standard EFGEFG repeats its tercet exactly, but Halligan's second tercet comes back out of order, E-G-F. Second, and decisively: the couplet never arrives. The English sonnet's couplet is the form's little engine of confidence — the two-line snap that resolves, summarises, moralises. Halligan's fourteenth line rhymes not with line 13 beside it but with line 10, four lines back — the longest rhyme-wait in the poem, so long that most readers half-lose the chime. Closure technically occurs and is barely audible. A poem about a creature that "looked uncertain where to go" is written in a form that, at its own ending, cannot find its expected way home.

Look at the rhyme distances: in the octave every rhyme-partner sits a tidy two lines back (1→3, 2→4, 5→7, 6→8). In the sestet the gaps go 3 (time→crime), 2 (go→know), 4 (shelf→myself). The metronomic alternation frays exactly as the creature loses its pattern. And the pairings are semantically loaded: time is made to rhyme with crime (the karmic equation in miniature — duration itself as offence); go with know (the two things neither roach nor speaker can do); shelf with myself — the self's rhyme-partner is the site of arrest, the bare ledge where movement ended. The last word of the poem chimes with the place where the creature stopped.

One more fact, easy to miss because it is an absence: every rhyme in the poem is full. No pararhyme, no half-rhyme anywhere. The disorder the poem describes is never allowed to roughen its sounds; the containment stays immaculate, table manners perfect throughout the breakdown. Disorder in this poem lives in the large structures (the withheld couplet, the inverted tercet, the drifting distances) while the local finish stays polished — which is precisely the speaker's own condition: outwardly composed, structurally lost.

Metre. The base is iambic pentameter, and the poem keeps it with almost sinister reliability. Scansion of eleven lines (stressed syllables in capitals, feet marked |):

  • L1: "i WATCHED | a GI- | ant COCK- | roach START | to PACE" — regular; but "cockroach" straddles feet 3–4 so that "-roach", a heavy syllable, sits in a weak slot: the creature bulges slightly against the frame that contains it.
  • L2: "SKIRT-ing | a BALL | of DUST | that RODE | the FLOOR" — initial trochee. The first foot swerves off the iambic path exactly as the roach swerves round the dust.
  • L4: "a PATH | be-TWEEN | the WAIN- | scot AND | the DOOR" — regular, with the fourth beat falling on a promoted "AND": a deliberately featureless, level line for the traced path between two fixed points.
  • L5: "but SOON | he TURNED | to JOG | in CROOK- | ed RINGS" — perfectly regular. The line about crookedness is metrically dead straight: at this stage the disorder belongs to the creature, not yet to the verse or the watcher.
  • L6: "CIR-cling | the RUST- | y TA- | ble LEG | and BACK" — initial trochee (with "circling" elided to two syllables). The line pivots at its head; it starts by turning.
  • L7: "and FLIP- | ping RIGHT | O-ver | to SCRATCH | his WINGS" — mid-line trochee in the third foot, jammed against the stressed "RIGHT": two stresses collide and the rhythm literally flips over in the middle of the line describing the flip. The poem's showpiece substitution.
  • L8: "as IF | the VIC- | tim of | a MILD | at-TACK" — pyrrhic third foot ("-tim of"): the line goes hollow in the middle, a mild dip before "attack" lands, enacting "mild".
  • L9: "of REST- | less-ness | that WORS- | ened O- | ver TIME" — pyrrhic-leaning second foot; and note what the enjambment has done: the octave's final, structurally most important line-position is handed to "Of", the weakest word available. Bathos built into the architecture.
  • L10: "AF-ter | a WHILE, | he CLIMBED | an O- | pen SHELF" — initial trochee, the third of three, and all three (Skirting, Circling, After) are pivot-words of ongoing motion or elapsing time: the inversions cluster where the creature changes course.
  • L11: "and STOPPED. | he LOOKED | un-CER- | tain WHERE | to GO" — five clean iambs. This is the line "widely said" to break the metre. It does not. The pentameter ticks straight through the full stop like a clock in an empty room — the pulse of the world entirely indifferent to the creature's arrest. That indifference is the effect; calling it a metrical break destroys the point.
  • L12: "was THIS | DUE PAY- | ment FOR | some VI- | cious CRIME" — spondaic pressure on "due pay-": the stresses bunch and thud where the karmic invoice is presented; the line audibly weighs something.
  • L13: "a FOR- | mer LIFE | had LED | to? I | don't KNOW" — the iambic template forces a beat onto "I" in the fourth foot, the metre picking out the ego at the exact moment the poem swings from roach to speaker; the question mark falls inside a foot, mid-stride.
  • L14: "ex-CEPT | i THOUGHT | i REC- | og-NISED | my-SELF" — regular, docile, the tamest line in the poem. The confession arrives deadpan, in perfect order — and the metre's final beat lands on "-SELF": four hedges in the syntax, but the last stress of the poem falls, without hedging, on the self.

The turn(s). Full adjudication in Cruxes; the structural facts belong here. The form appoints a turn at line 9 and the syntax refuses it: "a mild attack / Of restlessness" enjambs straight across the octave–sestet seam, the sentence (lines 3–9, seven lines, the poem's longest — restlessness as syntax) pouring over the boundary where the sonnet asks for a pause. The narrative hinge comes instead at line 11 — "And stopped." — the poem's shortest sentence, two syllables and a full stop, the only mid-line full stop in the poem, arresting ten and a half lines of continuous motion. The modal turn comes at 12, where narration becomes interrogation; the disclosure at 14. A sonnet is a machine with one pivot; this one distributes the pivot's functions across four sites, which is what a turn looks like when the turner is "uncertain where to go".

Syntax and punctuation. Six sentences: lines 1–2; 3–9; 10–11a ("After a while … And stopped."); 11b ("He looked uncertain where to go."); 12–13a (the question); 13b–14 ("I don't know, / Except …"). The shape is eloquent: a two-line establishing shot; a seven-line sentence that will not stop; then syntax shattering into short units exactly where the creature halts. The first three sentences all open with narrative time-markers ("I watched", "At first", "After a while") — the log-book of a vigil. The octave's interior carries no punctuation at all (its commas are all line-end): it streams. The sestet contains the poem's only mid-line full stop (11) and its only question mark (13): it stutters. Note too that "I don't know" is not even granted a full stop — a comma, and the sentence leans on into "Except": the poem's entire self-knowledge is grammatically a subordinate tail hanging off a confession of ignorance.

Enjambment. Four run-ons, each crossing a meaningful edge: 3→4 ("to trace / A path" — the path continues over the line as over the floor); 8→9 (the seam-crossing analysed above, which is also a bathetic reveal: "a mild attack / Of—" what? heart? panic? — "restlessness"); 10→11 ("an open shelf / And stopped." — the reader tips over the line-end and lands on the stop, the enjambment delivering the arrest bodily); 12→13 ("some vicious crime / A former life had led to?" — the line-break falls between the crime and the life, the white space standing where the gap between incarnations would be).

Line 11 as hinge. Everything before it is motion; everything after it is mind. "And stopped." ends the poem's kinetic subject; "He looked uncertain where to go." — six words, five of them monosyllables — is the plainest line in the poem and the first that reads mind into the creature wholesale. The caesura is the poem's centre of gravity: the silence after "stopped." is where watching turns into thinking, and the sonnet's remaining three and a half lines all happen inside that silence.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The poem's sound-world divides at the same hinge as everything else. The octave is built on friction: a scuttle of sibilants and fricatives — "Skirting", "dust", "seemed quite satisfied to trace", "soon", "rings", "scratch" — insect-leg noise carried in the consonants, so that the reading voice performs a light continuous rustle while the creature moves. The sestet drops the friction for stops and hollows: "stopped", "uncertain", "go", "don't know" — the mouth closing, the sound-floor falling away. Read aloud, the poem audibly loses its busyness at line 11, which is why the caesura lands so hard: the full stop after "stopped" is preceded by the plosive sandwich /st…pt/ — the word is a wall, consonants shutting at both ends — and followed by nothing the voice can rustle on.

The word "restlessness" deserves its own note: three hissing sibilants packed into the poem's diagnosis, the noun performing the fidget it names — and it arrives, after the line-break's suspension, as bathos: the octave's climactic enjambment sets up "a mild attack / Of—" and pays off with a word that merely seethes.

A hard-/k/ spine runs the poem's length and carries its argument: "cockroach" → "crooked" → "attack" → "climbed" → "crime" → "recognised" → "Except". The consonant of the creature's own name migrates through violence ("attack"), indictment ("crime") and finally cognition ("recognised") — the accusation travels phonetically from insect to speaker before the syntax admits it.

Vowel-length does the emotional shading at the rhymes. The octave's A and B rhymes are long and open — "pace/trace", "floor/door" — stately, unhurried sounds for the period of apparent purpose; against them the D rhyme "back/attack" snaps shut on a short vowel and a stop, the octave's two smack-shut sounds landing on its two violence-words. In the sestet, "go/know" leaves the mouth open on a long o — the vowel of irresolution, twice, the second time on the poem's confession of ignorance — while "shelf/myself" closes on the shut, shelved sound /ɛlf/: the self filed away on its ledge.

Cadence: the octave's rhymes ring at even two-line intervals, a metronome under the scuttle; the sestet syncopates (three, two, four lines between chimes). The final line is all evenness — five even iambs — and closes on the stressed "-self": the quietest line in the poem is the only one that lands its last beat squarely on its subject. Deadpan as a sound-effect: the voice is required to not rise precisely where the meaning does.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Distinguish the terms: a motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something. The cockroach itself becomes a symbol only at line 14, retroactively and hedged — for thirteen and a half lines it is stubbornly an insect, and the poem's power depends on how long it withholds symbolic status. Around it, four motifs run the poem's whole length.

1. The geometry of movement — the poem's plot told as shapes. "Pace" (line 1): a straight line, to and fro. "Skirting" (2): an arc around an obstacle. "Trace / A path between the wainscot and the door" (3–4): a fixed segment, two endpoints, the most ordered figure in the poem. Then "crooked rings" (5): closed curves, and deformed ones — a ring that fails at being a ring. "Circling the rusty table leg and back" (6): orbit around a point, radius shrinking. "Flipping right over" (7): rotation about the body's own axis — the locus of movement now the creature itself, going nowhere at all. "Climbed" (10): the sudden new axis, vertical, promising escape from the plane. "And stopped" (11): a point. Line → arc → segment → ring → orbit → spin → vertical → point: the degrees of freedom collapse one by one to zero. The whole existential argument is conducted in geometry before a single abstract noun appears.

2. Dust, rust, vacancy — entropy in three glimpses. "A ball of dust that rode the floor" (2): loose matter, mobile, passively carried. "The rusty table leg" (6): corrosion, fixed, eaten into structure. "An open shelf" (10): bare board, nothing stored — "open" as in empty. The decay migrates inward: from floating debris to corroded furniture to sheer vacancy at the top of the climb. Time is present in the room's objects long before it is named ("worsened over time", "After a while", "A former life"), and the neglected interior externalises the watcher's state eight lines before he admits to having one. The shelf is the one item that hardens into symbol: the summit that contains nothing, exposure and emptiness at the top of every climb.

3. The lexis of law and debt. "Victim" (8) — someone wronged; "attack" (8) — an offence, though here medicalised; "due payment" (12) — an invoice; "vicious crime" (12) — an indictment; "had led to" (13) — a case history establishing causation. Watch the register shift: medical ("mild attack … worsened") → forensic ("victim") → fiscal-judicial ("due payment for some vicious crime"). Across the poem a prosecution is quietly assembled out of natural history, and cosmic justice, when it finally surfaces, speaks in the language of bookkeeping — karma imagined as an unpaid bill. The verdict never comes: the court adjourns on "I don't know".

4. The epistemic verbs — the poem's real plot. "Watched" (1): confident perception. "Seemed" (3): appearance flagged as appearance. "As if" (8): open simile, interpretation admitting itself. "Looked uncertain" (11): projection wearing the grammar of observation. "I don't know" (13): the collapse. "Thought … recognised" (14): cognition twice-hedged. The trajectory runs from seeing to seeming to not knowing to thinking one recognises — a steady decay of epistemic confidence that is the poem's true narrative arc. The creature's movements degrade from line to point; the watcher's knowledge degrades in perfect parallel, from observation to confession. By the end the two collapses are revealed to have been one thing — which is what "recognised" means.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Restlessness and purposelessness

The cockroach moves from satisfied routine to crooked rings to a halt uncertain where to go. Restlessness is presented as a condition that worsens over time rather than resolves.

02

Self-recognition

The watcher sees himself in the watched. The distance of I watched collapses into I recognised myself, and the insect becomes a mirror more honest than direct self-examination.

03

Uncertainty

The speaker can only guess: seemed, As if, I don't know, I thought. The poem is honest about the limits of what we can know — about another creature, and about ourselves.

04

Guilt and punishment

The question of due payment for some vicious crime raises the possibility that suffering is deserved. The poem neither accepts nor rejects it; the guilt is left hanging, unexplained.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Where is the volta — line 9, 11, 12, or 14?

The difficulty. A sonnet reader arrives primed for one turn; this poem offers four candidates. Line 9 is the formal boundary (octave ends); line 11 is the narrative reversal ("And stopped."); line 12 is the modal shift (description becomes question); line 14 is the revelation.

The competing readings. For 9: the sestet's new rhyme-set (EFG) does begin here, and "restlessness that worsened over time" turns movement into diagnosis. Against 9: the syntax pointedly refuses the turn — the sentence enjambs straight across the seam, and the line it delivers opens on "Of", the least turn-like word in the poem. This is a refused volta, and the refusal is expressive. For 11: everything reverses here — motion becomes stillness, octave-matter becomes sestet-matter; the poem's centre of gravity is the full stop after "stopped". Against 11: the stance has not changed — the speaker is still outside, still reporting; arrest is an event, not a turn of mind. For 14: the allegory completes here, and the phrase "displaced volta" honours the fact that the poem's meaning arrives in its last breath. Against 14: a volta is a change of direction, and line 14 is better described as a landing — the direction changed earlier; this is where the ground arrives.

The strongest case is line 12. "Was this due payment for some vicious crime" changes what kind of poem this is: past-tense narration becomes present interrogation; the room's physics gives way to metaphysics; the speaker's mind, hitherto hidden behind observational grammar, enters as a questioner — and one line later the poem produces its only present-tense main verb, "I don't know". Tense, mood, register and subject all pivot at 12 in a way they do not at 9, 11 or 14.

What a strong answer does. Not pick a line and defend it to the death, but argue that the poem distributes the volta's functions — form's turn refused at 9, action's turn at 11, mind's turn at 12, meaning's turn at 14 — and then make the interpretive move: a sonnet whose turn cannot be located in one place is formally enacting a speaker who is "uncertain where to go". The scattered volta is not indecision in the writing; it is the poem's most precise mimesis of indecision.

2. "He looked uncertain where to go." — whose uncertainty is this?

The difficulty. "Looked" carries two grammars: appeared (the roach seemed uncertain to me) and gazed (the roach looked about, uncertain). And beneath both sits the harder question: can an insect be uncertain at all, or is this line the moment the speaker's projection completes itself and starts reporting his own interior as the creature's?

The competing readings. Taken as honest observation, the line is the poem's most touching moment: hesitation legible in an insect's body, creaturely experience continuous with ours — the reading the anthropomorphic "he" has been preparing since line 3. Taken as ventriloquism, the line is the crucial slip: earlier projections wore flags ("seemed", "As if"), but here the hedge is gone and the speaker states an insect's inner state as fact — the moment the mirror silvers, after which the karmic question and the recognition follow necessarily. The evidence tilts towards ventriloquism precisely because of that missing hedge: the poem has trained us in scrupulousness ("seemed", "As if") and then conspicuously drops it.

What a strong answer does. Refuses to choose, and locates the poem's honesty in the undecidability: the speaker cannot know whether he observed uncertainty or installed it — that is exactly what "Except I thought I recognised myself" concedes. The line is where watching and mirroring become indistinguishable, and the poem's final hedge ("thought") is its acknowledgement that they were never separable. Weak answers resolve the line one way and lose either the pathos or the self-knowledge; the poem keeps both.

3. "Was this due payment for some vicious crime / A former life had led to?"

The difficulty. Three tangles in fourteen words. Whose former life — the cockroach's (a soul demoted into vermin, paying off an old debt) or, proleptically, the speaker's (his own past conduct surfacing disguised as a question about an insect)? What is "this" — the restlessness, the paralysis, or existence-as-a-cockroach at all? And the strangest, least noticed: the causality runs backwards. The syntax does not say a crime was committed in a former life; it says the former life "had led to" the crime — the life is the cause, the crime the destination, as if simply living in a certain way accumulates, by itself, towards an offence.

The competing readings. Read as the roach's biography, the question is a genuine (if half-smiling) engagement with rebirth: demotion down the ladder of beings as penalty, the insect as a soul in debtors' prison — and the Buddhist frame of the poem's reported Asian setting gives the hypothesis local seriousness. Read as displaced autobiography, the question rehearses the speaker's private dread — that his condition is deserved, that restlessness is a sentence rather than a symptom — at one remove, where it is safe to ask. The reversed causality quietly supports the second reading: "a life that leads to a crime" describes not a discrete sin but a drift, a trajectory culpable in aggregate — much more like a watched life than a legal case. And the tone will not settle: "due payment" is bookkeeping language, cosmic justice as an invoice, which either deflates the metaphysics into comedy or renders it more sinister — debts fall due whether or not you remember incurring them.

What a strong answer does. Keeps the question double — asked about the roach, meant about the man — and reads "I don't know" as the only honest settlement of it; then presses the syntax: the poem's darkest suggestion, made available but never stated, is that the "former life" is simply the speaker's own earlier life, and the restless present is what it "led to". On that reading line 14 does not change the subject; it answers the question of line 12.

4. "Except I thought I recognised myself." — what, precisely, is being claimed?

The difficulty. The poem's entire payload is delivered through four stacked hedges, and careless readers bulldoze them into "the speaker realises he is the cockroach" — a paraphrase the line was engineered to prevent. Grammatically, the line is not even a sentence of its own: it is a subordinate tail on "I don't know," — the sole exception to a declaration of ignorance.

The hedges, in order. Except: a swerve, conceding one thing rescued from not-knowing — with the bleak consequence that the only certainty on offer is a resemblance to vermin. I thought: past tense and epistemically weak — the writing self reports an impression the present self declines to endorse; by the time we hear of the recognition it is already over, and "I don't know" (present tense) formally outranks it. Recognised: not "saw" or "realised" but a verb of fallible matching — you can recognise wrongly; yet the word also smuggles in intimacy, because recognition presupposes prior acquaintance. You cannot recognise what you have never met: the word hedges the assent while conceding that the face was familiar. Myself, withheld to the final stress: syntax delays the object of recognition to the last possible position, so the poem's whole meaning arrives on its closing beat — where, note, the metre lands its one unhedged commitment.

The competing readings. (i) Full allegorical identification, hedged only for politeness — the reading of most study guides, supported by everything the imagery has built. (ii) A momentary illusion, honestly reported and already disowned — supported by the tense structure and by "Except"'s subordination. (iii) The answer to line 12 — the "former life" was his; the recognition is an admission of guilt, not of kinship. (iv) A deadpan punchline — the mock-solemn form finally tips its hand. What a strong answer does: treats the hedging not as modesty about the claim but as the claim itself — the line asserts exactly as much as this speaker can honestly assert, and its four qualifications are the most precise thing in the poem, not the least. A reading that removes the hedges to get at "the meaning" removes the meaning.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Ten moments chosen because they repay pressure — the famous last line is treated in Difficult Moments; these are the lines most often skated over.

1. "Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor." (2) — initial trochee; participle; transferred animation. The metre swerves off the iambic path on "Skirting" exactly as the creature swerves round the obstacle: the first substitution in the poem is mimetic. "Skirting" also carries its social sense — evading, giving a wide berth — planting avoidance in the roach's repertoire twelve lines before the speaker's own avoidances surface. The dust "rode" the floor: passive matter given a jaunty verb of agency, while the genuinely self-propelled creature will end up going nowhere — the poem's first quiet joke about the difference between moving and being moved. The trivially precise detail (a dust ball, observed closely enough to see it drift) is also evidence about the watcher: this is the noticing of a man with nothing else to attend to. Intention and effect: Halligan grounds the allegory-to-come in verifiable small fact, so the reader trusts the eye long before doubting the mind.

2. "At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace" (3) — temporal frame; epistemic hedge; measured adverb. "At first" retrospectively announces a narrative — you only say at first when you know things changed — so deterioration is promised before it begins. "Seemed" is the poem's earliest confession that the creature's inner life is the watcher's construction; "quite" measures the constructed contentment and finds it moderate, faintly disappointing, the adverb of someone grading an experience they do not share. And "he": the third line quietly genders the insect, person-ing it long before line 14 admits why. Satisfaction, in this poem, is the state that exists only in report — never dramatised, only "seemed". Intention and effect: the reader is trained from the outset to read every subsequent mental-state word as speculation, which is what makes the unhedged "looked uncertain" of line 11 so loud.

3. "to trace / A path between the wainscot and the door," (3–4) — enjambment; verb connotation; bounded interval. "Trace" is not "choose" or "make": you trace a line that already exists, following a pre-drawn route — contentment defined at once as obedience to a given track. The enjambment sends the verb over the line-end to find its object, a small performance of path-following. The track runs "between the wainscot and the door": two fixed architectural limits, a life defined by its terminals — and "wainscot" is the traditional lodging of vermin in English domestic writing, an old-literary word that houses the roach in a long tradition of skirting-board lives. The path is real but closed: back and forth inside someone else's architecture. Intention and effect: purpose is introduced already ironised — the reader sees limits where the creature "seemed" to see satisfaction, an irony that will be turned on the speaker himself.

4. "But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings," (5) — conjunction pivot; register drop; oxymoronic geometry. "But" is the poem's first turn — a micro-volta at line 5, well before the form's appointed one, as if the poem cannot wait to start failing. "Jog" is superb comic casting: the leisure-exercise verb, aimless by design (jogging is motion whose destination is its starting point), demoting the creature's crisis to a fitness routine. "Crooked rings" is a geometry that fails twice — a ring returns you to where you began, and these rings are not even true circles. Meanwhile the metre stays perfectly iambic: the line about crookedness scans dead straight, the verse withholding its sympathy — disorder has reached the creature but not yet the poem. Intention and effect: Halligan lets aimlessness arrive in comic dress so that its later escalation ("worsened") catches the reader having laughed at symptoms.

5. "Circling the rusty table leg and back," (6) — initial trochee; synecdoche; floor-level perspective. The trochee makes the line pivot at its head — it starts by turning. The orbit has now shrunk to a single point of reference, and the point is telling: not the table but the "table leg", furniture seen from the floor, the poem's camera lowered to insect height eight lines before the speaker admits to sharing the view. "Rusty" puts corrosion at the centre of the creature's circuit — it orbits decay — and "and back" hangs off the line like the futile return leg it describes, syntax retracing its own steps. Intention and effect: the reader is brought physically down to the roach's scale, so the final identification has been rehearsed by perspective long before it is stated.

6. "And flipping right over to scratch his wings —" (7) — mid-line trochee; colloquial intensifier; suspended dash. The rhythm flips with the creature: "RIGHT O-ver" jams two stresses together and inverts the foot, the poem's one perfectly mimetic substitution. "Right over" is spoken register — the phrase you would use of a toddler or a beetle, affectionate, faintly amused — the watcher's voice warming as his subject loses dignity. The detail everyone forgets: wings. The creature has flight available and spends the poem on its back on the floor, scratching them — capacity unused, escape technically possible and never taken, which is as close as the poem comes to naming the speaker's own situation. The dash then suspends the line mid-air — the roach upended, the syntax withholding interpretation for a beat. Intention and effect: comedy and diagnosis arrive fused; the reader smiles at the tumble and inherits the image of unused wings.

7. "As if the victim of a mild attack / Of restlessness" (8–9) — simile; medical register; bathetic enjambment. "As if" flags the diagnosis as invention even while committing to it — the poem's most honest two words until "I don't know". "Victim" converts behaviour into affliction: the creature no longer acts but suffers, passive before its own movements. "A mild attack / Of—" is engineered suspense: the line-break holds open the grave possibilities (heart, panic, seizure) and pays off with restlessness — bathos that deflates and, in deflating, smuggles the medical frame past the reader's defences. The near-oxymoron of "mild attack" — a stock medical phrase, though attacks are rarely mild — captures precisely the low-grade, chronic, undramatic quality of the suffering at issue. Intention and effect: Halligan makes the reader laugh at the anticlimax and then discover the laughter has ratified a clinical account of the speaker's own state.

8. "that worsened over time." (9) — prognosis diction; end-stop; double time-scale. Three flat words close the octave with a chart-note: not an event but a course, the tense of chronic illness. The phrase quietly explodes the poem's realism — the vigil has lasted minutes, yet "over time" speaks of a longer duration than any cockroach-watching session contains: two clocks are superimposed, the insect's afternoon and the man's years, and the sentence only makes literal sense on the second clock. This is the poem's first unguarded autobiographical leak, eight lines before "myself". The full stop then seals the octave — the only end-stopped period since line 2 — closing the case-file section of the poem. Intention and effect: the reader registers, perhaps subliminally, that the diagnosis has outgrown its patient, and starts looking for the real one.

9. "After a while, he climbed an open shelf" (10) — initial trochee; vague duration; polysemous adjective. "After a while" is the diction of boredom — unmeasured time, the watcher no longer counting — and its trochee tips the line forward into the poem's final movement. "Climbed" introduces the vertical for the first time: after ten lines of floor-plane wandering, ascent — the allegory's career move, aspiration itself. But the summit is "an open shelf": open as in exposed (no cover, a predator's sightline), open as in available (nothing yet stored), open as in empty. The reward for the poem's one upward effort is a bare board. Every meaning of "open" converges on vacancy. Intention and effect: the reader receives the poem's bleakest structural irony — that climbing changes the view but not the condition — one line before it is enacted in "And stopped."

10. "A former life had led to? I don't know," (13) — mid-line interrogative; tense shift; refused full stop. The question mark falls inside the line, mid-stride, second of the sestet's two syntactic stumbles — and what follows is the poem's only present-tense main verb. Everything else is narrated from afterwards; "I don't know" is spoken now, the single thing the writing self will assert in its own moment, and it is a disclaimer. The causality of the question deserves pressure: the life "had led to" the crime — living itself as the road to the offence, guilt accumulated by trajectory rather than act. And the admission is not even granted a full stop: a comma, and the sentence leans into "Except" — ignorance immediately qualified, the poem's entire self-knowledge suspended from a confession of not-knowing. Intention and effect: the reader experiences the collapse of the poem's one metaphysical structure in real time, and is handed the question the speaker drops.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist. The lens under which the poem gives most, because its deepest ironies are structural: the couplet that never arrives after an octave that promised one; the sestet whose second tercet comes back out of order (EGF); the pentameter that ticks undisturbed through "And stopped."; the all-full rhymes polishing the surface of a breakdown; the seven-line sentence enjambing across the form's main seam at "attack / Of restlessness". Formalism sees the poem's true drama — a mind keeping perfect table manners while getting lost — enacted in verse-machinery rather than stated. What it flattens: the "I". Formalism can describe the hedges of line 14 as devices but has nothing to say about why a person hedges; it also brackets the karmic material, which is doing real work, as mere "content".

Psychoanalytic. Makes visible that the poem is a study in projection and displacement: the speaker deposits his own interior into a creature ("seemed quite satisfied", "looked uncertain") and then is ambushed by it — "Except I thought I recognised myself" is a textbook return of the repressed, the disowned self met as an other, and uncanny precisely because half-familiar ("recognised"). The choice of host matters: vermin, the culturally abject, the thing flinched from — self-disgust selects the one creature the self can safely despise, and the recognition therefore carries a charge of shame no neutral animal could deliver. What it flattens: the comedy, which it must read as defence; and the poem's epistemological scruple, which it converts into symptom — "I don't know" becomes resistance rather than honesty, and the reading starts diagnosing the patient instead of the poem.

Ecocritical. Makes visible what every other reading uses without noticing: the actual insect. What the speaker pathologises as "restlessness" is ordinary cockroach behaviour — exploration, grooming, edge-following; the disorder exists in the watching mind, not the watched body, and the poem half-knows it ("As if"). Ecocriticism catches the anthropomorphic machinery in the act — "he" from line 3, human verbs throughout — and names the poem's method for what it is: a colonisation of animal life by human meaning, in which the creature is never itself, only a mirror. Yet the lens also credits the poem's countercurrent: "giant" grants scale, "he" grants person-hood, and the final line levels the hierarchy — the human does not stoop to the insect but finds himself already there. What it flattens: the poem's actual interest, which is unashamedly the human; an ecocritical reading done stubbornly ends up reviewing the poem for a moral failure it openly performs and confesses.

Marxist / materialist. Makes visible the material preconditions nobody in the poem mentions: a man with time to watch an insect at length is a man released from labour — the vigil presupposes leisure, or unemployment, or expatriate vacancy, and the shabby interior ("dust", "rusty") is a material environment being read as a metaphysical one. Sharpest of all, the lens notices that when the speaker reaches for cosmic justice he can only imagine it as an economy — "due payment", a debt falling due — and that the roach "jogs", the leisure-exercise verb of the comfortable classes pasted onto subsistence movement. Even this poem's transcendence is denominated in money. What it flattens: the interiority; a strictly materialist account has to treat the epistemic drama — "seemed", "I don't know", "thought" — as superstructure, and so misses that the poem's subject is consciousness, whatever its economic base.

Reader-response. Makes visible that the poem's ending is completed in the reader or not at all. "I don't know" hands the metaphysical question across the page; the four hedges of line 14 leave a gap exactly reader-shaped — the poem never says and so are you, but the definite-article title's fable-promise, the universalising sonnet form and the pointed smallness of the occasion all pressure the reader into extending "myself" to themselves. The reader's own flinch at cockroaches is the poem's imported energy: revulsion converting to recognition happens in us, unstated. What it flattens: the historical and biographical specificity of the one speaker the poem actually has; and it licenses precisely the inflation ("this is all of us, the human condition") that the poem's deadpan holds at arm's length.

Postcolonial / historicist. Makes visible the direction of borrowing: a Western observer, reportedly in Buddhist Southeast Asia, reaches for karmic categories — "due payment", "A former life" — as a passing hypothesis for a private malaise, tries the doctrine on and shrugs it off within two lines ("I don't know"). The lens asks who gets to use whose metaphysics as metaphor, and notices that the poem's single room, with no street, no city, no named country, is legible as the expatriate's insulated bubble — the "outside" world present only as a system of ideas to be sampled. In the Cambodian frame, "some vicious crime" and undischarged guilt acquire a historical shadow. But the caveat is structural: the poem names none of this. No place, no religion, no history appears in the text; the entire postcolonial reading rides on thinly documented paratext, and it must be presented as context brought to the poem, not found in it. What it flattens: the possibility that the karmic question is doing exactly what it appears to do — expressing, in borrowed but seriously entertained terms, a guilt that has no local address.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The existential allegory (the standard reading). The roach's trajectory — purpose, restlessness, arrest — maps human aimlessness; the poem universalises through smallness. Evidence: the geometry's collapse (path → rings → stop); "uncertain where to go"; the fable-promising title. Weakness: it flattens the hedges — the poem says "myself", once, four qualifications deep, and never "ourselves"; read as universal statement it becomes the grand, solemn poem its deadpan was built to avoid.
  2. The clinical reading. The poem describes a psychological condition — anxiety or depression — in deliberate medical language: pacing, agitation ("a mild attack"), chronicity ("worsened over time"), psychomotor arrest ("And stopped."), anhedonia at the summit. Evidence: the sustained prognosis lexis; the double time-scale of line 9; the vigil itself as symptom. Weakness: the whole diagnosis sits inside "As if" — a simile, flagged as the watcher's invention; and the karmic question belongs to a different explanatory world the clinical frame cannot absorb.
  3. The karmic confession. The metaphysics is meant: the speaker half-believes his condition is "due payment", and line 14 answers line 12 — the "former life" is his own past, the recognition an admission of guilt. Evidence: "due payment", "vicious crime", the reversed causality of "had led to"; "I don't know" (not no); "Except" grammatically rescuing one certainty from the ignorance. Weakness: the tone will not hold still — "due payment" is bookkeeping comedy as much as doctrine; and the poem's only stated belief is unbelief ("I don't know").
  4. The mock-heroic comedy. The poem is a sustained joke: the grandest lyric form handed to vermin, "giant" inflation, the bathos of "a mild attack / Of restlessness", a punchline curtain-line. Evidence: the engineered anticlimax of the 8–9 enjambment; "jog"; the deadpan timing of 14. Weakness: it cannot account for the poem's residue — why "worsened over time" and "And stopped." are not funny, and why the last line, if a punchline, fails to release its tension rather than doubling it.
  5. The life-course allegory. The poem compresses a biography: the given track of youth ("trace / A path" between fixed limits), the crooked circling of the middle years, the climb, the summit that turns out bare, the arrest. Evidence: the sequenced time-markers ("At first", "soon", "over time", "After a while") — a lifetime's connectives spent in minutes; "climbed" as aspiration. Weakness: point-for-point mapping is mechanical and unfalsifiable (what is the dust? the table leg?); the poem offers a trajectory-shape, not a key, and readings that allegorise every noun end up writing their own poem.
  6. The meta-poem. The true subject is interpretation itself: a mind watching itself plant meaning in a neutral creature, with "trace" as the writer's own line-making and the sonnet failing to conclude as the essay-of-the-self fails to conclude. Evidence: the epistemic verb-chain ("watched, seemed, As if, looked, don't know, thought, recognised"); the dropped hedge at line 11; the confession that recognition, not observation, was the vigil's product. Weakness: nothing in the lexis names writing or reading; pushed hard, the reading turns a poem of felt unease into a seminar on epistemology — precisely the coldness the deadpan voice never has.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

1

”I watched a giant cockroach start to pace,”

Analysis
  • Line opens with first person pronoun “I”
  • Immediate and direct, places the speaker in the moment, lack of distancing suggests a connection between the cockroach and the speaker.
  • The speaker watched [watching] the cockroach implies sustained and deliberate attention rather than glancing, inviting the reader to question why the speaker chooses to watch a cockroach.
  • The intentionalness of this could hint towards the speaker’s boredom, drawing him towards a conventionally unattractive creature, showcasing the pointlessness of his life.
  • Hyperbolisation of the cockroach being giant captures the reader's attention, its size grants it a presence and allows it to be the centre of attention in a poem discussing its actions.
  • Otherwise, the hyperbolisation suggests the speaker’s unreliability, suggesting an unstable period of time.
  • Beginning to pace, the poet hints towards the cockroach's anxious restlessness, hinting towards its inevitable restlessness.
  • Subtly anthropomorphic as pacing is inherently a human quality, drawing a connection between humans and the insect.
2

”Skirting a ball of dust that rode the floor.”

Analysis
  • Diction in skirting suggests agility and movement, almost in a lively manner. Continuation from previous line + enjambment suggests how the cockroach’s movement cannot be contained.
  • Skirting also connotes avoidance, possibly of tasks till it snowballs at the end of the poem where the speaker is forced to confront what they avoid.
  • Personification of dust riding the floor as if it is drifting like it’s alive. As the dust moves, it suggests purpose as if it has a place to be, giving it a direction the cockroach doesn’t possess.
  • The dust cumulates on the floor, suggesting the unkempt state of the room, contrasting the even and tidy form of a sonnet.
  • Neglected room establishes atmosphere and the speaker’s inner state
3 / 4

”At first he seemed quite satisfied to trace” / A path between the wainscot and the door,

Analysis
  • Temporal: At first, introduces a narrative progression of the cockroach's journey.
  • The cockroach begins with a purpose, a defined path between two fixed points. As the poem progresses, the purpose deteriorates, the temporal verb indicates the baseline of where the cockroach begins.
  • The verb seemed introduces an uncertainty of the speaker not being able to identify the cockroach’s internal state, both reflecting his own uncertainty and permits the reader to recognise that a person will likely not fully understand another’s thoughts.
  • Introduces doubt from the start, the satisfaction may not be real, only apparent.
  • Tracing feels mechanical, as if the cockroach has a path designated to it from the beginning, paralleling the idea of humans having a set purpose by their peers or parents, further undermining the satisfaction the cockroach experiences. It also indicates the mindless motions the cockroach experiences rather than living.
  • At first, the cockroach has a defined path between the wainscot and the door, suggesting defined limits, representing the safe parameters of early adulthood as people chase goals they’ve set.
  • The intentions of the cockroach is evident, contrasting the restlessness and uncertainty further on
  • Wainscot: A usually paneled wooden lining of an interior wall
5 / 6

”But soon he turned to jog in crooked rings,” / Circling the rusty table leg and back,

Analysis
  • But indicates a flaw or a hiccup in a journey, suggesting a change between the previous certainty and the restlessness creeping into the cockroach’s motions.
  • Diction of crooked indicates a lapse in judgement and wobbliness, as if the cockroach is uncertain of which path to continue upon. The path is no longer laid out right in front of him, paralleling the experience of adults as they struggle to grasp the complexities of life.
  • Rings connote a circular path, indicating purposeless movement. The straight line satisfaction in early life dissolves into aimless circling, paralleling a midlife crisis.
  • Circling a table leg suggests how the cockroach is wound about a point rather than travelling in large circles to expand its knowledge. He refuses to leave a spot where safety is guaranteed, illustrating his own entrapment with no progress.
  • Circularness of the path seems to mimic a spiral, hinting towards the mental degradation of the speaker.
  • The rusty table leg implies the world the cockroach inhabits is degraded and neglected, also underlining the passing of time.
7

”And flipping right over to scratch his wings —“

Analysis
  • The physical action of the cockroach rolling onto its back suggests a momentary loss of control and vulnerability, paralleling a human’s willingness to sacrifice for momentary pleasure.
  • On the contrary, the cockroach flipping indicates a total loss of footing and ending up on its back captures his directionless journey.
  • Loss of composure seems undignified with em dash suspending the moment before explanation arrives.
  • Rhythm mirrors stumbles as Halligan inserts a trochee (right o-ver) that breaks the iambic pattern, allowing the line to lurch forward and mimic the action of the cockroach.
  • Dash permits pause before interpretation in the following line.
8 / 9

”As if the victim of a mild attack” / Of restlessness that worsened over time.

Analysis
  • Simile comparing the cockroach to a victim of its own behaviour. He’s passive rather than an active agent of harm and suffering beyond something beyond its control.
  • The cockroach falls prey into life’s pointless wander, unable to comprehend and therefore panicking till restlessness makes it worse.
  • Halligan captures the psychological impact of aimless wandering, suggesting a person’s panic from a lack of work done escalates from their urge to complete a task and reach a goal.
  • Use of victim suggests the cockroach is not choosing to behave erratically but rather suffering. This hints towards the speaker’s own emotions, being involuntarily consumed by existential crisis.
  • Enjambment from line 8 continues the idea, running over the stanza boundary between octave and sestet while ignoring the traditional volta, disrupting the rigid structure of a sonnet.
  • His condition worsened over time, a clinical and ordered interpretation towards a disorderly state. This implies restlessness is a condition deteriorating the cockroach where the passage of time exacerbates rather than heals.
10 / 11

”After a while, he climbed an open shelf” / And stopped. he looked uncertain where to go

Analysis
  • After a while indicates the passing of time and the cockroach aging
  • Cockroach has achieved something, reaching the metaphorical peak (top of the shelf) where the achievement brings not satisfaction but bewilderment.
  • Full stop indicates finality of previous movement, almost anticlimactic in the sense that the cockroach is still uncertain
  • The open shelf suggests possibility and exposure simultaneously where the cockroach decides his own path and there are no walls to guide him. Him and the speaker are confronted with freedom and find it paralysing.
  • The caesura after stopped pauses the reader and allows the reader to feel the silence, similar to the lack of direction the speaker feels. It formally enacts the epiphany of emptiness.
12 / 13

”Was this due payment for some vicious crime” / A former life had led to? I don’t know,

Analysis
  • Alludes to karma + reincarnation where the speaker ponders upon philosophical questions reaching beyond the cockroach. The speaker grasps at unrealistic strings to explain his confusion, implying the total degradation of his mentality.
  • Vicious crime introduces guilt where the speaker wonders if their own purposelessness is a punishment where all other answers have run dry, leading to self blame.
  • The answer of I don’t know brings the poem out of detached observation and serves as a direct link between the cockroach and the speaker.
  • The flat, simple and immediate answer suggests the speaker has been pondering for an extended period of time and reached the same conclusion and how the grand question deserves no grand answer. The speaker refuses to pretend to certainty he doesn’t possess.
14

”Except I thought I recognised myself.”

Analysis
  • The volta is situated at the end of the poem where the speaker realises he is the cockroach and the allegory completes itself. Despite his newfound self awareness, the speaker remains cautious and uncertain with thought rather than knew.
  • The final line is the poem’s entire point where the speaker recognises his own restless and aimless journey, realising his life trajectory took the same directionless path as a cockroach. The reader is invited to extend this further as a part of their lives. The poem universalises this concept through a cockroach, diminishing the reader’s ego.
  • The word recognised implies the speaker affirming a suspicion or like the self was meant to be found there.
  • The final line transforms the detached observation of the speaker into a confession of his own aimlessness ending with honesty rather than resolution.
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With "Love Armed" (Aphra Behn). Link: both poems give an inner state a body and watch it act — Behn enthrones desire as an armed tyrant, Halligan lodges restlessness in a roach — and both use immaculate formal poise to contain disorderly feeling. Shared technique: emblem-making (title as label for a staged figure) and the vocabulary of victimhood — each speaker casts himself as the injured party of his own emotion. Difference: Behn's harm has agents and a politics — the beloved's eyes arm the god, and the speaker's griefs are conscripted — so blame flows outward; Halligan's harm has no perpetrator at all, and the poem ends by suspecting the victim.

With "A Different History" (Sujata Bhatt). Link: both reach for South and Southeast Asian religious frames — transmigrating gods and sacred books in Bhatt, karmic debt and rebirth in Halligan — and both end without settling the questions those frames raise. Shared technique: the structural question — each poem's climax is interrogative, and the refusal to answer is the meaning. Difference: Bhatt's karma is collective and historical, asking how a people's tongue comes to love the conqueror's language; Halligan's is rigorously private, one man's afternoon — her unanswered question indicts history, his indicts (perhaps) himself.

With "The Chimney Sweeper" (Blake). Link: a small blackened creature moving through domestic architecture becomes legible as a condition its own perspective cannot name — the sweep inside the chimneys and coffin-dream, the roach on its wainscot track — and both poems run on the gap between what the figure knows and what the reader sees. Shared technique: dramatic irony from a limited viewpoint, plus confinement imagery doing symbolic work. Difference: Blake's irony indicts institutions — Church, parents, the trade in children — and demands the reader's outrage; Halligan's irony has no culprit to indict but the self, and asks for nothing louder than a wince.

With "Where I Come From" (Elizabeth Brewster). Link: both poems read interiors as minds — Brewster's claim that people are composed of their places, Halligan's dusty, rusting room externalising its watcher's state before he admits to having one. Shared technique: the inventory of particulars (her smells and door-yards; his dust-ball, wainscot, table leg, shelf) trusted to do the psychological work unstated. Difference: Brewster affirms formation — place composes a self that can be traced home; Halligan's room is placeless and anonymous, and the self it discloses arrives only as a hedged glimpse: her poem believes in origins, his doubts even recognition.

With "Report to Wordsworth" (Boey Kim Cheng). Link: the set's two subverted sonnets — Boey files an environmental elegy through the machinery of the Romantic sonnet of address; Halligan hands the love-lyric's form to vermin — both turning an inherited structure against its own tradition of consolation. Shared technique: sonnet subversion with a suppressed turn — in both, the sestet deepens rather than resolves the octave's trouble, and the close is diminuendo, not couplet-confidence. Difference: Boey's poem is public and apostrophic, petitioning a dead poet about a dying planet; Halligan's has no addressee at all — the largest possible audience versus a man talking himself into one admission.

With "Lament" (Gillian Clarke). Link: animals bearing human meaning — but pointed in opposite directions: Clarke's oil-choked, war-ruined creatures are real casualties of human action, mourned outward in a litany; Halligan's roach is perfectly fine — the suffering is projected onto it by the only casualty in the room. Shared technique: creaturely imagery carried by ritual registers — Clarke's elegiac dedications, Halligan's karmic audit of payment and crime. Difference: in "Lament" the grief is certain and the guilt collective; in "The Cockroach" both are hedged and private — Clarke writes the animal as victim of us, Halligan the animal as mirror of me, and the ethical weather of the two poems differs accordingly: mourning versus misgiving.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Gillian Clarke (b. 1937)

Clarke was born in Cardiff and is one of Wales's best-known poets: she edited The Anglo-Welsh Review, co-founded the Tŷ Newydd writers' centre, and was National Poet of Wales from 2008 to 2016. Her poetry is rooted in landscape, the natural world and Welsh history, and she has translated the early Welsh war-elegy Y Gododdin. 'Lament' was written in response to the 1991 Gulf War and collected in her Collected Poems (1997).

The Gulf War (1990–91)

Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A US-led coalition began bombing on 17 January 1991; a ground offensive followed on 24 February, and a ceasefire on 28 February. From late January, Iraqi forces released millions of barrels of crude oil into the Gulf — estimates run from about 4 to 11 million — in the largest oil spill of its kind, and as they retreated they set more than 600 of Kuwait's oil wells on fire. The fires burned until November 1991; the smoke made it, in Carl Sagan's words, 'pitch black at noon'. Tens of thousands of seabirds died, cormorants and grebes above all, and turtles, dugongs and dolphins were caught in the slick.

Clarke's own notes on the poem say that 'All the details in the poem came from reports in the media': newspaper photographs of oiled cormorants, a photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed, radio interviews with the mothers of young soldiers. The poem itself names no country, army or leader — only one human, Ahmed.

The Lament and the Litany

A lament — in Clarke's words 'an elegy, an expression of grief', and also 'a sad, military tune played on a bugle' — is one of the oldest forms of poetry: a song of grief for the dead or for something lost — from the biblical Lamentations to the early Welsh laments for fallen warriors and burned halls. Clarke's poem is also built like a litany, the church prayer of intercession in which each petition begins the same way: For…. It prays for everything lost, without ranking it — turtle, soldier, refugee and language mourned in the same breath.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Lament
Language & devices

Genre label: Lament — a song or poem of mourning, one of poetry's oldest forms. The word is both noun and verb: a lament, and the act of lamenting aloud. It can also mean a military tune played at funerals.

Meaning & effect

The single word announces mourning, not protest or report: the poem will grieve rather than argue. A lament is public and ritual — grief performed for a community — which suits a poem that mourns everything a war destroyed, human and non-human alike.

Lines 1–3
For the green turtle with her pulsing burden, / in search of the breeding ground. / For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness.
Language & devices

Anaphora: For… begins the litany. Metaphor: pulsing burden — the living eggs she carries, with a heartbeat. Paradox: nest of sickness — a place of safety made lethal. Sibilance: nest of sickness hisses.

Meaning & effect

The poem begins with birth: a turtle seeking the beach where she was born, to lay her eggs. Instinct leads her to poisoned sand, so the future is contaminated at its source. Opening with new life rather than death makes the war's damage reach forward into generations not yet born.

Lines 4–6
For the cormorant in his funeral silk, / the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.
Language & devices

Metaphor: in his funeral silk — oil-black, glossy feathers as mourning clothes. Imagery: the veil of iridescence — the rainbow sheen of oil, a mourning veil. Tricolon: bird, sand, sea.

Meaning & effect

The cormorant is dressed for his own funeral. The images are beautiful because oil really does shine — and that beauty is the horror: we are made to admire the thing that kills. The damage spreads outward, from one bird to the beach to the shadow on the sea.

Line 7
For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain.
Language & devices

Pun: lap — waves lapping the shore, and a mother's lap. Ambiguity: mortal stain — deadly, and close in sound to "mortal sin": a moral stain.

Meaning & effect

The sea, imagined as a lap that cradles life, now carries a fatal stain. The phrase quietly assigns guilt: this is not only pollution but sin, a mark on human conscience. The tercet ends by moving from creatures to the ocean itself.

Line 8
For Ahmed at the closed border.
Language & devices

Proper noun: Ahmed — the only named person in the poem, an ordinary Arabic name. Plain statement: no image, no adjective — at the closed border.

Meaning & effect

A civilian refugee, trapped, given one bare line. Naming him makes him a person rather than a statistic, but he stands for the thousands displaced. The plainness after the rich bird imagery is shocking: there is nothing beautiful to say.

Line 9
For the soldier in his uniform of fire.
Language & devices

Metaphor: in his uniform of fire — the soldier burning. Motif: clothing again — after the cormorant's funeral silk, another creature dressed for death. Anonymity: no side, no nation.

Meaning & effect

A uniform should identify and protect; this one consumes its wearer (Clarke took the image from a photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed). Because the poem does not say which army he belonged to, he could be any soldier — the lament refuses to take sides. The stanza's three lines move from the poisoned sea to a refugee to a burning man: every kind of victim in one tercet.

Lines 10–12
For the gunsmith and the armourer, / the boy fusilier who joined for the company, / the farmer's sons, in it for the music.
Language & devices

Listing: weapon-makers, then soldiers. Pun: joined for the company — companionship, and a military company. Colloquial idiom: in it for the music. Grammar: joined is the poem's only finite verb.

Meaning & effect

Even the gunsmith and the armourer — makers of weapons — are mourned. The young soldiers joined for friendship and the band, not for war: ordinary, innocent motives that led to death. Clarke took these phrases from radio interviews with the soldiers' mothers, so they are real voices of grief. Almost nothing in the poem acts: it is a list of losses with no agents.

Lines 13–15
For the hook-beaked turtles, / the dugong and the dolphin, / the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder.
Language & devices

Listing: the hook-beaked turtles (hawksbills), the dugong and the dolphin. Alliteration: dugong… dolphin. Metaphor: the missile's thunder — man-made thunder. Idiom: struck dumb.

Meaning & effect

The creatures of the sea are counted in, down to the rare dugong. The whale — a creature that lives by sound and song — is silenced by the noise of weapons. Human war drowns out nature's voice; struck dumb also anticipates the poem's final loss, of language.

Lines 16–18
For the tern, the gull and the restless wader, / the long migrations and the slow dying, / the veiled sun and the stink of anger.
Language & devices

Listing of birds: the tern, the gull and the restless wader. Parallelism and Antithesis: the long migrations and the slow dying. Echo: the veiled sun recalls the veil of oil. Synaesthesia: the stink of anger.

Meaning & effect

Birds that cross the world end their journeys in a slow death. The smoke veils the sun, and the smell of burning oil becomes the stink of anger — the war's emotion turned into pollution you can smell. The long vowels slow the stanza to the pace of dying.

Lines 19–21
For the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well. / For vengeance, and the ashes of language.
Language & devices

Apocalyptic imagery: the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well — earth, sky, water and fire all destroyed. Diction: scalded — a word for burnt skin, applied to the sea. Abstract nouns: vengeance, the ashes of language.

Meaning & effect

The poem widens to the elements themselves — creation undone, the sun put out (the smoke really did darken the day). Then the last line names the cause, vengeance, and the final casualty: language, burnt to ash by propaganda and by the silence of the dead. Clarke's own gloss: 'The ashes of language are the death of truth during war.' Ending on language, the poet's own material, also admits that even this lament cannot say enough.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Lament' is usually described as a sad catalogue: a list of the Gulf War's victims, human and animal, delivered with mounting grief. That description is accurate about the contents and wrong about the poem, because it misses what the poem withholds. The argument here: 'Lament' is built on a double refusal — it refuses to assert, and it refuses to accuse — and its power comes from performing, in grammar and ceremony, the only kind of speech it believes survives a war: naming without saying.
