The poem does not describe the death of honest language; it writes as if from inside it, and the form is the demonstration.

Start with what reading the poem actually feels like, line 1 to line 21. The title gives a genre-noun and stops. Then "For the green turtle" — and the ear understands at once that the title has not ended: Lament for. Every subsequent sentence re-attaches to that governing word, which means the reader is made to re-say "Lament" silently eleven times — the poem conscripts its reader into performing the rite, not observing it. This is the first sense in which the anaphora is the poem: it is not emphasis, it is liturgy, the structure of a litany of intercession — "For the sick… for the dying…" — in which a congregation offers up names. And a litany implies a hearer. The poem never names one. Prayers are said, in perfect order, into what may be an empty sky: that suspension — rite intact, addressee gone — is the poem's religious temperature, and one measure of what the war has burnt.

The sequence of the named is exact and means something. Two stanzas of sea-life first — turtle, eggs, cormorant, sand, sea — so that when the humans arrive in stanza 3 they arrive into a world already dying, not the other way round. Human suffering is not the context for environmental damage; environmental damage is the context for human suffering. Stanza 3 sets ocean, refugee and soldier as three grammatically identical, one-line, full-stopped sentences — the poem's strongest formal statement of its flattest claim: there is no hierarchy of grief here, a sea and a man take the same syntax. Ahmed, the only named being in the poem, stands at its threshold moment: the first human is not a combatant but a man stopped at a line someone drew. Then stanza 4, the poem's centre, does the hardest thing in it: it mourns the war's makers — gunsmith, armourer, fusilier, farmer's sons — in the same breath as its victims, because by the poem's logic they are its victims. After that the circle widens back out through species (stanza 5), flyways and atmosphere (stanza 6), to the elements themselves (stanza 7): earth, light, water, fire — creation's inventory, each item cancelled — and last of all the medium in which inventories are made: language.

Now the obvious objection, which any strong reading must meet head-on: a poem that ends by declaring language ash is self-refuting. Here is a poem — shapely, eloquent, anthologised, taught — whose final claim its own existence appears to disprove. If language were really ashes, 'Lament' could not have been written. The objection dissolves once you look at which language the poem has renounced. Go through all twenty-one lines looking for a statement — a main clause, something asserted of something — and you will not find one. The poem is eleven sentences with no predication in them: it never says the war is wrong, never says the turtle died, never says who set the fires. It has given up the assertive functions of language — the functions that reportage, propaganda, communiqués and euphemism share, the grammar in which a bombardment can be called a "surgical strike" — because in war those functions are the first corrupted. Clarke's own gloss is exact: "the ashes of language are the death of truth during war." What survives the fire is smaller and older: the capacity to name, and to set a name inside the dative of care — for. The poem is not self-refuting; it is self-exemplifying. It ends by mourning the language of saying in the only language left, the language of dedication.

The same withholding governs agency, and this is where the poem is most contestable. Its single finite verb is "joined"; its single agent is a boy; every act of destruction arrives as an agentless participle — laid, closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded. Nobody in 'Lament' does anything except enlist. One reading calls this the poem's deepest evenhandedness: grief refuses to become prosecution; at a funeral you do not read out the charge sheet. The other reading calls it evasion: the Gulf oil spill was not weather — it was a deliberate act, ordered by identifiable men, and a poem that mourns "the blazing well" without an arsonist converts a war crime into something like climate, to be grieved rather than judged. The defence, and it is a strong one, is that the poem does name the motive even as it withholds the men: "For vengeance". The last line files the accusation in the only grammar the poem allows itself — vengeance is not said to have caused anything (no clause could say so); it is simply set on the list, mourned-and-indicted in one word, the human faculty whose exercise fills the previous twenty lines. The charge is there; it has been folded into the rite.

And the rite itself is the answer to the poem's other great pressure: scale. A war's damage is uncountable, and the poem knows it — you can watch it running out of room, two griefs per stanza at the start, seven crammed into stanza 6, the singulars giving way to plurals — and a lesser poem would have answered scale with excess: piled adjectives, raised voice. Clarke answers it with ceremony and with terrible smallness of speech: "who joined for the company", "in it for the music" — the recruits' own idiom, or their mothers', lifted from radio interviews and left unimproved. The poem's tonal control is nowhere more severe: it will not translate a mother's flat phrase into poetry, because the flatness is the truth of it, and any eloquence added would be the first step back towards the language that ends in ashes. This is why calling the poem "sad" misses it. Sadness is an emotion the poem induces; the poem itself is doing something harder — holding grief, accusation, and a working ritual in a single unbroken posture, twenty-one lines at attention.

So the movement first line to last is best described not as a list but as a widening and a turning-inward at once: the circle of the mourned expands from one turtle to the four elements, while the poem's attention closes in on its own medium, until the two arrive together at the final line — the largest circle (everything, even abstraction) and the innermost point (the words this is written in). "For vengeance, and the ashes of language." — with the poem's one comma-before-"and", the drawn breath before the last name at a memorial, and then the full stop the owner's notes read exactly rightly: "no more words to be said proceeding last line". The lament ends because its medium has joined its subjects. What remains standing is the shape of the rite itself — seven equal stanzas, eleven dedications, order held all the way down — which is the poem's real, unstated claim: when truth has burnt, form is how grief keeps faith.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

The site has no other form section for this poem; this one is self-contained.

The governing grammar: a title with no sentence attached

The title is not a label but the poem's grammatical head. Every stanza — and in fact every sentence — completes the phrase "Lament / For…": Lament for the green turtle. Lament for Ahmed. Lament for vengeance. This is the oldest naming convention of the genre ("Lament for the Makaris", the Welsh marwnad or death-song tradition Clarke inherits, Lorca's Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías), broken open: Clarke snaps the conventional title after its first word so that the poem's whole body becomes the title's unfinished second half. Twenty-one lines try to complete the phrase "Lament for—" and none of them closes it.

The consequence is stark and almost never noticed: the poem contains no main clause. It is eleven sentences long, and every sentence is a prepositional phrase — a dedication, not a statement. Count the full stops: eleven (after lines 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15, 18, 20, 21), and each of the eleven sentences they close begins with "For". Nothing in the poem is asserted; nothing is predicated of anything. The poem cannot say "war destroys" or "grief is unbearable", because saying — assertion, the grammar of reportage and propaganda alike — is precisely what the last line declares burnt. What survives of language is the dative gesture: pointing grief at its objects, one by one.

Within this clause-less grammar there is exactly one finite verb: "the boy fusilier who joined for the company" (line 11). Every other verb-form is a participle with its agent deleted — laid, closed, struck, veiled, burnt, put out, scalded: things done to the world by no named doer. No Saddam, no Bush, no army performs an action anywhere in the poem; even the missile appears only as a possessive ("the missile's thunder"). The single completed action in 'Lament', and the single grammatical agent, is a boy joining up in innocence. That is the poem's ethics compressed into syntax: agency belongs to the naive, damage arrives agentless — either a profound evenhandedness or a deliberate refusal to prosecute, and the tension between those two readings runs through the whole analysis below.

The anaphora, mapped exactly

Eleven of the twenty-one lines begin "For" — Clarke's own count. The distribution is not even, and the unevenness is the argument:

StanzaLinesLines beginning "For"Pattern
11–31, 3two of three
24–64opening line only
37–97, 8, 9all three
410–1210opening line only
513–1513opening line only
616–1816opening line only
719–2119, 21two of three — incl. the poem's last line

So the shape is 2 – 1 – 3 – 1 – 1 – 1 – 2. Three observations, each worth exam space:

  • Every stanza restarts from the title. Whatever else varies, each tercet's first word re-sounds "Lament for—", so the reader silently supplies the title eleven times. The anaphora is not "repetition for emphasis"; it is the mechanism by which a one-word title governs a twenty-one-line poem.
  • The density peaks at stanza 3 — the pivot from nature to people. Ocean, refugee, soldier: the only stanza in which every line begins "For" is also the only stanza in which every line ends with a full stop (the owner's notes spotted this and it is the best single observation in them). Three self-contained, walled sentences: For the ocean's lap with its mortal stain. For Ahmed at the closed border. For the soldier in his uniform of fire. The stanza about a closed border is built of closed lines — each victim sealed in a grammatical cell, unable to reach the next line. Form performs border.
  • The frame: stanzas 1 and 7 have the same sentence-architecture. Each is a two-line "For" sentence followed by a one-line "For" sentence (lines 1–2 + 3; lines 19–20 + 21). The poem ends with the syntactic shape it began with — ritual returning to its opening posture — except that the opening's one-line sentence held eggs in a nest, and the closing's holds vengeance and ash. And line 21 is the only final line of any stanza to begin "For": after six stanzas in which the formula launches grief and lower-case lines absorb it, the last word-of-dedication arrives where a stanza should be subsiding. The lament refuses to end anywhere but on its own first word.

Where the anaphora does not hold, the exceptions are pointed. Nine lines begin with "the" — continuations, each victim still definite, still known. One line in the poem begins with neither: "in search of the breeding ground." (line 2). The line about searching is the only line that escapes the formula — syntax slipping off-pattern exactly where the turtle slips off her map.

Finally, the two lowercase "for"s. "Joined for the company"; "in it for the music". The same word that consecrates each victim reappears, small, inside the small print of motive — for meaning "in exchange for", "for the sake of". The elegy's word of dedication and the recruit's word of transaction are one word. That collision detonates in the last line, where "For vengeance" can be read with either grammar — dedication or motive — and the poem needs both (see Cruxes).

Metre: scansion and what the substitutions do

Free verse, but with strong local shapes; lines run from 6 to 12 syllables, mostly carrying 3–5 stresses. Stressed syllables are marked in bold; the notation beneath is x (unstressed) / (stressed).

Line 1 — "For the green turtle with her pulsing burden," x x / / x x x / x / x — an anapaestic lift into a spondee ("green tur-"): the line rises to its subject, then falls through two trochees, "pulsing burden", a dying fall on a feminine ending. The rhythm enacts dedication then weight: lift the creature up, feel what she carries.

Line 2 — "in search of the breeding ground." x / x x / x / — the poem's shortest early line, three stresses, ending on a stressed monosyllable plus full stop. After line 1's swell, the clipped masculine close is the search hitting its wall.

Line 3 — "For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness." x x / / x x / x / x — the spondee "eggs laid": two adjacent stresses where the line's weight is set down, as the eggs are. Then the cadence sags to another feminine ending, "sickness" — the stanza's last sound is an unstressed syllable failing.

Line 8 — "For Ahmed at the closed border." x / x x x / / x — eight syllables, the shortest human line. The name takes the first stress; the spondee "closed bor-" shuts the line like the border it names; the full stop completes the confinement. One line for a life: the brevity is the point.

Line 11 — "the boy fusilier who joined for the company," x / x x / x / x x / x x — a loose, ambling four-stress line with a falling triple ending ("company") — conversational cadence, someone talking, not intoning. The poem's only finite verb, "joined", takes a mid-line stress and no more: the one completed act in the poem is metrically unremarkable, a boy's ordinary decision.

Line 12 — "the farmer's sons, in it for the music." x / x / x x x x / x — after the caesura, four unstressed syllables in a row ("in it for the") — the flattest run in the poem — before "music" lands. The throwaway idiom is scored as throwaway rhythm. This is scannable proof of the tonal control discussed under Cruxes: the metre refuses to mourn here so that the reader has to.

Line 15 — "the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder." x / / / x x / x / x — three consecutive stresses, "whale struck dumb": the heaviest cluster in the poem, a metrical detonation, followed by the trochaic fallout of "missile's thunder". The line does to the reader's voice what the shockwave does to the whale.

Line 17 — "the long migrations and the slow dying," x / x / x x x / / x — the stresses fall on the two adjectives of duration, and the spondee "slow dy-" drags against the line's momentum. Add the long vowels (long, migrations, slow, dying) and the line takes longer to say than its syllables suggest: quantity, not just stress, stretching time — dying made durational.

Line 19 — "For the burnt earth and the sun put out," x x / / x x / / / — five stresses in nine syllables, the densest line in the poem, ending on three hammered monosyllables. Apocalypse compresses the metre: no unstressed syllable survives the line's end.

Line 21 — "For vengeance, and the ashes of language." x / x x x / x x / x — after line 19's pile-up, only three stresses: the poem's dying fall. The mid-line comma-pause, then the long subsiding curve to a feminine ending. Five of the seven stanzas end on unstressed syllables (sickness, music, thunder, anger, language) — the dying fall is the poem's structural signature — and the two that end stressed are the elemental ones ("the sea.", "of fire.").

End-stopping: the owner's system, kept and sharpened

Every one of the 21 lines is end-stopped — ten with commas, eleven with full stops; there is not a single enjambment in the poem. The owner's notes build a genuinely good two-term system on this (their strongest sustained work in the file, rescued here): hard end-stops (full stops) as finality — each death sealed, each victim "treated as its own separate loss" rather than blurred into the next, the reader halted and made to pay before moving on; soft end-stops (commas) as accumulation — victims "joining hands" within a stanza, grief rolling forward, the listing effect that overwhelms; and the interplay as a "push and pull… continuous sorrow flowing interrupted by sharp, overwhelming pain", which is a better description of the rhythm of mourning than most published criticism manages. Two sharpenings: (1) the alternation is not decorative but distributed — stanza 3 all hard (the border), stanzas 5–6 comma-led (the crowding lists), and the final line hard, "no more words to be said" after language's ashes, as the owner puts it; (2) the absence of enjambment is itself the claim. Enjambment is syntax surviving the line-break — continuation, spill-over, life exceeding form. Clarke forbids it for twenty-one lines. Nothing here survives its line.

Stanza logic: the arch

The sequence is precise: sea creatures (S1–2) → the pivot stanza where ocean, refugee and soldier stand as equals (S3) → the combatants, at the exact centre (S4) → sea creatures again (S5) → birds and atmosphere (S6) → the elements and the abstractions (S7). The human matter is embedded — stanzas 3–4, walled in by the animal world on both sides — humanity surrounded by the nature it is burning. The poem's numerical centre, line 11 of 21, is the boy fusilier: the only finite verb, the only agent, at the exact midpoint. The turns, then, are two: at line 8, where the first human enters and is the only victim in the poem to bear a name; and at line 21, where the lament turns from the world to the word — from casualties of war to the casualty that is the capacity to speak of them. Between those turns the poem does not develop an argument; it widens a circle — individual, species, element, meaning — until nothing stands outside it.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The tolled vowel. Read aloud, the anaphora is a sound before it is a device: "For" is a long open back vowel, /ɔː/ — the same vowel as mourn, forlorn, and the keening "aw" of a cry — struck eleven times at the head of eleven sentences. The owner's notes call it "a soft drumbeat… the steady beat of a funeral march", which is right; add that unlike a drumbeat it is pitched — a held, singable note, the bugle's note in Clarke's own gloss of a lament as "a sad, military tune played on a bugle". The word tolls, and each toll opens a breath that the rest of the line spends.

Stanza 1: plosives fading into sibilance. The owner's notes catch something excellent here, worth rescuing verbatim in idea: the opening line beats with /p/ and /b/ — "pulsing burden", "breeding" — the bilabial plosives that are as close as consonants come to a heartbeat; then across the stanza sibilance rises through "pulsing" and "search" to saturate line 3, "her eggs laid in their nest of sickness". One reading hears the transition as "the dying heartbeat of a living being which slowly fades away" — plosive life hushed into sibilant sickness. That is a genuinely fine piece of close listening: the stanza's sound-plot is its narrative.

Stanza 2: the hiss laid over everything. "Silk… iridescence… sand… shadow… sea" — five sibilants in three lines, the densest sibilance in the poem. Two effects at once, and a strong answer holds both: the hiss of something spreading (oil moving where it was never invited), and a hush — the sound of quieting, a finger to the lips, as the slick smothers birdsong and wave-noise alike. The stanza about a "veil" is voiced as a whisper; the sea's soundscape is being turned down.

Stanza 5: consonants as ordnance. The guttural /k/ of "hook-beaked" and "struck", the drumming /d/ of "dugong and the dolphin… struck dumb" and the thudding short-u assonance of "struck dumb" build the stanza's percussion before "thunder" names it. The scansion's molossus ("whale struck dumb") lands inside this consonant-field: sound and stress detonate together, and the softest creatures in the poem — dugong, dolphin — carry the hardest consonants of it, as if the blast has entered their names.

Stanza 6: keening, then stench. "The long migrations and the slow dying" is built almost entirely of long vowels and diphthongs — the mouth cannot say it quickly; it is the poem's line of pure keening, sung grief. Then the register snaps: "the stink of anger" — short vowel, ugly /k/, a word from the gutter not the elegy. The collision is deliberate and readable: mourning's long vowels belong to lament, but what hangs in the air over the Gulf is not song, it is smell; the line lets the genre's music be interrupted by the war's actual atmosphere. (The synaesthesia — anger as a smell — is analysed under Quotations.)

The last line's diminuendo. After line 19's nine syllables carrying five stresses ("burnt earth… sun put out") and line 20's paired hard stresses ("scalded… blazing"), line 21 drops to three stresses spread over ten syllables, with the poem's final feminine ending: "of language." falling away to nothing. The poem does not end with a bang of grief but with sound itself subsiding — a decrescendo into the full stop, the acoustic equivalent of ash after fire.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Distinction, then the tracing: a motif recurs and accumulates; a symbol stands for something beyond itself. 'Lament' runs at least four motifs through its 21 lines — and behind all of them stands one governing symbol that the poem never names.

1. Fabric — silk, veil, uniform, shroud. The cloth motif enters at line 4 ("the cormorant in his funeral silk"), where oil is mourning-dress: the bird wears his own funeral. It spreads in line 5 to the land ("the veil of iridescence on the sand") — the veil, Victorian mourning-wear and bridal wear at once, laid over the beach. At line 9 it becomes human and lethal: the soldier's "uniform of fire" — the garment that should identify and protect him is the thing consuming him. And at line 18 the motif reaches the sky: "the veiled sun" — the same veil, now planetary, the oil-smoke drawing mourning-cloth across the one light everything lives by. Trace the scale: one bird's plumage → a beach → a man's body → the sun. The fabric motif measures the disaster's expansion, and it carries a constant irony: everything the war dresses, it dresses for a funeral.

2. Voice, sound and silence. The poem's second motif is acoustic, and it runs straight into the final line. The ocean has a voice — its "lap" (line 7), the smallest, most domestic water-sound. Music is a motive — the farmer's sons "in it for the music" (line 12), the regimental band, sound as war's false promise. Then sound becomes a weapon: "the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder" (line 15) — the ocean's great singer silenced, and note the theft: "thunder", nature's own noise, is now the missile's possession; the war borrows nature's vocabulary to destroy nature's voices. By line 18 even the senses are scrambled — anger arrives as a "stink", emotion displaced into the wrong sense, as if the normal channels of expression are already down. And at line 21 the motif completes: "the ashes of language". Song promised, song silenced, speech burnt: the poem tracks the war's assault on every register of utterance, and ends by adding itself to the casualty list.

3. Fire and its residue. Fire enters on a single body — the "uniform of fire" (line 9) — and then runs the scale of stanza 7: "burnt earth", the sun "put out" (fire extinguished — the counter-image), "scalded ocean", "blazing well" (lines 19–20). Watch the grammar of the motif: blazing is a present participle — ongoing, unfinished — while burnt and scalded are past participles, damage already done; the stanza holds both tenses of catastrophe at once, still-happening and irreversible. Then the last line delivers fire's aftermath-noun: "ashes" (line 21). The motif's trajectory is combustion → residue; the poem ends after the fire, in what fire leaves. Against it runs water — lap, ocean, sea — until the two elements collapse into each other in "scalded ocean": fire's verb performed on water, the final impossibility made literal by burning oil on the Gulf's surface.

4. Motherhood and birth. The poem opens inside a reproductive emergency: "her pulsing burden… the breeding ground… her eggs… nest" (lines 1–3) — an entire vocabulary of birth, every term poisoned by its context ("nest of sickness"). It recurs in "the ocean's lap" (line 7), the mother's lap made mortal; in "the boy… the farmer's sons" (lines 11–12), where every soldier is implicitly somebody's child — and Clarke's sources here were literally the mothers, interviewed on radio; and in "the long migrations" (line 17), the journeys creatures make in order to breed. The motif inverts the elegy's usual consolation: laments traditionally set death against continuing life; here the continuing — eggs, nests, sons, migrations — is precisely what is being killed. War is figured throughout not as combat but as an attack on generation itself.

The governing symbol: oil, never named. Every motif above is oil seen without its name: the silk is oil, the veil is oil, the iridescence, the shadow, the stain, the scald, the blaze, the smoke that veils the sun — one substance behind a dozen appearances, and the word "oil" appears nowhere in the poem. This absence is the poem's most elegant structural fact. Oil is simultaneously the war's cause (what the invasion was for), its weapon (spilled and set alight), and its shroud (coating bird, beach and sky) — and Clarke treats it the way the poem treats every perpetrator: present everywhere, named never. It is a symbol in the strict sense — it stands for the whole system of greed and consequence the poem indicts — and its namelessness enacts the indictment: some things are too much the medium of the disaster to be seen as objects in it. Secondary symbols work inside its field: the sun (life-source, creation's first light) "put out"; the border (the human world's insistence on division, upheld even as the poison ignores it); ashes (what remains when meaning has been through fire).

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

War as a war on nature

Animals take up most of the poem: turtle, cormorant, dugong, dolphin, whale, birds. Human and animal casualties share the same For, so the poem refuses any ranking of victims.

02

One for many

Each casualty stands for thousands — one turtle, one cormorant, one Ahmed, one soldier. Making the catastrophe individual makes it imaginable; statistics would make it abstract.

03

Ordinary people caught up in war

The soldiers are not heroes or villains but boys who joined for the company and farmers' sons in it for the music. Even the weapon-makers, the gunsmith and the armourer, are mourned. War consumes people who never chose its causes.

04

Beauty and horror

The images are often beautiful — funeral silk, the veil of iridescence — because the oil really does shine. The beauty makes the damage harder to look away from, and slightly sickening to admire.

05

The failure of words

The poem ends with the ashes of language: war corrupts language into propaganda, silences the dead, and leaves poetry struggling to say enough. The lament is both an act of mourning and a confession of its limits.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. "For vengeance, and the ashes of language." — what is "For" doing in its own last line?

The difficulty. For twenty lines "For" has meant one thing: this lament is offered for — the dative of dedication. But English "for" has a second grammar, the grammar of motive and exchange ("for the sake of", "in return for"), and the poem has already used it twice, lowercase: "joined for the company", "in it for the music". When line 21 opens "For vengeance", both grammars are live. Reading A (dedication): vengeance is the last item mourned — the human faculty itself a casualty, pitied like the turtle; war has even ruined our anger. Reading B (motive): the line flickers into explanation — for vengeance all this happened; vengeance is not mourned but blamed, the war's cause smuggled onto its casualty list. Evidence for A: strict parallelism — every previous "For" is dative, and ritual repetition trains the reader to hear the eleventh as the first ten. Evidence for B: the two lowercase "for"s have already taught the motive-grammar inside this very poem; and "vengeance" is unlike every other item — not a creature or thing that can suffer, but an agent's reason. What a strong answer does: refuses to pick. The whole tragedy of the line is that in war the language of tribute and the language of transaction are the same word — the poem's formula of consecration is forced, at the last moment, to hold the war's motive inside it. Grief and accusation collapse into one preposition, and then the second half of the line tells you why no cleaner sentence was available: the language you would need for it is ash. Note also the comma — "vengeance, and the ashes" — the poem's only comma-before-"and": either a solemn pause before the final name, or the hinge of consequence (vengeance — and [therefore] ashes). Both, again.

2. "who joined for the company, / the farmer's sons, in it for the music." — is the flatness callous, tender, or ironic?

The difficulty. These are the poem's dead (or doomed) young men, and the poem describes their deaths' meaning in the language of a hobby: in it for the music, the idiom you would use of someone joining a pub band. Careless readers go two wrong ways: sentimental (the poem weeps over innocent boys) or ironic-superior (the poem mocks their naivety — they died for a band). The evidence cuts against both. Against mockery: Clarke sourced these phrases from radio interviews with the soldiers' mothers — the register is borrowed bereavement-speech, the way the families themselves talked, and the metre keeps it conversational (see the scansion of lines 11–12: the flattest stress-runs in the poem). A poem does not sneer in its sources' own words. Against sentiment: the lines refuse every available upgrade — no "brave", no "tragic", no elegiac vocabulary at all; the poem will not translate the mothers' flatness into poetry. What a strong answer does: names the technique — free indirect register, the vernacular of the bereaved incorporated unimproved — and reads the restraint as the poem's ethics in miniature. Understatement is the only register the poem trusts not to lie; eloquence about these boys would be recruitment's language ("the music" — the band, the parade — was the eloquence that got them killed). Add the pun the line quietly detonates: "the company" is companionship and a military unit — he joined for company and was issued a Company; the two meanings of the word are the two halves of his story, promise and machine. The flat register is where Clarke's power sits: the poem trusts the reader to supply the grief it declines to perform.

3. "For Ahmed at the closed border." — does the name individuate or tokenise?

The difficulty. Ahmed is the poem's only named being — turtle, cormorant, soldier, sons are all types with definite articles — and he is named with one of the commonest male names in the Arabic-speaking world. Reading A: the name is the poem's single act of full human recognition — everyone else is "the X", but a refugee is a person, with the kind of name that implies a family, a history, a face; his one line is the poem's moment of maximal dignity. Reading B (the uncomfortable one): a single, generic Arabic name — the Western newsroom's everyman-Arab — risks re-performing the anonymisation it protests; "Ahmed" as a name is close to "the refugee" as a category, and the poem gives him no verb, no face, no fate. Evidence for A: the capitalised name visibly breaks the definite-article system (it is the only capitalised word inside lines apart from the "For"s); his placement at the first human moment makes the civilian, not the soldier, the war's representative man. Evidence for B: the name's very commonness; the single line; the sourcing of the whole poem from Western media, which is where Clarke would have met him. What a strong answer does: holds the doubleness as the point — the name is deliberately both singular and countless; Clarke needs one man you could greet and a name ten thousand men answer to, because metonymy is the poem's entire method (one turtle for a species, one Ahmed for a displacement). Then it reads the line's form: hemmed in by full-stopped lines in the poem's only all-hard-stopped stanza, "at" (not "crossing", not "turned back from") holding him in arrested motion — the grammar builds the border it mourns, and the reader is left, like Ahmed, unable to get past the line's end.

4. "the sun put out" — hyperbole, or reportage?

The difficulty. Extinguishing the sun is the oldest apocalyptic hyperbole in the book — and in Kuwait in 1991 it happened: the smoke of more than six hundred burning wells turned midday dark — 'pitch black at noon', in Carl Sagan's words. So is line 19 the poem's most extreme figure or its most literal fact? Reading A (cosmic): the poem has left reportage for eschatology — un-creation, "Let there be light" reversed; the domestic phrasal verb "put out" (a candle, a lamp, a light at bedtime) makes the end of the world horribly easy, one breath. Reading B (documentary): the line is the plainest in the poem — it is what the photographs showed; Clarke, who built every image from media reports, is at her most factual precisely where she sounds most excessive. Evidence for A: the company the phrase keeps — "burnt earth", "scalded ocean" — a stanza systematically working through the elements; the Genesis resonance of ending with light and (next line but one) the word. Evidence for B: the verifiable smoke-darkness; Clarke's stated method of taking "all the details… from reports in the media". What a strong answer does: sees that the undecidability is historical, not verbal — the Gulf War closed the gap between apocalyptic rhetoric and weather report, so the line is unfalsifiable in both directions at once. And then connects that collapse to the final line: when hyperbole becomes literal, figurative language has lost its function — one more thing the war burnt. "The ashes of language" begins here, two lines early: the poem's most extravagant image is also its least invented, and there is no way of speaking that can keep those apart any more.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Ten moments chosen because they repay pressure — the famous set-pieces ("funeral silk", "the ashes of language") are treated at length elsewhere in this document.

1. "her pulsing burden" (l.1) — transferred epithet; pun; proleptic irony. The pulse belongs to the eggs (or to her own urgent blood) but is transferred to the "burden", so that the load itself beats — life felt as freight. "Burden" then opens twice more: the thing carried, and the archaic-technical sense of the refrain of a song — and this is the first line of a poem built entirely on a refrain ("For…"). The turtle carries her burden as the poem carries its own: the lament and the animal are doing the same labouring, rhythmic work of bearing something living towards ground that may not receive it. Intention/effect: Clarke fuses maternity, weight and song in two words, so the reader's first image already contains the poem's method — grief carried in repeating form.

2. "in search of the breeding ground." (l.2) — definite article; formula-break; terminal full stop. Not a breeding ground: the — green turtles return to the beach of their own hatching, one ground, non-negotiable, written into the body. The definite article makes the search unfalsifiable and therefore hopeless: there is no substitute to find. This is also the only line in the poem beginning with neither "For" nor "the" — the syntax itself off the map, searching — and the full stop ends the sentence where the search cannot end. Intention/effect: instinct meets the man-made in a single article; the reader feels the trap close grammatically before understanding it biologically.

3. "the veil of iridescence on the sand" (l.5) — metaphor; aestheticised toxicity. Oil-film genuinely is iridescent — rainbowed, shimmering, objectively lovely — and Clarke refuses to pretend otherwise. "Veil" holds bride and widow in one garment (silk in the previous line has already set a ceremony going, and the stanza cannot decide which ceremony it is). The horror is precisely the beauty: destruction that photographs well, poison you could mistake for ornament — an exact analogue for the war's own presentation, all tracer-light and precision-footage. Intention/effect: the reader is made complicit in finding the image beautiful, then made to notice what the beauty is made of; unease, not pathos, is the designed response.

4. "the ocean's lap with its mortal stain." (l.7) — polysemy stacked three deep. "Lap": the wave's smallest sound; the mother's lap (the poem's maternal motif reaching the sea); and the drinking animal's lap — the ocean tonguing its own poison. "Mortal": deadly; subject to death (the immortal-seeming ocean revealed as killable); and shadowed by "moral" — a stain of guilt, sin-language ("mortal sin" stands one consonant away). "Stain" is the crucial noun: not a wound but a contamination — wounds heal, stains are permanent and, crucially, stains implicate whoever made them. Intention/effect: in nine words the sea becomes intimate, mortal and wronged, and the reader receives the guilt without any accuser being named.

5. "For Ahmed at the closed border." (l.8) — onomastics; prepositional arrest; participial deleted agent. The poem's only name (see Crux 3) — but press the small words too. "At" is the preposition of arrest: not crossing, not before, not turned back from — held at, durationless and permanent. "Closed" is a past participle with its agent deleted: someone closed it, no one is named — the poem's ethics of agentlessness at its most political, because a border, unlike a storm, always has a closer. Intention/effect: eight words perform bureaucratic finality; the reader waits with Ahmed in a line that cannot move, and the anger the line refuses to state accrues to the reader instead.

6. "the soldier in his uniform of fire." (l.9) — genitive metaphor; irony of issue. The "of" construction does the violence: a uniform made of fire, as uniforms are of wool or cotton — flame as standard issue, listed like kit. A uniform exists to identify, protect and make-uniform; this one destroys identity, consumes its wearer, and makes him uniform with every other burnt body — fire being the great equaliser of corpses. (Some printings have "with his"; the variant only redistributes the horror between wearing and carrying.) Intention/effect: Clarke converts the war's most unpublishable photograph into eight words that can be printed, and the reader's imagination is forced to develop the image the newspapers refused.

7. "who joined for the company," (l.11) — the poem's only finite verb; pun; borrowed register. All the grammar of agency in 'Lament' is concentrated here: one boy, one completed act, and the act is joining — affiliation, the least violent verb available. "The company" doubles: companionship (the loneliness of a boy who enlisted to belong) and the military unit that word becomes the moment he signs — the pun is the recruitment, the warm word turning into the cold one behind his back. The register is the family's own flat idiom, unimproved (see Crux 2). Intention/effect: the reader performs the double-take the boy could not — hearing, inside the friendly word, the machine that will spend him.

8. "the whale struck dumb by the missile's thunder." (l.15) — idiom literalised; appropriated lexicon; molossus. "Struck dumb" is dead metaphor for astonishment; Clarke reanimates it into physiology — blast and sonar genuinely deafen and disorient cetaceans, whose whole world is acoustic. The possessive is the theft: the missile's thunder — ordnance has annexed nature's own word for sublime noise, so even the vocabulary of the sky now belongs to weapons. Three consecutive stresses ("whale struck dumb") detonate mid-line. Intention/effect: the ocean's largest voice is silenced by the war's borrowed one — and the reader is being prepared, six lines early, for what the poem will say about language itself.

9. "the long migrations and the slow dying," (l.17) — parallel syntax; gerund; quantitative metre. Two matched adjective-noun pairs, joined by "and" as if equivalent — and that false equivalence is the grief: an epic of navigation (Arctic-to-Africa flyways, species-memory older than any border) balanced against its new terminus. "Dying" as a gerund-noun is the masterstroke: not deaths (events, countable, over) but dying — a state, ongoing, possessed ("the slow dying") like a territory the birds now inhabit. The long vowels stretch the line's duration to match its subject. Intention/effect: the reader's voice must slow and lengthen — the poem makes you take the time that dying takes.

10. "the veiled sun and the stink of anger." (l.18) — synaesthesia; unowned emotion; register-collision. Anger has no smell; burning crude does — the line fuses them so that the atmosphere over the Gulf becomes an emotion you breathe. Crucially the anger is unowned: not Saddam's, not the coalition's, not the poet's — a free-floating rage hanging in the air like the smoke, which is the poem's agentlessness performed by weather. And "stink" — the lowest register in the poem, gutter-plain against elegiac "veiled" — refuses to perfume it. Intention/effect: the reader is denied the clean scapegoat and given nausea instead of blame; war's moral atmosphere is made physical, disgusting, and general.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Ecocritical. The lens this poem was practically written for — but push past "Clarke cares about nature". What the lens makes visible is the poem's structural biocentrism: the syntax grants a sea and a man identical sentences ("For the ocean's lap… For Ahmed…"), the pronoun system grants animals personal pronouns ("her pulsing burden", "his funeral silk" — the refusal of "it"), and the running order makes human suffering an episode inside an ecological catastrophe rather than the reverse (two stanzas of sea-life before any human appears). The poem also refuses the charismatic-species reflex: a cormorant (a bird fishermen hate), a dugong, a wader — the unloved mourned alongside the loved, grief without a favourites list. What the lens flattens: the war. Read purely ecocritically, 'Lament' becomes a pollution poem and loses "vengeance", Ahmed, the fusilier — the specifically human machinery of motive the last line indicts. The poem is not nature poetry with a war in it; it is a war poem that refuses to let "war" mean only humans.

Feminist. Makes visible the poem's maternal spine: it opens inside a female body's emergency ("her pulsing burden… the breeding ground… her eggs"), passes through the ocean's "lap" (the mother's lap made mortal), and mourns the combatants not as soldiers but as sons — "the boy", "the farmer's sons" — through phrases Clarke took from their mothers' radio interviews. The war's perspective in this poem is the perspective of those who bear and raise what war spends; its deepest definition of atrocity is the poisoning of generation itself (eggs, nests, breeding, migration — all reproductive acts). Male violence is present only as ownerless residue: agentless participles, a possessive missile. What it flattens: the poem's men are not only cyphers of a war-machine — gunsmith and armourer are mourned as workers, and the lens can reduce Clarke's inclusive grief to a gendered indictment the poem's evenhandedness pointedly withholds.

Postcolonial. Makes visible where the poem's knowledge comes from and who gets a name. A Welsh poet — from a small country with its own history of anglicisation, writing in the imperial language about a war conducted by Western powers in the Gulf — assembles her lament entirely from Western media: the one Arab in the poem has one line, no verb and a name that is also a category, while the detailed, tender particularity (joined for the company, in it for the music) is reserved for British soldiers whose mothers were interviewable in English. The lens sharpens the Ahmed crux: the poem's compassion crosses the border its information could not. It also notices "the closed border" as the colonial artefact par excellence — lines drawn by departed empires, upheld against the people who live there, ignored by the oil and smoke. What it flattens: the poem's genuine self-awareness — "the ashes of language" is, among other things, an admission that the reports the poem is built from are themselves burnt currency; the poem critiques its own sources from inside.

Marxist / materialist. Makes visible the commodity at the poem's centre and the class of its casualties. The war's cause, weapon and shroud is oil — the one substance never named, exactly as capital prefers to operate: everywhere effective, nowhere visible. The human dead are labour all the way down: the gunsmith and armourer (artisans of the arms economy, mourned as workers complicit without choice), the fusilier and the farmer's sons (rural recruits for whom the army is employment, company and a band — enlistment as economic fact dressed as adventure). No general, no minister, no shareholder appears; the poem mourns everyone the war-economy spends and no one it enriches. What it flattens: by deleting all agents, the poem also deletes the beneficiaries — a consistent Marxist reading wants the arms trade named and prosecuted, and Clarke's elegiac evenhandedness ("For the gunsmith…") grieves the system's instruments without indicting its owners. The lens calls that quietism; the poem would call it a funeral.

Historicist. Makes visible how precisely the poem is a document of the first television war watched live. 1991 was the war of pooled, censored, briefing-room coverage — "surgical strikes", "collateral damage", nose-camera footage with no bodies — and of a handful of images that escaped the management: the oiled cormorants, the burnt man in his vehicle. 'Lament' is built exclusively from that mediated seepage (Clarke says so), and its final line is a media-critique before it is a metaphysic: "the ashes of language" names what military euphemism and censorship had already done to public speech — Clarke's own gloss, "the death of truth during war". The poem's method — naming plainly what the coverage prettified or withheld — is counter-broadcasting: a litany against the communiqué. What it flattens: the poem's deliberate timelessness. Clarke strips away dates, nations and proper nouns (except Ahmed) precisely so the lament will fit the next war; a reading that chains it to 1991 mistakes the occasion for the subject.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

  1. The universal pacifist elegy. The poem deliberately erases sides — the soldier could be Iraqi or British, no nation is named, and Clarke's stripping of dates and places makes it a lament for war, applicable to any conflict (its afterlife on syllabuses through later wars supports this). Evidence: the agentless participles; the evenhanded mourning of combatants and makers of arms; the type-figures. Weakness: universality is bought with vagueness about a highly specific event — the spill and the fires were deliberate acts by an identifiable regime, the bombing a choice by identifiable coalitions, and a reading in which "everyone suffers, no one acts" converts crime into weather. The poem's one gesture toward cause, "For vengeance", is left doing an enormous amount of unassisted work.
  2. The ecocentric reading. This is primarily an environmental poem; the war is one instance of a general human assault on nature. Evidence: the running order (animals first, last and framing the humans); roughly two-thirds of the lines given to creatures, sea and sky; the endangered-species specificity (green turtle, hook-beaked turtle, dugong — from a Friends of the Earth list). Weakness: stanzas 3–4 are irreducibly a war poem — borders, uniforms, fusiliers, armourers — and "vengeance" is a human motive with no ecological meaning; read purely green, the poem loses its final line.
  3. The media-critique reading. The poem's true subject is mediation: it is a poem about watching a war on television in Wales, assembled from photographs and radio (Clarke's own account), and its last line mourns the corruption of public language — censorship, euphemism, propaganda — more than speech itself. Evidence: every image traceable to reportage; "the ashes of language" glossed by Clarke as "the death of truth during war"; the poem's plain naming as counter-euphemism. Weakness: nothing inside the text signals mediation — no screen, no newsprint, no aerial; the reading is built on paratext (Clarke's notes), and one can fairly ask where the poem itself knows it is second-hand.
  4. The liturgical reading. The poem is a litany of intercession — "For the sick… for the dying…" — a prayer form with the congregation's rhythm and the priest's repetitions, performed for a world war has unmade; stanza 7 reverses Genesis (earth, light, waters, word), so the poem is scripture run backwards. Evidence: the eleven "For" dedications; the ceremonial equality of all named; the un-creation imagery ("the sun put out"); the ending at language, the medium of "Let there be". Weakness: a litany has an addressee, and this poem conspicuously has none — no God, no "hear us"; prayer-shaped speech into silence may be the point, but the reading must then concede it is describing the ruin of liturgy, not liturgy.
  5. The self-elegy for poetry. The final line turns the lament on itself: an elegy whose last casualty is the elegist's medium, ending in the confession that poetry cannot hold this. Evidence: "the ashes of language" as terminal phrase; the poem's renunciation of statement (no main clause anywhere); the dying-fall prosody of the close. Weakness: flatly self-refuting if overstated — the poem exists, is eloquent and is taught; language demonstrably is not ash. The reading survives only in the softened form argued in this document: assertive language is burnt, naming survives — which is no longer quite the despairing claim the reading wants to make.
  6. The suppressed-rage reading. The lament is anger wearing ceremony: the tone hardens from "pulsing" to "stink… anger… vengeance" (the owner's notes track this diction-curve), and the ritual calm is a discipline clamped over fury — a protest poem in funeral dress. Evidence: "the stink of anger"; "For vengeance"; the accelerating crowding of griefs (2 per stanza to 7) as control audibly strains. Weakness: the form never actually breaks — no exclamation, no address, no rupture of the tercet or the formula; the anger is named twice but never voiced, and a reading that makes rage primary must explain why the poem's last sound is a diminuendo, not a raised voice.
REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

TITLE

Analysis
  • The title resonates with the poem in a multitude of ways as it encapsulates the poem’s purpose & tone, reflecting a deep // mournful song expressing grief for people, animals and environment lost during the 1990–91 Gulf War.
  • A Lament is both a passionate expression of mourning and sorrow which can be presented in the form of a song // poem // piece of music, tying into the poem’s elegiac form, or a complaint.
  • A lament captures both personal and public grief, beginning with an individual's sorrow branching towards universal mourning.
  • Reflective of the poem’s structure, Clarke opens the poem w/ singular losses to environmental damage resulting in widespread harm. Duality presents the poet mourning both single victims and the collective destruction caused by the Gulf War.
  • Private grieving: A lament provides a personal and raw expression of sorrow, indicating the poet’s full emotional transparency regarding the topic.
  • Public grief: Designed for community use to process collective crises. It twists personal sorrow into a shared experience of protest and pain, mirroring the poet voicing the complaints the media refuses to broadcast.
  • The title links to structure of the poem, using it to begin a list of lamented people // creatures // nature ([Lament] For…).
  • Allows poem to be read continually, permitting fluidity, travelling from one victim to another with destruction // suffering as a constant.
  • Connection between title & poem demonstrates the poet’s refusal to separate the act of naming from the act of mourning.
  • Simultaneously indicates elegiac form and beginning the elegy + consequently starting mourning // sorrowful tone
  • Having the title as a single word permits freedom to interpret what is lamented. Clarke provokes curiosity as the reader questions what is lamented, drawing them towards the poem. The poet answers it eleven times (each For) across seven stanzas, offering a broad scope of mourning, signaling the total destruction war creates.
  • The starkness permits multiple meanings for the reader to determine as the poem unfolds while implying the poem grieves over many things suggesting the encompassing damage war creates.
  • The lack of specificity upon which war acknowledges an inevitable impact, transcending a specific moment and discusses a universal impact. This opens Lament to be applied to any war // destruction, creating a timeless poem relevant to all losses.
  • Tone is established: Dignified and sorrowful, denies possibility of it being a partisan poem // triumphant war narrative.
  • Clarke ties in title to prevalent themes of war, the natural world and motherhood throughout the poem.
  • War and consequences: Traditionally associated with the aftermath of battle, Clarke titles the poem Lament to tie into the loss of soldiers and remembrance of war while expanding beyond the battlefield to include the natural world // civilians
  • Natural world: Poet laments both human loss and ecological destruction. She subverts the title's traditional association with human losses in battle by including victims in the natural world. Discussing both animal and terrestrial destruction under the same conditions, the poet captures the entirety of what is destroyed, mourning the natural world as she grieves human life.
  • Motherhood: A lament is deeply maternal with the title hinting towards maternal imagery w/ mothers of the boy soldiers and the pregnant turtle.
1 / 2 / 3

For the green turtle with her pulsing burden, / in search of the breeding ground. / For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness.

Analysis

Techniques:

→ Maternal imagery

her pulsing burden // breeding ground // her eggs

→ Hard end-stop

nest of sickness.

→ Transferred epithet

pulsing burden

→ Paradox

nest of sickness

  • The opening stanza mourns a green turtle futilely searching for a safe breeding ground to place her eggs in a shore poisoned by oil.
  • Clarke immediately counters nature’s instinct to reproduce and protect new life with manmade chaos, indicating nature’s losing battle against the destruction of war.
  • Poet doesn’t overly emphasise point, permitting reader to grasp stark reality as opposed to a metaphor (possibly) dampening the impact.
  • Bleak diction is prevalent within entire poem portraying Clarke’s honest outlook
  • Lack of hyperbolisation grounds point in reality, illustrating possible natural scenarios and not fictional harms
  • Poet dedicates her grief ([Lament] For…) to the turtle, elevating animals to the same status as soldiers // people → presents a fair judgement of losses + gives voice to creatures who cannot speak
  • Despite the green turtle being an individual victim, utilising the rather than “a” allows Clarke to mourn the entire species rather than an anonymous turtle
  • Single green turtle is symbolic of countless others → metonymy
  • Specificity of green turtle names an endangered species, stressing how war runs the risk of wiping out animals + makes it feel like a genuine possibility rather than a hypothetical situation
  • Green → Associated with nature, life and growth which is destroyed in the war. The deliberate choice to open the poem with green foreshadows Clarke’s complaints and establishes the stakes of war.
  • The poet's use of feminine pronoun (her) immediately establishes the turtle as a mother figure, tying into the theme of motherhood.
  • Continued in her eggs → Possessive pronoun reinforces maternal bond. Forms a feeling of protectiveness as if turtle claims eggs, not ambiguous.
  • ” Pulsing” connotes heartbeat, life and urgency, presenting the turtle’s immense urge to find a nest in a region plagued by oil. A heartbeat is indicative of life that will be taken before it is born, robbing the chance for the turtle’s young to escape.
  • No main verb (no tense) rejects the idea of a recap, displaying everything as unfolding in front of the reader’s eyes → Fresh impact + creates sense of realism
  • Carries pain of mother → Inability to provide adequately for young + the burden physically affects the turtle (not conditioned to not find a place, opposes nature’s call)
  • Burden is ambivalent. Traditionally signals a negative weight on a person that cannot be shaken but undermined with turtle’s pregnancy being the main purpose assigned to her.
  • Illustrates duality of motherhood → Gift of life and weight of failure // responsibility
  • Eggs end up in a nest of sickness, presenting the mother turtle’s failure and the burden upon her.
  • The turtle’s fear of not being able to fulfill duties criticises war’s disruption in natural cycles.
  • ”Pulsing burden” → Transferred epithet
  • Turtle pulsing w/ urgency, Clarke’s transfer of this to the burden (unborn children) blurs line between mother and child + strengthens idea of mother’s responsibility, like if child dies she dies too
  • Being in search of a familiar place implies effort and uncertainty, showcasing the disruption the manmade disaster had upon the biological programming of animals.
  • Futile search evokes helplessness, permits reader to feel sorrow for the turtle.
  • Resonates with humankind (stanza 3) → Blurs line between nature and human: People search for place to raise children // displaced refugees seek safety (Ahmed at the closed border)
  • Endstopping sentence after search sketches how turtle assumes pointlessness of looking for a place that doesn’t exist. End of sentence mimics end of search.
  • Clarke keeps the sickness plaguing the nest ambiguous, paralleling the turtle’s lack of knowledge of what it is.
  • Puts reader into turtle’s shoes, equally confused.
  • Permits the poem to be used in multiple contexts where the sickness may not be oil.
  • Subverts typical interpretation of nest from warmth and safety to a cradle of death → Paradoxical
  • Hard endstop at the end of the stanza indicates finality, definitively sealing the egg’s future without negotiation. The poet aims to capture the helplessness of unborn creatures against the poison of mankind, evoking an emotional response from the reader.
  • Poet aims to force the reader to pause and absorb the impact of loss in a harshly conclusive manner without hesitation.
4 / 5 / 6

For the cormorant in his funeral silk, / the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.

Analysis
  • Alludes to deliberate oil spill into the Persian Gulf and its effect on nature with a cormorant coated in oil and its spreading contamination to the sand & sea. Based on photographs, Clarke describes seabirds doused in oil and the shadow on the sea as a spreading oil stain due to bombed wells.
  • Cormorant: A medium to large seabird with black plumage covering its body. Their feathers are not fully waterproofed, creating a vulnerability to oil spills as it’s absorbed rather than repelled, making a large number of them victims to an oil spill as they dive beneath the surface of the water to catch fish, often fatally.
  • The cormorant is widely disliked by fishermen and fish farmers. Clarke deliberately chooses them over a conventionally favoured bird, insisting all creatures should be mourned, rejecting biases against certain species.
  • Clarke further respects the bird through a masculine pronoun rather than it, providing him with dignity and individualism.
  • Ties cormorant into the soldier in his uniform of fire and the boy fusilier, suggesting equality in mourning and war’s destruction. Hierarchical perspective between human and animal is dissolved to indicate the poet’s constant belief of grieving all victims appropriately.
  • The cormorant metaphorically wearing funeral silk refers to traditional black clothing worn at a funeral, suggesting he is symbolically attending his own death. Literally, the poet describes the oil as a shiny coating over the bird, elevating environmental destruction into a ceremonial image to humanise the bird and invite the reader to mourn it as a person. The weight of the oil prevents the bird from flying, transforming it into a suffocating funeral shroud (used to wind around dead bodies before burial) that ultimately seals his fate.
  • Silk carries connotations of beauty and luxury associated with wealth, ceremony and elegance in stark contrast with oil. Clarke offers a different interpretation of oil as beauty, colliding with its toxic and repellent qualities. Oil has a sheen and smoothness comparable to silk, forcing the reader to see its elegant yet destructive qualities. The poet forces the reader to recognise the lack of a clear answer between good and bad, suggesting an unsettling truth.
  • Silk’s prominence in weddings ties into a veil of iridescence, suggesting a glorified death of the environment as well as a falsified and deceiving beauty.
  • The veil of iridescence extends the funeral imagery with a veil being symbolic of mourning.
  • Refers to oil spreading across sand, mirroring contamination of the Gulf War spill laying itself across the ocean like a mourning veil.
  • Scene extends the funeral metaphor from cormorant to the entirety of nature as if the world is mourning itself.
  • Veil further suggests concealment as oil physically covers sand, obscuring traces of the natural world.
  • Drags wedding connotations from silk. The poet glorifies death as people glorify war, using the same tone // attitude to showcase deaths as others would describe war. Creates a sense of unease and permits the reader to question whether it’s right to celebrate something as destructive as battle.
  • Soft endstop implies a slight pause, permitting continuation and creating the sense that the shadow is spreading similar to the oil.
  • The shadow on the sea metaphorically suggests a shadow of death and human destruction poisoning the natural world as well as foreshadowing the inevitable damage to the ocean. Adapting from the shadow of death, its foreboding nature captures the poet’s warning of war’s destruction.
  • Use of sibilance throughout stanza (silk // iridescence // sand // shadow // sea) allows a hissing quality, evoking an insidious sense and a spreading of evil. Also creates a quiet tone as if hushing // using a tarp (oil) to cover natural sound and life.
7 / 8 / 9

For the ocean’s lap with its mortal stain. / For Ahmed at the closed border. / For the soldier in his uniform of fire.

Analysis
  • The ocean’s lap evokes the gentle rippling sound of the water as it washes against the shore
  • The rhythmic motion of the sea creates a peaceful and reassuring sound, evoking a sense of calmness and serenity.
  • Lap evokes a sense of motherhood, describing safety and comfort, and strengthens maternal imagery expanding from the pregnant turtle. Clarke corrupts nurture and protection with oil’s mortal stain, suggesting mankind’s disruption to nature.
  • The mortal stain is physically the black coating of oil that brings death and destruction, literally staining and poisoning the land. Metaphorically, this evokes a blood stain as if the ocean has been mortal[ly] wounded and injured in a manner that will ultimately lead to death.
  • Moreover, the diction mortal suggests a temporary, finite, and impuissant (powerless, unable to take action) revealing the destruction caused by man, resulting in nature eventually perishing
  • A stain is not a wound, rather than breaking, it seeps and corrupts, suggesting the inability to be completely removed, paralleling an oil spill. The contrast between lap’s gentleness and the stain's corruption suggests war poisoning fundamental sources of comfort and safety, erasing comfort permanently.
  • Hard endstop after mortal stain closes line with finality suggesting the ocean’s wound is an incurable disease spreading to the shore. Mourning the ocean as a victim of war, Clarke establishes the ecological effects of the Gulf War’s destruction, mourning nature as she would a human casualty. She takes a radical position, insisting the natural world has an equal claim on grief.
  • Clarke moves to the human collateral damage of this war, encompassing everything and everyone.
  • The proper noun Ahmed introduces specificity to the generalised image of suffering, indicating individual tragedy. A name brings Ahmed individuality, acting as a human with an identity and history rather than a statistic or representing a category. Clarke insists his suffering is irreplaceable and acts as a voice for countless other refugees as an individual rather than an abstraction.
  • Highlights the toll of war takes, not only on the environment but on the lives of innocent people
  • The closed border is especially poignant as it symbolises the hopelessness and entrapment of refugees unable to escape the conflict that ravages both their homes and their futures.
  • The preposition of at indicates the inability to cross, unable to flee the horrors of war. Use of the implies a known and established sequence, chosen over “a”, the poet suggests routine entrapment.
  • The casual phrasing normalises injustice within war and simplistic refusal to grant a person safety, refusing to acknowledge their humanity as war does to countless innocent victims.
  • The ambiguity of Ahmed’s fate permits multiple interpretations and applications to voice other experiences of people turned away at borders.
  • The soldier brings the poem back to an ambiguous state contrasting the deliberate naming of Ahmed. His suffering originates from his role as a soldier, different to the citizens affected by the war.
  • The soldier burns in a metaphorical uniform of fire that transcends the literal image of a burning person to represent the inescapable destruction of war.
  • A uniform defines a soldier, allocating them to a place and group as well as serving as a garment of protection via either camouflage or design. The uniform burning signals the destruction of a soldier’s identity and cause, an ironic scene where the very thing that’s supposed to protect and identify him turns against him and consumes him whole. Being in close physical proximity, it prevents the soldier from escaping his fate, illustrating war’s destruction.
  • The poet alludes to a photograph of a soldier burnt when his tank was bombed. Clarke doesn’t invent the events of war but bases it off of real world images, warning the reader of the immediate risk of war.
  • Fire further links to broader imagery of burning destruction in the blazing well and burnt earth. The soldier’s burning body is a microcosm of the burning world, possibly foreshadowing the eventual outcome.
  • The word uniform carries irony in the sense of the reversal of protection and the uniform grieving // loss of three different victims of war, spanning from the natural world to innocent citizens and finally to soldiers
  • This stanza is the only one with all hard end-stops and every line beginning For, which emphasises the containment seen through the closed border.
  • Moreover, Ahmed is seemingly trapped in between a few juxtaposing elements:
  • The vast ocean coated with oil
  • The soldier burning alive
  • The contrast between fire and water indicates the duality of warfare on both man and nature, yet it’s simultaneously linked where the oil which the fire burns also poisons the sea.
  • The literary image of the border is conveyed through endstopped lines and isolation of stanzas, illustrating Ahmed’s hopelessness and inability to access others from physical separation.
  • This stanza develops the scope of Clarke’s lament where war is shown to not only destroy wildlife but everything it can. The ocean, refugee and soldier are placed in the same stanza as equals, suggesting the lack of hierarchy in suffering and war’s equal and universal devastation.
  • Intensifies hellish imagery of war where death is extremely visceral. The image of being burnt to death adds a layer of horror, suggesting the brutal, unrelenting nature of violence.
  • Shifts from the natural world to the human world, showing how the devastation of nature parallels the suffering of people caught in war
10 / 11 / 12

For the gunsmith and the armourer, / the boy fusilier who joined for the company, / the farmer’s sons, in it for the music.

Analysis
  • Clarke begins the stanza with a gunsmith and the armourer who furnish and maintain weapons and defence systems, being part of people who can profit financially from warfare.
  • Despite their contribution to war, Clarke insists that all should be mourned equally, a recurring idea throughout the poem. Deepens the sense of mourning of not just victims of war, but those who perhaps without choice become complicit in it by making weapons. The poet forgives those that take part in war, suggesting financial instability during wartime and the fight for survival and taking care of family outweighs moral choices.
  • Adds complexity and moral ambiguity to Clarke’s critique of war, it’s not only the soldiers and civilians who suffer but those whose livelihoods are tied to the production of violence. She suggests the lack of a definitive good and bad in war.
  • By mourning the gunsmith and armourer, the poet suggests that no one in a society at war is fully exempt from its horrors.
  • The next line creates an image of innocence and vulnerability through the description of a boy, with their naivety distancing them from brutal dictatorships and governments waging the war.
  • The poet’s portrayal of young men joining for the company and music indicates innocence and vulnerability. This shows their lack of driven motivation by political affiliation // propaganda being caught in conflict due to personal reasons. The gap between their motivations and the larger political forces enables the reader to feel sympathy towards the clueless soldiers, making their involvement tragic rather than provoking anger.
  • Use of boy reduces the soldier to a child, shattering the illusion of military heroism, revealing a human being inside the uniform. A child carrying a gun in a warzone seems ironic as his version of an adventure is twisted into a nightmarish scene of death and brutality.
  • Connected to poem’s maternal theme: Clarke took the boy + sons from radio interviews with their mothers.
  • boy fusilier is an ironic juxtaposition with the antiquity of military violence following something that carries heavy connotations of innocence.
  • joined → only finite verb in the whole poem; boy = only agent → the one completed act is a boy signing up
  • the company → pun: companionship + military unit (joined for friends, issued a Company)
  • The diction boy and sons reinforce the theme of lost potential, highlighting the youth of individuals with lives cut short by the war.
  • Choice of sons rather than son suggests a recurring pattern of young enlistments for naive reasons.
  • Regardless of survival, the war leaves a permanent indent in their mindset, being victims of the system and misguided reasons that led them to the war.
  • War corrupts the innocence that brought them there in the first place, an irreversible act of damage even if they survive the conflict itself.
  • Contrasting other stanzas, Clarke directly confronts the human cost of war on those who fight and fuel it as ordinary, often naive, humans tangled in a conflict beyond their control. As pawns in a game, the poet idealises them as citizens without a choice, being forced to accept duties against their morals to survive or given a falsified idea of war only to face its brutality with no way of backing out.
  • Though war is thought of as a conflict with two sides, Clarke’s choice to mourn the gunsmith, armourer and boy soldiers with other innocent victims without judgement indicates a universal experience of suffering regardless of what aspect war impacts them.
13 / 14 / 15

For the hook-beaked turtles, / the dugong and the dolphin, / the whale struck dumb by the missile’s thunder.

Analysis
  • The hook-beaked turtle is another name for the Hawksbill turtle, a critically endangered species
  • Choice of using hook leads to connotations with entrapment, suggesting that the turtles themselves are snared in the destruction surrounding them.
  • The shift from a singular turtle in stanza one escalates to many, mirroring the scale of the poem’s grief increasing from one lament to the next.
  • The reader moves from mourning a single animal to an entire species.
  • Similar to a snowball effect, overwhelms the reader in terms of destruction, revealing the true extent of devastation.
  • A dugong is a sea cow, similar to a manatee
  • Clarke draws attention to the diversity within the natural world, selecting more obscure species as they are often left out to give them a voice. Unfamiliarity acts as a reminder to the reader that war kills things that they haven’t recognised as a species.
  • Suggests universality of war’s harm, all forms of life regardless of popularity or uniqueness are at risk due to human callousness.
  • The whale is the largest marine animal and being the final and climactic image of the stanza, Clarke builds a crescendo of loss from small to large, mirroring the poem’s increasing emotional intensity.
  • Associated with wisdom, depth and peace, its silencing acts as a reminder of the ease of human destruction, silencing or killing the largest animal without deliberately intending to, and the consequent death of those qualities.
  • Being struck dumb, the poet literally describes the whale as speechless, being shocked into silence. Suggests the acoustic damage caused by underwater explosions. Relying on sound to communicate, this would disrupt and confuse the whale and dolphin, effectively silencing them or forcing them to travel directionlessly. Metaphorically, the whale’s peace is drowned by the missile's thunder, indicating the voices of reason being drowned out by the chaos of warfare
  • Two soft end-stops between the stanza emphasises a continuation of ideas and gentleness of life while ending with a hard end-stop after thunder mimics the ferocity and viciousness of human weapons.
16 / 17 / 18

For the tern, the gull and the restless wader, / the long migrations and the slow dying, / the veiled sun and the stink of anger.

Analysis
  • Tern and gull are seabirds, spending most of their time airborne, searching for food and relying on fish for survival
  • Terns are known for long migrations, introducing the theme of migration in the stanza
  • Waders are shorebirds which are often found wading along shorelines and mud flats to find food
  • The bird’s anxiousness suggests its unfamiliarity with this environment, unable to find safety and cannot stop moving, similar to refugees escaping war.
  • The restless wader suggests the struggle to find food to survive in a polluted habitat where water has become contaminated.
  • The long migrations initially refers to the disrupted migrations of seabirds due to the Gulf War’s environmental effect with burnt oil wells clouding the sky. Clarke mourns not only the deaths of the birds but the loss of a structured routine nature has developed over long periods of times.
  • Simultaneously, the migrations refer to the migrations of displaced refugees and stateless people such as Ahmed.
  • ”Long” suggests a physical distance and the endurance required for the journey where safety isn’t guaranteed.
  • The poet links the human and animal world, implying their similarities in attempting to find a safe end after a long arduous journey.
  • The slow dying refers to the gradual death of creatures affected by oil contamination due to a lack of food, inability to fly or those that die slowly due to poisoning. The poet enables the reader to feel sorrowful for the inescapable fate of the birds.
  • In the context of human victims, it refers to the death of people who have been displaced and died on the journey of trying to find shelter without adequate water. Clarke implies a painfully slow and aware death where people are helpless yet conscious of their impending death.
  • The personification of the veiled sun creates an image of a veneer made of smoke from the burning oil fields acting as a funeral veil
  • Symbolises the death of nature and offering a mournful tone, emphasising the theme of the death of the planet
  • The veiling // concealment of the sun diminishes its warmth and light, foreshadowing its death in the following stanza.
  • The stink of anger could literally refer to the smell of burning oil created by the environmental devastation in the Gulf War
19 / 20 / 21

For the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well. / For vengeance, and the ashes of language.

Analysis
  • Stanza opens with apocalyptic imagery with total environmental destruction at the centre of the first line, ascending war’s devastation to a cosmic level within a line.
  • A burnt earth literally refers to the Gulf War’s oil well fires. As a past participle (burnt), the poet suggests the earth’s total destruction has already happened beyond a repairable point. The lack of conditionality and prevention indicates the finality of the situation where the poet leaves no room for negotiation, a direct warning of the consequences of war.
  • The earth not existing eradicates all victims mentioned previously where its destruction crushes the medium of life.
  • The sun being put out captures the extinguishment of the ultimate source of life. Due to its simplicity, the poet suggests an astronomical amount of damage due to human carelessness. Paralleling snuffing out a candle, Clarke connects the destruction of the sun to an everyday task, contrasting the climactic point the poem has reached.
  • Escalation of the veiled sun from veiled obscurement to total extinguishment
  • The poet personifies the ocean with it being scalded, attributing a sense of suffering and vulnerability in a way the reader can relate (e.g. burning hand on stove)
  • Refers to theme of nature being a victim of human actions and inevitable consequences
  • The blazing well directly alludes to oil wells set on fire during the Gulf War, illustrating the magnitude of human destruction
  • Beyond extinguishing life on earth, the poet captures an image of wastefulness, an intentional move to pollute the environment partially understanding the consequences
  • Signifies human greed and personal benefit as underlying themes during conflict
