  • The metaphorical ashes of language references the death of truth during war, suggesting damages beyond physical grasp. Clarke critiques media censorship obscuring truth from the public audience.
  • The inclusion of abstract concepts (language and vengeance) contrasts tangible imagery, broadening the scope of her laments.

Structural + General Analysis

Analysis
  • 7 stanzas of three lines (tercets)
  • 7 stanzas ↔ 7 days of creation? Stanza 7 undoes Genesis (earth, light, water, finally the word) → argue from imagery, not the number
  • Free verse
  • No fixed metrical (or rhythmic) structure
  • No set rhyme scheme
  • Rhyme suggests order, closure in a musically pleasant way; absence of rhyme removes chime // consolation (no resolution) — but form is strict (7 equal tercets, every line end-stopped) → ritual order containing chaos, not chaos
  • Each line is end-stopped with either a comma (soft) or a full stop (hard)
  • Lack of enjambment contributes to this slow and deliberate pace with each line standing on its own as a self-contained thought
  • Mimics the style and solemnity of a prayer or elegy, allowing the reader to pause and reflect on the gravity of each lamentation
  • Offers a sense of finality and mourning with each image or event carefully and respectfully acknowledge before moving onto the next
  • Measured rhythm enhances the poem’s tone of sorrow and reverence for the victims of environmental destruction and war
  • First three stanzas: One item/ image attributed to each line (line 10 already has two)
  • In further stanzas, this structure isn’t present, structure slowly falls as poem continues, expands to two subjects per line
  • As if Clarke doesn’t have enough time/space to lament all affected/destroyed by the war
  • The entire poem is built around a series of For phrases, expressing sorrow for different subjects
  • From endangered animals to the individuals involved in warfare
  • Anaphora: For opens 11 lines (1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 19, 21) + 2 lowercase mid-line fors (for the company, for the music) = 13
  • Creates a solemn, rhythmic quality that echoes the tolling of a funeral bell, acts as a soft drumbeat
  • Reflects steady beat of funeral march, reinforces elegiac form
  • The repetitive structure alongside the asyndetic nature of each lament reinforces the mournful tone, as each for introduces another casualty or loss to be grieved
  • The repetition invites contemplation, emphasising the sheer scale of destruction
  • Each toll marks a life, a species, or an aspect of the natural world devastated by the war
  • This effect is both hypnotic and haunting, mirroring the persistence of grief and the unrelenting nature of the damage cause
  • Clarke’s diction is lyrical, often carrying a musicality and emotional resonance, enhancing the elegiac tone of the poem
  • Heightens the poignancy of the subject matter, making the destruction made even more vivid and heartrending

Lament

Analysis

Similar: wail // weeping

Similar: elegy // requiem // dirge

[Lament] For Ahmed at the closed border.

  • The one-word title
  • The start of a list of lamented people, events, creatures, and other things hurt in the war
  • A Lament is a song expressing grief for something lost or someone who has died
  • Noun
  • a passionate expression of grief or sorrow
  • his mother’s night-long laments for his father
  • a song, piece of music, or poem expressing grief or sorrow
  • the piper played a lament
  • a complaint
  • there were constant laments about the conditions of employment
  • The diction lament is understood to be tacitly (in a way that is understood or implied without being directly stated) present before each instance of the word For
  • [Lament] For the ocean’s lap with its mortal stain.
  • Clarke puts a slight twist to the traditional lament by painting her sorrow onto a broader canvas, focusing as much on the environmental cost as on the human cost of the Kuwait oil Disaster
  • Her theme beyond the expression of sorrow at the scale of destruction, is that human wars waged against one another are also waged against the natural world
  • Her usage of metonymy (individuals or small things to represent many)
  • Allows her reader to connect in a concrete way
Effect, style & response
  • Relevance to the poem
  • Establishes form as an elegy
  • Introduction of mournful tone
  • Structurally significant, allows the poem to list what the poet laments

“For the green turtle with her pulsing burden, / in search of the breeding ground./ For her eggs laid in their nest of sickness.”

Analysis

Consider the consequences of environmental damage

  • The imagery of a pregnant turtle seeking the exact beach where her instincts tell her to lay her eggs is particularly poignant
  • The burden becomes simultaneously a literal physical weight, and metaphorically a natural responsibility
  • Highlights the turtle’s vulnerability and the significance of her journey
  • The act of carrying the weight of life but also the curse of survival in a poisoned world adds to the tragic dimension of the turtle’s mission
  • Noun burden has a dual meaning (life vs. suffering) deliberately made ambiguous:
  • Literal: the turtle’s eggs (new life)
  • Connotative: weight, struggle, or suffering
  • This duality creates tension, as the turtle carries future life, but also carries the threat of destruction
  • Highlight the tragic irony that reproduction (hope) becomes vulnerability
  • The adjective pulsing not only evokes the life that she carries with her, but also suggests the urgency of her mission
  • Emphasise that what is at risk is not abstract, but living, breathing life bringing tension and anxiety
  • Focus on the immediacy of life being endangered
  • The plosive /p/ and /b/ enhances the sense of vitality and tension, mirroring the heartbeat of new life within the eggs
  • Juxtaposed with the despair of the nest of sickness in the oil-saturated poisoned sand
  • The diction of nest is often associated with birth, new life, and vitality, yet this one will only breed death, and disease emphasising the tragic futility of her instinctual journey as her offspring are doomed by the polluted environment even before they are hatched
  • This metaphor effectively implies the toxic pollution that’s going to contaminate her and her new babies
  • The gradual increase in sibilance from the pulSing, to the Search, and her eggS laid in their neSt of SickneSS reveals the rapidly yet subtly approaching death which encroaches on the mother turtle and her children
  • The transition from the plosive /p/ and /b/ to the sibilant /s/ mimics the dying heartbeat of a living being which slowly fades away
  • The definite article the in THE breeding ground, conveys the way that these creatures are hard-wired to go back to their ancestral breeding ground
  • That even though it is poisoned they are unable to adapt to sudden environmental changes
  • This contrast sets the tone for the rest of the poem, highlighting the clash between nature’s resilience and the destructive impact of human activity
  • The visual imagery of green suggests a miracle of nature, encapsulating life in words like pulsing, breeding and eggs while offering a sense of stability, growth, and fertility
  • The faint movements in the pulsing burden hints at the tiny heartbeats, the birth of new life, which elicited the sympathy of readers who recognise the protective maternal instincts driving her on
  • Adjective Green portrays natural innocence and ecological identity
  • Symbolises nature, life, and ecological harmony, also specifically identifies the green sea turtle, grounding the image in reality
  • Connotes purity and a creature that belongs wholly to the natural world
  • Emphasise the turtle as part of an untouched, balanced ecosystem
  • Noun turtle shows vulnerability and ancient life
  • Turtles are often associated with longevity and ancient continuity, slow movement (vulnerability to human harm)
  • Represents a species that has survived for millennia, now threatened by modern human actions
  • Highlight the scale of destruction—impacting even the most enduring creatures
  • Feminine possessive pronoun her (not “it”) humanises the turtle, bringing empathy, while encouraging emotional identification
  • Suggests maternal vulnerability, especially in relation to reproduction
  • Create a personal, emotional connection between reader and animal
  • Contextual implication pollution and human impact:
  • Transforms something natural (eggs) into something toxic and unnatural

“For the cormorant in his funeral silk, / the veil of iridescence on the sand, / the shadow on the sea.”

Analysis
  • Alludes to the oil deliberately spilled into the Persian Gulf by the occupying Iraqi army (Jan 1991)
  • A cormorant is a medium-to-large seabird, which is a reference to a photograph that Clarke saw in the newspaper, of one of these birds covered with oil
  • The diction funeral silk is a reference to the black clothes that are worn to a funeral, which evokes the shiny, viscous black coating of oil over the bird’s feathers
  • Almost like a shroud used to ritually wind around dead bodies before burial
  • The personification creates the visual image of a mourner dressed for a funeral after the death of his habitat/home
  • This funeral imagery is further developed in the next line as the oil has left a veil of iridescence on the sand reinforcing the poem’s tone of sorrow and loss
  • Black veils were traditionally worn by women at funerals up until the mid-twentieth century
  • Iridescent means luminous colours that seem to change when seen from different angles due to the way light interferes with the surface, both reflecting and refracting different wavelengths and is typical of the appearance of oil
  • Evokes how the oil has left a beautiful yet poisonous sheen
  • The shadow on the sea acts as a metaphor for death and the foreboding inevitability of death that is to come to the living animals
  • The extensive use of sibilance throughout this stanza Silk/irideSCenCE/Sand/SHadow/Sea allows a hissing quality which evokes an insidious sense of a spreading evil
  • This illustrates not only the physical damage, but the emotional toll it takes on the natural world
7 / 8 / 9

For the ocean’s lap with its mortal stain. / For Ahmed at the closed border. / For the soldier in his uniform of fire.

Analysis
  • The diction lap evokes the gentle rippling sound of the water as it washes against the shore
  • Yet the mortal stain is physically the black coating of oil that will bring death and destruction, as it in turn will literally stain and poison the land
  • Metaphorically evokes a blood stain as if the ocean has been mortal[ly] wounded and injured in such a manner that it will ultimately lead to death
  • Moreover, the diction mortal suggests a temporary, finite, and impuissant (powerless, unable to take action) revealing the destruction caused by man, even resulting in nature eventually perishing
  • Clarke moves to the human collateral damage of this war, which encompasses everything and everyone now
  • The proper noun Ahmed is the name of the refugee, which moves from a generalised image the suffering to one of individual tragedy
  • Highlights the toll of war takes, not only on the land but on the lives of innocent people
  • The closed border is especially poignant as it symbolises the hopelessness and entrapment of refugees unable to escape the conflict that ravages both their homes and their futures
  • This stanza is the only one all with hard end-stops and anaphorically emphasised through for which emphasises the containment seen through the closed border
  • Moreover, Ahmed is seemingly trapped in between a few juxtaposing elements:
  • The vast Ocean coated with oil
  • The soldier burning alive
  • The contrast between fire and water shows the duality of warfare on both man and nature, yet it’s simultaneously linked where the oil which the fire burns in, is also the one that poisons the sea
  • The physical/literary imagery of the border, between the lines, and the entirety of the poem, shows Ahmed’s hopelessness and inability to access others, whether he’s being separated by stanza, or be line
  • The intensification of the hellish imagery of war, where death is not abstract but extremely visceral
  • The image of being burnt to death adds a layer of horror, suggesting the brutal, unrelenting nature of the violence
  • Shifts from the natural world to the human world showing how the devastation of nature parallels the suffering people caught in the war
Effect, style & response
  • Evokes a more personal and engaging empathy with the author, as almost this is someone of familiarity, someone close to the reader
  • Allows the reader to feel, ponder, and experience the true tragedy of warfare, harming everyone, without exception
10 / 11 / 12

“For the gunsmith and the armourer, / the boy fusilier who joined for the company, / the farmer’s sons, in it for the music.”

Analysis
  • Clarke begins with the gunsmith and the armourer who furnish and maintain weapons and defence systems and those who can be said to profit financially from warfare
  • Deepens the sense of mourning of not just the victims of war, but those who perhaps without choice become complicit in it by making weapons
  • Adds complexity and moral ambiguity to Clarke’s critique of war it’s not only the soldiers and civilians who suffer but those whose livelihoods are tied to the production of violence
  • The lament for them could be seen as an indictment of a system that perpetuates destruction suggesting that their work , though essential to the war machine, contributes to the cycle of death
  • The next line creates an image of innocence and vulnerability, and distances these people from the dictators and governments who are really waging the war
  • Clarke’s portrayal of these young men as joining for personal reasons ie. human connection or a desire to be part of a military band
  • Show’s innocence and vulnerability
  • Lack of driven motivation by political affiliation or motivations
  • Caught up in more personal and even naive reasons
  • This disconnect between their motivations and the larger political forces at play adds to the tragic nature of their involvement
  • The diction boy and sons reinforces the theme of lost potential, highlighting the youth of these individuals and the bright futures that have been cut short by war
  • Whether they survive or not they are victims in a different sense, victims of:
  • The system
  • Their own vulnerability
  • The misguided reasons that led them to war

“For the hook-beaked turtles, / the dugong and the dolphin, / the whale struck dumb by the missile’s thunder.”

Analysis
  • The hook-beaked turtle is another name for the Hawksbill turtle which are critically endangered species
  • Dugong is a sea cow, similar to the much better-known manatee
  • Clarke is drawing attention to the diversity within the natural world
  • All forms of life–no matter how unique or less widely known are at risk exposing the widespread impact of human activity on the full spectrum of life forms
  • The missile’s thunder not only suggests the physical destruction caused by war, but also the psychological and sensory impact on the natural world
  • Whale’s complex communication and reliance on sound would be profoundly affected by the noise of missiles and explosions, disrupting their ability to navigate and communicate
  • The repetition of harsh sounds
  • Guttural consonance of hooK-beaKed and struCK
  • Acts as a foreshadowing to the violence that is about to be experienced by the animals
  • Plosive alliteration of Dugong, Dolphin, Dumb
  • Assonance of short uh in strUck dUmb
  • Draws attentions to these creatures’ collective peril, heightening the emotional weight of their inclusion
  • This stanza returns from the focus on man back to nature and its natural inhabitants
  • The lexical field, encompassing turtles, dugong, dolphin, whale reveals a sense of life, vitality, and continuity within the cycle of life, yet this calm serenity is juxtaposed and destroyed by the diction missile’s thunder
  • Creates a harsh dissonance and cacophony compared to the melodic euphony experienced
  • The term is placed at the end of the fifth stanza showing the fast paced development of the violence and warfare
  • The two soft end-stops while discussing the animals emphasises the gentleness of life while the hard end-stop after thunder shows the ferocity and viciousness of human weapons
  • The diction thunder links the missile to nature making this moment even more devastating
16 / 17 / 18

“For the tern, the gull and the restless wader, / the long migrations and the slow dying, / the veiled sun and the stink of anger.”

Analysis
  • Tern and gull are related seabirds which spend much of their time airborne, searching for food, relying on fish for survival, while waders are shorebirds which are often found wading along shorelines and mud flats to find food, often probing or digging in the mud and sand
  • The adjective restless has negative connotations implying unease or discomfort
  • Reflects the bird’s struggle to survive in its polluted habitat, where the water it wades (its life long) in has become a source of harm
  • The long migrations a natural and instinctual behaviour has been made more arduous and more fraught with danger, through the polluted air which they have to fly
  • The diction slow dying conveys prolonged suffering, suggesting the harm inflicted on the environment in not immediate but lingering
  • Creates a sense of inevitable decline and helplessness
  • The personification of the veiled sun creates an image of a veneer made of smoke from the burning oil fields obscures it, acting as a funeral veil
  • Symbolises the death of nature and the world as it once was
  • Offers a mournful tone, emphasising the theme of mourning for the planet
  • stink of anger → synaesthesia, fusing the sense of smell with an emotional state
  • This merging of sensory and emotional realms conveys the palpable (able to touch) overwhelming rage and grief that hangs in the air
  • Or literally refers to the acrid smell of burning oil linking the physical to the emotional devastation caused by war
19 / 20 / 21

“For the burnt earth and the sun put out, / the scalded ocean and the blazing well. / For vengeance, and the ashes of language.”

Analysis
  • The last stanza is concluded with an apocalyptic vision of death and destruction
  • The image of the burnt earth evokes the devastating aftermath of human conflict where the land itself is scorched and rendered lifeless
  • Scorched earth policy is a military strategy of burning or destroying crops or other resources
  • Alludes to the way the defeated Iraqi army sought to set everything on fire as they retreated
  • The sun being put out is a chilling metaphor, by taking this imagery to its ultimate conclusion: the extinguishing of life itself
  • The casual diction of put out making it seem as easy as flipping a switch, emphasises the human recklessness and the fragility of the natural world
  • Portrays a terrifying imbalance, where something s monumental as the sun can be destroyed by human actions
  • The adjective scalded personifies the ocean giving it a sense of suffering and vulnerability, as if it were a living entity capable of feeling pain
  • Refers to the theme of nature being a victim of human actions and the consequences which follow
  • The blazing well directly refers to the oil wells set ablaze during the Gulf War
  • A striking image of wastefulness and destruction, and a calculated move to wreak havoc, pollute the environment, and depriving others of resources
  • Not only signifies environmental devastation but the greed and violence that underpin and fuel such conflicts
  • The final line ends the entire poem on a sombre note, with a shift in the final tone suggesting the human motivations behind war:
  • Retaliation
  • Anger
  • Endless cycle of violence
  • The metaphor of the ashes of language is glossed by Clarke herself as “the death of truth during war”, suggesting much more than the physical is lost
  • The inclusion of these abstract concepts contrasting with the tangible imagery previously, adds a broader philosophical layer
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

  • Love Armed (Behn). Link: both poems anatomise who pays for a grand abstraction — Behn's Love "in fantastic triumph sat" while only one heart bleeds; Clarke's "vengeance" sits unnamed at the head of a casualty list it never joins. Both are structured on unequal ledgers (thy joys / my pains; the mourned / the never-blamed). Shared technique: patterned repetition building a rhetorical case (Behn's balanced antitheses; Clarke's anaphora). Difference: Behn's suffering is performed within courtly wit — symmetrical, musical, self-delighting even in pain; Clarke's register is documentary restraint, and her asymmetry (eleven dedications, no verdict) refuses the closure Behn's final couplet snaps shut.
  • A Different History (Bhatt). Link: both end at the same wound — language after violence. Bhatt asks "which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?" and marvels that the descendants love it; Clarke ends with the tongue itself in ashes. Conquest corrupts language from within; war burns it down. Shared technique: the pivot from concrete scene to abstract linguistic close; sacred framing (Sarasvati and book-reverence; litany and rite). Difference: Bhatt's poem holds a future — "the unborn grandchildren" will speak, strangely, lovingly, something; Clarke's ends in residue with no generation to follow (the eggs of line 3 were already doomed). Bhatt's is a history; Clarke's is a terminus.
  • The Chimney Sweeper (Blake). Link: children recruited by warm words — the sweep consoled with an angel's promise, the fusilier with "the company", the farmer's sons with "the music"; in both, the institution's language of comfort is the mechanism of exploitation. Shared technique: devastating use of the victims' own naive idiom, left uncorrected so the reader must do the condemning (Blake's "So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm"; Clarke's "in it for the music"). Difference: Blake gives his children voices and a consoling (ironised) theology; Clarke's recruits never speak and no heaven is on offer — her irony is quieter and her frame is planetary, where Blake's is a single city's economy of soot.
  • Where I Come From (Brewster). Link: both are catalogue-poems in which a list builds a world — Brewster's "People are made of places", itemising woods, farms, chromium-plated offices; Clarke's litany itemises a world being unmade. The catalogue as memory versus the catalogue as obituary. Shared technique: asyndetic listing; the definite, plain noun-phrase as unit of meaning. Difference: Brewster's list is generative and ends on an opening — "a door in the mind blows open" to spring and frogs; Clarke's ends on a full stop and ash. One poem trusts accumulated detail to preserve; the other uses the same device to count losses that accumulation cannot restore.
  • Report to Wordsworth (Boey Kim Cheng). Link: the closest pairing in the set — both are eco-elegies that end by doubting their own medium as the sky itself fails: Boey's "sky slowing like a dying clock", where "poetry and piety have begun to fail" and God labours "to utter his last cry"; Clarke's "sun put out" and "ashes of language". Both mourn nature and the tradition of mourning nature. Shared technique: inherited elegiac machinery under strain — Boey crams his report into a sonnet addressed to a dead poet; Clarke strips the lament to its ritual skeleton. Difference: Boey's poem is thick with literary ancestry (Wordsworth, Milton, Neptune, Proteus) and speaks to someone; Clarke's has no addressee and almost no allusion — Boey laments that the tradition cannot help; Clarke writes as if it is already ash and only the bare rite remains.
  • The Cockroach (Halligan). Link: both use an animal to dissolve the human/animal boundary — but in opposite directions: Halligan scrutinises one insect until it mirrors himself ("I thought I recognised myself"); Clarke mourns many creatures as fellow victims who mirror no one and matter in themselves. Introspection versus intercession. Shared technique: minute animal observation carrying moral weight; a closing turn that reframes the whole poem (Halligan's unanswered question, Clarke's abstract final line). Difference: Halligan's is allegory — the animal exists to read the self, in a private room; Clarke's animals refuse allegory — the turtle is not a symbol of humanity but a casualty alongside it, on the scale of a biosphere. One poem ends in a question about the self; the other in a full stop over everything.

Follower

Seamus Heaney · 1966

The son gets ahead of his father but never out from under him: the expert who now stumbles behind him keeps the last verbs, the last rhymes — and the will not to go away.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet and His Father

Seamus Heaney (1939–2013) was born at Mossbawn, the family farm in County Derry, Northern Ireland, the eldest of nine children. The farm was small, some fifty acres, and the father's real commitment was to cattle-dealing, so a cattle dealer's son chose to remember his father at the plough, the farm skill most like his own craft of laying down lines. The Nobel Foundation's biography calls the father 'notably sparing of talk', and the poem never gives him a word.

Patrick Heaney was alive when the poem was published; he died in 1986. Whatever the last stanza means, it is not about a dead man.

Death of a Naturalist (Faber, 1966)

'Follower' comes from Heaney's first full collection, published when he was twenty-seven. The book opens with 'Digging': pen in hand, the poet watches his father's back bend and come 'up twenty years away', admits he has 'no spade to follow' his elders, and resolves to dig with the pen. 'Follower' makes that verb of succession its title and runs the other way, from the past up into today. It refuses the consolation: it never mentions the pen, and it ends not on a resolution but on a father who will not go away.

The Scholarship: Leaving the Land

At twelve Heaney won a scholarship to St Columb's College, a Catholic boarding school in Derry. The Nobel biography calls this first departure from Mossbawn 'the decisive one', a move from 'the earth of farm labour to the heaven of education'; Heaney remembered the proverb adults pressed on schoolchildren, 'the pen's lighter than the spade'. The poem never mentions school, but the departure is its buried subject: in the field the son is behind; by the last stanza he is ahead, in a life the father does not share. That is why the ending can carry guilt as well as tenderness.

The Horse-Plough and Its Words

A pair of horses, the team, draws the plough; the ploughman walks behind, gripping its handles, the shafts, and steering with reins. The sock is the share, the blade that cuts beneath the slice; the wing is a blade on the plough's body whose angle governs how the slice is cut and lifted; both are set before work. Set well, the plough turns the slice, the sod, over whole, its face left shining by the steel. At the headrig, a strip left unploughed at the field's end, the team wheels round for the next furrow, and the ploughman sights along the line to keep it straight: the squint the boy longs to copy. From the early 1950s tractors steadily replaced horses in Ireland, so by 1966 the scene recorded a skill on its way out.

Sock and headrig are Scots and northern words, used without a gloss: the son speaks his father's language from inside, the part of the inheritance he did receive. Even verse comes from the field: Latin versus, from vertere, 'to turn', was the plough's turning round, and so a furrow, a row, a line of writing.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Follower

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper.

6he fixes the shining steel-tipped ploughshare in place

9on the lines swings the lathered pair about
10and they return to work; then his gaze
11squints and slants down towards the soil
12charting each furrow's course with precision
13the boy totters along in the track of his studded boots

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Follower
Language & devices

Title: a bare agent noun with no article, Follower rather than 'The Follower', so it names a role, not a person. Polysemy: one who walks behind; a disciple who imitates a master; a successor in a trade, the sense 'Digging' gives the verb ('no spade to follow'). The noun never appears in the poem; the verb follow occurs once, in line 19, and it is the son's.

Meaning & effect

The poem is about the father, but the title names the son's position: behind, secondary. All three senses fit the boy, who walks behind the plough, copies its master, and was the eldest son of a farm he did not take on. Yet the poem never pins the noun on anyone: when the father ends up behind, he keeps stumbling; he does not follow. The reader makes the transfer: a role can change hands, and by the end this one has.

Line 1
the speaker remembers his father ploughing behind a team of horses
Language & devices

Declarative opening in plain words; the compound horse-plough sets two stresses together at the line-end (spondee). The son exists only as the possessive My. Frame: my father returns in line 23, the phrase's only repetition.

Meaning & effect

A statement of record: the father is defined by labour, worked, before anything else, and horse-plough dates the memory to before tractors took over, a craft already passing. When my father returns, his verb has changed from worked to keeps stumbling: a job done has become an accident that keeps happening.

Lines 2–3
the father's shoulders swell, rounded like canvas filled by wind / his body taut between the plough's handles and the cut earth
Language & devices

Simile: globed like a full sail, the first nautical image; globed, a verb made from a noun, reads as a participle, so the line holds a picture with no main verb. Three stresses pile up on full sail strung, and enjambment carries the sail across the line-end to its two fixings: the shafts, the plough's handles, and the furrow. Sibilance (shoulders, sail, strung, shafts) breathes like wind in canvas; half-rhyme plough / furrow.

Meaning & effect

The father is seen from behind and below, at a child's height, as a huge rounded back. Arms out to the handles, back bowed over the earth, he is the taut point between plough and furrow, a sail filled not by wind but by the team's pull, which he holds and steers into a line. It is the first of the parts in which the boy sees him: shoulders, tongue, eye, back, shadow, never the whole man.

Line 4
the horses heave forward at a small click of his mouth
Language & devices

Onomatopoeia: clicking, hard /k/ closed by the nasal of tongue. The horses take the main verb; the father's act sits in a phrase after a preposition, at his clicking tongue. Full rhyme strung / tongue and a full stop close the stanza firmly.

Meaning & effect

Mastery is economy: two straining horses obey a click, with no whip and no shout. The father is the cause without being the grammatical subject, a pattern that runs through his stanzas. The click is the only sound he makes in the poem; the son's, when it comes, is Yapping.

Lines 5–6
a two-word verdict on his skill; he adjusts a blade / he fixes the shining steel-tipped ploughshare in place
Language & devices

Minor sentence: An expert., a verbless verdict, then a caesura; expert (Latin expertus, 'proved by experience') is a word of judgement among plain words of work. Technical diction: he sets the wing, angling the blade that governs how the slice is cut and lifted, and fits the sock, the Scots and northern word for the share. Bright steel-pointed stacks three stresses and a run of plosives.

Meaning & effect

The child's verdict comes first and the evidence follows, and the fragment admits no qualification: hero-worship kept intact inside an adult's poem. The evidence is preparation, not effort: set and fit are adjustments made before a furrow is cut, two of the very few verbs he owns, and both act on the plough. The habitual would makes one day a ritual repeated season after season, and it is a form of will, the verb of the father's last refusal.

Line 7
the turf turns over in one whole, unbroken strip
Language & devices

The sod takes the verb, rolled over, in long rounded vowels after line 6's clatter. Perfection defined by a negative: without breaking. Feminine ending; half-rhyme wing / breaking.

Meaning & effect

Cause and effect in successive lines: the settings of lines 5–6 make the slice turn over whole, so the skill shows in the earth's response, not in the man's effort. Rolled keeps the sea in view, the sod turning like a wave. Wholeness becomes the poem's standard, and everything after is measured against it: the boy who stumbled and Fell, and in the end the father himself.

Lines 8–10
at the turning-strip by the field's edge, one light tug / on the lines swings the lathered pair about / and they return to work; then his gaze
Language & devices

Scots headrig: the strip left unploughed at the field's end so that the team can turn. The father's act is a noun again, a single pluck of the plough-reins (strings are plucked: compare strung). Enjambment across the stanza break, the only sentence in the poem that crosses one, delays the subject, the sweating team, until after the white space; the stresses cluster on team turned round.

Meaning & effect

One tug turns the whole team, and the syntax turns with it. The headrig is a margin, ground kept for turning, and the stanza break becomes the page's headrig: the pluck hangs at the edge, and the horses come back into view on the far side, back into the land. Sweating keeps the labour honest: the strain is the animals', the light touch the man's.

Lines 10–12
and they return to work; then his gaze / squints and slants down towards the soil / charting each furrow's course with precision
Language & devices

A mid-line full stop leaves His eye hanging at the line-end (enjambment). Synecdoche: the eye stands for judgement. Semantic field of measurement (Narrowed and angled, Mapping, exactly), with a trochaic inversion on Narrowed and a metaphor of ploughing as map-making. Exactly closes a loose three-beat line on a feminine ending and a half-rhyme with eye.

Meaning & effect

The focus cuts from horses to face, a wide shot narrowing to a close-up: strength was in the shoulders, skill is in the eye, sighting along the furrow. Mapping makes ploughing the drawing of lines on a blank surface, so field and page come close. Exactly is the father's standard, yet the line that names it is itself inexact; his half of the poem ends on an adverb of precision, and the son's will end on one of distance, away.

Lines 13–14
the boy totters along in the track of his studded boots / now and then tumbling onto the shiny turned earth
Language & devices

I enters at line 13 of 24 with a verb of accident, stumbled, against the father's set and fit. Metaphor: wake, the churned track behind a ship, here made by hob-nailed (nail-studded) boots. Initial inversion: line 14 falls on its first syllable, Fell. The definite article in the polished sod points back to line 7.

Meaning & effect

The son enters at the exact halfway mark, already falling behind, and his entrance reveals where the watcher of the first three stanzas was standing: in the wake. He follows in his father's footsteps in the most literal sense and fails even at that, falling onto the polished sod, the master's finished work.

Lines 15–16
at times his father carries him piggyback / the boy bobbing up and down with each heavy step
Language & devices

Repetition: Sometimes answers sometimes across the semicolon. Rode me: the father as active subject, the son as object. Rhythmic mimesis: Dipping and rising falls, then rises, and the participles have no stated subject. Nautical imagery, a boat on a swell; full rhyme sod / plod.

Meaning & effect

The expert stoops to lift the nuisance, the poem's only touch, and the repeated adverb rations it: neither the falling nor the carrying is claimed as constant, which is why the tenderness convinces. Dipping and rising fits the riding boy and the walking man alike, so in the one embrace the grammar cannot separate their bodies. Plod, heavy and unheroic, keeps the hero human.

Lines 17–18
the child longed to become a ploughman himself / to copy the one-eyed squint and the braced arm
Language & devices

A plain statement of desire, then a chain of infinitives: grow up and plough, then close one eye and stiffen in asyndeton. Plough returns as an end-word from line 1, now a verb. Eye echoes line 10; arm is the first rhyme-word that belongs to the son.

Meaning & effect

To the boy, growing up and ploughing are one thing; life split the pair, and he grew up without ploughing. Being a ploughman means two gestures he has watched, so he copies the outward signs of the skill, not the judgement behind them, and his verbs act only on his own body. Stiffen shows how a child imagines manhood: rigidity, strain, holding firm.

Lines 19–20
but all he managed was to trail after him / in the big man's shade, all over the farm
Language & devices

Pseudo-cleft: the construction saves its one verb for the end, follow, the title-word's only appearance. The line is wholly trochaic, the only one that falls from start to finish, and runs on (enjambment) into the broad shadow (symbol). Half-rhyme plough / follow; round repeats line 9.

Meaning & effect

A whole childhood reduced to one verb: ever is a child's absolute and an adult's sigh, and the falling rhythm and run-on syntax trail after the verb as he trailed after his father. Follow takes the rhyme-place furrow held in stanza 1 and nearly its sound: the father made furrows; the son followed them. The shadow shelters and eclipses at once, and where the team turned round with a purpose, the boy goes round the farm with none.

Lines 21–22
he admits he was a pest, forever losing his footing / forever chattering like a pup; then the present breaks in
Language & devices

Adult self-judgement in one noun, a nuisance, answering An expert. from the first line of stanza 2. Asyndetic list of participles, tripping, falling, running on into Yapping (onomatopoeia: a small dog). Anaphora: the first person opens stanzas 4, 5 and 6.

Meaning & effect

The adult names the child bluntly, in the word a grown-up uses of a child underfoot, completing the poem's only two verdicts on a person, one for each man. The participles are continuous and unfinished, the opposite of the father's single exact acts, and Yapping makes the boy a pup at a working man's heels: noise against the father's purposeful click.

Lines 22–23
forever chattering like a pup; then the present breaks in / now the roles reverse: the father is the unsteady one
Language & devices

Volta in mid-line: a full stop after always, then But today, the poem's only But, in its shortest line (seven syllables). Cleft sentence: my father is moved into the focus slot, so the clause after him is taken as given and only he is news; first present tense. Verbal echo: stumbled (line 13) returns as keeps stumbling, which half-rhymes with the son's falling.

Meaning & effect

Two words of time collide across the full stop, always, the whole of childhood, and today, and the turn arrives late and mid-line, like a thought that interrupts the speaker. The cleft treats someone stumbling behind as a fixture of the poem's world and changes only who it is: the follower is a role that outlasts its occupant, as the title implied. Keeps makes the stumbling as constant as the boy's always, and the poem never says why.

Line 24
he trails his son and refuses to leave
Language & devices

Behind me: after the place-phrases built on the father (his wake, his back, his shadow), the first built on the son, and it is the father it places. The modal will not means both 'refuses to' and plain 'won't', as one says of a problem or a memory, and it answers the habitual would of line 5. Idiom: the closing phrase is what one says to a pest; full rhyme today / away seals the poem.

Meaning & effect

The son is in front at last but has no verb: he is only me, the point the father is behind. The father keeps both verbs, and the second is a modal of will, so what survived the stumbling was his will. Behind me also means 'in my past', and the refusal to leave denies that comfort. The pest's idiom implies 'nuisance' without saying it: the son spares his father the word he used of himself.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Follower' is usually read as a clean reversal: the boy stumbles behind his father, and then, today, the father stumbles behind the man. The symmetry is real, and the poem works hard to make it exact. But its grammar keeps a different account. What passes from son to father in the last stanza is the weakness, the stumbling and the place behind, while the authority stays where it was. The son gets in front of his father; he never gets his father's sentence. That is the poem's harder discovery: overtaking a parent is not the same as leaving him. The way to see it is to track who owns the verbs and the positions.

In the first three stanzas the father owns very few verbs. He worked, he would set the wing and fit the sock, adjustments made before the work begins; everything else that moves is something obeying him. The horses strained, the sod rolled over, the team turned round, and even His eye takes its own verbs, while his decisive acts are tucked into small phrases, at his clicking tongue, with a single pluck. Mastery appears as causation: he is rarely the subject, and the world does what he means. The son, meanwhile, is almost absent. For twelve lines he exists only as the poem's first word, My, a possessive attached to someone else, and only when I arrives, already in the father's wake, do we learn where the watcher has been standing. The portrait was a follower's view all along, and at its centre is the child's verdict, An expert., a sentence with no verb.

When the son becomes a grammatical subject, it is of accidents: I stumbled, Fell. Every place he occupies belongs to the father (his wake, the sod he turned, his back, his plod, his shadow). In the one embrace the grammar cannot tell them apart, since Dipping and rising has no stated subject. The wish of stanza 5 is all infinitives that never become deeds, and the pseudo-cleft of line 19 loads a whole childhood onto one verb, follow, which takes the rhyme-place, and nearly the sound, of the father's furrow.

The last stanza opens with the son's label for himself, a nuisance, answering An expert.: one verdict for each man, each in a stanza's first line. Then two time-words collide across a full stop, always and But today, and the reversal comes as a cleft sentence, which takes the stumbling as given and makes only the stumbler news. The place behind is still there; the father now fills it, and keeps stumbling, the boy's verb from line 13. The rhymes follow suit: the son's words open them and the father's close them. So far the exchange is complete. But look at the last sentence. The son, in front at last, has no verb in it; he is only me. The father has both verbs, and the second is a modal of will. The poem has used that modal once before, in its past form, when he would set the wing, and the would of his habit has become the will not of his refusal. What the father kept, when he lost his footing, was his will. And the present has no image: no field, no plough, no sea, no shadow, only a man, a pronoun and a direction.

The strongest objection is that this makes too much of grammar. The poem's plain sense is the reversal: the strong man is now the stumbling one, the son leads, and the title, which named the boy, now names the father. But is the poem's only adversative, and it announces exactly that change. On this view the ending is simply a grown son's mixed feelings about a father who has come to depend on him.

That reading is right about what changes and wrong about what it means. The poem never calls the father old, ill or dependent, and the son does nothing for him in the last sentence. It gives the father the boy's verb and the boy's place, and stops; it withholds the boy's noun, and it leaves the will where it was. The reversal is a mirror, not a handover. The son sees in his father the child he was, and finds himself in his father's old place, the one with a follower at his heels.

Behind me has a second sense: what is behind us is supposed to be over. This past will not stay there, and the poem is the proof. The son who could not cut a furrow has cut twenty-four lines in six even quatrains, and the father is held in them for good, still the subject of the last verbs and the owner of the last sound. Yet only five of the twelve rhyme-pairs are full, as if the son's lines come close to the father's exactly and never quite meet it. 'Follower' does not settle whether the presence at his back is comfort, haunting or reproach. It settles only that he cannot see it, and cannot leave it.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form

Six quatrains, twenty-four lines: a first-person lyric of memory in three movements. The father works (stanzas 1–3), the child follows (4–5), the present arrives (6).

Metre

A loose four-beat line with an iambic tendency, seven to nine syllables: not strict iambic tetrameter.

Rhyme

ABAB in every stanza: five full rhymes, seven half-rhymes, six feminine endings.

Turns

Two: at the headrig, where a sentence wheels across the stanza break (lines 8–10), and the volta, But today, in mid-line 22.

Stanza logic

The poem is laid out like a field: twelve lines for the father, twelve for the son. The father's half moves from the whole man to the smallest organ of his skill: shoulders, tongue, hands, the earth's response, the turn and, last, the eye. The son's half moves from what he did (stumbled, Fell) to what he wanted, to what he was (a nuisance), and I opens each of its stanzas, so it reads as a run of confessions. The proportions shrink, twelve lines of mastery, nine and a half of childhood, two and a half of the present, yet the shortest movement overturns everything before it, as a single pluck turns the whole team.

Metre: a four-beat line that stumbles

The ear hears a walking four-beat pulse, the plod, constantly varied, and the variations carry the meaning. The father's lines gather stresses on the work: horse-plough, full sail strung, bright steel-pointed, team turned round, so the verse feels the weight he handles. The full stop after An expert. halts the metre on the third syllable: awe heard as a pause. The son's lines fall. Line 14 drops on its first syllable, Fell, as the boy does; Dipping and rising goes down, then up, the rocking walk felt from the father's back; and line 19, four trochees, is the only line that falls from start to finish, the verdict follow trailing behind its own beat. In the last stanza the metre itself stumbles: nine syllables, then seven (the shortest line, at the turn), then nine and nine, the last crowded with stresses in its refusal, unsteady and immovable at once.

Rhyme, worked out

Stanza A rhyme (lines 1, 3) B rhyme (lines 2, 4)
1 plough / furrow: half strung / tongue: full
2 wing / breaking: half sock / pluck: half (/k/)
3 round / ground: full eye / exactly: half
4 wake / back: half (/k/) sod / plod: full
5 plough / follow: half arm / farm: full
6 falling / stumbling: half today / away: full

Every stanza keeps its ABAB shape, but only five of the twelve pairs chime fully, and every stanza except the second has exactly one full pair. Stanza 2, the stanza of technical words, has none: there the exact word (sock, headrig) matters more than the chime.

The repeated rhyme tells the story. In stanza 1 plough is the father's tool, a noun rhymed with furrow, the thing it makes; in stanza 5 it is a verb the boy wants, rhymed with follow, the thing he did. Furrow and follow share their first and last sounds and differ only between them, so the son's word sounds like a slightly mis-made copy of the father's.

Who owns the rhyme-words is as telling. All sixteen line-ends of stanzas 1–4 belong to the father's world, his tools, his body, his work, even in stanza 4, the son's own (wake, sod, back, plod). The son's words reach the line-end only in stanza 5, and the first is arm, a borrowed gesture. In stanza 6 the son's words open both rhymes (falling, today) and the father's close them (stumbling, away): the father now follows the son in the rhyme scheme itself, but the last sound is his.

The six feminine endings (furrow, breaking, exactly, follow, falling, stumbling) each leave a weak syllable trailing after the last beat, a small follower at the end of the line. In the final stanza both A-rhymes are feminine, so the falling-away sound gathers where the father stumbles, before the poem closes on its most emphatic full rhyme.

Lineation, enjambment and caesura

Nine line-ends run on without punctuation. In the father's stanzas they carry movement: the body strung across lines 2–3, the linked operations of 5–6, the headrig turn across 8–9 and on into 10, and the eye left hanging at the end of 10. In the son's they carry following: the piggyback across 15–16; follow running on into the shadow (19–20), so the syntax trails its own verb; and, in the last stanza, two in a row, so that Behind me arrives at the start of the last line, literally behind the stumble.

Lines 10 and 22 share a design: a full stop in mid-line, then a new sentence begun at the line-end and run over, first the father's eye, then But today. The poem uses one device for its two great shifts of attention, the first narrowing in on his skill, the second turning from past to present.

Two clefts

The son's half has two emphatic constructions that answer each other. The pseudo-cleft of line 19 takes the doing as given and shrinks it to one verb, follow; the cleft of line 23 takes the stumbling as given and makes only the stumbler news, my father. In both the action is fixed and only its size or its agent changes: the follower's place outlasts whoever fills it. Between them the tense moves from past to present, and the present arrives with the father as its subject.

The two turns

The headrig turn and the volta answer each other. At the headrig the team wheels and comes back down the field alongside the furrow it has just cut. At But today the poem turns and comes back over its own material: stumbled returns as stumbling, following becomes being followed, the boy behind becomes the man in front. The last stanza is the return furrow, laid beside the first and running the other way.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Stanza 1 is full of breath and hiss, shoulders, sail, strung, shafts, horses, strained: wind in canvas and effort under strain. Against that soft background clicking is a sharp signal, and the click goes on under the rhymes. Two half-rhymes are pure /k/ consonance, sock / pluck and wake / back, and all four words name the father's doings: the share he fits, the tug he gives, the track he leaves, the back that carries the boy. A pl- family binds tool, gesture and gait, plough, pluck, plod, with polished close by, so the man who plods behind the plough and turns it with a pluck is one person in sound.

The father's stanzas are rich in long, rounded vowels, the /əʊ/ of shoulders, globed and rolled over, the /aʊ/ of plough, round and ground, as rounded as the shoulders and the turning sod. The son's turn to short vowels and the unstressed -ing of participles, Dipping and rising, tripping, falling, Yapping: the sounds of small, repeated, unfinished movements. One family crosses over. The weak -ow of the father's furrow and Narrowed returns in the son's follow and shadow, so the words of his following are made from the sounds of his father's work. By the last stanza the father's /əʊ/ and /aʊ/ have almost gone; only go keeps one, in the very phrase that says he will not leave.

Onomatopoeia carries two kinds of voice. The father's sounds are signals that work: a click sets two horses straining, a pluck turns the team. The child's is noise that achieves nothing, Yapping, a pup at a working man's heels. Yet the yapper grows into the family's man of words, and the poem is his voice doing at last what the click did: directing a heavy, living material with small, exact signals.

The ending is built in sound before it is stated. The second syllable of the boy's always is nearly the stressed syllable of away, so his endless yapping already holds the rhyme that will seal the father's refusal. Then will not go is a run of heavy monosyllables that slows the voice almost to a halt before away: the refusal is heard as weight, and the stumbling last line lands on the poem's firmest rhyme.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. Following and being behind

The title's motif runs through the son's whole life. First it is physical: the boy stumbles in the father's wake, the boot-print track, and the idiom 'in someone's wake' (left behind) is part of the meaning. Then it is imitation, To close one eye; then eclipse, his broad shadow, where to follow is to live in someone's shade, sheltered and unseen. Finally it changes owner, and the father is the one behind, out of sight at his son's back.

2. The sea in the field

Nautical imagery runs through a poem set on dry land: the full sail of the shoulders, strung like rigging; the sod that rolled over like a wave; the team going back into the land as a boat returns to sea; the boy in the wake; the piggyback Dipping and rising like a small boat on a swell. The images make the father a ship moving with grace through a heavy element, and they chart the relationship: the boy first bobs in his wake, then rides on him. In the last stanza the sea has gone, and so has every other image. The father has lost his element.

3. The eye

Skill lives in the eye. The father's eye is isolated at a line-end, then Narrowed and angled, then Mapping: the part that stands for his intelligence. The boy's ambition is to copy it, To close one eye, and the poem is the work of another eye, the child's, which watched closely enough to remember how his father's face changed. But the father's eye is always on the ground; it never turns on the son. In the last stanza the looking stops altogether: the father is behind, felt rather than seen.

4. Breaking and stumbling

Perfection is wholeness: the sod turns over without breaking. The definite article brings it back in stanza 4, where the boy falls on the polished sod, his father's finished surface, and the last stanza's tripping, falling piles up the opposite of the unbroken sod. Then the breaking reaches the father, who keeps stumbling, and the rhythm of the last line stumbles with him. What was whole at the start, the sod and the father, cannot stay whole, except in the poem.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Inheritance: the standard, not the trade

The son does not inherit the plough (the wish to grow up and plough ends in following), but he inherits the words (sock, headrig), the habit of exact attention, and the standard itself, exactly. The inheritance is also a debt: 'Digging' settles the account with the pen, while 'Follower' leaves it open, its mostly inexact rhymes keeping the shortfall audible.

02

Craft as art

Ploughing is a sequence of exact settings and signals: the plough set before work, then a click and a single pluck while the horses do the straining. By getting the craftsman's words right, the poem refuses the snobbery that treats farm work as unskilled, and judges field and poem by one standard.

03

Love without words or looks

The love is never stated. It shows as attention, the child's minute record of every gesture, and in one rationed moment of touch, carried Sometimes. The father speaks only in clicks and his eye stays on the ground, so father and son never meet face to face; the poem ends with the son facing forward and his father at his back.

04

Time turns the relationship over

Twenty-one and a half lines of past tense end in But today, and the reversal is built from words already used: stumbled becomes keeps stumbling, behind becomes Behind me. Time turns the people over as the plough turns the sod, but the places stay: someone is always behind, and only weakness and position change hands, never the father's will.

05

The land left, the memory that will not leave

The son has gone ahead into a life the father does not share. Guilt is never stated; it lives in a father left behind who will not leave, and the poem, a memory that would not go away, keeps him for good.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Is the stumbling literal?

The difficulty. The poem never says why the father stumbles. Old age is an inference: he is never called old, ill or dependent.

Competing readings. (a) Literal: years have passed and the body is failing. Evidence: today, the present continuous keeps, a physical verb, and the piggyback inverted, the man who carried the boy now trailing him. (b) Figurative: a memory or conscience that follows the son through adult life. Evidence: after But today the poem has no setting, only a direction; Behind me can also mean 'in my past', and the closing idiom is what one says of a thought. (c) Social: the expert of the field is out of step in the educated world his son now lives in, the life the scholarship opened and the father does not share. (d) Retrospective: since Patrick Heaney's death in 1986, readers hear a ghost.

What a strong answer does. It holds the literal and figurative senses together and uses the bareness of the last lines as evidence that the poem has left the field. The father of the past had shoulders, tongue, eye and back; the father of today has none of them, only a verb of failing and a verb of will.

2. The closing idiom: exasperation, haunting or devotion?

The difficulty. The last words are what one says of a pest, but they could equally describe a love that lasts.

Competing readings. Exasperation: the son has just called himself a nuisance, so the roles swap, irritation included; a man stumbling at your back slows you, keeps makes the drag as constant as the boy's always, and the modal hardens the tone. The hero of the field has become an encumbrance. Haunting or guilt: the son who left the land cannot escape his father's example, and the father is now out of sight, felt rather than seen, like a conscience. Devotion: the father goes on following because he loves, and the full rhyme with today makes his presence permanent.

What a strong answer does. It shows which words produce which tone. The pest's idiom brings the impatience; the modal splits the readings, since will not as refusal makes the persistence the father's choice (pestering or devotion), and as plain futurity makes it a fact, like a memory that will not fade (haunting). And the son withholds a noun: he gives his father his own childhood verb but not his childhood label, so the line implies 'nuisance' without saying it. The impatience is audible, and that honesty is what makes the earlier love credible.

3. Is the father idealised?

The difficulty. Stanzas 1–3 read as hero-worship. Is the portrait a child's myth?

Competing readings. Idealised: the child's-eye view enlarges him (globed, broad shadow), the sea imagery makes him a captain, An expert. admits no qualification, and he fills the first half of the poem as completely as he filled the field. Realistic: the labour is kept honest (strained, sweating, plod), and the kindness is rationed: he carried the boy Sometimes.

What a strong answer does. It separates the child's view, preserved intact in An expert., from the adult's frame (a nuisance, today), and adds one more piece of evidence: the father is never seen whole. He is shoulders, tongue, eye, back and finally a shadow, the parts that do the work, and the one time he is named whole in the present, he is out of sight behind his son. The monument is real to the child; the stumbling man is real to the son.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. globed like a full sail

Simile; absolute construction; stress cluster.

The first image of the father is a back seen from below, and the simile turns muscle into canvas. This sail is strung from the shafts, the plough's handles, down to the furrow, with no mast or yard, so the comparison never leaves the field: the man is rigged into his own apparatus, and the wind that fills him is the horses' pull. Read globed as a participle and the line has no main verb, so the father is held as a picture before he does anything, and the closing stresses make the voice carry his weight.

Intention and effect: Heaney opens at a child's eye-level, so the reader feels the scale against which the son will measure himself.

2. his clicking tongue and a single pluck

Onomatopoeia; musical overtone; enjambment across the stanza break.

Two tiny acts move two heavy horses. Clicking is the only sound the father makes in the poem, a hard /k/ obeyed without whip or shout; a single pluck carries a musical overtone (strings are plucked, and the back was strung), so control becomes an art. Set against the sweating team, the single tug measures skill as the gap between his ease and their labour. At the field's end the pluck hangs over the stanza break, and the team it turns comes into view only on the far side, so the line turns where the furrow turns.

Intention and effect: mastery is economy, and the form performs it: the reader goes round the headrig with the horses instead of being told about it.

3. An expert. and a nuisance

Minor sentence; paired verdicts; register.

These are the poem's only two verdicts on a person, and each sits in a stanza's opening line: the father's in stanza 2, the son's in stanza 6. An expert. is the child's word, a verbless fragment that admits no argument; a nuisance is the adult's, passed on himself in hindsight. Both are abstract words of judgement among concrete words of work, and expert (Latin expertus, 'proved by experience') names knowledge earned in the field rather than in school.

Intention and effect: the pair frames the poem as a judgement, the father's verdict delivered by the boy, the boy's by the man.

4. Mapping and exactly

Metaphor; semantic field of measurement; feminine ending; half-rhyme.

Narrowed and angled is the ploughman sighting along his line; Mapping makes ploughing map-making, a line drawn on a blank surface, so field and page come close. Exactly is the father's standard and becomes the poem's, yet the line that names it falls to a weak close, and its rhyme with eye is inexact.

Intention and effect: Heaney sets exactness up as the measure of everything, and lets his own verse admit that it cannot quite match the furrows.

5. his hob-nailed wake

Metaphor fusing land and sea; idiom; grammar of position.

The son's first appearance reveals where the watcher has been standing all along: behind. Iron-studded boot-prints become a ship's churned track, and the idiom 'in someone's wake' (left behind) belongs to the meaning: he follows in his father's footsteps literally, and fails even at that. From here every place the boy occupies is a his phrase: wake, back, plod, shadow.

Intention and effect: the son introduces himself through failure and position, so the reader meets a boy who can only be located in relation to his father.

6. rode me on his back

Repetition; causative verb; participles without a subject.

The poem's only touch is rationed: the boy fell sometimes and was carried Sometimes, and neither is claimed as constant, which is why the tenderness convinces. Rode me makes the father rider and horse at once, bearing the weight like his team, and it is the last time he acts on anything: his later verbs take no object. Then Dipping and rising arrives with no stated subject and fits the riding boy and the walking man equally.

Intention and effect: the moment humanises the hero and plants the image the last stanza inverts, when the weight falls the other way.

7. follow and his broad shadow

Pseudo-cleft; trochaic line; rhyme shift; symbol.

The wish of stanza 5 is all infinitives, and this is its verdict: the pseudo-cleft loads a whole childhood onto the one appearance of the title-word. The line falls in four trochees and runs on over its end, so even the syntax follows. Follow takes the rhyme-place, and nearly the sound, of the father's furrow: he made furrows; the son only followed them, into a shadow that shelters and eclipses at once.

Intention and effect: the rhyme scheme tells the story of a failed inheritance before the sentence confesses it, while the poem's own furrow-like quatrains quietly contest the verdict.

8. But today and keeps stumbling

Volta; cleft sentence; verbal echo; rhyme transfer.

The turn comes late and mid-line, in the poem's shortest line, like a thought that interrupts the speaker. The cleft then takes the stumbling for granted and makes only its subject news: someone is still stumbling behind; the surprise is who. He inherits the boy's verb, stumbled returning as keeps stumbling, and keeps makes it a pattern as constant as the boy's always. Even the rhyme hands it over, the father's stumbling answering the son's falling.

Intention and effect: Heaney builds the reversal entirely from recycled material, so the reader recognises the father's new state as the boy's old one: the mirror the poem turns on.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Formalist

Shows how much of the poem's feeling lives in its machinery: a field of twelve lines up with the father and twelve back with the son, one sentence that turns across a stanza break at the headrig, a rhyme scheme that narrates (furrow, then follow), and a last quatrain that runs back over the poem's own words like a return furrow.

What it flattens: the human relationship. A purely formal reading makes the father a pretext for craft and loses the raw feeling: tenderness, inadequacy, the impatience of will not go away.

Psychoanalytic

Sees a son defining himself against a powerful father. The father is all body and authority, globed shoulders and a broad shadow that shelters and eclipses; the son is small, noisy and falling, and wants not just to farm but to be the father (To close one eye). The figure who will not go away is a voice within the son, close to what psychoanalysis calls the superego, the internalised parent who judges. The son steps out in front; he cannot step out of the shadow.

What it flattens: the love. The poem shows no rivalry, only devotion and patience, and this lens can turn the piggyback into a power struggle the text does not support.

Marxist / materialist

Looks at labour, skill and class. The poem gives a farmer's skill the dignity of precise language (An expert, set the wing, Mapping), and it records a change in how the work was done: the horse-plough belonged to a world the tractor was replacing, so the expertise was becoming obsolete even as it was praised. The son's path from farm to education to writing is a story of social mobility in which the next generation leaves manual labour and the father is left behind.

What it flattens: the intimacy. The father is not a type of the rural worker but a particular man who carried his son.

Gender

The poem's world is entirely male: a father, a son, a team of horses, a farm with no mother in it. Masculinity means size, strength, silence and control, and the boy fails on every count, small, noisy, falling. Yet he grows into a man of words, so the poem quietly values the tongue as well as the arm, and inheritance runs entirely through the male line and the field.

What it flattens: the gentleness. The father who carries the boy is not only a model of hard masculinity, and the poem's tenderness is part of its idea of what a man is.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. An elegy written in advance

The poem as a memorial that fixes the father at his best, at the plough, for good: a eulogy that works as a funerary monument, with a funeral half-hidden in its vocabulary, the wake, the sod, and a father who will not leave, like a ghost.

Evidence: the monumental first half; the past tense of stanzas 1–5; wake and sod; the poem's later life after Patrick Heaney's death in 1986.

Weakness: in 1966 the father was alive, and the last stanza is in the present tense. The funeral puns are a reader's associations: the wake kept for the dead is a different word from a ship's wake.

2. A poem about writing poems

The furrow is the line, the field the page, the headrig the line-break, and exactly the poet's standard: the son who could not plough becomes a ploughman of verse, his father's follower in another medium.

Evidence: 'verse' from versus, the plough's turning; the sentence that crosses a stanza break exactly at the turn; Mapping; the poem's even quatrains; 'Digging', where the pen replaces the spade.

Weakness: 'Follower' never mentions writing, and the reading can turn the father into a metaphor for the son's career. It also struggles with the last stanza, which is about a presence, not a craft.

3. The son's departure from tradition

The father stands for a whole way of life, rural, manual, traditional, and the son is the one who left it: the father's halting gait in the last stanza admits that the poet is moving away from a tradition he loves.

Evidence: the horse-plough, already passing; the failed wish to grow up and plough; the father now out of step behind him; Heaney's own scholarship at twelve.

Weakness: it makes the father an emblem. The poem's details are personal (the piggyback, the click, the eye), and nothing in the text mentions education, the city or modernity: those come from the biography.

4. The resentful son

Some readers hear hostility: an overbearing father whose shadow blots the boy out, and a last line of pure exasperation.

Evidence: the broad shadow; the son's harsh words about himself (a nuisance, Yapping), which may echo what the child was told; the pest's idiom, go away.

Weakness: there is no cruelty anywhere in the poem. The father carries the boy, the boy longs to be like him, and the admiration is total; whatever impatience the ending holds is the son's, not the father's.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

Follower

Analysis
  • No article → a role, not a person → can change hands
  • Walks behind / disciple / successor (eldest son; never took the farm)
  • 'Digging': 'no spade to follow' → follow = succeed in the trade
Effect, style & response
  • Noun never in poem; follow once (l. 19) = the son's
  • Father only keeps stumbling, never 'follows' → reader makes the transfer

Context

Analysis
  • Heaney 1939–2013; Mossbawn, Co. Derry; eldest of 9
  • Father Patrick: small farm, cattle dealer; 'notably sparing of talk'
  • Scholarship at 12 → 'the decisive' departure; 'the pen's lighter than the spade'
  • Tractors replacing horses from early 1950s → craft already passing
Effect, style & response
  • Father alive in 1966 (d. 1986) → NOT about a dead man
  • 'Digging': pen for spade → 'Follower' refuses the consolation

Structure

Analysis
  • 6 quatrains: 12 lines father / 12 son (last 2½ = now)
  • Loose four-beat line, iambic tendency; 7–9 syllables
  • I opens st 4, 5, 6 → confessions
  • Pseudo-cleft l. 19 (what he did: follow) ↔ cleft l. 23 (who does it now) → place fixed, person changes
Effect, style & response
  • Last stanza = the return furrow

Rhyme

Analysis
  • ABAB; 5 full, 7 half; 6 feminine endings
  • plough: noun + furrow (st 1) → verb + follow (st 5)
  • St 1–4 rhyme-words all the father's (even st 4: wake / sod / back / plod)
Effect, style & response
  • St 6: son opens (falling, today) → father closes (stumbling, away) → father follows in the rhyme
  • Close, never exact → imitation never perfect
1–4

globed like a full sail

Analysis
  • My father worked → defined by labour; son only My for 12 lines
  • Sail strung between shafts (handles) + furrow; filled by the team's pull → he holds + steers it
  • Horses strain at his clicking tongue → father = cause, not subject
Effect, style & response
  • Child's-eye view: from behind, from below
  • Only parts: shoulders, tongue, eye, back, shadow
5–7

An expert.

Analysis
  • Minor sentence → absolute verdict; hero-worship
  • ↔ a nuisance (st 6) = only 2 verdicts on a person
  • set the wing (angled blade: cut + lift); fit the sock (= share) → preparation, not effort
Effect, style & response
  • Settings (l. 5–6) → sod turns without breaking (l. 7): cause → effect; wholeness = the standard
  • sock, headrig → he inherited the words
8–12

a single pluck

Analysis
  • Headrig = unploughed strip for turning → only stanza-crossing sentence → break = the page's headrig
  • single pluck vs sweating team → ease vs labour = skill
  • Eye = synecdoche for judgement: narrowed / angled / mapping / exactly
Effect, style & response
  • Eye on the ground → never on the son
  • Exactness line itself loose (eye / exactly); half 1 ends exactly ↔ half 2 away
13–16

hob-nailed wake

Analysis
  • Son enters at l. 13 → halfway → watcher was behind all along
  • stumbled vs father's set, fit
  • Falls on the polished sod = l. 7's sod → father's finished work
  • sometimes ×2 → honest, rationed
Effect, style & response
  • rode me = father's last verb with an object
  • Dipping and rising → no subject → one body
  • plod → unheroic, human
17–20

broad shadow

Analysis
  • grow up and plough → grew up, didn't plough
  • Infinitives = wishes; only objects = own body (one eye, my arm)
  • Pseudo-cleft → all weight on follow; line wholly trochaic
Effect, style & response
  • Shadow = shelter + eclipse
  • round: team turned round (purpose) → boy round the farm (circling)
  • Hidden pride: quatrains = furrows → followed in another field
21–22

a nuisance

Analysis
  • Blunt hindsight (rue? fond?)
  • tripping, falling → asyndeton, restless
  • Yapping (noise) vs clicking (signal)
Effect, style & response
  • always ↔ today → time-words collide; shortest line
  • Only But → volta mid-line, like a sudden thought
22–24

keeps stumbling

Analysis
  • Son's verb (l. 13) → father's → mirror
  • Cleft: stumbling = given, stumbler = news → role outlasts its occupant
  • Son = me, no verb; father has both verbs
  • would → will not (refuses / won't) → will survives
  • 'nuisance' withheld → implied by the pest's idiom
Effect, style & response
  • Behind me = at my back + in my past
  • No image after the volta
  • Never says old / dependent → age / memory / guilt / love

Sound

Analysis
  • /k/: clicking → sock / pluck, wake / back (father's doings)
  • pl-: plough, pluck, plod, polished
  • Long round vowels (father) vs short + -ing (son)
Effect, style & response
  • -ow: furrow, Narrowed → follow, shadow
  • always → away: the rhyme hidden in the yapping
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Storyteller' (Liz Lochhead)

Link: an older figure practising a craft, her storytelling 'like spinning', his father An expert at the plough. Shared technique: a tongue at work (her 'tongue clacked', his clicking tongue) and an ending that carries the old into the young: her stories hang in 'the sleeping heads of the children', his father will not go away. Difference: Lochhead's inheritance succeeds and the stories fly again; Heaney's son fails to inherit the craft and carries his father instead, half burden, half blessing.

With 'Before the Sun' (Charles Mungoshi)

Link: a boy and adult work: Mungoshi's splits a big log with 'the sharp axe', because 'when you are fourteen' big logs are what you want; Heaney's wanted to grow up and plough. Shared technique: a grown-up presence seen by a child, a sun that 'winks / like a grown-up', a father globed above him. Difference: Mungoshi's boy can do the work, joyfully, in the present tense; Heaney's can only follow, and writes from a reversal Mungoshi's morning never reaches.

With 'The Cockroach' (Kevin Halligan)

Link: the watcher and the watched: Halligan's speaker begins 'I watched'; Heaney's spends three stanzas watching his father. Shared technique: a late turn that collapses observer into observed ('I thought I recognised myself'; the watched man now following the watcher). Difference: Halligan's mirror is a stranger's aimless 'crooked rings'; Heaney's is the most familiar person in his world, and the mirror is time: the son sees the child he was in the father behind him.

With 'Sonnet 18' (William Shakespeare)

Link: lines that keep a person against time: Shakespeare's beloved lives 'in eternal lines', Heaney's father goes on ploughing in lines that are kin to furrows. Shared technique: a volta on 'But' ('But thy eternal summer'; But today) and a shadow (Death's 'shade'; the father's broad shadow). Difference: Shakespeare's 'But' defeats time and Heaney's admits it: the beloved never fades, the expert stumbles, and the only consolation is that he will not go away.

With 'Where I Come From' (Elizabeth Brewster)

Link: 'People are made of places', and Heaney's speaker is made of a farm and a father, a rural childhood carried into adult life elsewhere. Shared technique: concrete country detail (hens 'clucking aimlessly'; a hob-nailed wake) and a last movement in which the past breaks into the present ('A door in the mind'; But today). Difference: Brewster's memory is of a place and arrives like bracing weather; Heaney's is of a person, a relationship with obligations, which is why it can feel like a burden as well as a gift.
