CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Liz Lochhead (b. 1947)

Born in Lanarkshire in 1947, Lochhead is a poet, playwright, translator into Scots and a performer of her own work, and is well known as a feminist writer. She was Scotland's national poet, the Makar, from 2011 to 2016.

The Grimm Sisters and the Grimms' tellers

'Storyteller' is the opening poem of The Grimm Sisters (1981), whose title swaps the Brothers Grimm into the feminine and whose poems retell familiar fairy tales from a female viewpoint, often ironically.

Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm's Kinder- und Hausmärchen (1812, 1815) was presented as the voice of the German folk, but most of its informants were educated young women in and around Kassel, none named on the title page. The famous exception is Dorothea Viehmann, a tailor's wife whom Wilhelm's preface praised, unnamed, for telling her tales vividly and repeating them without alteration; her portrait in the 1819 edition fixed the image of the peasant 'tale-wife'. Where the 1970s feminist re-visions of the fairy tale — Anne Sexton's Transformations (1971), Angela Carter's The Bloody Chamber (1979) — rewrote the tales, 'Storyteller' rewrites no tale at all: it restores the teller.

Spinning and telling

Until mechanisation, spinning was the defining women's labour of Europe: 'spinster' first meant a woman who spins, and 'the distaff side' is still the female line. Women spinning together on winter evenings — the German Spinnstube, the Scots 'rocking' — shared songs, gossip and tales. The fairy tales keep the link: Rumpelstiltskin spins straw into gold, Sleeping Beauty pricks her finger on a spindle, and the frontispiece of Perrault's tales (1697) shows an old woman with her distaff telling stories to children. English keeps it in 'to spin a yarn'.

The kitchen and the dawn

A dresser is the shelved cupboard on which a household displayed its plates; delftware is tin-glazed earthenware, originally from Delft, and in Scots 'delf' came to mean any crockery. Scouring meant scrubbing with sand, soda or ash; clogs were the footwear of field and mill workers across northern Europe.

The details locate no single village. A Scots-sounding kitchen (delf, sloven, shiftless) sits beside a Low Countries or north German dawn of clogs and flat fields, the landscape of the Grimms' tales. The setting is deliberately once-upon-a-time, and the unnamed woman is not identified with Viehmann or any real teller: she is a composite, standing for every woman who told tales by a fire.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Storyteller

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper.

TStoryteller
1she takes her seat — no capital letter, no name
2by a table scrubbed clean
3in a kitchen already brushed tidy
4by shelves of chipped blue-and-white Dutch-style crockery.
5The last scraps of light are hoarded away like food.
6Nobody could call the tales pointless,
7because while her voice rattled on
8one hand, or four women's hands, kept sewing;
9grain was scraped from its casing;
10scraps of cloth were joined into a quilt;
11or worn socks were mended.
12Nobody would ever smear her as lazy.
13Whether her housekeeping was slack or immaculate,
14whether her broth was thin or good —
15telling tales was her job: the central claim.
16A simile: it resembled making thread,
17drawing nothing but air into one unbreakable strand —
18the strand completed. Then, every evening,
19she kept us in suspense, breath stopped,
20for a conclusion we had long memorised.
21Then, as dawn broke,
22while the women roused themselves to light the hearth,
23while a farm-worker groped for wooden shoes,
24while pale, colourless light spread across level land,
25the tales melted away in the spiral of the ear —
26yet they (the turn)
27roosted head-down, like bats,
28inside the dreaming children's minds,
29until they took wing once more
30in the night that belongs to the teller(s).

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Storyteller
Language & devices

Title as a bare noun — no article, no name, no possessive — so it reads like a trade ('Weaver', 'Blacksmith'), the compound joining the thing made to its maker. It returns, pluralised and without an apostrophe, as storytellers in the last line, so title and ending frame the poem.

Meaning & effect

The woman is given a role before anything else, and never a name: in one word, storytelling is an occupation, a skill practised and valued like any other. At the head of The Grimm Sisters, it points to the tellers, many of them women, behind the most famous fairy-tale collection in Europe. By the last line the role has widened to storytellers: what survives is the office, handed on, not the individual.

Line 1
sat down
Language & devices

Lower-case opening on a pronoun with no antecedent: we are never told who she is. Three evenly stressed monosyllables. In medias res: the poem begins as if a story were already under way.

Meaning & effect

The missing capital makes the opening a continuation rather than a start, as if picking up a tale about someone who needs no introduction. Sitting down is a double change of state — the day's chores end and the evening's other work begins — and the teller's authority starts when she takes her seat. Like most of the women whose tales reached print, she is never named.

Lines 2–4
scoured table … cracked delft
Language & devices

Parallel prepositional phrases move the eye outward from table to room. The past participles scoured and swept describe finished labour without saying who did it, bound by sibilance from sat onward; plosives then harden cracked delft (blue-and-white crockery). The first full stop closes the opening sentence.

Meaning & effect

The setting is built out of housework already done — the hard, daily, unseen jobs of a poor household — so the stanza's order, labour then story, is the order of the woman's day. The agentless participles raise the question the whole poem asks: whose work counts, and who gets the credit? The only decorative things in the room are damaged but kept and displayed, like the stories themselves: old, worn by handling, still treasured and in use.

Line 5
every last crumb of daylight
Language & devices

Metaphor: daylight as food — crumb, and the idiom salted away (hoarded, as meat or fish is preserved in salt). Hyperbole of thrift in every last; an agentless passive names no hoarder. Sentence-initial And is the connective of spoken narrative.

Meaning & effect

In a household this poor even daylight is rationed like bread, used to the last scrap and put away. The idiom cuts two ways — used up, and also preserved — which anticipates the ending, where the stories are stored, unseen, in the children. Darkness is not a loss but the start of the storyteller's time.

Line 6
No one could say
Language & devices

Litotes: nobody could call the stories useless — praise by denying an accusation. useless is the poem's first evaluative word; the definite article in the stories implies a known repertoire. A falling rhythm that line 12 will repeat exactly.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from description to argument, anticipating a hostile voice — practical, thrifty, suspicious of idleness — and answering it in its own terms. The praise is deliberately grudging: not 'the stories were wonderful' but 'nobody could call them useless'. That is how a hard-working community expresses approval, and it convinces more than enthusiasm would.

Lines 7–8
the tongue clacked
Language & devices

Causal for introduces the evidence. Synecdoche: the tongue for the teller, fingers for the women working. Onomatopoeia: clacked, a hard, wooden sound. Alliteration in five or forty fingers, over a regular trochaic beat like a needle going in and out.

Meaning & effect

The stories are first justified by what happens while they are told: the listeners' hands keep sewing. Clacked, the verb for a gossip's tongue, becomes the sound of a tool keeping time with the needles. Five or forty is a teller's offhand arithmetic — one hand or four women's worth — and the tongue, not 'her tongue', describes a function as much as a person.

Lines 9–11
grated from the husk
Language & devices

An asyndetic list of chores in three agentless passives (was grated, was pieced, was done), with alliteration in patchwork / pieced and darning / done. The lines shrink and settle on a firm full stop; or offers alternatives, a typical evening rather than one night.

Meaning & effect

A catalogue of women's making-do — husking grain, piecing patchwork, darning — each turning waste or raw material into something of use, and each a figure for how a tale is made: pieced from inherited scraps, mended where it has worn thin. The passives erase the workers; the work simply gets done, by no one in particular, which is exactly the invisibility the poem sets out to correct.

Lines 12–14
slander her shiftless … sloven or spotless
Language & devices

Ellipsis: line 12 has no main verb ('[There was] never the one to…'), a spoken, almost proverbial idiom. slander is quasi-legal, a false and damaging accusation, and shiftless (lazy) echoes useless in line 6's exact rhythm. Then inversion in a verbless sentence of two antitheses bound by sibilance — sloven or spotless, Dishwater or tasty — Dishwater being a blunt, homely insult for thin soup.

Meaning & effect

The second defence moves from the stories to the woman: nobody ever called her lazy, a serious charge where women are measured by industry. She is exempt from the two standards every other woman is judged by, a clean house and a good table, because her real work lay elsewhere: she is valued as one would value an artist. The scrambled syntax makes us rebuild the sense like a listener following a run-on speaker, and Dishwater keeps the portrait honest — no idealised peasant kitchen.

Line 15
To tell the stories
Language & devices

A plain declarative, almost all monosyllables, in the poem's one regular line of iambic tetrameter. End-stopped at the hinge, the fifteenth of thirty lines, it ends on the stressed work.

Meaning & effect

The thesis, stated with the flat certainty of a proverb. Two stanzas of defence end not with 'as good as work' but with an outright claim — her work — that answers both useless and shiftless. Against a tradition that dismissed women's talk as chatter and left their unpaid labour uncounted, the line insists that cultural labour is labour, and the regular metre makes it sound like something everyone has always known.

Lines 16–18
like spinning … single strongest
Language & devices

Simile: storytelling was like spinning, the governing comparison, playing on 'to spin a yarn'. Paradox: gathering air into the strongest thread; superlative single strongest. Enjambment leaves the adjectives hanging until thread arrives on the next line, closed by a hard caesura.

Meaning & effect

Having called storytelling work, the poem says what kind: spinning, for centuries the defining female craft. The storyteller twists air — breath, words, almost nothing — into the strongest thing the community owns, the narrative thread that holds it together, and the line-break draws the thread across the gap. Spinning also outranks the stitching and darning of stanza 2, since it makes the thread they use; read as Lochhead's own art, it defines a poem's line, breath gathered into one strong strand (an 'air' is also a tune).

Lines 18–20
Night in … knew by heart
Language & devices

Night in clips 'night in, night out' — ellipsis compressing habit into two words. The first-person plural enters for the only time (us, we), with habitual she'd. Enjambment across held / breath; paradox of suspense over an ending known by heart.

Meaning & effect

The speaker is revealed as one of the listening children, remembering from adulthood. The teller's power is physical — she stops her audience breathing, and the line-break makes us do the same. Everyone knew the ending and the suspense was real anyway, because the pleasure lay in the telling and the ritual, not in surprise; by heart means memorised, and also says where the stories live.

Lines 21–24
first light … thin grey light
Language & devices

Sentence-initial And echoes line 5, and first light answers every last crumb, framing the night. Then anaphora and tricolon: three clauses beginning as hold back the main verb, with synecdoche in the peasant's feet, alliteration on f (fire, feet felt for, flat fields) and drained, monochrome imagery in thin grey light.

Meaning & effect

The clock turns: light in this poem is the medium of labour, so its return sends the stories into retreat and begins the women's day, again, with work at the fire. The day is thin, colourless and watery, like the Dishwater soup, reversing the usual values: day is meagre, night rich. The delayed verb builds suspense — the form has learned its technique from the woman it describes.

Line 25
whorl of the ear
Language & devices

The main clause arrives at last: the stories dissolved, a metaphor of melting into liquid, like a dream at waking. whorl is a pun: the spiral of the outer ear and, in its oldest sense, the weighted wheel on a spindle that keeps it turning. A rocking, anapaestic rhythm.

Meaning & effect

At first this sounds like loss: daylight dissolves the stories as it dissolves dreams. But the pun completes the spinning simile — the teller's thread is wound onto the listener's ear, so listening finishes the craft. What dissolves is held, invisibly, in solution: absorbed rather than remembered, the stories begin their survival in their apparent defeat.

Lines 26–28
but … sleeping heads
Language & devices

Volta: but, on the shortest line (two syllables), turns loss into survival. Implied metaphor: the stories become bats, never named, roosting upside down; the reflexive hung themselves echoes stirred themselves (line 22), with a faint shadow of 'hanged' — personification shading into zoomorphism. Synecdoche: sleeping heads; the speaker now says the children, not us.

Meaning & effect

The stories do not die with the night; they roost. Bats are an exact emblem for oral tales — creatures of the dark that find their way by sound, invisible by day, hanging above the children they now live in — and as the women stir themselves awake the stories put themselves to sleep, needing the teller no longer. Upside down suits the inverted logic of dreams and of fairy tales, where the youngest child wins. The shift to the children puts the speaker outside, watching a new generation receive what she once received.

Lines 29–30
flew again … storytellers night
Language & devices

flew completes the unnamed bat metaphor and again makes the ending cyclical; the last word, night, echoes Night in (line 18). storytellers is printed without an apostrophe — an ambiguity: her night, every teller's night, or a compound like 'market day'.

Meaning & effect

The cycle closes and reopens: night returns, and with it the stories, flying free of the heads that kept them. Ending on night, not on the teller or the children, confirms darkness as the generative time. The open apostrophe is the poem's last act of handing on, and the poem itself is the proof: the stories she told are flying again, in Lochhead's words.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Storyteller' is an argument dressed as a memory. It sets out to win a case — that a woman's storytelling is work — and wins it in the language of the people who would deny it: thrift, use, industry. Then, having won, it leaves that language behind. The stories end the poem not as tools that kept the sewing going but as wilful creatures that roost and fly on their own terms. The poem travels from a kitchen economy, where everything is scoured, salted, grated, pieced and counted, to a natural history of the imagination, and it makes the journey in the shape of a told tale — dusk, night, dawn, night again — so that it demonstrates the craft it defends.

The opening is all economy. The woman arrives without a capital or a name, in a room made of finished labour — a scoured table, a swept kitchen — where not even light is wasted: every last crumb of daylight is salted away, stored like food against hard times. The participles and passives name no worker, and that invisibility is the poem's real subject: women's work everywhere, credited nowhere. The storyteller sits down exactly where the countable work stops.

Stanza 2 imagines the charge — that the stories were useless — and answers it shrewdly, in the accuser's own currency. Nobody could say so, because while the tongue clacked the listeners' hands stitched, grated, pieced and darned. Lochhead does not yet claim the stories are valuable in themselves, only that they kept the work going: tongue and fingers share one sentence, one rhythm, one function.

Stanza 3 is the hinge, in three steps. First the woman herself is defended: nobody would slander her shiftless, whether her house was slovenly or spotless, her soup Dishwater or tasty — she alone is exempt from the standards every other woman is judged by. Second, the defence collapses into a verdict at the exact midpoint: telling the stories was her work — not like work, work. Third, what kind of work, and the tone turns from argument to wonder: like spinning, gathering air into the single strongest thread. Spinning is the craft the others depend on, since stitching and darning need its thread; the storyteller does not merely accompany the household's work but produces its most necessary material, out of breath. Then the poem lets slip who is speaking — she'd have us waiting, breath held, for an ending known by heart. The speaker was one of the children, and the case is now made by evidence rather than argument: a remembered body, holding its breath.

The final stanza is a single sentence that performs the teller's craft. Three as clauses hold back the main verb while dawn arrives — the women rousing themselves to the fire, feet groping for clogs, a thin grey light over flat fields — a day as meagre as the dishwater soup, whose arrival seems to defeat the night: the stories dissolved. Then comes the two-syllable turn, but, and the stories hang themselves upside down in the children's sleeping heads until they fly again.

The bats answer everything the poem has argued. They are not useful; they grate no corn and darn no socks. They belong to the dark, find their way by sound, keep their own hours and need no teller. The reflexive hung themselves answers the women who stirred themselves: one shift wakes as the other sleeps. And the speaker who was one of us now says the children, an adult outside the scene. The poem we are reading is the proof: the stories are flying again, in another teller's voice.

The strongest objection is that the poem concedes too much. Defending stories because they kept the needles moving, and calling telling work, it seems to accept the very work-ethic that dismissed women's talk: art must earn its keep. A second objection is nostalgia — a placeless peasantry of delft and clogs, as manufactured as the Grimms' own image of the tale-wife. Both describe real features of the poem, and both are answered by its shape. The language of use is tactical: Lochhead meets the hostile voice on its own terms (No one could say), wins, and moves beyond it into an image no utilitarian could value. And the poem's honesty keeps spoiling the idyll — the delft is cracked, the soup may be dishwater, the dawn is grey and the day begins in labour. The composite setting is deliberate: a poem about stories is told as a story, with an unnamed she, a once-upon-a-time kitchen and a fairy-tale logic of creatures and flight. It honours the woman behind all the villages and shows her art outliving her, which is the only credit the oral tradition ever gave.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form

Free verse: no rhyme scheme, no fixed metre, no regular stanza length. A portrait that is also a defence (stanzas 2–3 argue a case), a memory (the speaker was a listener) and, as the opening poem of The Grimm Sisters, a frame for the collection.

Stanzas

Thirty lines in four stanzas of 5, 6, 9 and 10 lines, each longer than the last, each a stretch of time.

Voice & tense

Third person, with one brief break into the first-person plural (us, we, lines 19–20). Past tense, much of it habitual (she'd have us waiting).

Turns

A shift at lines 15–16 from argument to celebration (verdict, then simile), and a volta at line 26, the shortest line, where but turns loss into survival.

A shape that grows

The stanzas lengthen — five lines, six, nine, ten — as a thread is drawn out and a story gathers force. They also make a complete cycle of time: dusk, the chores done and the last light put away; the working evening, voice and fingers together; the night's telling and the held breath; then dawn to the following night, so the poem ends where the next telling begins. It opens with daylight salted away, ends on night and brings the title word back in its last line. Nothing is resolved because nothing needs to be: the cycle is the point.

Inside the cycle the poem argues in sequence: description, a defence of the stories (not useless), a defence of the woman (never shiftless), then the verdict, her work, at line 15 — the fifteenth of thirty, closing the first half. Everything after it is demonstration rather than argument: the spinning simile, the remembered suspense, the stories' survival.

Metre and rhythm

Lochhead's free verse is not shapeless; its rhythms change with what is being described.

Line Stress pattern What it does
6 and 12 (No one could say, slander her shiftless) / x x / x / x x / x one falling rhythm for both accusations, so useless and shiftless sound like one voice
8–9 (five or forty fingers, grated from the husk) / x / x / x / a regular trochaic beat: the chores keep time like a needle going in and out
15 (her work) x / x / x / x / the only regular iambic line, giving the thesis the ring of a proverb
18 (Night in) / / / three stresses split by a full stop: the thread is finished, the night begins
25 (whorl of the ear) x / x x / x x / x x / a rocking, lullaby rhythm as the stories melt into sleep
26 (but) x / the shortest line, two syllables, and the turn

Line 24 is heavy by contrast — as many as seven of its nine syllables can take a stress — so the dawn light spreads slowly and flatly across it. Lines lengthen for the big tableaux (line 5, the longest; 13; 22; 25) and shrink to two or three syllables at the hinges: the opening, Night in, the volta.

The one rhyme that matters

There is no rhyme scheme; the music is the music of speech — stress, alliteration, the repeated '-less'. The single full chime is structural. Light and night recur through the poem (daylight, Night in, first light, grey light, night), and the last stanza's first and last lines end on exactly that rhyme. The final sentence travels from one to the other, and the chime makes the return of the storytelling night feel inevitable.

Syntax: who does what

The grammar carries the poem's argument about invisible labour. Stanza 1 uses agentless participles (scoured, swept) and a passive (salted away); stanza 2 lists chores in three agentless passives (was grated, was pieced, was done). Work is everywhere and the workers nowhere: the only active agents in the first two stanzas are she and parts of bodies, the tongue and fingers. In the last stanza the women stirred themselves, feet feel for clogs, light washes the fields — and then the stories become the subject. They dissolved, hung themselves, flew: by the end they are the poem's most independent actors.

Stanza 3 bends word order like speech. Line 12 has no main verb, and lines 13–14 form a verbless sentence the reader must rebuild, as a listener follows a run-on speaker; sentence-initial And (lines 5 and 21) is the connective of oral narrative, events simply following one another. The last stanza is a periodic sentence: three as clauses delay the main clause for four lines, the stories dissolved seems to end the story, and but reverses it. Setting, apparent loss, reversal, resolution — the sentence has the shape of a tale, and builds suspense exactly as the storyteller did.

Lineation and punctuation

The line-breaks are placed for meaning. single strongest / thread draws the thread across the gap as a spinner draws out fibre; held / breath makes the reader pause, breath held; line 26, two syllables ending on a bare pronoun, suspends the reader before the stories hung. Short lines act as hinges and long lines carry the tableaux — the rhythm of a voice drawing breath. Punctuation is sparse (the ten-line final sentence runs without a comma), and capitals appear only at sentence starts, with one exception: Dishwater, mid-sentence at the start of line 14, which gives the homely insult a proverbial weight. The opening has no capital at all — an unexplained she, as if the tale were already under way.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sibilance

Stanza 1 is hushed with s-sounds — sat, scoured, swept, salted — a room going quiet before a performance. Stanza 3 brings a second wave — slander, shiftless, sloven, spotless, spinning, single strongest — the whisper of a wheel turning.

Plosives

Hard k, t, d and p sounds cluster on objects and tools — cracked delft, clacked, crumb, husk, pieced, darning, done, clogs — the material world knocking against the soft sibilance of voice and breath.

F-alliteration

five or forty fingers (line 8), then the dawn's fire, feet felt for and flat fields (22–24), and finally flew (29): one consonant travels from working hands to hearth and fields, and ends in flight.

The '-less' words

useless, shiftless, spotless: one suffix, the vocabulary of a community that measures people by what they lack. The poem answers with a word that lacks nothing: work.

The most telling pattern is the st-cluster that runs through the poem like the thread it describes: stories, stitched, strongest, stirred, storytellers. It binds the stories to stitching and to strength, so the claim that telling is a kind of making, and the strongest kind, is made in the ear as well as in the argument; the stories are told while fingers stitched and dissolve as the women stirred. Clacked is the poem's one clear onomatopoeia: a hard, wooden double click, a busy tongue and busy needles keeping one time.

The final stanza changes the sound-world. After the hard consonants of chores and clogs, the stories dissolved in the whorl of the ear, a phrase of liquid l and r and open vowels — whorl even sounds like 'whirl', the turning of a spindle. Then softer still: the nasals of hung, down, children, again and the long vowels of sleeping and flew hum like breathing in sleep. Silence is part of the music too — the hard stop inside line 18 between the finished thread and Night in, and the two-syllable line 26, almost all white space, a breath held before the stories come back to life.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Thread and textile

The textile vocabulary rises in status as it goes. In stanza 2 it is the language of chores — fingers stitched, patchwork pieced, darning done — the thrift crafts of a household mending what it cannot replace. At line 16 it becomes a figure for art: telling was like spinning, gathering air into the single strongest thread, the craft the others depend on. At line 25 it completes itself in the pun on whorl, which makes the listener's ear the spindle on which the teller's thread is wound. Chore, then art, then transmission: by the end, thread is what passes from one generation to the next.

Light and dark

Light is scarce and poor. It is rationed like bread — every last crumb of daylight is salted away (line 5) — and when it returns at first light it is thin grey light (24), watery and colourless, the medium of labour; it washed over the fields as if the day were scrubbing the night away. Night is abundance: Night in (18) is the time of the stories, and the poem's last word is night. Lochhead reverses the usual symbolism: darkness is where imagination is fed, and the day is what has to be endured.

Food, salt and dissolving

The opening treats daylight as food (crumb, salted away) in an economy of scarcity — grain grated from the husk, soup that may be Dishwater. Salt preserves; to salt something away is to store it against hard times. When the stories dissolved at dawn, the image recalls salt in water: gone from sight but still present. The stories are both nourishment and preserved store, kept invisibly in the children for later use.

The working body

Lochhead shows parts of bodies at work rather than whole people: the tongue that clacked, five or forty fingers, the held breath, the ending known by heart, the peasant's feet, the ear, the sleeping heads. The synecdoche makes storytelling one bodily labour among others — the tongue is a tool, like the fingers — and it maps the path of a story: out of the teller's tongue, into the listener's ear, held in the breath and the heart, stored in the head, released into flight.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Storytelling as women's work

The central claim, at the midpoint, is that telling the stories was her work, earned in stages: the telling accompanies labour (the tongue clacked while fingers stitched), then is labour, then is a craft, like spinning. Clacked, a word that belittles women's talk, is reclaimed as the sound of a tool.

02

How women are judged

A woman here is measured by industry (shiftless), cleanliness (sloven or spotless) and cooking (Dishwater or tasty). The storyteller alone is exempt, because her real work lay elsewhere — a tribute to her as an artist, and a critique of how every other woman is valued.

03

Art and use

The poem answers the charge that stories are useless on its own terms, then outgrows it: bats are not useful, and stories that hang and fly by their own will are valuable because they live.

04

Oral tradition and survival

Stories pass from tongue to ear and lodge in the sleeping heads of the children until night lets them fly; the speaker, once a listener (she'd have us waiting), is now the teller. Survival is cyclical and alive, not fixed in a book.

05

Who gets the credit

Agentless passives, synecdoches and a heroine who is only she reproduce the anonymity of folk culture, and of the women behind the Grimms' collection. The poem supplies no name, only the title Storyteller and an argument that the work deserves the credit.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Does the poem defend stories for being useful — or against the idea that they must be?

The difficulty. Stanza 2 justifies the stories by what got done while they were told: nobody could call them useless, because the sewing, grating and darning went on. Stanza 3 then calls telling her work. Is Lochhead accepting the work-ethic that dismissed women's talk — art must earn its keep — or arguing against it?

Competing readings. A concession: the defence runs entirely in productive terms; even the praise is grudging litotes, and the climactic claim is that storytelling counts because it is labour — a woman's worth still measured in output, with one more output added to the list. A tactic, then a transcendence: the poem meets the hostile voice in its own currency and wins, then moves beyond it — the simile makes something out of air, and the bats, which do nothing useful at all, value the stories simply because they live. A redefinition: the poem neither concedes nor escapes but enlarges what counts as work, in the spirit of 1970s feminist arguments that women's unpaid domestic and cultural labour is real labour.

What a strong answer does. It traces the movement — practical defence, verdict, simile, image — rather than freezing one stage. It hears the grudging early defence as a community's voice, not the poet's last word, and lets the 'useless' bats be the final answer without pretending the earlier stanzas avoid the accuser's language.

2. At dawn, are the stories lost or saved?

The difficulty. the stories dissolved sounds like defeat. Then the stories hung themselves, a phrase with a dark echo of 'hanged themselves', and roost upside down like bats. Is the ending consoling, elegiac or uncanny?

Competing readings. Elegy: everything is past tense, the world of delft and clogs is gone, and flew again may be a hope rather than a fact. Survival: what dissolves is absorbed, not destroyed; but reverses the loss; bats sleep by day and fly by night, so again makes the survival cyclical and certain. The uncanny: bats are gothic creatures, the reflexive verb has a shadow of death, and the stories lodge in children's heads beyond anyone's control — fitting for Grimm tales of wolves, witches and cruelty.

What a strong answer does. It reads dissolved and but together, takes the darkness of the image as part of the tales' power rather than a contradiction of the consolation, and notices that survival depends on night: the stories live only when told again.

3. Whose night is it?

The difficulty. The last line prints storytellers with no apostrophe.

Competing readings. Singular possessive: her night — the tribute ends with the night belonging to the woman the poem has defended. Plural possessive: the storytellers' night — every teller's, including the children who will grow up to tell, and the poet telling us now. Compound noun: a 'storytellers night', like 'market day' — a fixture of the calendar, a communal institution rather than anyone's property.

What a strong answer does. It works from the printed form, shows how each reading changes the ending, and connects the openness to the poem's central idea: the role is not owned but handed on, the singular Storyteller of the title becoming plural at the close. The apostrophe's ambiguity is the poem's whole balance in small: it gives the texture of one remembered woman (us, the soup) while withholding name and place, so that she can stand for a whole tradition.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. every last crumb of daylight — salted away (line 5)

Techniques: metaphor, idiom, hyperbole of thrift, agentless passive.

Daylight is imagined as bread, used down to every last crumb, then salted away — the idiom for hoarding, from preserving meat or fish in salt. Poverty is made concrete without self-pity: even the light is rationed. But the idiom also means 'saved for later', so the line holds the poem's pattern in miniature: what seems used up is in fact preserved.

Intention and effect: nightfall becomes a beginning rather than an ending, and we are taught to read later disappearances — the stories dissolving at dawn — as storage rather than loss.

2. the tongue clacked (line 7)

Techniques: synecdoche, onomatopoeia, reclaimed pejorative.

The teller is reduced to her working organ, as her listeners are reduced to fingers: storytelling becomes one bodily labour among others. Clacked is a hard, wooden sound — needles, a loom, a busy tongue — and also the verb for a gossip's chatter, the kind of word used to dismiss women's talk. Lochhead keeps the insult and changes its meaning: the clacking tongue keeps time with the work.

Intention and effect: women's speech is re-valued from inside the very vocabulary that belittled it.

3. slander her shiftless — sloven or spotless (lines 12–13)

Techniques: ellipsis, inversion, antithesis, sibilance, the '-less' suffix.

Line 12 has no main verb and line 13 begins a sentence the reader has to rebuild, so the syntax sounds like an older speaker. The antitheses set out the standards — industry, cleanliness, good soup — by which women in this world are judged, and slander shows how damaging the charge of laziness would be. The storyteller alone is exempt, whatever her housekeeping.

Intention and effect: the poem praises a woman as one would praise an artist, and in doing so exposes the narrow scale on which every other woman is weighed.

4. like spinning — single strongest — thread (lines 16–18)

Techniques: simile, paradox, superlative, enjambment, caesura.

Spinning, the archetypal female craft and the source of 'to spin a yarn', is done here with air — breath, words — and makes the single strongest thread, the narrative line that holds a community together. The enjambment draws the thread across the line-break, and the full stop after thread snaps it off, finished.

Intention and effect: storytelling is promoted from accompaniment to the most fundamental craft of the house — and, read as Lochhead's own art, the image defines a poem's line: breath gathered into one strong strand.

5. held / breath — knew by heart (lines 19–20)

Techniques: enjambment, first-person plural, habitual modal, paradox.

The only us and we in the poem reveal the speaker as one of the listening children. The line-break after held makes the reader pause mid-phrase, as the children did. The paradox — suspense over an ending everyone knew — captures oral storytelling: the pleasure is in the telling and the shared ritual, not in novelty.

Intention and effect: the argument becomes testimony; the speaker's remembered body is the evidence that the stories worked.

6. whorl of the ear (line 25)

Techniques: pun, metaphor, anapaestic rhythm.

The main clause finally arrives and seems to announce defeat: the stories dissolved. But whorl is both the spiral of the ear and, in its oldest sense, the small wheel on a spindle that keeps it turning, so the spinning simile completes itself as the teller's thread is wound onto the listener's ear. What dissolves is absorbed, not destroyed.

Intention and effect: transmission becomes bodily and unconscious — the stories become part of the listener rather than something she remembers.

7. hung themselves — sleeping heads — flew again (lines 27–29)

Techniques: implied metaphor (bats, never named), reflexive verb, synecdoche, cyclical again.

The stories roost like bats in the children's heads: nocturnal, invisible by day, finding their way by sound. The reflexive verb echoes the women who stirred themselves at dawn, so one group wakes as the other sleeps, and the faint echo of 'hanged' adds a Grimm shadow. Then they flew again, and the poem ends on night.

Intention and effect: survival becomes a living cycle, and the stories pass on — to the children, and to the poet whose poem is the stories flying again.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Feminist

What it makes visible. Three gestures: the poem names women's cultural labour as work (her work); it frees one woman from the domestic standards by which all women are judged (sloven or spotless, Dishwater or tasty); and it makes the handing-on of stories a line of women and children, from the teller to us to the children. At the head of The Grimm Sisters, it also restores the teller to a tradition that men wrote down and signed.

What it flattens. The poem's women are not only victims of an unfair measure: the community's voice is grudgingly approving (No one could say), and the storyteller holds real power over her audience. A purely protest reading misses the poem's warmth and its pleasure in the craft.

2. Materialist

What it makes visible. The poem is about value and production — what counts as useless, what counts as work — and precise about the economy of a poor household: rationed light, grated grain, patchwork, darning, thin soup. Storytelling appears as social reproduction, the community remaking its shared culture nightly as it remakes its clothes, and the anonymous passives show labour without workers, the condition of unpaid domestic work.

What it flattens. The final image escapes economics altogether: bats are not productive. A materialist reading risks treating the stories as one more commodity when the ending insists on their freedom.

3. Psychoanalytic

What it makes visible. The stories end in the sleeping heads of the children, the place of dreams. Bruno Bettelheim's The Uses of Enchantment (1976) argued that fairy tales work on a child's unconscious, helping children master fears they cannot name; Lochhead's bats, roosting unseen in the dark of the sleeping mind and flying at night, are an image of that hidden work, and the echo of 'hanged themselves' suits the dark material of the tales.

What it flattens. The social world — the kitchen, the women's work and the question of credit — which is the poem's main concern for three stanzas out of four.

4. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The poem makes its reader behave like its listeners. We are thrown into a scene with an unexplained she; we rebuild the scrambled syntax of stanza 3; we pause, breath held, at a line-break; we wait four lines for the final sentence's main verb. And many readers, like the children, know the ending already — the fairy tales are part of their own childhoods — which makes the paradox of suspense by heart our own.

What it flattens. It can make the poem about us. The poem keeps its focus on her: her work, her night.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A portrait of the poet's own art

The storyteller is Lochhead's model for herself: a woman who holds a room with her voice. Lochhead performs her own poems, and the poem defines poetry as voiced craft — air spun into a strong thread — absorbed by listeners rather than possessed by readers.

Evidence: the spinning simile as a definition of the poetic line; the speaker who was one of us and is now the teller; free verse shaped like speech; the plural storytellers.

Weakness: the poem's attention is on the woman and her community, not the poet. Reading it as self-portrait repeats the very move it criticises, giving the credit to the writer rather than the teller.

2. An elegy for a vanished oral culture

The poem mourns a world that has gone: scoured tables, cracked delft, children who learned their culture by ear. The past tense governs everything, and flew again may be a hope rather than a fact.

Evidence: the habitual past (she'd have us waiting); the archaic details (clogs, the dresser, the peasant); the thin grey dawn that dissolves the stories.

Weakness: the poem refuses elegy at its turn — but and again insist on survival — and a grown listener retelling the scene is evidence that the stories did fly again.

3. A frame for The Grimm Sisters

As the collection's opening poem, 'Storyteller' sets up the book's project: to give the fairy tales back to the women who told them, after men had collected, edited and signed them. The unnamed she is the source from which the book's other voices descend.

Evidence: the book's title; the teller's anonymity; the agentless passives of women's work; the insistence on her work.

Weakness: the poem never mentions the Grimms, books or writing; a reader with only the anthology page has to infer the reclamation.

4. A Scottish, vernacular reading

The idiom is Scots-inflected — delft (Scots 'delf', crockery), sloven, shiftless, Night in, the proverb-like Never the one to — and the storyteller belongs to a culture whose ballads and tales were carried largely by women's voices. Lochhead, a Makar who writes and performs in Scots, writes as its heir.

Evidence: the spoken syntax of stanza 3; the vernacular words; the kitchen with its dresser of delf.

Weakness: the setting reaches beyond Scotland — clogs, flat fields, a generic peasant — into the continental world of the Grimms: Scottish in voice, universal in scene.

CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

With 'Follower' (Seamus Heaney)

Link: a child watches an adult's craft with awe — Heaney's father is ‘An expert’ at the plough, Lochhead's storyteller spins the single strongest thread — and both poems are about what passes down the generations. Shared technique: synecdoche of the working body (the father's shoulders and eye; tongue, fingers, ear) and a final reversal of roles: Heaney's son now leads, Lochhead's listener has become a teller, speaking of the children. Difference: Heaney's inheritance is a burden, the father who ‘will not go away’; Lochhead's is a release, stories that flew again.

With 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (Carol Rumens)

Link: women's and children's work with thread, and craft as the way a culture carries itself forward. Shared technique: textile imagery as a figure for time and transmission — Rumens's ‘flickering knots’ and the carpet that ‘will travel’, Lochhead's spinning and whorl. Difference: Rumens's children are workers whose product leaves them behind; Lochhead's are listeners, and what the women make stays with them, roosting in their heads.

With 'Sonnet 18' (William Shakespeare)

Link: both claim that something made of words survives. Shared technique: breath as the medium of survival — Shakespeare's poem lives ‘So long as men can breathe’; Lochhead's stories are spun from air and depend on held / breath. Difference: Shakespeare's survival is fixed, written and signed, ‘eternal lines’ for a named beloved; Lochhead's is oral, anonymous and cyclical, dissolving each dawn and flying again each night.

With 'A Married State' (Katherine Philips)

Link: both weigh how women's lives are measured by domestic roles — Philips reads misery in ‘wives' careful faces’, Lochhead's storyteller might be sloven or spotless. Shared technique: antithesis as a weighing-scale. Difference: Philips escapes the measure by refusing marriage; Lochhead's woman escapes it from inside the household, through the value of her art.

With 'A Different History' (Sujata Bhatt)

Link: both ask how a culture survives through language — Bhatt through reverence for books and the inherited ‘oppressor's tongue’, Lochhead through the unwritten tongue that clacked. Shared technique: a closing turn to a future generation — Bhatt's ‘unborn grandchildren’, Lochhead's sleeping heads. Difference: Bhatt's inheritance comes through conquest and print and ends uneasily; Lochhead's comes through a woman's voice and is celebrated.

Up before the sun, a boy turns a chore into a feast and the feast into a rite — and when the late guest only winks, he eats its share too.
