CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Charles Mungoshi (1947–2019)

Born at Manyene, near Chivhu, in what was then Southern Rhodesia, into a farming family, Mungoshi wrote in both Shona and English and was first of all a prose writer. Childhood runs through his work: his novel Waiting for the Rain (1975) is about the gap that education opens between a son and the people who raised him. That matters here. This is a storyteller's poem, built from a sequence of small events rather than an argument.

The Milkman Doesn't Only Deliver Milk (1981)

'Before the Sun' comes from Mungoshi's only collection of poems, first published in 1981, the year after Zimbabwe's independence (18 April 1980). He called poetry “a sideline, a mere finger exercise”, which reads best as a clue to method: poems as practice in compressing language to exactness. He admired the haiku of Bashō, and the Shona work song, such as the threshing song for rapoko (finger-millet), offers a second, local analogy: it makes work feel like play and play feel like work.

The real morning: firewood, green maize and the rains

Everything in the poem is ordinary rural work. In a homestead that cooks on wood, splitting logs and lighting the fire is a daily early-morning job, often given to older children. The maize is roasted on the cob — “green mealies” in Southern African English, fresh maize picked before the grain hardens — and a cob with its kernels bitten away is a pale, ridged core: skeletons is an exact picture before it is a symbol.

Zimbabwe's rains fall roughly from November to March. A rainy-season day starts hot and clear and builds to an afternoon storm, which the first stanza forecasts; dew on the grass means the sun is not yet up to dry it. Green maize is ready from about February, before the main harvest, so the first cobs often end the lean months — part of why two cobs can be a feast, though the poem never mentions hunger.

The sky and the sacred

The smoke rising to the distant sky is a signal of some kind, or else a sacrificial prayer, and two traditions make the second reading available. In Shona religion, as usually described, the high God Mwari (also Nyadenga, a name tied to the sky) is approached through the ancestral spirits, the vadzimu, with offerings of beer or snuff. Mungoshi was educated at a mission school, and in the Bible the smoke of a burnt offering rises to God (Genesis 8:21). But the poem names no god, ancestor or ceremony, and the boy's fire is a cooking fire: the religious meaning is a possibility the speaker entertains, not a rite the poem records.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Before the Sun

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper.

TBefore the Sun
1a vivid, deep-coloured dawn sky (no verb)
2foretelling hot weather soon
3and, once midday has passed,
4a downpour to come.
5glinting splinters of wood
6leap off the keen blade
7travelling a way across open space,
8[one word: the curve of their flight]
9and, after what feels like forever,
10come to rest, falling like rain
11onto grass still wet from the night.
12plain fact: the log is a large one
13but at the age of fourteen
14[two words: large logs, now plural]
15are exactly what one craves.
16the timber releases
17a pleasant scent that clears the nostrils
18which, in brackets, compared with sawn wood-dust,
19won't set off a sneeze.
20the fire lifts a slender smoke-twist
21which, after a while, rises straight
22and widens like a flute's bell
23toward the far-off heavens: perhaps a message
24of an unspecified kind,
25or an offering made in worship.
26the burning timber fizzes,
27embers leap upward (a capital opens the clause).
28once the sun
29at last appears
30over the eastern horizon, like a
31guest arriving late to a banquet
32the speaker has a pair of corn cobs
33prepared for its arrival.
34he invites the sun to join him
35in eating the fire-cooked corn
36but it merely gives a wink
37the way an adult would.
38so he starts without it, with large
39turn-taking mouthfuls:
40a bite on the sun's behalf,
41a bite for himself.
42again, pointing: this bite for the sun,
43this bite for himself:
44until both cobs
45are only a pair of small bony frames
46lying in full sunlight.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Before the Sun
Language & devices

The Preposition Before holds two senses (Ambiguity): earlier than — the boy is up before sunrise — and in the presence of, as one stands before a king or an altar. The sun is not mentioned until line 28, so the first twenty-seven lines literally happen before the sun; the poem's last word returns to sun (Circular structure).

Meaning & effect

In the time sense the title is a small boast: the boy beats the sun to the day, so when it arrives his work is done and the sun is the latecomer. In the presence sense, everything he does — the fire, the rising smoke, the portion set aside — is done in front of a great power, almost as an offering. The poem keeps both alive, a race the boy wins and a ceremony he performs, and ends with him no longer before the sun but sitting in its light.

Lines 1–4
Intense blue
Language & devices

A Minor sentence: four lines with no main verb, a Noun phrase carried to its full stop by the Participle promising. Intense belongs to heat and feeling more than to colour, so the blue presses. Personification makes the morning a speaker giving a pledge, and the lines are a forecast (Prolepsis): heat first, then heavy rain.

Meaning & effect

Perception comes before person: we are given what is seen before we know who sees it, and the morning is a state the reader is placed inside rather than an event. The speaker reads the sky like a farmer — hot morning, afternoon storm, good news for the maize — so the opening is hopeful. But the forecast reaches into an afternoon the poem never gets to: the bright morning is enclosed from the start in a day that will move on.

Lines 5–7
bright chips
Language & devices

The chips are the grammatical subject and the axe only where they fly from; the person swinging it is left out (Ellipsis). Paired adjectives give light and edge, bright and sharp, and the hard /b/, /ch/, /sh/ and /ks/ of bright chips and sharp axe make the blow audible. for some distance is a watcher's vague measure, the first of three somes.

Meaning & effect

The work begins without a worker: the boy is so absorbed in what he sees that he disappears from his own sentence. bright is exact, since freshly split wood is pale and catches the early light, and treating the chips as a spectacle turns the chore into something worth watching. What matters is the flight, not its length.

Line 8
arc,
Language & devices

A One-word line, the shortest in the poem, with white space on both sides. arc, a noun from geometry, is used as a Verb, the middle of three: fly … arc … settle. The comma suspends the sentence rather than ending it, and Enjambment runs into and out of the line.

Meaning & effect

The line does what it says: the chip hangs at the top of its curve and the eye hangs with it on one word, so a single flight becomes launch, peak and landing. Geometry, the language of perfect shapes, lends a scrap of firewood its dignity. It is the poem's method in one word: exact naming, placed in space, instead of description.

Lines 9–11
eternities later
Language & devices

Hyperbole: a chip falls in about a second yet lands eternities later, the plural stranger than the cliché “an eternity” (Time dilation). The Phrasal verb settle down is gentle and domestic against fly, and the Metaphor in showers makes the chips rain. Sibilance and longer vowels (settle, showers, dewy grass) soften the stanza after its hard opening.

Meaning & effect

Deep attention stretches time: to an absorbed fourteen-year-old the fall really does seem endless, so the exaggeration is accurate, not boastful. Stanza 1 squeezed a day into four lines; this stretches one second to eternity, because the poem's clock is attention. The axe makes a small private weather before the sky delivers its promised rain, and dewy is a time-stamp: the sun is not yet up to dry the grass.

Lines 12–15
big logs
Language & devices

The log is sized up in a blunt Declarative of five monosyllables, a drop in Register to flat fact, ending on a Colon that poses a problem. A Conjunction turns the difficulty into the attraction, and the Second person you makes the feeling a rule. Repetition with a change of number — one log becomes big logs, alone on a two-word line — widens a task into an appetite.

Meaning & effect

The poem's funniest, truest moment: at fourteen the difficulty is the point, because what you can split measures what you are becoming. The age arrives as a law of life rather than a fact about I, so the speaker is defined by what he wants. Only someone past fourteen can generalise about being fourteen: an older voice shows through.

Lines 16–19
(unlike sawdust)
Language & devices

Olfactory imagery: sight gives way to smell, and the coined-sounding Compound adjective nose-cleansing names an effect on the body rather than a scent. The Parenthesis (unlike sawdust), the poem's only brackets, is Bathos: from sweet to sneezing. The impersonal one is formal; the contraction doesn't is colloquial.

Meaning & effect

Even the fuel is a pleasure: the wood gives off its scent generously, and nothing in this morning is drudgery. The bracket then deflates it with a practical, knowing aside, which keeps sweetness from becoming sentiment and sounds like the older voice again. The detached one returns, transformed, as the counting word of the final chant.

Lines 20–22
a thin spiral
Language & devices

Ellipsis: the lighting of the fire is never shown; between stanzas the wood is simply burning. The Phrasal verb sends up implies sending something to someone, and the visual sequence is exact: thin spiral → straightens → flutes out. flutes turns a noun into a verb, the smoke widening like a flute's bell, and Sibilance links sends, spiral, smoke, straightens.

Meaning & effect

The gap between stanzas tells part of the story. The smoke is watched precisely — a curl, then a straight column in still morning air, then spreading higher up — and sends up turns it into communication, something dispatched upward. flutes gives a silent image music, and the column joining the boy's fire to the sky prepares the question of what it means.

Lines 23–25
a signal … sacrificial prayer
Language & devices

A Colon after the distant sky introduces an interpretation: two alternatives joined by or, the practical signal and the religious sacrificial prayer, and neither chosen (Juxtaposition of registers). The hedge of some sort shrugs. Sibilance carries on through sky, signal, sacrificial.

Meaning & effect

At the poem's exact centre (lines 23–24 of 46) the speaker sees the smoke as possibly a message, possibly an offering, and refuses to choose; the shrug keeps solemnity off. Both readings share one assumption: the smoke is addressed to someone, so the sky is imagined as a listener. sacrificial prayer is the poem's only openly religious phrase, and it looks ahead to the end, where food really is offered to a power in the sky, and then eaten.

Lines 26–27
hisses
Language & devices

The shortest stanza: two clauses in Parallelism, article, noun, verb, twice. Onomatopoeia in hisses; fly returns from line 6 as chips become sparks. The second line takes a capital after a comma, the only such capital in the poem, so the clauses stand side by side as equals.

Meaning & effect

The fire takes hold in two lines: sound, then light. The bare matched clauses sound like a formula or chant, and the poem slows into ceremony. This is the hinge between preparation and guest, and it gets the least space of any stanza: the turn happens as quickly as a fire catching.

Lines 28–31
some latecomer
Language & devices

the sun is mentioned for the first time, twenty-eight lines in, in a sentence opening on a storyteller's And. finally signals impatience, and shows up is a colloquial Idiom for people arriving late, not stars (Personification). The Simile like some / latecomer is delayed by Enjambment, and the poem's one close rhyme, East … feast (Internal rhyme), chimes as the guest arrives.

Meaning & effect

Sunrise is told as a friend turning up late: the boy has been working for some time and the sun is behind schedule. The idiom cuts the most powerful thing in the sky down to a slack guest, and some is mock-scornful but affectionate, since you only complain about lateness when you were expecting someone. Two cobs of maize become a feast because the boy has decided they are one.

Lines 32–33
two cobs of maize
Language & devices

The first I in the poem, at line 32 of 46, in the same sentence as the sun's arrival. The colloquial I have got is childlike and proud; the number is exact, two; ready is a host's word.

Meaning & effect

The speaker names himself only when company arrives: I appears when there is someone to be “I” in front of. Two cobs means one each, planned before the guest appeared, which recasts the log, the fire and the smoke as preparations for a visit.

Lines 34–35
come share
Language & devices

The verb tell, not “ask” or “beg”, is confident, even bossy: the boy addresses the sun in reported speech, a kind of Apostrophe. share is placed at the line-end by Enjambment, and roasted is a Participle used as an adjective.

Meaning & effect

The boy speaks to the sun as an equal: no prayer, no awe, an invitation from host to guest. This is a different relation to the sky from the sacrificial prayer — friendship rather than worship, sharing rather than giving up. share is the poem's key moral word: the meal becomes a feast only when it is shared.

Lines 36–37
just winks
Language & devices

Personification is completed: the sun winks, with just meaning “merely”. A second Simile, a grown-up, brings in the poem's only adult. A wink is a one-eyed gesture of shared understanding, and also a picture of the sun's first glint over the horizon.

Meaning & effect

The perfect answer: neither accepting nor refusing, the sun acknowledges the game as an amused adult humours a child's pretend party, and just carries a small disappointment the boy takes cheerfully. The wink sets the limit of the poem's closeness to nature — the world plays along, kindly, from a distance. With no parent anywhere in the poem, the sun takes the adult's role: benign, knowing, uninvolved.

Lines 38–43
for the sun
Language & devices

So takes the wink as permission, go ahead is what a host does when a guest is delayed, and big, the third, waits alone at the line-end. alternate sets a rule, and the chant follows: four short lines of Repetition and Parallelism in the counting formula of a children's sharing game. Assonance binds one to sun while me stays outside the sound, and the Deictic This in the second pair points, as if a cob is held up.

Meaning & effect

Form becomes action: the lines take turns as the eaters do. The formula is the way children divide sweets, but the measured repetition also sounds like a liturgy, an offering portioned out in words, so a game and a rite are the same gesture. big ties the bites to the big logs, the same appetite now turned to pleasure. And since the sun cannot eat, the boy eats every bite: the sharing is generous in spirit and comic in fact.

Lines 44–46
two little skeletons
Language & devices

till runs the ritual to its natural end. Metaphor: the stripped cobs are skeletons, ridged and pale like bone; little, the poem's only diminutive, reverses the three bigs, and just deflates once more. The last word returns to the title's noun (Circular structure), but the preposition has changed from Before to in.

Meaning & effect

The meal ends in an image of death, and the poem refuses to be simply cheerful. The picture is accurate and funny first — a gnawed cob does look like a small spine — but whatever is eaten leaves remains, and the appetite for bigness ends in something small. The boy who began before the sun now sits in its full light with the morning over, and the poem ends on an image, not a comment, leaving the joy weighed against the bones.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Before the Sun' can look like a charming snapshot: a boy splits a log, lights a fire, roasts two cobs of maize and invites the sun to breakfast. Read closely, it is a poem about what attention does to an ordinary chore — it turns work into play, play into something like a rite, and a meagre breakfast into a feast — and about the limits of that transformation, which the poem marks every time with a shrug, a bracket or the word just. Its joy convinces because it is never naive: each enchantment is followed by a small deflation, and the poem ends by admitting that what was enjoyed has been used up.

The opening establishes the power of attention. The first sentence has no verb and no I: the morning is a state the reader is placed inside, already promising like someone who talks, and already enclosed in a longer day, since the forecast heat and rain belong to an afternoon the poem never reaches. In the chips stanza the worker vanishes from his own sentence, absorbed in what he sees; the sentence breaks at the top of the flight on the single word arc, and the landing comes eternities later. The hyperbole is accurate rather than boastful — to a fourteen-year-old wholly inside the moment, one second really is endless — and the falling showers make the axe a private weather before the sky's. A chore has already become a spectacle.

Then attention turns into appetite, and the first deflation arrives. The big log is the attraction, not the problem: at fourteen the hard version of the job is the one you want, because what you can split measures what you are becoming. The wood's sweet smell is followed at once by the bracketed, almost scientific (unlike sawdust). The poem will not let sweetness stand unqualified; it stays loyal to the actual texture of the morning, sneezes included.

At the exact centre of the poem the transformation reaches furthest. The fire is lit off-stage; we see only smoke climbing to the distant sky, which the speaker reads as a signal, or else a sacrificial prayer. This is the poem's nearest approach to the sacred, and the shrug of some sort keeps it from solemnity: both options imagine the sky as a listener, and neither is chosen. The two-line fire stanza that follows has the bare, matched rhythm of a chant, the hinge between preparation and guest, given the least space in the poem.

The sun, withheld for twenty-seven lines, arrives as some latecomer, demoted to a slack guest, and the one close rhyme (East … feast) greets it. Only now does I appear: the speaker becomes a self when he has company, and the two cobs he has ready recast the whole solitary morning as preparation for a visit. His invitation is friendship, not supplication — he tells the sun to come and share — and the sun's reply is the second deflation: it just winks, as an amused adult humours a child, acknowledging the game without joining it. The limit of the poem's communion with nature is stated without complaint.

So the boy goes ahead, and the lines alternate as the bites do. The counting formula is a child's sharing game and also the shape of a liturgy; play and rite are one gesture, and since the sun cannot eat, the boy eats every bite. The ending is the final deflation: the cobs are two little skeletons. little cancels the poem's three bigs, just shrinks once more, and skeletons brings the first image of death into a poem that has had none — exact first (a gnawed cob does look like a small spine), funny second, and then an admission that whatever is consumed leaves remains. The boy who began before the sun ends in its full light, with the morning and the feast over.

The strongest objection is that the poem is slight: a pleasant anecdote, or nostalgia that prettifies a hard rural childhood. The reply is its construction and its restraint. It is built more carefully than its casual voice suggests — the sun withheld for twenty-seven lines, the I withheld until the guest arrives, the smoke at the exact centre, big reversed into little — and it refuses sentiment exactly where sentiment is easiest: after the sweet smell, after the invitation, after the feast. The opposite objection, that the poem is a disguised rite and the boy is really worshipping, has support in the smoke and the portioned offering, but it must ignore the poem's own shrug and the wink that declines. The better account is the poem's own: a morning attended to this fully is a feast, a game and very nearly a prayer — and by the last line it has been eaten.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Free verse: 46 lines, nine stanzas, no metre, no rhyme scheme, no regular stanza shape. A dawn poem, childhood lyric and small narrative of work that becomes, in its last stanza, a ritual chant — a reversed aubade: the traditional dawn poem resents the sunrise, this one waits for the sun as a guest.

Stanzas

4, 7, 4, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4 and 9 lines. Each is a single sentence except the last, which has two. The shortest (the fire catching) is the hinge; the longest (the shared meal) is the ending.

Lines

Very short, mostly two to five words. The one-word arc (line 8) and the two-word big logs (line 14) are the extremes.

Two halves: before the sun, and with it

Stanzas 1–6 (lines 1–27) never mention the sun: sky, chips, log, smell, smoke and fire — the boy's work, done in the half-light. Stanzas 7–9 (lines 28–46) begin when it arrives and are given to the guest and the meal. Twenty-seven lines happen before the sun and nineteen in its presence, and the change of preposition from the title's Before to the last line's in measures the morning's passing.

One sentence, one act of attention

Because each stanza but the last is one sentence, each reads as a single act of noticing, lasting as long as the noticing takes. The chips stanza is the longest sentence (seven lines) because the flight is being slowed down: launch, arc, eternities, landing. The log and smell stanzas are four lines each, quick judgements; the smoke stanza runs to six as the column climbs, three short lines tumbling down the page to its two interpretations; the fire stanza is two lines because a fire catching is sudden. The last stanza breaks the pattern: one sentence states the rule of alternate bites, and a second repeats it with more emphasis (This one) and runs through a colon straight into the result. The counting leads directly to the skeletons.

Lineation and white space

The short lines control the reader's speed. arc stands alone with white space on both sides, so the eye stops where the chip pauses. big logs sets two heavy words alone, the boy's desire held up like a slogan before its verb arrives. The break in like some / latecomer is a comic pause before the punchline. Elsewhere enjambment holds a word back so it lands as a small surprise: the chips hang before fly, big waits alone at a line-end before alternate, and skeletons is delayed by the line-break after the cobs. Almost every line runs on, which gives the poem the feel of a voice thinking as it goes and makes its few end-stops moments of settling.

Rhythm in key lines

There is no metre to scan, but the stress patterns change with the subject.

Fragment Stress Effect
Intense blue x / / stresses crowded together: an opening as heavy as the colour
bright chips / / a spondee, hard and quick like the axe-blow
eternities later x / x x / x few stresses among light syllables: the moment drifts and lengthens
big logs / / the weight of what he wants
two little skeletons / / x / x x stresses, then a falling run of light syllables: the energy runs down

The movement across the poem is from heavy, clustered stresses (sky, axe, logs, fire) to the light, sing-song beat of the counting chant and then the dying fall of skeletons: effort, then play, then ending.

Rhyme and echo

There is no rhyme scheme, but there is one close rhyme, and it falls exactly where the sun arrives: East mid-line 30, feast at the end of line 31, a chime of welcome at the guest's entrance. Three far-spaced line-endings also rhyme fully — air (7), prayer (25), share (34) — joining the poem's three outward movements: chips into the air, smoke into the sky as prayer, the meal held out to the sun.

Beyond rhyme, the music is repetition. sun ends four lines. big comes three times and is cancelled by little. some comes three times (some distance, some sort, some / latecomer), a habit of loose, unpretentious measuring. later comes three times too, linking three scales of time: the afternoon, the chip's eternities, the smoke straightening.

Punctuation

The colon is the poem's characteristic mark. Each of its four appearances (lines 12, 23, 39, 43) holds something out for inspection: the log, the meaning of the smoke, the ritual, and the ritual's result. It suits a poem that displays objects rather than explaining them. The brackets of (unlike sawdust) are its only parenthesis, an older, knowing voice stepping in and out. Line 27 is the one line that takes a capital without beginning a sentence, which makes the fire's two clauses equal and separate, like two lines of a chant.

Pronouns and tense

The pronouns build an architecture of their own. Nobody swings the axe in stanzas 1–2; then comes a generalising you, then a formal one. The first I arrives at line 32 with the sun, and me follows: the speaker becomes a self at the moment he has company. Meanwhile one changes job, from detached pronoun (line 19) to counting word (lines 40–43).

The present tense throughout is the poem's boldest formal decision: a remembered childhood told without the frame of memory, with no “I remember”, so the reader is inside the fourteen-year-old's morning rather than looking back at it. The older voice shows at only two seams, the generalisation about being fourteen and the knowing bracket.

The turn

If the poem has a volta, it is line 28, where the sun appears and work turns to company. With it come the first simile, the one close rhyme and, four lines later, the first I; the two-line fire stanza just before it is the hinge. A smaller turn comes in the last two lines, where the game stops and skeletons lets time and loss into the poem. The poem sets that turn down without comment.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sharp to soft. The chips stanza is one sound-movement. It opens on clipped, edged sounds — the /b/, /p/, /ch/, /sh/ and /ks/ of bright chips and sharp axe, packed round short vowels — so the blow is audible. arc stands alone, an open vowel shut by /k/, a hard sound held in silence. Then settle, showers and dewy grass bring in hushed /sh/, voiced /z/ and long vowels: the stanza comes to rest as the chips do.

Sibilance from axe to fire. One sound, /s/, runs through every stage of the morning and changes its job each time: sharp in sharp and axe, soft in the landing, curling upward in the smoke (sends, spiral, smoke, straightens), literally audible when the wood hisses, and finally lifted into the sky by signal and sacrificial. The consonant carries the poem from cutting to burning to prayer.

Fire and flute. hisses is the fricative hiss of damp wood; sparks wraps /sp/ and /ks/ round one short vowel, a crack, before fly opens into a long vowel as the spark rises. Earlier, the long /oo/ of flutes rounds the mouth as the column widens: the poem's one musical instrument gives a silent image a sound.

The welcome chime. East … feast greets the sun, and gathers a long /ee/ that has run quietly through the poem — heat, fourteen, sneeze — until it ends in me, closing the boy's own shares. The vowel that announced the day's heat ends in his pronoun.

The counting chant. The four lines alternate in length and stress as the bites alternate between eaters. The falling-rising beat of a counting-out rhyme gives the passage its innocence; its call-and-response, like an antiphon, gives it its solemnity. one and sun share a vowel while me stands outside the echo: bound to the sun in sound, the boy is separate from it in fact, since he eats every bite.

The dying fall. The last lines run down. skeletons trails off through light syllables after its stresses, and the poem ends not on a strong beat or a chime but on a quiet fall, like a fire burning down.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

1. The sun: absent host, late guest, impartial light

Named in the title, the sun then disappears for twenty-seven lines; the early stanzas are lit by a sky Intense blue before sunrise, with dew still on the grass. When it comes it is cut down to human size — it shows up, some latecomer — then spoken to, answering like an adult (just winks), and given a share in the chant. In the last line it is no longer a person but simply the light the cobs lie in. Absence, guest, playmate, impartial day: the sun's course is the poem's attitude to nature — intimate, playful, and not quite equal.

2. Fire and smoke: the upward offering

The fire is never lit on the page, but it fills the poem's middle: wood that gives off its smell, smoke that sends up a spiral and flutes out to the sky, then hissing and sparks. The verbs make burning an act of sending, something going up from the boy to the sky, and the speaker names the possibility — a sacrificial prayer — before hedging it. The motif completes itself at the end, where the roasted maize is portioned out for the sun: the offering rising, then the offering shared.

3. Big and little: the scale of fourteen

The log, the logs, the bites: three times the poem measures by size, with big, and size is what the boy values. The one reversal is the last stanza's two little skeletons. The appetite for bigness ends in littleness, and that single diminutive gives the ending its quiet ache: at fourteen you want everything big, and the reader sees, without the boy saying so, that consuming things makes them small.

4. Weather and time: the day around the morning

Rain is forecast in the first stanza; the chips fall in showers on dewy grass, so the axe makes a miniature rainfall before the sky's real one, and the promised rain, good news for the maize, keeps the poem hopeful. The time-words are elastic: later three times, eternities, finally, till. The first stanza compresses a day into four lines and the second stretches a second into eternity, because time is measured by attention and appetite, not by a clock. till marks the one limit attention cannot stretch, the end of the food and of the morning; the dew will dry and the storm will break, but the poem ends before any of it happens.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Childhood and absorbed attention

The boy is so absorbed that he vanishes from his own sentences and a falling chip lands eternities later: attention is the poem's clock. At fourteen he wants difficulty (big logs) and takes a host's pride in being ready, yet still lives where the sun can be invited to breakfast.

02

Work made into play, and play into ritual

Heavy work arrives without a word of complaint: difficulty becomes appetite, the chips a spectacle, the cooking a game, and the game a rite of alternate bites with a portion for the sun. Two cobs become a feast and a solitary breakfast a social occasion — the same gestures are work, play and ritual at once.

03

Kinship with nature, and its limits

Nature is company: a promising morning, generous wood, a sun invited like a friend. But the sun just winks, like a grown-up humouring a child, and the boy eats both shares; the closeness is real, one-sided, and accepted without disappointment.

04

The sacred inside the ordinary

Religious language enters once, hedged: the smoke is a signal of some sort or a sacrificial prayer. Close, loving attention comes very near to reverence, and the poem will not say where one becomes the other.

05

Transience

The morning is framed by a day it never reaches, the forecast heat and rain, and inside that frame time stretches (eternities) and then runs out (till). The feast ends as two little skeletons in the sun, the poem's one image of death, with nothing said about loss.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. What is the smoke — a signal, or a sacrificial prayer?

The difficulty. At the poem's exact centre the smoke reaching the distant sky is a signal, of some sort, or a sacrificial prayer: the poem's only openly religious phrase, set beside a practical alternative the speaker will not give up. How much religious weight can it bear?

Competing readings. Religious: sends up and flutes out make the smoke a dispatch to the sky, and both of the poet's traditions, Shona religion and mission Christianity, supply a God above to receive it. The ending supports this: food portioned out for the sun in a repeated formula, then eaten, is the pattern of many offerings. Secular: it is smoke from a cooking fire; a signal is what smoke on a hillside can be, of some sort is a boy's shrug, the poem names no god, ancestor or ceremony, and Shona offerings are usually beer or snuff, not smoke. Both at once: the two options share one assumption — the smoke is addressed to someone — so either way the sky is imagined as a listener.

What a strong answer does. It keeps the hesitation in view rather than resolving it. The religious reading is available, and the ending strengthens it, but the poem presents it as a possibility the boy entertains, not a rite he performs. The same column of smoke can be practical, playful and devout at once, and Mungoshi will not say which.

2. What does the sun's wink mean?

The difficulty. Invited to share, the sun just winks like a grown-up. A wink can mean many things, and just suggests disappointment.

Competing readings. Indulgence: the sun humours the boy as a kind adult humours a game, acknowledging it without joining in. Permission: the boy reads it as “go ahead”, and the next line begins So I go ahead. Refusal: just means “merely”; the offering is declined and the communion is one-sided. Complicity: a wink shares a secret — both know the sun cannot eat, and the game goes on anyway. Beneath all of these, a wink is exactly how a rising sun's first glint looks, so the personification grows out of a visual fact.

What a strong answer does. It sees that the wink works because it is all of these at once — affectionate, permissive, non-committal — and that the boy's response is cheerful, not hurt. The sun is the poem's only grown-up, and the limit of the relationship is stated without complaint, which is why the poem is warm about nature without being naive.

3. How dark is the ending?

The difficulty. The meal ends with the cobs as two little skeletons, and the last word is sun. A cheerful image of a meal finished, or a shadow of death across a happy poem?

Competing readings. Not dark: a gnawed cob genuinely looks like a small spine, little is affectionate, and the joke is that the boy has eaten the sun's share too. Quietly elegiac: little cancels the three bigs, just deflates, and skeletons brings death into a poem that had none; the morning is over, and the hot day forecast in line 2 is about to begin. Ritually complete: if the sharing was an offering, it has been consumed, as offerings often are by those who make them, and the bare cobs are the proper remains of a rite done right.

What a strong answer does. It holds the humour and the shadow together and shows how the language produces both: an exact picture that also carries mortality, and a diminutive that reverses the poem's scale. It ties the ending to the poem's habit of deflation (unlike sawdust, just winks) and to the opening forecast. As with the smoke, Mungoshi places the image and withdraws.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Close analysis

1. arc (line 8)

One-word line; noun as verb; white space. The chip's flight is broken into three verbs and the middle one is set alone, so the eye pauses where the chip pauses, at the top of its curve. arc comes from geometry, the language of perfect shapes, and lifts a scrap of firewood into it. Intention and effect: the poem's method in one word — exact naming, placed in space, instead of description — so the reader experiences a split second as a held moment.

2. eternities later (line 9)

Hyperbole; plural; time dilation. A chip falls in a second; the poem says eternities, and the plural is stranger than the cliché. To a wholly absorbed fourteen-year-old the fall does seem endless, so the exaggeration is truthful about attention. A grand, strange word in a poem of plain words, it also brings in a time beyond human measure, quietly preparing the religious language of line 25. Intention and effect: the reader feels time stretch and learns the poem's clock: a day squeezed into four lines, a second stretched to eternity.

3. when you are fourteen (line 13)

Second person; generalisation; stated age. The age arrives as a rule of life, not a fact about I, and the conjunction before it turns the problem of the big log into its attraction: at fourteen, difficulty is what you want, because what you can split measures what you are becoming. you universalises the feeling and lets an older voice show through. Intention and effect: the reader smiles in recognition, and the speaker is defined by his appetite — a boy on the edge of adulthood turning a chore into a challenge.

4. (unlike sawdust) (line 18)

Parenthesis; bathos; practical comparison. Straight after the sweet smell comes a bracketed aside: this wood, unlike sawdust, won't make you sneeze. The brackets mark a remark from slightly outside the scene, and the impersonal one that follows sounds grown-up: this is someone who knows wood well enough to compare kinds of work. Intention and effect: the deflation keeps sweetness from sentimentality, and the reader trusts the poem's pleasure because it is so matter-of-fact.

5. sacrificial prayer (line 25)

Alternatives joined by “or”; register shift; hedge. Two meanings are offered for the smoke — a signal, of some sort, or this — and neither is chosen. sacrificial is the poem's heaviest word before skeletons, and the shrug keeps it light. Intention and effect: placed at the exact centre, the phrase opens the possibility of the sacred and leaves it open, preparing the ending's portioned offering without turning breakfast into ceremony.

6. some latecomer (lines 30–31)

Simile; personification; internal rhyme. The sun shows up like a guest late to a feast: some is casually dismissive, the idiom shrinks the sun to human size, and East … feast chimes as it arrives. Two cobs become a banquet in a single word. Intention and effect: the comedy of a boy grumbling at the sun's lateness hides a real reversal of scale — the boy, up first, is the host, and the greatest power in the sky is the one who has to catch up.

7. just winks (line 36)

Personification; deflating adverb; simile. Asked to share, the sun just winks like a grown-up, acknowledging the game without joining it; just registers a small, cheerful disappointment, and the wink is also the rising sun's first glint. Intention and effect: the poem's closeness to nature is given its limit — the world plays along kindly, at a distance — and the sun becomes the only adult in a childhood with no parents in it.

8. two little skeletons (line 45)

Metaphor; diminutive; deflation. The gnawed cobs look like small bony spines, which is accurate and funny. But little reverses the poem's three bigs, just shrinks them further, and skeletons is the poem's first image of death, with the last word returning to the sun. Intention and effect: the feast ends in remains, and the reader is left to hold the morning's joy against its using-up, with no comment from the poet — the same suspension as the smoke.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. A relation with nature that is neither scenic nor exploitative but social: the morning promising, the generous wood, the smoke sent upward, the sun teased, invited and humoured. The boy's cutting, burning and cooking sit inside a cycle of dew, heat and rain — the set's most intact natural world, beside the damage in 'Report to Wordsworth' and 'Lament'.

What it flattens. The poem's honesty about limits: the sun just winks and the boy eats both shares, so the communion is imagined, and the poem knows it.

2. Postcolonial

What it makes visible. What is absent. A rural childhood in Rhodesia is presented with no colonial frame — no white farmer, school, church, money, law or war — in a collection published the year after independence by a writer whose work the Rhodesian regime had banned for a time. The poem asks for no explanation and offers its world as complete.

What it flattens. The evidence: the poem contains no political reference, and reading absence as resistance can make every quiet poem a protest. The defensible claim is that its self-sufficiency can be read as significant in its moment, not that it was designed to be.

3. Materialist

What it makes visible. The facts under the lyricism: a fourteen-year-old up before dawn doing heavy household work and cooking his own breakfast of two cobs, in a season that often follows the lean months. Does the poem's joy disguise labour and scarcity — a child taught to want the chore (big logs) he cannot avoid? The contrast with Blake's sweep and Rumens's weavers is sharp.

What it flattens. The boy's own experience. The poem reports how the work felt, which was pleasure and pride; no one in it exploits him and nothing suggests he is hungry, so overriding that with an adult economic verdict is a different falsification.

4. Psychoanalytic / developmental

What it makes visible. A mind at the edge of adolescence: the wish for big things, the pride of being ready first, the invented rule of alternate bites, the game of feeding an adult figure who cannot eat — a child rehearsing independence and hospitality while still playing. The winking grown-up is a benign parental figure, present but not intrusive, in a poem with no actual parent, and the skeletons can be read as the first awareness of loss arriving inside play.

What it flattens. The poem's lightness: reading the sun as a displaced father imposes a depth the plain, comic surface does not invite.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A celebration of childhood

A hymn to a childhood morning: physical work enjoyed, every sense open, an imagination free enough to invite the sun to breakfast, and an ending that is just the cheerful debris of a good meal. Evidence: no word of complaint; the pleasure in big logs; the comedy of some latecomer; the sharing game. Weakness: it must ignore the deflations (unlike sawdust, just winks, little) and the forecast that encloses the morning in a day that will move on.

2. An elegy in the present tense

An adult writing about a world he has left uses the present tense to refuse to let the memory be past; the ache lies in what the poem does not say. Evidence: the generalising when you are fourteen, which only someone older can say; the knowing bracket; the ending's skeletons. Weakness: nothing in the poem mourns. The tone is playful throughout, and elegy imports a sadness the text only glances at.

3. A rite performed without being named

The poem records a ritual — a fire built, smoke sent to the sky, a power invited, food portioned out to it and consumed — performed in the shape the boy's culture has given him, without being called prayer. Evidence: sends up, sacrificial prayer; the chant-like fire stanza; the portion for the sun. Weakness: the poem hedges (of some sort), names no god or ceremony, and lets the sun decline with a wink. The ritual is at most a resemblance the poem notices.

4. A haiku-like poem of attention

In the manner of Bashō, whom Mungoshi admired, the poem is a sequence of exact images with the commentary removed, set in a marked season, cut by the isolated arc, and ending on a bare object rather than a conclusion: its subject is attention itself. Evidence: the one-sentence stanzas; the present tense; the season-markers of dew, storm and fresh maize; the refusal to explain the smoke or the skeletons. Weakness: it is also a story with a plot, a joke and a host-and-guest drama, closer to a Shona narrative work song than to haiku. The haiku is an analogy, not a form.

CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Connections

1. Seamus Heaney, 'Follower'

Link. The closest pairing: rural childhood, physical work and the wish to be bigger — Mungoshi's boy wants big logs, Heaney's wants to “grow up and plough”, and both poems hold an adult's one-eyed look (Heaney's “To close one eye”; the sun's wink). Difference. Heaney writes in the past tense and turns the relationship round at the end (the father “will not go away”); Mungoshi stays in the present with no verdict, and his boy is competent, alone and in charge.

2. Judith Wright, 'Hunting Snake'

Link. Suspended time in an encounter with nature under the sun: Wright's walkers “froze half-through a pace”, Mungoshi's chip lands eternities later, and both poems end in an unexplained return to ordinary life. Difference. Wright's is awe and fear before a creature that ignores the humans; Mungoshi's is friendship with a sun that answers with a wink.

3. William Shakespeare, Sonnet 18

Link. The selection's two great suns: Shakespeare's “eye of heaven”, sometimes “too hot”, and Mungoshi's late guest who winks — the sun as an eye, made intimate and comic — in two poems aware of transience. Difference. Shakespeare argues against time and claims victory through verse; Mungoshi lets the morning end as two little skeletons, without argument.

4. Carol Rumens, 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco'

Link. Children, work and the sacred, in the present tense: Rumens's children weave a carpet for a mosque, where it will be “heaped with prayer”; Mungoshi's boy sends up smoke that may be a sacrificial prayer. Difference. Rumens's children are watched from outside, labouring for others; Mungoshi's boy works for himself and turns the chore into a game, which sharpens the question of when children's work is a pleasure and when a cost.

5. William Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper'

Link. Two children at work early in the day, with religion in the background: Blake's “little black thing” in the snow, sent out while his parents pray, and Mungoshi's boy, warm, fed and unsupervised by his own fire. Difference. Blake is bitterly ironic about adults who exploit a child's happiness; Mungoshi has no irony and no exploiting adult. Both ask what a child is owed, and answer completely differently.
