CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Katherine Philips (1632–1664)

Katherine Fowler, a London Presbyterian cloth merchant's daughter, moved to Pembrokeshire when her widowed mother married Sir Richard Phillipps in December 1646. In August 1648, aged sixteen, she married James Philips, a twenty-four-year-old Parliamentarian kinsman of her stepfather. As "Orinda" she became the most admired woman poet of her generation, above all for poems on friendship between women.

'A Married State' comes from before the wedding. The only copy is untitled and unpunctuated, in her teenage hand, on a folded leaf dated between her mother's marriage and her own: she was fourteen to sixteen. The same leaf holds her poem describing the husband she would accept ("some man of sence", with "a good estate") and a mock "receipt" curing lovesickness with "the Powder of good advise". Thirteen of this poem's lines reappear in a later, longer anonymous satire to "Madam", apparently by several hands.

The married state in law and church

Under coverture an unmarried woman (feme sole) could own property, make contracts and sue; a wife (feme covert) was "covered" by her husband's legal person, her goods became his, and she could not normally act at law in her own name. A 1632 legal handbook, The Lawes Resolutions of Womens Rights, observed that a wife might "doubt whether shee bee either none or no more than halfe a person". The 1559 Prayer Book called matrimony "an honourable state, instituted of God in paradise, in the time of man's innocency", gave "the procreation of children" as its first cause, and asked the bride, "wilt thou obey him and serve him". Behind it stood Eve's sentence: "in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee" (Genesis 3:16). Pain, desire and a husband's rule were one curse; lines 7–8 and 15 refuse all three. The pain was literal: a married woman's lifetime risk of dying in childbirth was about one in eighteen.

St Paul's case for staying single

The poem's key words come from 1 Corinthians 7, the chief scripture ranking the single life above marriage (King James Version):

1 Corinthians 7 'A Married State'
"I would have you without carefulness" wives' careful faces; all the cares
"how she may please her husband" so hard to please
"attend upon the Lord without distraction" distract your prayers; Attend on matrimony
"he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better" be advised by me
"it is better to marry than to burn" Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel

The last two rows are where the poem leaves its authority: Paul gives the choice to the man who gives a virgin in marriage and lets those who cannot master desire marry; the poem gives the choice to one woman advising another, and allows nobody that exit.

The apes in hell

Satires against marriage were almost all men warning men off wives; this one warns a woman off husbands, against the "go marry" advice of poems like Herrick's 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' (1648). Its last line meets the threat behind that advice, the proverb that a woman who died unmarried would "lead apes in hell". In Lyly's Euphues (1578) a father uses it on his daughter, who later declares she will lead a virgin's life "though I lead apes in hell"; Shakespeare's Katherina dreads it, Beatrice jokes about it, and both end up married. Philips's speaker neither fears the penalty nor accepts it: she denies it exists.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

A Married State

This is the Songs of Ourselves text, with modernised spelling and punctuation. Versions online often keep Philips's manuscript spellings ('wifes Carefull faces', 'desemble', 'inocent'); quote the anthology's wording.

TA Married State
1A married state affords but little ease;
2The best of husbands are so hard to please:
3This in wives' careful faces you may spell,
4Though they dissemble their misfortunes well.
5A virgin state is crowned with much content,
6It's always happy as it's innocent:
7No blustering husbands to create your fears,
8No pangs of childbirth to extort your tears,
9No children's cries for to offend your ears,
10Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers.
11Thus are you freed from all the cares that do
12Attend on matrimony, and a husband too.
13Therefore, Madam, be advised by me:
14Turn, turn apostate to love's levity.
15Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel,
16There's no such thing as leading apes in hell.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
A Married State
Language & devices

Editorial title: the manuscript is untitled, so editors took the poem's first three words. Key noun: state is a condition of life, a legal status and, in the 1640s, a polity; the Prayer Book called matrimony "an honourable state". Indefinite article: A makes it any marriage, the institution rather than one couple.

Meaning & effect

The title names the thing on trial, in a phrase with its praise removed: the Prayer Book's "honourable state" becomes a bare married state, a status a woman enters, not a feeling she has. The generic A blocks the obvious reply ("but my marriage is happy") before anyone makes it. As printed, the title names only the state the poem rejects; the one it recommends arrives in line 5, worded as its mirror.

Line 1
A married state affords but little ease;
Language & devices

Aphorism: a general truth with no speaker, example or grievance, in perfectly regular Iambic pentameter. Verb: affords means yields or supplies, as land affords a crop, so the state is valued like an estate. Understatement: but little, not "none"; ease is freedom from pain, care and anxiety.

Meaning & effect

The case opens as a verdict everyone already knows: a complaint invites sympathy or dismissal, but a maxim in faultless metre invites agreement, and but little is harder to refute than "nothing". The poem begins by coining a proverb; it will end by abolishing one. affords also starts it keeping accounts in quantities (little, much, No, Few, all, no such thing), so the two lives are weighed like two estates.

Line 2
The best of husbands are so hard to please:
Language & devices

Concession turned into attack: The best of husbands argues from the finest case. Generic plural: husbands names a type; no single husband appears until line 12. Missing agent: hard to please never names who must do the pleasing. Embedded rhyme: please contains ease.

Meaning & effect

The poem's sharpest tactical choice. To call husbands cruel could be refuted by one kind man; to say that even the best are so hard to please makes the arrangement itself the fault, because pleasing is a standard never met once and for all. The wife does all the pleasing yet is missing from her own sentence, and in the rhyme her ease disappears inside his please.

Line 3
This in wives' careful faces you may spell,
Language & devices

Metaphor: faces as texts; spell (glossed "observe") is to make out letter by letter, reading what is not said. Diction: careful means full of care, anxious, not cautious. Demonstrative: This points back to line 2 as the claim to be proved. Possessive: wives appear only as the owners of faces.

Meaning & effect

The evidence is open to anyone who reads slowly: spell implies that most people look at wives without reading them, and you may spell makes the listener a witness who can test the claim herself. The grammar already divides the poem's women: the unmarried reader gets the active verb, while the wives are a possessive, the surface on which care is written. careful plants the word that line 11 returns as all the cares the single woman escapes.

Line 4
Though they dissemble their misfortunes well.
Language & devices

Concession: Though meets the objection that many wives look content. Verb: dissemble, to hide the truth under a false appearance, is the wives' only verb in the poem. Euphemism: misfortunes makes suffering bad luck, nobody's fault. End stress: well, skilfully, lands on the rhyme, and it is also the word a wife gives when asked how she is.

Meaning & effect

The strongest counter-evidence becomes more evidence: wives who look happy are simply good at hiding, because composure is part of what marriage requires of them. The move makes the case unanswerable, since a contented face now proves it. The unruffled metre performs the composure it describes, and the dry well admires the skill even as it exposes it.

Line 5
A virgin state is crowned with much content,
Language & devices

Parallelism: A virgin state answers A married state slot for slot. Antithesis: crowned against affords, much against little, content against ease. Metaphor: crowned joins the crown of virginity to the proverbial crown of the contented mind ("my crown is called content", 3 Henry VI). Turn: the case changes sides.

Meaning & effect

The alternative is built as the mirror of line 1, so choosing it looks like a fair comparison of two states, not defiance. Where marriage merely affords, the single life is crowned: honoured, and sovereign over itself, a pointed word when the first state absorbed a wife's legal person into her husband's. content is exactly what the careful faces lack.

Line 6
It's always happy as it's innocent:
Language & devices

Ambiguity: as means "because" or "in proportion as". Diction: innocent is guiltless and, at its Latin root (in-nocens), harmless. Contraction: It's… it's is brisk after the ceremonial crowned, and always allows no exception. Light rhyme: stressed content against the unstressed last syllable of innocent.

Meaning & effect

Happiness is tied to innocence, and the barb is left implicit: if the single life is happy because innocent, marriage must cost innocence, and the poem has just shown which kind, the daily pretence of line 4. The marriage service said matrimony was instituted "in the time of man's innocency"; this line gives innocence to the woman who stays out of it. And notice what is happy: It, the state. No woman in the poem is ever said to be happy.

Line 7
No blustering husbands to create your fears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: No… opens a three-line run, and Ellipsis removes the main verb ("[there are] no…"). Diction: blustering is used of gusting wind and of loud, bullying men full of empty threat. Infinitive of purpose: to create your fears makes causing fear the husband's function; your is the first of four possessives.

Meaning & effect

The first freedom is from a husband's temper, and blustering makes him menacing and faintly ridiculous, all wind; create says the fears are manufactured, not answers to real danger. From here each harm is the subject of an infinitive (create, extort, offend, distract), and the reader appears only as the owner of what they act on: your fears, then tears, ears and prayers. In the married state, as the grammar draws it, everything acts on a woman and she acts on nothing.

Line 8
No pangs of childbirth to extort your tears,
Language & devices

Anaphora: the second No. Diction: pangs is the Bible's word for labour ("as the pangs of a woman that travaileth"). Verb: extort, glossed "extract forcibly" (Latin extorquere, to twist out), is what an extortioner does to money. Plosives: pangs, childbirth, extort.

Meaning & effect

The darkest line, in the plainest rhythm. In the 1640s childbirth carried a real risk of death, and extort makes tears something wrung out of a woman, not shed by her: labour is force done to her. Eve's sentence bound sorrow in childbirth to a husband's rule, and lines 7–8 escape both halves of the curse at once, the ruling husband and the pangs.

Line 9
No children's cries for to offend your ears,
Language & devices

Archaism: for to is an older infinitive marker that fills the metre. Triplet: fears / tears / ears, the third rhyme being the first two with their opening consonant removed. Bathos: from mortal danger to noise.

Meaning & effect

After the risk of death comes the sound of crying children, a deliberate, funny drop that stops the catalogue becoming a lament; the list follows a married life in order (husband, labour, children) on a falling scale from terror to pain to irritation. The claim is narrower than callous: children are one more demand on a woman who already has no time of her own. Counting them among the burdens is still the poem's boldest departure from the marriage service, which named "the procreation of children" as marriage's first cause.

Line 10
Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers.
Language & devices

Broken anaphora: Few, not No. Diction: crosses (glossed "troubles") keeps Christ's cross behind the word, and worldly sets them against the soul; distract is Paul's word for what marriage does to devotion. Rhyme: prayers carries the triplet's sound into a fourth line. Climax: the catalogue ends on the soul.

Meaning & effect

The list's one concession is also its climax. Few is required by piety as much as honesty: a Christian must "take up his cross", so the single woman is promised fewer worldly crosses, not none, and the admission makes the speaker credible. The worst cost of marriage turns out to be not pain but the crowding-out of prayer, Paul's own ground, which no one could call irreligious; and with four lines on one sound, the catalogue is the one place where the couplets fail to close.

Line 11
Thus are you freed from all the cares that do
Language & devices

Logical connective: Thus draws the conclusion. Inversion and Passive: Thus are you freed is formal and oratorical; the reader is at last the subject, but of something done to her. Echo: cares returns to careful (line 3). Enjambment: the only run-on line, hanging on the filler auxiliary do.

Meaning & effect

The case closes in the language of release: marriage is bondage, and the single life is freed, a word with weight in a decade of civil war fought over liberty. The present tense says the reader is free already, so nothing has to change: the advice will be to stay as she is. cares closes the ring begun at careful faces, and the sentence spills over the empty do as the cares spill over a wife's days.

Line 12
Attend on matrimony, and a husband too.
Language & devices

Alexandrine: twelve syllables and six stresses, the only line longer than a pentameter. Personification: the cares Attend on matrimony as servants wait on a household, reversing Paul's "attend upon the Lord". Bathos: and a husband too, the poem's only singular husband, tacked on after the institution like an afterthought.

Meaning & effect

The poem's best joke carries one of its gravest claims. The line about marriage's burdens runs two syllables past the pentameter, and what overloads it is the add-on husband; too makes him an extra charge on the institution. Meanwhile the wife has vanished: the attendance a bride promised ("obey him and serve him") is performed by her cares, as if she had been absorbed into them, which is close to what coverture said happened to her.

Line 13
Therefore, Madam, be advised by me:
Language & devices

Logical connective: Therefore brings the application, as at the end of a sermon; Madam is the courteous Vocative of a verse letter. Passive imperative: be advised keeps the reader on the receiving end. First person: me is the poem's only first-person word; there is no "I". Headless line: nine syllables, so the address starts on the stress of Therefore.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns from proof to counsel, and only now does the speaker appear, in the object case inside a passive: not "I advise you" but be advised by me, authority claimed and veiled in one phrase. The claim is bold all the same. Paul left the decision to the man who "giveth her in marriage", read in the period as her father; here it passes to one woman advising another.

Line 14
Turn, turn apostate to love's levity.
Language & devices

Epizeuxis and Spondee: Turn, turn doubles the prophet's call to repentance ("turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways", Ezekiel 33:11) on two stresses. Religious diction: apostate, glossed "religious traitor", is one who deserts a faith. Diction: levity is lightness, frivolity, fickleness, the opposite of gravity. Light rhyme: stressed me against the weak last syllable of levity, a light rhyme on lightness.

Meaning & effect

The language of conversion demands its opposite: Ezekiel calls sinners back to God, Turn, turn calls the reader out of a faith, love's, so conversion and apostasy become one act seen from two sides. The whole charge against love's religion is one word, levity, set against the gravity of the poem's couplets and connectives. The syntax wobbles (Turn… to sounds like turning towards something) before the line settles it: renounce love's lightness.

Line 15
Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel,
Language & devices

Imperative and Political diction: Suppress is the verb for putting down a rising, rebel the rising. Personification: wild nature is a female rebel; she is the poem's only feminine pronoun. Subjunctive: if she dare is a challenge. Spondee: wild nature swells the line before regular iambs restore order.

Meaning & effect

The most honest line admits the cost: desire will rise, and the crowned woman of line 5 has a rebellion to put down inside herself. The irony is that the "rebel" is the urge towards the most conventional choice of all, so the unconventional life is cast as lawful order. Here the poem also leaves its scripture behind: Paul let those who "cannot contain" marry, since "it is better to marry than to burn"; the poem allows no such exit.

Line 16
There's no such thing as leading apes in hell.
Language & devices

Allusion: the proverb that women who die unmarried "lead apes in hell" (glossed "the proverbial fate of spinsters"). Colloquialism and Bathos: There's no such thing is plain speech after apostate, levity and Suppress. Rhyme: rebel / hell repeats the -ell of spell / well, in perfectly regular Iambic pentameter.

Meaning & effect

The last threat used to push women into marriage is not argued with but denied: a deadpan literalism that treats a scare-story as a factual claim and corrects it. Earlier heroines dreaded the proverb, joked about it or accepted the penalty; this line abolishes it in one plain sentence. Yet the rhyme leaves one road to hell open, through rebel, the desire of line 15, and the poem's last word is still hell.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'A Married State' is usually read as a list of marriage's miseries followed by brisk advice. That is accurate, and it undersells the poem. This is an argument about authority, about who may decide how a woman lives, and it wins by borrowing authority's own voices: the maxim, the marriage service, St Paul, the preacher, the ruler putting down a rising. Each is made to speak against marriage, and the one power left standing at the end, a folk threat with nothing behind it, is dismissed in a sentence. The poem opens by coining a proverb and closes by abolishing one. Underneath, the grammar moves the power to decide: wives have a single verb, dissemble; the unmarried reader ends with two commands.

The opening speaks as a maxim speaks. A married state affords but little ease has no speaker, instance or grievance; its metre is faultless and its verb a steward's, as land affords a crop. Line 2 makes the concession that wins the case: not cruel husbands but The best of husbands, so the fault lies in an arrangement where one person's occupation is to please another, a standard never met once and for all. The person doing the pleasing is missing from the sentence, and the rhyme buries her ease inside his please. When wives appear they are a possessive, wives' careful faces, a surface on which care is written, while the active verb goes to the reader: you may spell. Line 4 gives wives their only verb in the poem. They dissemble, and do it well. In the married state a woman has authority over nothing, not even her own face; her one act is to hide what is done to her.

Line 5 replays line 1 slot for slot, so the alternative arrives as a comparison, not a rebellion, but its verb is a sovereign's: the virgin state is crowned. What follows is St Paul's case for the single life, and the poem keeps his vocabulary of care, pleasing, distraction and attendance because nobody could call it impious. Its argument lies where it departs from him. The catalogue frees the reader from both halves of Eve's curse at once, the ruling husband and the pangs, and extort makes labour a kind of extortion. It counts children's cries among the burdens, against the marriage service's first cause, "the procreation of children". There is no main verb: each harm is the subject of an infinitive (create, extort, offend, distract), and the reader exists only as your, the owner of what they act on. Then the pattern breaks on Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers: the one concession is also the climax, and it lands on the soul, the safest ground the poem could choose.

Thus are you freed is the verdict. For the first time the reader is a subject, though of a passive, and the present tense says she is free already: the advice will be to stay as she is. Then comes the joke that carries the gravest claim. The cares Attend on matrimony, and a husband too: the bride's promise to "obey him and serve him" is kept by her cares, as if she had dissolved into them, while the poem's one singular husband arrives as an add-on that pushes the line two syllables past its measure.

Only now does a speaker appear, and even then not as "I": be advised by me. Authority is claimed and veiled in one phrase, and the claim is large, because Paul gave the decision to the man who "giveth her in marriage" and the poem gives it to one woman advising another. Then the borrowed voices change. Turn, turn is the prophet's call to repentance, conscripted to command apostasy from love's religion. Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel is the ruler's, and the reader now wields it: the crowned woman of line 5 has a province to govern, her own desire. Here the poem parts from its scripture, which let those who "cannot contain" marry. Last comes the threat behind the age's "go marry" advice, and the poem treats it as a factual claim and corrects it: There's no such thing as leading apes in hell.

The strongest objection is that this turns a game into a manifesto. The poem survives on one leaf beside a mock cure for lovesickness and a poem by the same girl describing the husband she would accept; within two years she married. Advice poems end in imperatives, satire exaggerates, and the jokes keep everything light. But the objection, followed through, strengthens the reading. The companion poem makes the same claim from the other side: accepting a husband on her own terms or refusing marriage outright, the girl assumes the decision is hers, and in the 1640s that assumption, more than any preference for the single life, was the bold thing. Nor is the wit a retreat. The jokes fall exactly on the gravest claims, the wife absorbed into her cares and the sanction that is only a story, and a joke can say what a complaint could not.

What the poem finally offers is not happiness, which it never claims for any woman (what is always happy is the state), but authority over oneself, and it is honest about the price. The verbs it hands its reader are Turn and Suppress: refusal and self-command. That is less than liberty in a modern sense and more than the married state offered, where a woman's one act was to hide. The last line removes the fear that might stop her using those verbs, and removes it with a shrug. The shrug is the argument: a threat that can be laughed out of existence was never a law.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A verse letter of counsel to Madam in heroic couplets: sixteen lines of rhymed iambic pentameter, built as an argument rather than a lyric.

Four movements

Lines 1–4: the case against marriage (axiom, then evidence). Lines 5–10: the case for the virgin state (axiom, then catalogue). Lines 11–12: the verdict (Thus). Lines 13–16: the advice (Therefore), ending by refuting a threat. 4 + 6 + 2 + 4.

Metre

Iambic pentameter, mostly very regular. Three lines break the measure: line 7 (eleven syllables unless blustering is elided), line 12 (the only alexandrine) and line 13 (nine syllables, headless).

Rhyme

aabbccdddd eeffbb: six couplets around one sound held for four lines at the centre (fears / tears / ears / prayers). The last couplet (rebel / hell) returns to the sound of lines 3–4 (spell / well).

Punctuation

The manuscript has none, so every stop in the anthology is an editor's; but it follows the syntax, so the shape it shows is the poem's own. Only lines 11–12 are enjambed; only lines 12–14 pause inside the line.

The form is not a container for the argument; it is the argument's credential. Closed couplets in pentameter were becoming the measure of polished public verse in the 1640s, and a generation later they would be the voice of Dryden and Pope. Each couplet clicks shut like a proposition proved. A girl writing against marriage in this measure claims the register of reason rather than of complaint, and the poem's few irregularities are placed where the argument needs them.

A proof in four movements

The poem moves like a proof, or like a sermon's doctrine, reasons and application, and its line-opening connectives are the signposts: This (the evidence), Though (the objection answered), Thus (the conclusion), Therefore (the application). The two halves of the case are built alike. Each opens with a two-line axiom, A married state… (1–2) and A virgin state… (5–6), and each axiom ends on a colon that opens its evidence: wives' faces (3–4), then the catalogue (7–10). The proportions matter. The case for the virgin state is the longest section, but it is made almost entirely of negatives (No… No… No… Few): the poem describes the good life by what is absent from it, which is rhetorically safe, since it never has to say what a single woman does with her days, and also its most exposed point.

The one formal surprise falls at the centre of the catalogue, where the grievances accumulate. A couplet poem trains the ear to expect closure every two lines; here one sound returns three times, then a fourth, and the form stops closing exactly where the troubles stop ending. It closes again only when the soul is reached, on prayers.

Scansion

Stresses in capitals; feet divided by |.

Line Scansion What it does
1 a MAR- | -ried STATE | af-FORDS | but LIT- | -tle EASE Perfectly regular. The axiom arrives with total composure.
2 the BEST | of HUS- | -bands are | SO HARD | to PLEASE Pyrrhic then spondee in natural speech: the stresses pile up on so hard, and the effort of pleasing is audible.
4 tho THEY | de-SEM- | -ble THEIR | mis-FOR- | -tunes WELL Perfectly regular. A composed line about composure: nothing in the sound betrays the strain it describes.
7 no BLUST'- | -ring HUS- | -bands to | cre-ATE | your FEARS Elision needed. Unelided, blustering gives eleven syllables: the husband's bluster overfills the line.
10 FEW WORLD- | -ly CROSS- | -es to | dis-TRACT | your PRAYERS Spondee on Few worldly: the word that breaks the anaphora takes a full stress, so the concession is heard.
12 at-TEND | on MA- | -tri-MO- | -ny AND | a HUS- | -band TOO Alexandrine: six feet. The line about matrimony's burdens runs two syllables over, and what overloads it is a husband too.
13 THERE | -fore MA- | -dam BE | ad-VISED | by ME Headless: nine syllables, the opening off-beat missing, so the address starts on a stress. The metre breaks where the voice turns personal.
14 TURN, TURN | a-POS- | -tate to | LOVE'S LEV- | -i-TY Spondee, pyrrhic, spondee: the urgent command jolts the rhythm; the final stress falls on a weak syllable for the rhyme with me.
16 there's NO | such THING | as LEAD- | -ing APES | in HELL Perfectly regular. Plain speech in perfect metre: the threat is dismissed with complete calm.

The pattern is clear. The case (1–6) is almost perfectly regular, as befits a demonstration. Disturbance gathers in the catalogue (7, 10), peaks in the verdict's overloaded line (12), and breaks at the turn to direct address (13–15). The last line returns to perfect order.

Rhyme

The rhymes are tight where the poem argues (ease / please, spell / well) and loosen where it praises or exhorts: the light rhymes content / innocent and me / levity each set a stressed syllable against an unstressed one. prayers is a near-rhyme to modern ears; in the 1640s, when these vowels were still shifting, it may have chimed fully, and either way it extends the run. The rhyme of lines 11–12 falls on the weak auxiliary do, which forces the only run-on. And the matching -ell rhymes link the beginning of the evidence to the end of the advice: what you may spell in wives' faces is set against the hell the poem abolishes, and the final couplet pairs that hell with rebellion, not with virginity.

Syntax and punctuation

The editors' stops make the syntax visible. A semicolon and a colon tie the first axiom to its evidence (1–2), a second colon does the same for the virgin state (6), and full stops close the married case (4), the catalogue (10) and the verdict (12); the advice then comes in two crisp two-line sentences, the first hinged on the poem's last colon (13). The catalogue itself has no main verb, which is why its harms seem to act by themselves. The pauses inside a line come only at the end of the case and the start of the advice: before and a husband too (12), then Therefore, Madam, and Turn, turn (13–14), exactly where the speaker turns to address her reader.

The turns

There are three. Line 5 is the argumentative turn, from the married state to the virgin state, marked by the parallel phrasing rather than by a conjunction. Line 10 is a small swerve inside the catalogue, Few for No. Line 13 is the main turn, from proof to command, from general to personal, from third person to first, and it is the most metrically disturbed line in the poem. The command that follows begins with the word itself: Turn, turn.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

ease inside please

The first rhyme is embedded: the wife's peace sits inside the husband's pleasure, and the long /iː/ lets both words linger.

Shrinking rhymes

ears is fears and tears without their first consonant: the chime returns as the troubles do, and shrinks as they do, from terror to noise.

Plosives at the points of force

blustering, pangs of childbirth, extort, crosses, Suppress: hard consonants gather where the poem names violence and effort.

The opening four lines are hushed by sibilance (state, so, spell, dissemble, misfortunes), which suits a diagnosis delivered almost confidentially, about something wives do not say aloud. Then a firm /k/ runs through the poem's key words, careful, crowned, content, crosses, cares: care and crown begin with one sound, and the two states are distinguished by what follows it.

The catalogue is where the poem becomes physical. blustering is close to onomatopoeia, a gust of /bl/ and /st/, and extort hisses and then snaps shut on /t/, the sound of something being wrung out. Against these, cries and ears are open and long, so the anticlimax of line 9 is audible as well as logical. Each No is a long, open vowel at the head of its line, a refusal said three times before Few softens it.

In the verdict the sound slows. Thus are you freed from all the cares that do is ten monosyllables, ending on the weak do, which cannot end anything, and the alexandrine that follows drags its six beats to the long vowel of too. Then the voice changes. Therefore, Madam, breaks into two falling words fenced off by commas; Turn, turn brings two stresses into collision, the hardest jolt in the poem; Suppress is a hiss of control before wild nature swells with long vowels and the clipped rebel puts the rising down.

The final line is the quietest: ordinary speech in regular rhythm, held together by the /l/ of leading and hell. Its no picks up the three Nos of the catalogue.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. The state: condition, status, kingdom

The poem's governing noun appears once for each life: A married state (1), A virgin state (5). At first it means simply a condition. But the second state is crowned, and from then on the word gathers political meaning: the single woman is freed (11), and at the end she must Suppress a rebel (15). By the close the two states are rival constitutions. In one the woman is a subject who must please and Attend on a ruler; in the other she is a crowned sovereign, with the duty every sovereign has of governing her own territory, which here means her own desire.

2. Care, pleasing and attendance

A chain of words makes married life a form of service. Husbands are so hard to please (2); wives' faces are careful (3); the single woman is freed from all the cares (11) that Attend on matrimony, and a husband too (12). Attend on is the verb of servants waiting on a household, and behind it stands the Prayer Book bride who promised to "obey him and serve him". The chain moves from the wife's obligation (please), to its mark on her (careful faces), to its personification (cares as attendants), and the single life is defined as release from the whole retinue.

3. Faces, reading and performance

The poem is preoccupied with the gap between what is shown and what is true. Wives' faces must be read slowly (you may spell, 3) because wives dissemble their misfortunes well (4); the virgin state is happy because innocent (6), free of the need to pretend. The motif ends with a story told to frighten girls, the apes in hell (16): an appearance with nothing behind it. The poem has moved from reading a mask to exposing a fiction.

4. Borrowed religion

Religious vocabulary runs from start to finish, and it changes direction as it goes. It first honours the single life (crowned, innocent, 5–6), then names marriage's spiritual cost (worldly crosses, prayers, 10), then treats love itself as a false religion (Turn, turn apostate, 14), and finally abolishes a false hell (16). Faith is the poem's licence: it lets a girl argue against marriage without sounding impious. But it is also its target, because the one sanction it dismisses outright is a religious one.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Marriage as an institution, not a relationship

The poem never attacks a husband: the generic A, the plural husbands and the concession The best of husbands are so hard to please make the complaint structural. Marriage is a state in which one person's occupation is pleasing another, close to the legal truth of coverture, and no individual kindness can change that.

02

What wives hide

The evidence is what wives conceal: they dissemble their misfortunes well, and the catalogue names what lies behind the composed face, down to the childbirth that will extort your tears. The calm voice and regular metre mimic the composure they expose.

03

Faith turned against custom

The case is religious before it is social: it climaxes on prayers, takes its key words from St Paul's argument for the single life, and frames its command as a conversion (Turn, turn apostate). Yet it outruns Paul at line 15 and laughs off a religious threat at line 16: faith is both its licence and something it is willing to correct.

04

Freedom as self-government

The single woman is crowned and freed, the vocabulary of rule and liberty in years when England was fighting over exactly those words. But sovereignty must be exercised: Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel admits that the crowned woman has a rebellious province to govern, her own desire.

05

Authority: who decides a woman's life

The poem's real question is who may decide, and it answers by borrowing authority's own voices (the maxim, St Paul, the preacher's Turn, turn, the ruler's Suppress) to hand the decision to Madam, advised by me. Wit is how the claim gets made: each joke (and a husband too, the crying children, the apes) falls on a serious claim and makes it sayable.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Counsel or game?

The difficulty. The facts are grave (a wife's legal erasure, death in childbirth) and the manner is playful (the crying children, the husband as afterthought, the apes). The addressee, Madam, is never named, and the speaker is never "I", only me.

Competing readings. (a) Real counsel. One girl warns another in a world where families arranged marriages, and every cost named was real. (b) A coterie game. The only copy shares a leaf with a mock "receipt" for lovesickness and a poem by the same girl setting terms for a husband she would accept; she married within two years, and thirteen of these lines turn up in a later, longer anonymous satire, as if they were common property for wits. (c) Roles, not persons. me is whoever has learned to read wives' faces, Madam whoever has not yet had to.

What a strong answer does. It refuses the choice. The jokes fall exactly on the gravest claims (the wife absorbed into her cares, 12; the sanction that turns out to be a story, 16), so play is how the poem says them, not proof that they are unmeant. And both poems on the leaf make the same bold assumption: that a girl may set the terms of her own life.

2. Suppress wild nature: liberation or a new confinement?

The difficulty. The poem promises freedom (freed, 11) and ends by demanding self-suppression (15).

Competing readings. (a) Sovereignty. Self-government replaces government by a husband. Suppression is the price any ruler pays, and it breaks the mechanism of Eve's curse, "thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee": no desire, no rule. (b) Ascetic confinement. Freedom from a husband is bought by denying one's own body; the ideal resembles the convent life Protestant England had abolished, without any of its institutions. (c) A claim about capacity. Paul let those who "cannot contain" marry; the poem assumes that a woman can contain, which is a claim about women's self-command as much as a renunciation.

What a strong answer does. It sees that the poem names its own cost, notices the irony that the rebel is the urge to conform, and holds (a) and (b) together: the freedom is real, and it is not free.

3. The last line: triumph or residue?

The difficulty. There's no such thing as leading apes in hell could be a victory or an anticlimax, and its last word is hell.

Competing readings. (a) Triumph. Earlier heroines dreaded the proverb, joked about it or accepted the penalty; this line declares it non-existent, in the plainest words and the most regular metre in the poem, which is the right way to treat a bogey. (b) Residue. Straight after conceding that nature will rebel, the poem ends on the place of punishment, and the rhyme of rebel with hell leaves one road there open, through desire. (c) A limit. It abolishes an imaginary hell but says nothing of the real costs of staying single: money, dependence, contempt.

What a strong answer does. It reads the line as the end of an argument about authority, in which law, scripture and custom are borrowed or weighed and the one threat with nothing behind it is simply thrown out. It hears no such thing completing the catalogue's No… No… No…: the last absence the single life is promised is hell itself. And it can say what the poem leaves unsaid.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. The best of husbands are so hard to please (2)

Concessive superlative; generic plural; missing agent; embedded rhyme. Arguing from the best case makes the complaint structural: no single man's kindness can fix an arrangement measured by his satisfaction, and hard to please names a standard, not a mood. Natural speech crowds the stresses onto so hard, so the effort of pleasing is audible, and the rhyme buries the wife's ease inside the husband's please. Intention and effect: the reply "some husbands are kind" is answered before it can be made, and the person who does the pleasing has already vanished from the sentence.

2. This in wives' careful faces you may spell, / Though they dissemble their misfortunes well (3–4)

Metaphor of reading; period diction; concession; euphemism. The couplet sorts women by their verbs. The unmarried you reads, letter by letter (spell); the wives dissemble, their only verb in the poem. careful is full of care, and misfortunes calls the cause bad luck, blaming no one. Line 4 runs perfectly smooth, a composed line about composure. Intention and effect: a contented face now counts as proof, and the reader is trained to read appearances against themselves.

3. A virgin state is crowned with much content, / It's always happy as it's innocent (5–6)

Parallelism; double metaphor; ambiguous conjunction; etymology. Line 5 replays line 1 slot for slot (crowned for affords, much for little, content for ease), so the choice reads as a comparison. crowned joins the crown of virginity to the crown of a contented mind; as means "because" or "in proportion as"; innocent keeps its Latin sense, harmless. Intention and effect: the barb is left to the reader (marriage costs innocence, the innocence spent in line 4's pretence), and the brisk contractions make a radical preference sound like common sense.

4. No blustering husbands to create your fears, / No pangs of childbirth to extort your tears, / No children's cries for to offend your ears, (7–9)

Anaphora; verbless syntax; infinitives of purpose; triplet; bathos. Three Nos, three harms, three infinitives, and three rhymes that shrink, ears being the bare remainder of fears and tears. The order is a married life's (husband, labour, children); the scale falls from terror to pain to noise. extort is the pivot: tears wrung out by force. Intention and effect: the reader, present only as your, sees a life in which everything acts on her, and the comic drop of line 9 keeps lament from taking over the argument.

5. Few worldly crosses to distract your prayers (10)

Broken anaphora; religious diction; extended rhyme; climax. Few is the one concession, and theologically exact: a Christian must bear a cross, so the single life is promised fewer worldly crosses, not none. distract is Paul's word, and the climax falls on the soul. The rhyme sound runs into a fourth line, so the catalogue is the one place where the couplets fail to close. Intention and effect: honesty buys credibility, and the case ends on Paul's own ground, where no one could call it impious.

6. Thus are you freed from all the cares that do / Attend on matrimony, and a husband too. (11–12)

Conclusion; passive; enjambment; personification; alexandrine. freed makes marriage bondage. The sense spills over the empty do, the only enjambment, and the next line swells to twelve syllables, overloaded by the add-on and a husband too, the poem's first singular husband. The cares do the attending a bride promised, and the wife disappears from her own sentence. Intention and effect: the verdict lands as a joke, and the joke carries the poem's gravest claim.

7. Turn, turn apostate to love's levity. (14)

Epizeuxis; spondee; inverted religious diction; light rhyme. The doubled verb is the prophet's call to repentance, but it calls the reader out of a faith, fusing conversion and apostasy. levity (Latin levitas, lightness) is the whole charge against love's god, set against the gravity of the poem's connectives, and its rhyme with me falls on a weak syllable. Intention and effect: love is demoted from sacred passion to a frivolous cult, and after the passive be advised the reader receives her first command to act.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

Feminist

The lens under which the poem looks most radical. It makes visible a woman's analysis of marriage as an institution that costs women: the duty to please (2), the mask of contentment (4), legal subordination in a state that affords little, the mortal risk of childbirth (8), and one woman's claim to advise another against the order arranged for her (13). What it flattens: the poem's class (it speaks to gentlewomen with families to keep them), its religious frame (the climax is prayers, not independence), and its ending in self-suppression, which some readers find a bleak substitute for liberty. It also risks treating as a manifesto a teenager's witty piece, written on a leaf that also sets out the husband she would accept.

Historicist

Puts the poem in 1646–48: a defeated king, a Second Civil War breaking out in the poet's own Pembrokeshire, a Parliament that had abolished the Prayer Book, and the law of coverture. Under this lens state, crowned, freed, rebel and Suppress carry the charge of the decade, and Madam faces a choice between two constitutions. It also shows what the poem answers: the Prayer Book's "honourable state" and its "remedy against sin". What it flattens: intention. Nothing shows the girl meant a political allegory, and the lens can turn a witty counsel poem into a pamphlet.

Theological

Reads the poem as a versified 1 Corinthians 7: care, pleasing, distraction, attendance, wife and virgin, happiness in remaining single. On this view Philips is less a rebel than a conservative, reviving the Christian preference for celibacy that Protestant England, having closed the convents, had quietly dropped, and the climax on prayers is sincere. It makes visible the poem's licence to speak and the precise point where it outruns Paul (Suppress wild nature against "better to marry than to burn"). What it flattens: the wit, and the last line, where a religious threat is dismissed as folklore.

Formalist

Shows the argument built into the verse: closed couplets as the sound of reason; a near-regular demonstration (1–6) disturbed in the catalogue (7–10), overloaded in the alexandrine (12), broken at the turn (13–15) and restored in the last line. It hears ease inside please, the triplet that refuses closure at the centre, the light rhymes on innocent and levity, and the -ell frame. What it flattens: everything outside the text, including the conventions the girl was playing with, and the question the form lets her avoid: what a single woman will actually do.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. The proto-feminist protest

One of the earliest arguments in English by a woman that marriage is bad for women as a class and that the single life is a legitimate, better choice. Evidence: The best of husbands (an institutional complaint); the dissembling wives; extort your tears; freed; be advised by me. Weakness: the alternative is defined almost wholly by negatives, its highest good is prayers, it ends in self-suppression, and it is a teenager's piece in a satirical genre whose lines turn up in a later anonymous satire, so it is risky to treat it as a personal manifesto.

2. Pauline counsel

A devout, conservative poem: St Paul's case for celibacy in verse, with his vocabulary almost intact. Evidence: careful, please, distract your prayers, Attend on, A virgin state, always happy. Weakness: it departs from Paul at the decisive point, refusing his concession that those who cannot contain should marry, and it ends by laughing at a religious threat. Piety is its licence, not its whole meaning.

3. Anti-romance, not anti-marriage

The real target is romantic love, not marriage: a clever girl's warning against marrying for feeling. Evidence: what must be renounced is love's levity and wild nature; the companion poem on the same leaf hopes for a husband "of sence" and "good estate"; the receipt beside it cures love with reason; its author married within two years. Weakness: lines 1–12 condemn the institution, not the motive for entering it. The companion poem trusts that a husband of sense will do; this one says that even The best of husbands is so hard to please, and childbirth and children come with any marriage, sensible or not.

4. The sceptic's reading

A brilliant piece of rhetoric that proves less than it claims. Evidence: line 4 makes the case unfalsifiable (happy wives are only dissembling); the good life is described only by what it lacks; the cost of the single life is reduced to desire, ignoring money and dependence. Weakness: the poem itself concedes (Few, Suppress), and its job is to persuade one reader, not to prove; its honesty about cost is unusual in advice of any kind.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

"A Married State"

Analysis
  • MS untitled → heading = first three words
  • state = condition / legal status / estate / polity
  • Prayer Book: "an honourable state" → poem drops "honourable"
  • A = generic → the institution, not one marriage
  • Names only half the case → the other state wins
1–2

The best of husbands

Analysis
  • Aphorism + understatement but little → verdict as common knowledge
  • Opens by coining a proverb … ends by abolishing one
  • affords = yields (like land) → marriage judged like an estate
  • Even the best → problem = system, not man
  • so hard to please → the pleaser (wife) erased; please swallows ease
3–4

wives' careful faces

Analysis
  • Faces = texts → spell (= observe) = read letter by letter
  • careful = full of care ≠ cautious
  • Reader reads; wives hide → dissemble = wives' only verb
  • well = skilfully / "I'm well"
Effect, style & response
  • Happy face = good dissembler → unanswerable
  • Smooth l. 4 = composure itself
5–6

crowned with much content

Analysis
  • Mirror of l. 1: married → virgin, affords → crowned, little → much, ease → content
  • crowned = crown of virginity + crown of content → her own sovereign
  • innocent = guiltless / harmless → marriage costs innocence (the pretence of l. 4)
  • Only a state is happy → no woman is
7–10

No… No… No… Few

Analysis
  • No main verb: harms act, reader = your ×4
  • blustering = storm wind + empty threats
  • extort = extract forcibly → childbirth as force (real risk of death)
  • Husband + pangs = both halves of Eve's curse escaped
  • fears → tears → ears = terror → pain → irritation (bathos)
  • Children = burden ≠ Prayer Book's "procreation of children"
  • Few = only concession → climax prayers (Paul's ground)
  • 4 lines on one sound → troubles won't close
11–12

and a husband too

Analysis
  • Thus → verdict; freed → marriage = bondage
  • are you freed → passive, present: already free → just stay
  • cares closes ring with careful; only enjambment
  • Alexandrine: 12 syllables, overloaded by and a husband too → only singular husband, an add-on
  • Cares do the attending → wife vanishes (coverture)
13–14

be advised by me

Analysis
  • Therefore → application (sermon / proof); headless line, 9 syllables
  • No "I"; me inside a passive → authority claimed, veiled
  • Paul: man who "giveth her in marriage" decides → here woman advises woman
  • Turn, turn = Ezekiel's "turn ye, turn ye" → conversion words command apostasy
  • levity = lightness, fickleness ≠ gravity of the couplets
15–16

Suppress wild nature

Analysis
  • Suppress, rebel → self as kingdom, desire as revolt
  • she = only feminine pronoun = nature, not a woman
  • Irony: the "rebel" = urge to conform (marry)
  • Paul: "better to marry than to burn" → no such exit here
  • There's no such thing → denial, not argument → threat = story
  • rebel / hell → hell for rebels, not virgins
Effect, style & response
  • Punchline wit… but last word = hell

Who decides

Analysis
  • Borrowed voices: maxim (1) → Paul (3–12) → preacher Turn, turn (14) → ruler Suppress (15)
  • Wife: erased (l. 2) → a possessive (l. 3) → only verb dissemble (l. 4) → absorbed into cares (l. 12)
  • Reader: may spell → your ×4 → are you freed, be advised (passive) → Turn, Suppress (commands)
  • Speaker: no "I", only me

Attitudes to marriage

Analysis
  • Institution, not a man → The best of husbands
  • Performance → dissemble
  • Danger, pain → extort your tears
  • Servitude → please, Attend on
  • Distraction from God → distract your prayers
  • Single life = crowned, freed … but Few, not No
Effect, style & response
  • Tone: cool verdict → witty catalogue → urgent command → deadpan shrug

Structure

Analysis
  • 16 lines, heroic couplets (iambic pentameter)
  • 4 + 6 + 2 + 4: case against → case for → Thus verdict → Therefore advice
  • aabbccdddd eeffbb → one sound ×4 (ll. 7–10); -ell frame (3–4, 15–16)
  • Alexandrine l. 12; l. 13 headless (9 syllables)
  • MS unpunctuated → stops = editors'; colons after both axioms (ll. 2, 6)
  • Turns: l. 5 (states), l. 10 (Few), l. 13 (advice)

Context

Analysis
  • c. 1646–48, aged 14–16, before her marriage (Aug 1648; James was 24, not 54)
  • Only copy: her hand, untitled; same leaf: husband "of sence", receipt "Powder of good advise"
  • 13 lines turn up in a later anonymous satire → lines circulated
  • Coverture: wife = feme covert; 1632: "none or no more than halfe a person"
  • Prayer Book: "obey him and serve him"; Gen 3:16: childbirth + husband's rule = one curse
  • Apes in hell = fate of spinsters: Lyly (1578) a father's threat; Katherina dreads it, Beatrice jokes → poem denies it
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Behn, 'Song: Love Armed' (01)

Two seventeenth-century women on love as a false god: Behn's lovers "set him up a Deity", Philips tells Madam to Turn, turn apostate to love's levity, and both arguments turn on "Thus" ("Thus thou and I, the God have armed"; Thus are you freed). But Behn writes from inside desire, after the harm is done, and freedom belongs to the indifferent beloved ("the Victor is, and free"); Philips writes from outside, advising escape before it begins, and freedom belongs to the woman who never marries.

2. Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper' (03)

Both expose suffering hidden behind a cheerful face, and an institution that uses the cheerfulness as its alibi: the sweep's "because I am happy and dance and sing, / They think they have done me no injury" beside wives who dissemble their misfortunes well. Both turn religious language on its users. Blake's victim is a child who cannot escape, and his voice is angry; Philips's addressee still can, and her voice is cool and strategic.

3. Pope, 'An Essay on Man' (12)

Two arguments in heroic couplets that open on a maxim ("Know then thyself, presume not God to scan"; A married state affords but little ease) and think in states: Pope's man hangs "between" on "this isthmus of a middle state", while Philips's reader must choose one of two, and is told to Suppress wild nature if she dare rebel. Pope later mocked the "needless Alexandrine" that "drags its slow length along"; Philips's line 12 drags on purpose, overloaded by the husband. His couplets describe a riddle; hers make a case and end in a command.

4. Shakespeare, Sonnet 18 ('Shall I Compare Thee…?') (14)

Both are short pentameter arguments borrowing legal and commercial language ("summer's lease hath all too short a date"; marriage affords but little ease). Sonnet 18 follows the seventeen sonnets urging a young man to marry and have children; Philips urges a woman not to marry and counts children's cries among the burdens. Shakespeare promises permanence ("So long lives this"); Philips calls love levity, and promises only release.

5. Bhatt, 'A Different History' (02)

Both examine customs enforced by sacred language: Bhatt's India makes it "a sin / to be rude to a book", and Philips's world threatens unmarried women with apes in hell. Both argue in the oppressor's own terms: Bhatt asks "Which language / has not been the oppressor's tongue?", and Philips argues against marriage in the Bible's words. Bhatt accepts a mixed inheritance with irony and tenderness; Philips refuses the inherited role outright.

An Essay on Man

Alexander Pope · 1733

Forbidden to scan God, man studies himself — and finds a creature so evenly divided that the only exact definition is a contradiction: the glory, jest, and riddle of the world.
