CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Alexander Pope (1688–1744)

Pope was born in London in 1688, the son of a Catholic linen merchant. The law treated Catholics as suspects — no university, no vote, no public office — so he was largely self-taught, reading his way through Latin, Greek, French and Italian literature outside the institutions that certified learning. Tuberculosis of the spine, contracted at about twelve, left him about four and a half feet tall and in constant pain; he called his existence “this long disease, my life”. He became the dominant poet of his age anyway. The man who wrote Great lord of all things, but a prey to all was a celebrated outsider in a frail body, though the passage speaks of “man”, not of Pope.

An Essay on Man (1733–34)

The Essay is a philosophical poem in four epistles, verse letters addressed to Pope's friend Viscount Bolingbroke, on man in relation to the universe, himself, society and happiness. Its aim is to “vindicate the ways of God to Man”, echoing Milton: a theodicy, arguing that the universe is well designed even though humans, seeing only a part of it, complain of disorder and evil. Epistle I ends “Whatever is, is right”, and Epistle II, published in 1733, opens with this extract: Know then thyself. After it comes a mocking survey of human achievement (“Go, wondrous creature!”), and then the constructive argument that self-love and reason must work together.

The Great Chain of Being

Behind a middle state lies the Great Chain of Being: everything that exists ranked on one ladder, from God through the angels (pure spirit) to man, animals, plants and lifeless matter, every rung filled. Man is the one link that is both spirit and matter, with a rational soul like the angels and a body and appetites like the animals. To wish to be higher than man is to wish creation broken — the pride the extract keeps returning to. The picture was under new pressure in 1733: Newton had shown that the heavens obey mathematical laws, and an age that could measure the planets might think it could measure God. presume not God to scan is aimed at that confidence.

Sceptics, Stoics, “Know thyself” — and Pascal

“Know thyself” (gnōthi seauton) was inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, and Socrates made it the first task of philosophy. The ancient Sceptics held that nothing can be known for certain, so the wise suspend judgement; the Stoics that virtue is the only good and the wise man, ruled by reason, is unmoved by pain, passion or fortune, a self-sufficiency Christian moralists called pride. The diagnosis of man as a contradiction comes largely from Pascal's Pensées, whose man is a “confused chaos”, “hanging” between the infinite and nothing. The difference matters as much as the borrowing: Pascal piles up the contradictions to drive the reader to God, while Pope keeps the diagnosis and, in his first line, forbids man to scan God.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

An Essay on Man
TAn Essay on Man
1Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;
2The proper study of mankind is man.
3Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,
4A being darkly wise, and rudely great:
5With too much knowledge for the sceptic side,
6With too much weakness for the stoic’s pride,
7He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,
8In doubt to deem himself a god or beast,
9In doubt his mind or body to prefer,
10Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;
11Alike in ignorance, his reason such,
12Whether he thinks too little or too much:
13Chaos of thought and passion, all confused;
14Still by himself abused or disabused;
15Created half to rise and half to fall,
16Great lord of all things, but a prey to all;
17Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:
18The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
An Essay on Man
Language & devices

The anthology prints the passage from An Essay on Man: these are the first eighteen lines of Epistle II of a four-part poem in verse letters. Essay is French essai, “attempt, trial”, and Man is a Generic noun for the species, the way a naturalist might write “on the horse”. The indefinite An is modest: one attempt.

Meaning & effect

The title promises a treatise, a general account of what a human being is; the extract shows that the subject resists exactly that kind of definition, so an essay, a trial, is the right word for an inquiry that ends on riddle. The then of line 1 points back to Epistle I, so the passage opens mid-argument, as a conclusion drawn from what came before.

Line 1
Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;
Language & devices

Two Imperatives, positive and negative, balanced across the Caesura: Know and presume not. Know… thyself is an Allusion to the Delphic maxim gnōthi seauton, and then means “therefore”. A Chiasmus (verb, object | object, verb) brings thyself and God together at the comma; scan means to examine minutely and to measure verse, and the Trochaic inversion on Know lands the command before the metre settles.

Meaning & effect

The whole passage starts on a hinge: left of the comma the inquiry Pope permits, right of it the inquiry he forbids — a door opens and a door shuts in one line. He does not deny God; he forbids man to scan him, to measure and judge God's ways like a line of verse, because that is presumption. The irony the next seventeen lines deliver is that the permitted object will prove almost as hard to scan as the forbidden one.

Line 2
The proper study of mankind is man.
Language & devices

An Aphorism: a complete, quotable proposition in ten syllables, ending in the passage's only full stop, with no comma to break it. Polyptoton narrows mankind to man, the species to the specimen, and the rhyme pairs the forbidden act, scan, with the permitted object. proper means fitting to our rank and also (Latin proprius) our own.

Meaning & effect

The line's shape — X is man — sounds final and self-evident, and that confidence is the set-up: the study is announced as a programme, and the next sixteen lines report that its subject is a mass of contradictions. The polyptoton hides a trap, since if mankind studies man the investigator is the specimen and can never get outside his object. proper also concedes a limit: not the highest study, but the one fitted to our station.

Line 3
Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,
Language & devices

The agentless Past participle Placed, stressed in an inverted first foot, implies a placer who is never named. The Metaphor isthmus is a narrow neck of land between two seas, and middle state is man's rank on the Great Chain of Being, state meaning both condition and rank. Suspended syntax: the sentence that starts here does not reach its main verb until line 7.

Meaning & effect

Placed carries the theological premise quietly: man did not choose his position, so complaining about it misunderstands the arrangement. The isthmus is exact on three levels — it joins, since man is where spirit and matter touch; it separates, with sea on either side; and it is narrow and exposed. The grammar does what the image says: we are placed in mid-sentence and kept waiting four lines for the subject.

Line 4
A being darkly wise, and rudely great:
Language & devices

Two Oxymorons balanced across the Caesura in exact Parallelism, adverb plus adjective twice: darkly wise, rudely great. darkly means dimly, as in poor light (“through a glass, darkly”), not sinisterly; rudely means roughly made, unfinished (Latin rudis, raw), not impolitely. A being is the vocabulary of the Chain, classifying man as one item in creation's inventory.

Meaning & effect

Pope grants man his two great claims, wisdom and greatness, and qualifies each in the same breath: wise, but in the dark; great, but rough-hewn. Nothing is denied and everything is diminished — the passage's method in miniature — and the balance makes the qualification sound like a measurement rather than an insult. The reader told to know thyself is shown a specimen in a catalogue.

Lines 5–6
With too much knowledge for the sceptic side, / With too much weakness for the stoic’s pride,
Language & devices

Anaphora (With too much) and exact Syntactic parallelism across the couplet, with Antithesis of knowledge and weakness, sceptic and stoic. The Sceptics held that nothing can be known, so the wise suspend judgement; the Stoics that the wise man, ruled by reason, is unmoved by pain or passion. The rhyme side / pride names stances, not doctrines, and both disqualifications come from excess.

Meaning & effect

The couplet explains line 4 by closing antiquity's two escape routes from the human condition. Man knows too much to doubt everything and is too weak to rise above pain, appetite and grief: the same middle position fails him in both tests, by making him too much of two things at once. The matched lines make the double exclusion feel like proof, and calling Stoicism pride ties it to the presumption of line 1.

Line 7
He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,
Language & devices

The Main clause at last: He and hangs arrive four lines after Placed. hangs means suspended, without footing, like the beam of a pair of scales, and the semicolon after between is the heaviest Caesura in the passage. The Anaphora of in doubt begins, with the Antithesis act or rest, and the Pronoun shift from thyself to He puts the reader outside the specimen.

Meaning & effect

After four lines of description the sentence finally lets man do something, and what he does is hang. between takes no object, because the objects are everything already named, and the semicolon leaves the reader dangling in the pause the word describes. The first doubt is the most practical — whether to do something or nothing — so the ordinary paralysis of a day sits under the grander doubts that follow.

Lines 8–9
In doubt to deem himself a god or beast, / In doubt his mind or body to prefer,
Language & devices

With line 7, the Anaphora In doubt builds a Tricolon of doubts — act/rest, god or beast, mind or body — now taking the line-openings. The Reflexive himself makes line 8 a doubt about self-assessment. In line 9 the Hyperbaton his mind or body to prefer postpones the verb to the end.

Meaning & effect

The doubts widen and then turn inward. Line 8 is cosmic: man cannot tell which end of the Chain he belongs to, the half that shares in the divine or the half that shares with animals, and he is the one doing the deeming. Line 9 brings the question inside his own skin, the delayed verb stumbling as though the choice keeps being put off. The three doubts descend from what to do, to what to be, to what to value in oneself.

Line 10
Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;
Language & devices

Parallelism across the Caesura — participle, but to, infinitive, twice — with Antithesis in Born / die and reasoning / err. but means “only”, and the heavy Trochaic inversion on Born opens the line on a blow; reasoning must be said as two syllables for the line to scan.

Meaning & effect

Line 10 answers line 9 by disposing of both options: the body exists to die, the mind to err. but to makes the end sound like the purpose — not merely that we die and make mistakes, but that this is what birth and reason are for. It is the bleakest line in the passage, and its neatness is half its force: a life's sentence in ten syllables, stated at full strength because the passage is building a case against pride.

Lines 11–12
Alike in ignorance, his reason such, / Whether he thinks too little or too much:
Language & devices

Ellipsis and Inversion: Alike in ignorance, his reason such means his reason is such that he is equally ignorant — result before cause, verb missing. The Antithesis too little or too much brings back the too much of lines 5–6, and the rhyme such / much is the flattest in the passage, two vague words of quantity. A Colon opens the final catalogue.

Meaning & effect

This goes further than line 10: not just that reason errs, but that more thought is no cure. The person who thinks too little stays ignorant through idleness, the person who thinks too much through over-subtle speculation, and they finish level — there is no right dose. The dull rhyme lands like a shrug, and the colon opens six lines that no longer argue at all; they simply list.

Lines 13–14
Chaos of thought and passion, all confused; / Still by himself abused or disabused;
Language & devices

From line 13 there is no main verb: man is defined by noun phrases in Apposition to He. Chaos, stressed in an inverted foot, is an Allusion to the formless state before Creation, and confused keeps its Latin sense, “poured together”. In line 14 Still means always, abused deceived and disabused undeceived (Archaic sense); the Polyptoton — one root with and without its negating prefix — rhymes with confused, and the metre stresses dis.

Meaning & effect

In a poem about an ordered creation, man alone is called Chaos, the condition of matter before God sorted it, and the chaos is a precise mixture: thought and passion poured together so that neither works alone. Line 14 adds an endless cycle — man fools himself, catches himself out and fools himself again — with no outside villain, since deceiver and deceived are one mind. himself is the last pronoun man is given; after it he becomes a list of titles.

Lines 15–16
Created half to rise and half to fall, / Great lord of all things, but a prey to all;
Language & devices

Created, like Placed, implies a maker. Parallelism and Antithesis split line 15 like a fraction, half to rise and half to fall, with fall carrying Adam's Fall. Line 16 is the only line divided exactly in half, five syllables either side of the comma: lord against prey, all doubled and rhyming back to fall, a heavy first half against a light, quick second.

Meaning & effect

The Chain is restated as arithmetic: man is built from both tendencies in equal measure, and Created removes both blame and any hope of escape, since you cannot climb out of your own specification. His relation to the world runs both ways at once — he rules everything, and anything can destroy him — and the doubled all leaves no safe remainder. prey drops him back among the animals, answering god or beast with both at once.

Line 17
Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:
Language & devices

Antithesis and Chiasmus: judge of truth / error hurled, truth and error meeting at the caesura, the seated judge and the flung body at the edges. Sole means the only one, with no higher court; hurled, a violent, involuntary Passive participle, is an Allusion to Milton's verb for Satan's fall. Alliteration and Assonance in endless error, which also brings back line 10's err.

Meaning & effect

Forbidden to scan God, man is the only judge of truth left, and that judge is being flung endlessly through error. Judging is an act of stillness and authority, being hurled is helpless motion, so the line pictures a judge whose bench is falling. endless removes the hope that error might run out, and the colon makes the last line a sentence passed on the judge himself.

Line 18
The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!
Language & devices

A Tricolon — glory, jest, riddle — after fifteen lines of pairs. Two commas make it the only line with two marked pauses, isolating jest between them, and the passage's only Exclamation closes the sentence that began at line 3. The rhyme hurled / world ends the passage on world, not “man”.

Meaning & effect

The verdict refuses to be a verdict: three terms instead of two, as if man cannot be summed up even as a pair. glory is what we may be proud of, jest what we may be laughed at for, riddle what neither settles. The exclamation holds wonder and exasperation together, and the last word places the creature we were told to study inside the larger spectacle of creation — and a riddle, unlike a sentence, invites another attempt.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

The passage obeys its own first line. Forbidden to scan God, it scans man, with every measuring instrument the heroic couplet possesses — balance, antithesis, half-line set against half-line — and the reading it gets is a contradiction. Pope's achievement is to make that failure exact: the more precisely man is measured, the more clearly he refuses to come out as a single quantity. So the extract is neither a lament for human weakness nor a hymn to human greatness. It demonstrates that the “proper study” begins with the student discovering how much of himself he cannot see.

Know then thyself, presume not God to scan opens a door and shuts one in the same ten syllables: the Delphic command that began Greek philosophy, then a prohibition. then means “therefore” — Epistle I has argued that the universe looks disordered only because we see a fragment of it — and scan names the forbidden activity in a line that itself scans perfectly. Line 2 states the programme in the passage's only sentence of untroubled confidence, The proper study of mankind is man. It sounds like the opening of a research project. Everything after it is the research report, and the report is unsettling.

The second sentence begins with Placed, a participle with no agent named: someone put man here, and complaining about the placing would repeat the presumption of line 1. this isthmus of a middle state locates him at the one rung of the Great Chain that is both spirit and matter, a strip of land that joins, separates and endangers. Then Pope grants man his two great claims and qualifies each as he grants it, darkly wise, and rudely great, and lines 5–6 close antiquity's two escape routes: too much knowledge to be a sceptic, too much weakness for the Stoic's pride. Both disqualifications come from excess.

After four lines of description the subject finally appears, and his one action is hangs. The grammar mirrors the image: He is suspended between four lines of description before him and eleven after. Three doubts follow, each widening the gap — what to do, what to be, what to value in himself — and line 10 removes the grounds for choosing: Born but to die, and reasoning but to err. Lines 11–12 go further still. Thinking more is no cure; man is Alike in ignorance at either dose, and the flattest rhyme in the passage, such/much, lands where reason runs out.

From line 13 the verbs go. Man is no longer allowed to do anything; he is renamed, six times: Chaos, the state of matter before Creation; a mind by himself abused or disabused, deceiving and undeceiving itself in an endless cycle; a creature Created half to rise and half to fall. Two titles are awarded and snatched back within their lines — Great lord of all things, but a prey to all, split exactly down the middle, and Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled, a judge whose bench is falling. The participles are passive throughout (Placed, Born, Created, hurled), so even the grammar treats him as something acted upon.

Then the form breaks its own habit. After fifteen lines of pairs, the last line gives three terms, as if man cannot be summed up even as a contradiction between two things: glory, what we may be proud of; jest, what we may be laughed at for; riddle, what neither pride nor laughter settles. The exclamation mark holds wonder and exasperation together, and the last word is not “man” but world: the student told to study himself ends by seeing himself as one strange item in a spectacle he cannot see whole.

The strongest objection is that this is either commonplace philosophy in brilliant clothes, or despair without a remedy — Pascal's indictment of fallen man with Pascal's cure removed. Both charges misread the extract's job. It is the opening of an argument, not its end: the next line of the poem is “Go, wondrous creature!”, and later in the epistle Pope begins the constructive case, “Two principles in human nature reign; / Self-love, to urge, and reason, to restrain”. The extract does contain a remedy, and it sits in line 1: humility. To know that you cannot scan God, and that your own reason misleads you, is the self-knowledge the Delphic command asked for. Nor is the tone despairing: jest and riddle are comic, puzzled words. As for the ideas being old, the poem does not merely state them; it acts them out. The subject that hangs between its modifiers, the verbs that vanish, the antitheses that speed up to one per line, the exact central split of line 16, the pattern of pairs broken by the last line: these are the argument, carried out on the reader's ear. The study of man is “proper” because it is the one study whose failure teaches something true — what kind of creature is doing the studying.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Nine heroic couplets, the first verse paragraph of Epistle II: didactic verse in a public voice, with general nouns and no “I”. It argues; it does not confide.

Metre

Iambic pentameter, regular enough that every departure is audible. reasoning is said as two syllables.

Rhyme

Nine full, masculine couplet rhymes; only rest/beast is imperfect to a modern ear.

Syntax

Two sentences: a command and its reason (1–2), then one sixteen-line sentence whose only main clause is He hangs between (7).

The heroic couplet: a form built for weighing

A heroic couplet is a pair of rhyming pentameter lines; when sense and syntax finish with the rhyme it is “closed”, and each couplet lands like a small, complete proposition. The form offers balance at two levels: line answers line across the rhyme, and inside each line the caesura divides the ten syllables into halves that can be set against each other. Line 2, one of the most quoted lines in English, shows what the form does to an idea: it makes it memorable and final. The irony is that a machine designed to weigh and settle is turned on a creature who will not settle. Couplet after couplet clicks shut on a judgement, and each judgement is that no judgement holds; the form's confidence and the content's uncertainty pull against each other, and that tension is the passage's main effect.

Four movements

Lines 1–2, the command and its reason, are the only couplet that is a complete sentence, sealed by the passage's only full stop. Lines 3–6 begin the second sentence but withhold its subject: a participle (Placed), a noun phrase (A being), two parallel phrases (With too much), all describing a man not yet named. Lines 7–12 deliver the main clause, the three doubts and reason's double failure, closed by a colon. Lines 13–18 are a catalogue with no main verb, one contradiction per line, ending in the three-part verdict. The movement runs from instruction to description to pure paradox, and the imperative of line 1 never returns: Pope commands once, then spends sixteen lines showing why the command is so hard to obey. The decisive turn is the last line, which breaks the form's habit of pairs.

Metre and caesura: the key lines

Capitals mark stressed syllables, · the division between feet, ‖ the caesura.

Line Scansion What the variation does
1 KNOW then · thy SELF, ‖ pre SUME · not GOD · to SCAN Inverted first foot: the command lands before the metre settles, then four regular iambs restore order.
2 the PROP · er STUD · y OF · man KIND · is MAN Fully regular, with no punctuated pause: the line runs in one breath to man, and certainty sounds seamless.
7 he HANGS · be TWEEN; ‖ in DOUBT · to ACT · or REST Regular feet, but the heaviest pause in the passage falls after between: the line hangs where it says hangs.
10 BORN but · to DIE, ‖ and REAS · 'ning BUT · to ERR Inverted opening on Born; the halves are built alike, so the second blow repeats the first.
13 CHA os · of THOUGHT · and PAS · sion, ‖ ALL · con FUSED Inverted opening; a late caesura, after the seventh syllable, leaves all confused as a short, sagging tail.
16 GREAT LORD of ALL THINGS, ‖ but a PREY to ALL The only exact 5 ‖ 5 split: stresses crowded into the first half, two quick light syllables after the pause — the title heavy, the fall fast.
18 the GLO · ry, ‖ JEST, ‖ and RID · dle OF · the WORLD Pauses after the third and fourth syllables isolate jest; then an unbroken run of six syllables to world.

Most pauses fall after the fourth or sixth syllable, the standard Augustan positions, so the three exceptions stand out: line 16's perfect central balance for the passage's most total reversal, line 13's late collapse, and line 18's break into three. Several unpunctuated lines still divide sharply on a conjunction — a god or beast, too little or too much, abused or disabused, half to rise and half to fall — so the balance is carried by syntax alone.

Rhyme

The rhyme-words trace the argument. scan / man pairs the forbidden act with the permitted object, so the first rhyme already contains the whole programme; side / pride rhymes two stances; rest / beast, the one rhyme that does not quite close to a modern ear, falls on the doubting couplet; prefer / err answers a choice with a mistake; such / much, the flattest pair, sits where reason runs out; confused / disabused packs three “-used” words into two lines, a rhyme that goes round in a circle; fall / all joins the Fall to the totality. The passage opens by pairing scan with man, examining a creature, and closes by pairing hurled with world, that creature flung across the universe he was meant to study.

Syntax: where the subject is, and what it does

The subject of the long second sentence is a single word, He, and it does not appear until line 7: four lines of description come before it and eleven of renaming phrases after, so the grammar does what the main verb says. There are only five finite verbs in eighteen lines — Know, presume, is, hangs, thinks — and man is the subject of just two of them. From line 13 there is no verb at all, only noun phrases set beside He to rename him, and the participles describing him are things done to him: Placed, Born, Created, hurled. The only active participle, reasoning, is but to err.

The pronouns fade the same way. Man is thyself, then He, himself, his, and after line 14 he has no pronoun at all. A passage that begins by addressing you ends with the noun world: as the sentence proceeds, man loses first his actions, then his person.

Antithesis accelerating

About fifteen antitheses run through the passage — sceptic/stoic, act/rest, god/beast, mind/body, born/die, rise/fall, lord/prey, truth/error — and their rate rises: early on one opposition fills a couplet, and from line 13 there is one per line, six lines running. Two chiasmi frame them (lines 1 and 17), and two tricolons break them: the three doubts and the three nouns of the last line.

Punctuation and pace

There is one full stop (line 2) and one exclamation mark (line 18). Between them the marks are commas, semicolons and colons, which suspend rather than close. Each colon opens onto something larger — the explanation of lines 5–6, the catalogue of 13–18, the final verdict — and because every line ends on punctuation, the sixteen-line sentence is built by accumulation, unit added to unit, piling up the way the contradictions do.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Soft half, hard half. Know then thyself runs on soft, continuous sounds — n, th, s, f — while presume not God to scan is full of stopped consonants, p, t, g, d, k. The permitted inquiry sounds easy; the forbidden one sounds hard-edged, a door closing on scan.

The hum of line 2. mankind is man is built on nasals, and the line has no internal pause, so it is spoken in one breath and ends on its strongest syllable. Its smoothness is the source of its authority.

Doubt and excess. in doubt… In doubt… In doubt restarts three times from the same sound without moving forward, the audible shape of indecision, with a d alliteration in doubt to deem. too much sounds three times, and too little or too much is clipped and repetitive. Every repeated sound in the passage repeats an amount or a doubt.

Blows and circles. Line 10 is packed with plosive b, t and d, with no liquids to soften them, and its matching halves land like a repeated blow. such / much is the dullest rhyme, two colourless syllables where reason runs out; then confused, abused and disabused put three buzzing “-used” endings into two lines, with a beat on dis, so the ear hears one word turned inside out — a sound going round in a circle, like the self-deception it describes.

Weight and speed. Great lord of all things is slow, with long vowels and crowded stresses; after the comma, but a prey to all tumbles fast. Sole judge of truth is grave and long-vowelled, then endless error hurled runs short e sounds into rolling r and l: stillness turning into a tumble.

The last line. glory, riddle and world are full of liquid l and r, so the line rolls; jest is the one word without them — short, sibilant, ending on a hard t, isolated between commas — so the joke-word sounds different from everything around it. The passage that began with the bright, open -an of scan / man ends on hurled / world, a dark vowel and an -rld cluster that rolls and does not close cleanly.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

1. Measuring

It begins with scan, to examine minutely and to count the beats of verse, and the words of quantity multiply: middle, too much twice, too little or too much, half… half, all… all, Sole, endless. Man is weighed and calculated, and the answer never comes out — too much for one philosophy, too much for the other, equally ignorant at either dose, exactly half one thing and half another. By the end the measurements are total (all) or infinite (endless), and measurement turns into riddle. The motif turns the age's confidence in calculation back on the measurer.

2. Rank: up, down and between

The Great Chain is vertical, and the passage keeps moving on that axis: presume is the upward overreach, a god or beast names the top and bottom of man's neighbourhood, half to rise and half to fall makes the motion his design, and Great lord against prey, the seated judge hurled and finally glory mark the extremes. Between them runs a vocabulary of position — isthmus, middle state, side, He hangs between — and the hinge-word or, five times. Man is never allowed to stay at any height: his place is in between, and his characteristic motion is a drop.

3. The self as its own object

thyself, himself, by himself: the reflexive keeps returning, because in the study of man investigator and specimen are the same person. The polyptoton mankind… man states it, and Still by himself abused or disabused shows its cost: deceiver and deceived, corrector and corrected, are one mind. Pope also keeps the specimen at arm's length — A being, He — as if self-knowledge required treating oneself as a third person.

4. The hidden maker

God is named once, in the command not to scan him, yet he is everywhere in the grammar: Placed, Born and Created are passive participles whose agent is never named but is obviously present. The motif ends in glory, the word Scripture uses for God's own splendour, here given to man. The maker cannot be examined, but his handiwork is the whole subject; the design is felt in every line, which is why complaint about it would be presumption.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

The limits of human knowledge

The passage opens with a prohibition, presume not God to scan, and spends seventeen lines showing why it is wise: man is darkly wise, reasons but to err, and is Alike in ignorance whether he thinks too little or too much. Reason's range is fixed, and pushing it harder only gives a different ignorance of the same size.

02

Self-knowledge: the proper study

Know then thyself makes the Delphic maxim the only licensed inquiry, and the study yields not a portrait but a list of contradictions, with the self as its own deceiver. Knowing oneself as The glory, jest, and riddle of the world is still real knowledge, the kind Socrates meant.

03

Man's middle place

this isthmus of a middle state puts man on the Great Chain between angels and animals, Created half to rise and half to fall, both lord and prey. The middle is honourable, as the link joining two halves of creation, and unstable, since he belongs wholly to neither.

04

Pride and presumption

The vocabulary is theological — presume, pride, fall, hurled — and the sin attacked is the one that destroyed Satan and Adam: wanting a knowledge and a status not one's own. Each grand title (Great lord of all things, Sole judge of truth) is cut down in the same line; Pope condemns not weakness but the refusal to accept its terms.

05

Reason and passion

Chaos of thought and passion, all confused names the conflict the rest of Epistle II takes up, and line 10 disposes of both halves of a person: the body Born but to die, the mind reasoning but to err. The chaos is a problem stated in order to be worked on.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. The proper study of mankind is man: a programme or a retreat?

The difficulty. The line is quoted everywhere as a humanist slogan, a celebration of studying human beings. In the poem it follows a prohibition, and what follows it is a list of human failures.

Competing readings. Programme: the line launches a new science of human nature, in the age of Locke, which wanted to audit the mind before trusting it. Retreat: forbidden to scan God, we fall back on the only object within range — the study of man instead of God, not as the crown of knowledge. The line echoes Pascal's “The study of man is the proper employment and exercise of mankind”, but Pascal meant studying man instead of mathematics, never instead of God. Irony: the confident announcement sets up a study whose result is riddle.

What a strong answer does. It takes proper seriously — fitting to our rank, not the highest study — and notices Pope's revision: the first edition read “The only science of mankind is man”, and he softened an exclusive claim into a humble one. The line is both programme and limit, and the passage tests it at once.

2. presume not God to scan: piety or deism?

The difficulty. The line sounds like Christian humility, yet within a few years of publication the poem was attacked as fatalistic “natural religion”, a religion of reason that needs no revelation.

Competing readings. Orthodox: this is the angel's advice to Adam in Milton, and Job's question whether man “by searching” can “find out God” — humility before mystery; and the poem's stated aim, to “vindicate the ways of God to Man”, is Milton's own. Deist: the extract mentions no Christ, grace, soul or afterlife; Born but to die leaves out what a Christian would add, and where Pascal's identical contradictions end in a call to listen to God, Pope forbids the inquiry and offers no Saviour; the first edition's line 8, “To deem himself a part of God or beast”, could even sound pantheist. Strategic: Pope, a Catholic in a Protestant country, wrote a theodicy broad enough for any believer.

What a strong answer does. It notices what is present and what is absent. God is everywhere in the grammar (Placed, Created) but never approached, and the passage's remedy is humility, not grace — which is why it could be praised as pious and attacked as deist.

3. What tone is the last line?

The difficulty. The glory, jest, and riddle of the world! can be read as awe, contempt or comedy, and the exclamation mark fits all three. It is the passage's only exclamation, so there is no earlier one to measure it against.

Competing readings. Awe: glory is the word Psalm 8 uses for man “crowned… with glory”, and the next line of the poem is “Go, wondrous creature!” Contempt: jest is the operative word; the passage has earned exasperation, and a riddle has no answer. Comic mastery: the satirist's flourish — Pascal had called man the “glory and refuse” of the universe, and Pope replaces refuse with jest, trading disgust for laughter.

What a strong answer does. It argues that the line is built not to resolve. The tricolon breaks the pattern of pairs, the words rise, drop and suspend, and the comparison with Pascal shows which way the tone leans: away from revulsion, towards amused wonder. A line about irresolvability would be poorly served by a single resolved tone.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. Know then thyself, presume not God to scan;

Two imperatives across a caesura; Delphic allusion; chiasmus; pun on scan. The permitted half is the founding command of philosophy; the forbidden half names the sin, presumption. The pattern crosses — verb, object | object, verb — so thyself and God, the two possible objects of knowledge, meet at the comma while the two verbs of knowing stand at the edges. Intention and effect: Pope fences philosophy's first command at once, so the reader starts with a limit, and the tidy form makes the restriction feel reasonable rather than arbitrary.

2. The proper study of mankind is man.

Aphorism; polyptoton; only full stop; no punctuated caesura. A complete thesis in ten syllables, its predicate held back to the last two, is man. mankind… man narrows the species to the specimen, so student and object become one. Intention and effect: the line sounds self-evident, which is the set-up for what follows: the passage's most confident sentence introduces a study whose result is a riddle.

3. Placed on this isthmus of a middle state,

Agentless passive participle; metaphor; the Great Chain of Being. Placed implies a placer who is never named, and the isthmus — a neck of land that joins two land masses and separates two seas — makes man the joint between spirit and matter, honoured by the position and endangered by it. Intention and effect: the reader feels the precariousness, and the passive verb quietly forbids complaint: we did not choose our station.

4. He hangs between; in doubt to act or rest,

Delayed main clause; the heaviest caesura; start of the in doubt anaphora. The subject arrives after four lines of description, and his one action is to hang; the semicolon leaves between dangling, and He is suspended between his own modifiers. in doubt then repeats three times, moving from mid-line to the line-openings as the doubt takes over. Intention and effect: the reader is held in the pause the word describes, so indecision is heard and felt, not just stated.

5. Born but to die, and reasoning but to err;

Parallel halves; but meaning “only”; antithesis; plosives. Body and mind are each reduced to their failure, and but to makes death and error sound like the purposes of birth and reason; the halves share a rhythm, so the second blow repeats the first. Intention and effect: the bleakest line in the passage, stated at full strength because the passage is building a case against pride, not pronouncing a final sentence.

6. Still by himself abused or disabused;

Archaic sense; polyptoton; reflexive; metrical stress on dis. abused meant “deceived”, disabused “undeceived”, and Still means always: man fools himself, catches himself out and fools himself again, with no outside deceiver. The two words differ only by a prefix, and the metre stresses it. Intention and effect: a strikingly modern idea of the self as its own deceiver, in a sound that circles as the mind does.

7. Great lord of all things, but a prey to all; / Sole judge of truth, in endless error hurled:

Antithesis; exact 5 ‖ 5 balance; chiasmus; Miltonic verb. Each line grants a title and takes it back. The doubled all makes line 16 airtight — the same totality is his kingdom and his predator — and line 17's judge is hurled, Milton's word for Satan's fall, so a seated authority becomes a body in flight. Intention and effect: the comic timing of satire, set up and knocked down in ten syllables, carrying a frightening idea: forbidden to scan God, man is the only judge left, and there is no higher court to appeal to.

8. The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

Tricolon breaking the pattern of pairs; two caesuras; the only exclamation; final word world. After fifteen pairs, three terms: what we are proud of, what we are laughed at for, what settles neither, with jest standing alone between two commas. Intention and effect: the form breaks to prove its point — man cannot be summed up even as a pair — and the last word sets the specimen inside the whole spectacle of creation, which the next line of the poem greets with “Go, wondrous creature!”

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Historicist

What it makes visible. A poem written in the decade after Newton, when measurement seemed limitless and Pope had just written Newton's epitaph: presume not God to scan is aimed at that confidence, and the passage's own measuring words (too much, half, all) turn calculation back on the calculator. It also places the author — a Catholic barred from university and office, self-taught, publishing anonymously to dodge his enemies.

What it flattens. A general account of humanity becomes a period document, when the extract has lasted precisely because its paradoxes are not tied to 1733.

2. Psychoanalytic

What it makes visible. A divided self: Chaos of thought and passion, a mind by himself abused or disabused, unable to choose between mind or body. Self-deception without an outside deceiver anticipates later ideas of the unconscious, and the shift from thyself to He looks like a mind that can only examine itself by stepping outside itself.

What it flattens. History: the lens is anachronistic, since Pope's passions are not repressed drives, and the rest of Epistle II proposes not analysis but balance, self-love urging and reason restraining.

3. Feminist

What it makes visible. The generic masculine — mankind, man, He, himself, lord: the universal human being is grammatically male, and the middle state between god and beast is described as if it were a man's position. Set beside Katherine Philips, who weighs women's legal and bodily lot in the same couplet form, Pope's state of man looks like a view from a particular place.

What it flattens. The eighteenth-century convention in which man meant humankind; the extract makes no claim about women at all.

4. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. The Chain as an ecology of ranks, and man's double place in nature: Great lord of all things, with Genesis's dominion over creation, but a prey to all, hunted and vulnerable, one link among many. Epistle I mocks the pride that thinks the universe was made for us. Read today, after Boey's ‘insatiate man moves in for the kill’, lord of all things sounds like a warning.

What it flattens. History again: the lens imports modern environmental worries into a poem whose hierarchy is fixed and God-given, not a web to be protected.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Alternative readings

1. The problem stated, not the verdict

The extract is the first step of an argument: Pope's own marginal summary calls it “His middle nature”, and the constructive case follows later in the epistle. Evidence: the next line, “Go, wondrous creature!”, is a challenge, not an epitaph, so the dark picture provokes the search for truth rather than ending it; and the epistle goes on to propose self-love and reason as the two principles that order the chaos. Weakness: the anthology prints these eighteen lines alone, and they must stand on their own; their eloquence goes into the indictment, not the cure.

2. Satire: mock-heroic anthropology

The author of The Dunciad sets up grand titles and knocks each down in the same line. Evidence: Great lord of all things and Sole judge of truth, each reversed within ten syllables; jest is a satirist's word, and the exclamation can be heard as a flourish. Weakness: the satire has no target but everyone, the poet included, and the passage's seriousness about knowledge and God is not a joke. Satire is one register among several, not the whole.

3. A humanist celebration of range

The proper study of mankind is man became a humanist slogan, and the man of these lines contains glory and is lord of all things, a creature whose very contradictions make him the most interesting object in creation. Evidence: the slogan itself; glory; the wonder of the exclamation. Weakness: the line is framed by a prohibition and followed by error, ignorance and chaos. The celebration is real but always qualified.

4. A disabled poet's body in the argument

Pope stood about four and a half feet tall, lived in constant pain from spinal tuberculosis and called his life “this long disease”. Evidence: rudely great, his mind or body to prefer and a prey to all had a personal meaning for him. Weakness: the passage speaks of “man”, not of Pope, and its terms come from Pascal and the Chain of Being; biography may explain the force of the physical vocabulary, but it cannot be its meaning.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

“An Essay on Man”

Analysis
  • Essay = attempt, trial (French essai) → modest, provisional
  • Man = humankind (generic), not the male sex
  • extract = first 18 lines of Epistle II (of four verse letters)
  • Pope's own summary: man's business is not to pry into God but to study himself

Context

Analysis
  • Alexander Pope (1688–1744): Catholic → no university, no office; largely self-taught
  • spinal TB → c. 4 ft 6 in, constant pain; “this long disease, my life”
  • An Essay on Man (1733–34): four epistles; a theodicy — to “vindicate the ways of God to Man”
  • Epistle I ends “Whatever is, is right” → Know then thyself follows
  • Great Chain of Being: God → angels → man → animals → plants → matter
    • man = only link both spirit + body → middle state, a god or beast
    • wishing to be higher = pride; breaks the chain
1

Know then thyself

Analysis
  • Delphic gnōthi seauton; Socrates' first task of philosophy
  • then = therefore → follows from Epistle I
  • two commands across the caesura: Know (allowed) vs presume not (forbidden)
  • scan = examine minutely + measure metre (the line scans perfectly)
  • presume = the sin of overreaching (Satan, Adam)
2

The proper study of mankind is man

Analysis
  • aphorism: thesis in 10 syllables; only full stop; no mid-line pause → sounds final
  • polyptoton mankind… man → student = specimen
  • proper = fitting to our rank + our own
  • 1st edition: “The only science…” → humbler revision
  • irony: confident programme → the study produces a riddle
3–6

isthmus of a middle state

Analysis
  • Placed = passive; God the unnamed placer → no complaining
  • isthmus = joins (spirit + matter), separates, narrow → precarious
  • darkly wise (dimly) / rudely great (roughly made, rudis) → each claim granted, then limited
  • With too much… ×2: too much knowledge for Sceptics, too much weakness for Stoics
  • disqualified by excess; pride → the sin of line 1
7–9

He hangs between

Analysis
  • main clause at last; He hangs between descriptions (4 lines before, 11 after)
  • semicolon = heaviest pause → the line itself hangs
  • in doubt ×3 → tricolon: act/rest → god/beast → mind/body
    • doing → being → valuing
10–12

Born but to die

Analysis
  • but = only; body → death, mind → error
  • but to sounds like a purpose → bleakest line; plosives b / t / d
  • 11–12: equally ignorant at either dose of thinking → no right amount
  • flat rhyme such / much → reason runs out
13–14

Chaos of thought and passion

Analysis
  • no main verb from here → man only renamed, never acts
  • Chaos = before Creation; confused = poured together
  • abused = deceived; disabused = undeceived; Still = always
    • self-deception cycle, no outside villain
  • himself = last pronoun → then only titles
15–17

Great lord of all things

Analysis
  • half to rise and half to fall → built from both; fall = Adam's Fall
  • exact 5 | 5 balance; all doubled → kingdom = predator
  • Sole judge of truth → no higher court; hurled = Satan's fall (Milton)
  • passive participles throughout (Placed, Born, Created, hurled) → man acted upon
18

The glory, jest, and riddle of the world!

Analysis
  • tricolon after ~15 pairs → man can't be summed up even as a pair
  • two commas isolate jest
  • glory (pride) → jest (laughter) → riddle (unsolved)
  • Pascal: glory + refuse → Pope swaps in jest → comic wonder, not disgust
  • only exclamation: awe + exasperation
  • ends on world, not man; next line: “Go, wondrous creature!”

Structure

Analysis
  • 9 heroic couplets, all end-stopped
  • couplet + caesura = balance at two levels → irony: form of order, content of chaos
  • 2 sentences: 1–2 command + thesis; 3–18 one long sentence
  • command → description → pure paradox
  • antitheses speed up: one per couplet → one per line (13–18)
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Katherine Philips, 'A Married State'

Link. The set's two poems in heroic couplets, both weighing a human state — Philips's 'married state' against the 'virgin state', Pope's man in a middle state — with balance, antithesis and but meaning “only” (marriage 'affords but little ease'; Born but to die). Difference. Philips argues a woman's practical case and reaches a firm conclusion; Pope shows that no conclusion about man will hold.

2. Kevin Halligan, 'The Cockroach'

Link. Aimlessness that becomes self-knowledge: Halligan's insect 'looked uncertain where to go', Pope's man is in doubt to act or rest, and in both a creature described from outside turns back on the describer ('I thought I recognised myself'; Know then thyself). Difference. Pope generalises (mankind) and ends on a confident exclamation; Halligan works privately through one small creature and ends in a hesitant 'I don't know'.

3. Aphra Behn, 'Song: Love Armed'

Link. Passion at war with reason, with a shared rhyme ('hurled' / 'the Amorous World'; hurled / world) and a shared vice (the stoic's pride; 'his Pride and Cruelty'). Difference. Behn's lovers make a god who then rules them; Pope's man is forbidden even to scan God, and is himself the thing hurled.

4. William Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper'

Link. The order of things and who pays for it: Pope's poem argues that 'Whatever is, is right', while Blake's child is a link in a social order run by 'God and his priest and king'. Difference. Pope forbids man to question the design (presume not God to scan); Blake's poem exists to question it, and his child sees through the adults who justify his suffering.

5. Boey Kim Cheng, 'Report to Wordsworth'

Link. Man's place in nature: Pope's man is Great lord of all things, but a prey to all; Boey's 'insatiate man moves in for the kill', a lord turned predator. Difference. Pope's universe is intact and God beyond scanning; in Boey the sea-gods are 'entombed' and 'God is labouring to utter his last cry'.

Carpet-weavers, Morocco

Carol Rumens · 1987

The carpet is given a journey, a purpose and a future; the children who knot it get only more knotting — and the instant in which all-that-will-be becomes all-that-was.

Lines
12
Form
