ContextThe PoemThe Whole PoemForm & StructureSoundMotifs & SymbolsThemesDifficult MomentsClose AnalysisCritical LensesOther ReadingsRevision NotesConnections
CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Carol Rumens (1944–2026)

A London-born poet and translator, and from 2007 until her death the writer of the Guardian's weekly 'Poem of the week' close readings, Rumens is often compared to Larkin for her plain, level, end-stopped sentences, which is the manner of this poem. Her later work turns increasingly to foreign places, languages and customs. 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' was first collected in her Selected Poems (1987). It names no speaker, date or place beyond the title: it records a scene, not an anecdote.

Children at the looms

Hand-knotted carpets were one of the trades in which child labour drew international attention. In 1978 the Anti-Slavery Society published Child Labour in Morocco's Carpet Industry, and the problem outlasted it: in 2001 a reporter found some fifty children, some about six or younger, weaving in a back room in Fes. The employers' defence — small hands weave better, and the work teaches a trade — is a justification, not a finding. Morocco's Labour Code raised the minimum working age to 15 only in 2003. The poem names no workshop, wage or employer, but these facts show what the scene meant at the time, and why hard at work and the school of days are not neutral phrases.

How a knotted carpet is made

A pile carpet is built on an upright loom. The weaver ties short lengths of coloured wool round pairs of vertical warp threads, row by row across the width, and each row is beaten down under the next. Because the carpet is made from the bottom up, the design rises with the work, top border last, and on a fixed loom the weavers' plank or bench is raised as the weaving climbs. So the raised bench of line 5 is plain workshop fact before it is anything else, and the tree-tops of a garden design really are woven last.

Prayer, the mosque and the garden

Muslim prayer involves standing, bowing, kneeling and prostration with the forehead to the ground, which is one reason mosque floors are carpeted. The Qur'an's word for paradise, al-janna, means 'the garden', and Persian 'garden carpets' of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries map a formal garden seen from above and are often read as images of paradise. the garden of Islam is Rumens's own phrase, not a technical term: it gathers the carpet's trees and flowers, the paradise they evoke, and the faith the carpet will serve.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Carpet-weavers, Morocco

This poem is still in copyright, so its words are not reproduced here: each line shows a short summary. Read it alongside your anthology or the exam paper.

TCarpet-weavers, Morocco
1young workers at the weaving frame of somewhere else entirely
2hair plaited and glossy-dark; clothes vividly coloured
3graded in size, they would sound like a set of bells
4eyes fixed on the shimmering knots, as if at a screen
5the paradise pattern rises, so their seat must go up too
6next, they'll thread red branchwork through the highest foliage
7the finished rug will leave on a trader's lorry
8mosque attendants will unroll it across the floor
9thick and yielding, it'll sink beneath the worshippers' weight
10back in the workshop: still labouring, time their only teacher
11the hues of the future leap off their fingertips (runs on)…
12…and set solid, locked within the finished past

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Carpet-weavers, Morocco
Language & devices

The title is a Caption: occupation, comma, place — the label under a photograph or a museum exhibit. The Compound noun Carpet-weavers names people by their product, with no article, number, age or name, and the comma sets the job beside the country without a verb.

Meaning & effect

The title promises documentary neutrality — workers, located — and the poem keeps that promise in its tone while breaking it in its first words, where the weavers turn out to be The children. That gap between weavers and children is the poem's subject. The caption also places the reader where a visitor to an exhibition stands, looking at people labelled by what they make.

Line 1
young workers at the weaving frame of somewhere else entirely
Language & devices

The Definite article presents the children as already in front of us, not introduced. Polysemy: loom is the weaving frame and also the verb to loom, to rise up threateningly. Ambiguity: another world has no stated referent, and a plain Declarative in the simple present, closed by a full stop, sets the pattern of the first ten lines.

Meaning & effect

The line holds three worlds at once: the paradise garden the carpet depicts; a world of work apart from the childhood the reader assumes; and, to a British reader, the kind of faraway place people call another world, a phrase that can make Morocco exotic. Rumens does not choose, and the flat statement makes the ambiguity sound like a fact. Before we see a weaver, we see a child.

Line 2
hair plaited and glossy-dark; clothes vividly coloured
Language & devices

Visual imagery in two balanced halves either side of a Caesura (Parallelism), with Alliteration on b (braids, black, bright) and black set against bright. oiled implies grooming, and the only verb is are. It is the poem's one perfectly regular line of Iambic pentameter.

Meaning & effect

Rumens makes the children particular — cared for, dressed, individual — so they cannot dissolve into a statistic about child labour. But the details are a photographer's: colour, sheen, arrangement, and the children do nothing. The line's balance and neat metre make the scene attractive, and the poem goes on to ask what it means to find working children attractive.

Line 3
graded in size, they would sound like a set of bells
Language & devices

The Conditional would, the only one in the poem, makes the image hypothetical. Synaesthesia turns sight into sound: children graded by height become a set of bells (Implied metaphor). assorted is a word for goods, and the m and l sounds of melodious make the line itself lilt.

Meaning & effect

The poem's most beautiful image is marked as imaginary: no chime sounds, and would is the one place the unseen observer's fancy shows. Rumens turns the children into music and flags that she has done it. The image carries its own warning — chimes are instruments, arranged and struck by someone else — so harmony and use arrive in a single line.

Line 4
like television
Language & devices

Simile: like television comes from the observer's world, not the children's, and flickering fits both a screen and fast fingers. The children's first action Verb is one of watching, not tying or weaving. Irony: television is passive consumption, but these viewers are producing an image; the line trails off on the unstressed end of television.

Meaning & effect

The simile measures the distance between the reader's childhood, where television is what children do instead of working, and this one. It is also an exact picture of skilled repetition — hands going on, eyes following, absorbed or hypnotised. Either way the work seems to happen by itself while they look on: the first sign that the poem gives the making to the material rather than to the makers.

Line 5
the garden of Islam
Language & devices

Metaphor: the pattern is the garden of Islam, and it grows, an organic verb for knotting that evokes the Qur'an's paradise, al-janna, the garden. After the comma comes the poem's first Future tense, in an Agentless passive: the bench is to be raised, by whom we are never told. It is literal too, since at an upright loom the weavers' seat goes up as the carpet rises.

Meaning & effect

The sacred and the practical share one sentence: paradise grows, furniture is adjusted. The labour is credited to the garden, which grows as if unaided, and the children's only advancement in the poem is a bench that rises with the product. The missing agent matters: whoever owns the workshop is never named.

Line 6
dark-rose veins
Language & devices

lace means to thread delicately and to tie tight. Metaphor: veins are a leaf's and a body's, so the woven trees are alive. The Compound words dark-rose and tree-tops crowd the stresses — three in a row in dark-rose veins — so the line is as dense as the pile.

Meaning & effect

Carpets are woven upward and trees grow upward, so the children reach the tree-tops last, at the top of the frame: they will climb a garden they cannot enter. This is their only future verb in the poem, and it promises more work, higher up the same frame. veins gives the carpet life and raises the question of whose life is in it.

Lines 7–8
the merchant's truck
Language & devices

A new subject, the carpet: the children vanish for the whole of stanza 3. The object is given a verb of travel normally used of people (Personification), and the trader appears only as a Possessive attached to a vehicle, truck a hard, modern drop in Register after the tree-tops. Line 8's Passive voice is the only one that names its agent, the servants of the mosque, and Consonance links truck and mosque on the same closing /k/.

Meaning & effect

The politics are done by grammar: the product gets movement, a route and a destination, while the makers stay where they are. The one adult who turns the children's work into money has no name and no action, only ownership — which is how a supply chain looks from inside a workshop. Trade then hands the carpet to worship with no seam between the lines: one journey, a chain of hands all serving something, and only the first link is children.

Line 9
heaped with prayer
Language & devices

Fronted Tactile imagery: the line opens on touch, soft, the language of a hand run over a carpet before buying it. Polysemy: give means to yield under weight and to bestow. Metaphor: heaped with prayer makes worship physical, the weight of kneeling bodies, in a word for piled goods.

Meaning & effect

This is the carpet's purpose: to cushion worshippers who kneel and press their foreheads to the floor, so the children's labour becomes the softness under other people's devotion — a gift, in the second sense of give. Yet heaped measures prayer by bulk, as a market measures goods. The poem neither places the children among those who pray nor shuts them out; it moves on.

Line 10
the school of days
Language & devices

Repetition: the line repeats the opening words of line 1, a Framing device that returns the poem to the present tense. The Idiom hard at work is the praise-phrase for a diligent pupil, and the Metaphor the school of days unpicks schooldays into a school made of days, echoing the school of life.

Meaning & effect

After the carpet's journey the children are exactly where they were nine lines earlier: the carpet has a story, they have a condition. the school of days says two things at once — they are learning a real craft by apprenticeship, and their only school is the passing of working days. Commendation and accusation arrive together, and the poem lets both stand.

Lines 11–12
all-that-will-be … all-that-was
Language & devices

The poem's only Enjambment: fly ends line 11 and the sentence runs on into freeze (Antithesis). The Hyphenated compounds all-that-will-be and all-that-was turn clauses into nouns, so future and past become things, and Alliteration chains fingers, fly, freeze, frame. frame is the loom's frame, a picture frame and a film's freeze-frame.

Meaning & effect

The closing paradox: as each knot is tied, the future — the colours still to come — leaves the fingers and at once becomes the past, fixed in the woven part held by the frame. There is no lasting present, only the instant of the knot, which is the tense the children have lived in all along. The line-break acts this out, the colours crossing the one boundary the poem allows and caught by the first word on the other side; what is frozen — the pattern, the children's futures, or a permanence that will outlast them — is left open.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' is usually read as a choice between two verdicts: a quiet protest against child labour, or a celebration of craft and faith that the protest reading ignores. The better account is that the poem withholds verdicts so that its grammar can deliver something harder to argue with: a distribution of time. Tense by tense, the carpet is given a future — a journey, a destination, a use — while the children who make it are given the present and a single future verb, which promises more of the same work; and in the final sentence even that present turns out to be no more than the instant in which their future becomes the carpet's past. The poem never calls this wrong. It makes it visible row by row, as a carpet makes its pattern.

The method is announced by the gap between title and first line. The title is a caption — trade, comma, country — and the first line corrects it: the weavers are The children, at the loom of another world that is at once the paradise in the pattern, the world of work apart from the childhood the reader assumes, and an outsider's name for somewhere far away. Stanza one then does what a camera does. Line 2 is all surface, and the poem's one perfectly regular pentameter: the children are composed, in both senses. Line 3 turns them into music, graded by height into a chime — but this is the one line governed by would. The prettiest image is the only one marked as invented, and in marking it Rumens admits that somebody is standing in this workshop turning children into art; assorted, a word for goods, confesses the cost.

Stanza two moves the eye from the children to the work, and quietly takes the work away from them. They watch their knots like television, the reader's emblem of a child's leisure laid over a child's labour. Then the making passes to the pattern: the garden of Islam grows as if by itself, and the only thing done in answer is that the bench is raised, by nobody, since the passive has no agent and no employer appears anywhere in the poem. Their one advancement is furniture adjusted to the product. Next they will work the woven tree-tops, a garden they will climb but never enter.

Stanza three makes the argument without the children. Every verb is future and every subject is the carpet: it will travel, be spread, give. The object acquires everything its makers lack — movement, destination, community, purpose — and the adults who handle it are glimpsed only as a possessive (the merchant's truck) and as the agent of a passive (the servants of the mosque). Commerce and worship sit in consecutive lines with no seam. The stanza ends in the poem's softest line, where give means both to sink under weight and to bestow: the children's work becomes the floor beneath other people's devotion, and the poem neither mocks that devotion nor places the children within it.

Stanza four returns to the opening words and finds the children where they were, hard at work in the school of days: a pupil's praise attached to labour, so that commendation and accusation arrive together. Nine lines of narrative have happened to the carpet and none to them. Then the last sentence, the only one longer than a line, turns the tense-pattern into a paradox. The colours of all-that-will-be fly from the children's fingers over the poem's only run-on, and the next word is freeze: the future leaves the hands and lands as the past, held in the frame — loom, picture, freeze-frame. The sentence has no present except the instant of the knot, which is exactly the tense the children have been given throughout.

The strongest objection comes from two sides at once. One side says the child-labour reading is too quick: the children belong to a community whose work will be honoured in a mosque, the school of days can echo the proud school of life, and fly suggests escape. The other says the poem is too comfortable: a British poet finds other people's working children beautiful, gives them braids and heights but no thoughts, and makes from their labour an object as portable and decorative as the carpet. Both describe something real, and the design answers both. The celebration is there and fully felt — the craft is skilled, the faith treated with dignity, give generous — but the grammar keeps a ledger that celebration cannot erase: the carpet gets the future and the children do not, and the colours fly only into a freeze. And the poem has already confessed its gaze. would marks the aestheticising as the onlooker's, and the television simile casts the reader as a viewer consuming the image of children who are producing one. The missing 'I' is not innocence but a refusal to make these children an occasion for an observer's feelings.

What the poem finally says is not that the children are victims, or artists, but that making turns time into objects, and that it matters whose time is spent. A carpet, like a poem, outlives the moment of its making and travels to people who will never meet its makers. Rumens builds her poem like the carpet — twelve sealed rows, a single thread allowed to cross — so that its paradox applies to her own lines too.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

Twelve lines in four unrhymed tercets. An observational lyric with no speaker — no 'I', no addressee, no question, no verdict — closer to documentary forms (caption, photograph, report) that record without comment.

Line & metre

No fixed metre: a long, level line of 10–13 syllables, mostly four or five stresses, steadily rising. Only line 2 is regular iambic pentameter; only line 9 opens on a stress.

Rhyme

None. Faint end-echoes stand in: truck / mosque (7–8) on the same /k/; raised / days (5, 10).

Syntax

Eleven sentences in twelve lines: lines 1–10 are each one end-stopped sentence. Three commas; no colon, dash or question mark. One enjambment, after fly (line 11).

Four tercets, four movements

The stanzas divide the poem's attention cleanly, and their order is the argument. Stanza 1 looks at the children, stanza 2 at their work; stanza 3 follows the finished carpet out of the room — truck, mosque, prayer — with no children, no they, no their; stanza 4 returns to the workshop with the poem's opening words. The shape is an envelope, children / work / carpet / children: the outer stanzas are present tense and open alike, while the inner ones carry the poem into the future and away from the makers. Three-line stanzas read as bands of pattern, four equal blocks as regular as rows of knots, and a tercet cannot fall into two balanced halves, so no stanza settles into a neat either/or.

The turns

There is no single volta, but two quiet shifts and one return. The first is the comma in line 5: the subordinate clause is still present tense, and the main clause after it brings the first future verb, so the tense turns as the pattern starts to grow, as if the future belongs to the product. The second is line 7, where the grammatical subject changes from the children to the carpet. The return is line 10, which repeats the opening words: after the carpet's journey, the children are where they were. The final sentence then turns from scene to idea, from what the children do to what their doing does to time.

Metre: a level line and its disturbances

Rumens writes a long line that never settles into a pattern, so the reader feels steadiness without song, the rhythm of a report or of captions read aloud. Against that surface, small disturbances fall on the lines that matter. Line 2, balanced on its comma, is the one perfectly regular pentameter: the children are composed metrically as well as visually. Line 3's double light syllables (as-SORT-ed, me-LO-di-ous) give a rocking lilt, so it sounds like the chime it imagines. Line 4 is the only line not to end on a stress: it trails off on television, like attention drifting to a screen. Line 6 crowds three stresses together in dark-rose veins, as thick as the pile. Line 8 has only three strong stresses among the passive's small words, as unemphatic as its grammar; line 9 is the only line to begin on a stress, the hand pressing the pile; line 11 loads two colliding stresses onto its edge just before the break. The three ten-syllable lines are the children's appearance (2), the carpet's softness (9) and the frozen past (12): the three moments at which something is presented as finished.

Sentences as rows

Each of lines 1–10 is a complete sentence ending in a full stop, mostly in the plainest English pattern, subject–verb–complement. The effect is of separate statements laid side by side, each finished before the next begins, like a row of knots tied and beaten down before the next row starts. Nothing is subordinated to anything else, so nothing is said to cause anything else: the poem never says because or but. The reader has to make the connections — between the merchant's truck and the children's bench, the soft carpet and the hard work — and that is where the poem's judgement happens.

The single enjambment

After ten closed lines, line 11 does not stop. Its last word is fly, and with no punctuation the colours cross the line-break, the only thing in the poem that crosses a boundary; the first word on the other side is freeze. The flight is the run-on and the arrest is the next word, so the ending's energy lasts exactly one line-break. The sentence also runs future-first and past-last, performing the passage it describes, and it shrinks as it goes: thirteen syllables, then ten; all-that-will-be four syllables, all-that-was three. Time contracts as it passes through the children's fingers.

Tense: the poem's hidden structure

Stanza Verbs Tense Grammatical subjects
1 are · are · would make present; one conditional the children; their braids; their heights
2 watch · grows · will be raised · will lace present → future they; the garden; the bench; they
3 will travel · will be spread · will give future only the carpet; it; it
4 are · fly · freeze present the children; the colours

The future arrives with the garden, so the tense belongs to the design first. The children receive a single future verb, they will lace, which promises more of the same work, higher up the same frame; in stanza 3 the future belongs wholly to the carpet, while the makers drop out of the grammar. No verb in the poem is past: in the closing sentence past and future are hyphenated nouns, things that can fly and be frozen. And the design is known in advance, so all-that-will-be is as settled as all-that-was. For the carpet, the future is a journey; for the children, it is the next row.

Hyphens and the frame

Hyphens bind the poem at both ends: Carpet-weavers fastens people to their product, the last two lines fasten whole clauses into single words, and between them dark-rose and tree-tops knot the design together. The last image of form is the frame: the loom that holds the carpet, the picture-frame round a scene, and the poem itself, which holds these children in twelve fixed lines.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

The pleasure of the picture. Stanza 1 is the most enjoyable to say, which is part of its point. Line 2 runs on bright plosive b's — braids, black, bright — in strict iambic alternation, so the description sounds as neat as the children look. Line 3 moves to liquids and nasals, the m's of melodious closing on the m of chime, whose long i rings with heights and bright. It is music describing music, in the line governed by would: the sound is loveliest at exactly the moment the loveliness is marked as an onlooker's fancy.

Work and density. Line 4 is quicker and thinner — short vowels in flickering, clicking k's and t's — and sounds like many small, identical actions. Then a long a runs from raised into lace and veins, and line 6 piles up its stresses before closing on the hard t's of tree-tops: the sound thickens as the pattern does.

From commerce to worship. A hard /k/ marks the carpet's journey — carpet, truck, mosque — the last two sharing the closing sound that keeps trade and worship in one chain. Line 8 softens into sibilance (spread, servants) and line 9 into long vowels and gentle p's; the long ee of heaped is the sound of sinking into pile. The consonants relax as the carpet passes from trade to devotion, doing tonal work the poem refuses to do in statement.

The f-chain. The ending turns on one consonant: fingers, fly, freeze, frame — source, motion, arrest, enclosure. fly and freeze begin almost identically, f followed by a liquid, for two opposite actions, so escape and capture sound like versions of one word, and the long ee of freeze recalls the carpet's softness. The closing compounds share their first two syllables and differ only at the verb, so future and past are heard as near-twins, one small sound apart. The first line ended on world; the last ends on the short, closed was — a place, then a tense.

Silence. Eleven full stops make eleven silences, each line set down before the next begins, at the level pace of someone recording what they see. Against that, the unpunctuated line-end after fly is heard as much as seen: the one place the voice is not allowed to rest, and only until freeze.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

1. Another world, and the garden

The first noun phrase, another world, is left open, and the poem fills it three ways. By line 5 it is the world in the pattern, the garden of Islam, paradise knotted into wool; by stanza 3 it is the world the carpet will enter, the mosque and its prayer; and all along it is the workshop, apart from the reader's idea of childhood. The garden gathers the central irony. The children make paradise row by row and are never placed in it: the garden climbs, they climb with it on a raised bench, and then the garden leaves on a truck.

2. Watching, screens and the frame

Someone looks throughout, though no one says 'I'. The look shows first in the would of line 3, where an onlooker imagines a chime; then the children watch their knots like television, bringing in the onlooker's world of screens, where children are viewers, not workers. The motif ends in freeze and frame: a freeze-frame, the moment a moving picture stops and is held. Film language — flickering, television, freeze, frame — runs through a poem about hand-weaving, and it implicates the reader, who is also watching children and is shown, in the end, a frame.

3. Height and rising

Vertical movement accumulates: assorted heights; the garden that grows and the bench that is raised; the tree-tops; the carpet heaped with prayer; the colours that fly. Everything rises, but the children rise only because the product does — their one ascent is a bench adjusted to the carpet. The motif ends with the one upward movement that looks free, the flying colours, and stops it at once with freeze.

4. Hands, colour and the chain of service

The carpet passes through a chain of hands: the children's fingers tie and lace; the merchant is implied only by a possessive; the servants of the mosque spread it; the worshippers press it with their bodies; and the poem ends back at the children's fingers. Every link serves something — trade, a mosque, God — and only the first link is children. Colour travels the same way. Line 2 gives the children their braids oiled and black and their bright dresses; after that the colour belongs to the carpet, first the dark-rose veins, then the colours that leave the children's fingers and become the carpet's fixed past. The makers' hands are where everything starts, and the grammar keeps moving the credit elsewhere.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Child labour, seen without a verdict

Children doing skilled adult work are described without one word of judgement; the evidence is in the grammar and idioms — hard at work in the school of days, the bench raised by no one, the employer who exists only as the merchant's truck. Yet the children are cared for, absorbed and expert, so the reader must hold the craft and the missing childhood together.

02

The object outruns its makers

The carpet is given a future (it will travel, be spread, give), a vehicle, a destination and a use; the children get the present and one future verb that promises more work. Anything made by hand leaves its makers, and the poem asks what that means when the makers are children.

03

Faith, trade and the chain of hands

Workshop, truck and mosque follow in consecutive lines with no seam, and the vocabulary mixes goods (assorted, heaped) with worship. The faith is treated with respect; the question left is placement, since the children make the floor of other people's devotion.

04

Time turned into objects

Weaving converts time: all-that-will-be flies from the children's fingers and freezes into all-that-was, with no lasting present between. On one reading it is their own futures spent into an object someone else will own; on another, a permanence that will outlast them.

05

Beauty and the watcher's eye

The poem's loveliest lines are the ones that make the scene attractive to an outsider, and Rumens marks the most aestheticising image with its only conditional, would. There is no 'I', but the act of watching is everywhere.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. a melodious chime — admiration or complicity?

The difficulty. The poem's prettiest image turns working children into music. Is Rumens celebrating them, or showing how easily an onlooker turns children into a picture?

Competing readings. Tender admiration: the graded heights look harmonious, and the image honours the children's order and grace. Self-exposure: would, the only conditional in the poem, marks the chime as imagined, so the one place an onlooker's mind shows is the moment of aestheticising, and the poem confesses it. Critique: a chime is a set of instruments, graded, arranged and struck by someone else, and assorted is a word for stock; the image contains the use it seems to celebrate.

What a strong answer does. It notices that the conditional and the stock-word sit inside the beautiful line, so admiration and its cost arrive together, and that the line belongs to stanza 1, where the children are only looked at and no work has yet been shown. The image is both a real response and a test of the reader's.

2. the school of days — deprivation or education?

The difficulty. Line 10 returns to the poem's opening words and fixes the children in place with two phrases, hard at work and the school of days, that can sound proud or bitter.

Competing readings. Deprivation: there is no school, only days; the children's education is the passing of working time, and the pupil's praise hard at work becomes an accusation. Education: a craft is being learned by apprenticeship, and the phrase echoes the proud school of life, honouring learning that does not happen in classrooms. Time as teacher: whatever the children learn, the subject is time itself, which prepares the closing paradox.

What a strong answer does. It reads the line against line 1 — nine lines of the carpet's progress and none of theirs — and lets commendation and complaint stand together, exactly as the idiom hard at work does. The repetition is the evidence: their situation has continuation but no story.

3. The ending — what is frozen, and is fly an escape?

The difficulty. The last sentence is a paradox, and its subject, the colours of all-that-will-be, is deliberately unspecified. Whose future flies, and what does the freeze mean?

Competing readings. The pattern: the carpet's colours, waiting in the future of the design, become fixed past the instant they are knotted — a general truth about making. The children's futures: their days and possibilities leave their fingers and are frozen into an object others will own; on this reading it is the coldest line in the poem. Permanence and agency: fly is escape and possibility, and the ending almost magical — the children, passive watchers at the start, are finally responsible for everything that was and will be, and the carpet will carry their work long after them. Determinism: the design is already known, so line 6 can say what they will weave next, and all-that-will-be is as settled as all-that-was.

What a strong answer does. It ties the meaning to the form. The colours fly over the poem's only enjambment and are caught by the next word, freeze: the flight is real but lasts one line-break. A strong reading lets the magic and the arrest coexist — the children make something lasting, and what lasts is fixed in a frame they stay behind — and notices that the poem's last word, was, closes on the past with a full stop.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. The title against The children

Caption title; compound noun; correction. The title has the shape of a label under a photograph: a trade, a comma, a country. Carpet-weavers names people by their product, with no age, number or name. The poem's first words replace the label — the weavers are The children — and the definite article presents them as already in front of us. Intention and effect: Rumens lets the reader see the scene as a market or a museum would, workers located, and corrects that view at once, so every later description of skill is shadowed by the word children.

2. oiled and black (line 2)

Visual imagery; alliteration; balanced halves; regular pentameter. Four concrete details in two halves either side of a comma, with b-alliteration running on into bright. oiled implies care — someone prepared these children this morning — so they cannot dissolve into a statistic. But the only verb is are: they are described, not doing, in the poem's one perfectly regular line. Intention and effect: the children are made individual and attractive in the same breath, composed in both senses, and the line's neatness is part of what the poem examines: how easily working children become a pleasing picture.

3. like television (line 4)

Simile; irony; register shift; unstressed ending. The comparison comes from the observer's world, not the children's. flickering fits a screen and fast fingers, and the line trails off on the unstressed end of television. Intention and effect: television is what children in the reader's culture do instead of working, and the simile measures the distance without comment. It also catches the trance of skilled repetition and reverses the usual roles: these viewers are producing an image, while the reader watching them is the one consuming it.

4. the bench will be raised (line 5)

Agentless passive; first future tense; literal detail with figurative force. At an upright loom the weavers' plank is raised as the carpet climbs, so this is plain workshop fact. But the passive names no agent, no employer appears anywhere in the poem, and the clause follows an organic verb that credits the work to the design. Intention and effect: the children's one advancement is a piece of furniture adjusted to the product — they rise only because the carpet does — and the grammar keeps the authority over them invisible.

5. dark-rose veins (line 6)

Metaphor; compound words; stress cluster; double-edged verb. veins belong to a leaf and to a body, so the woven garden lives and circulates; lace means to thread delicately and to tie tight; three stresses in a row make this the densest line in the poem. And they will lace is the children's only future verb: more work, at the top of the frame. Intention and effect: the children will reach the tree-tops of a garden they can never enter, and the carpet comes alive as its makers move out of view, raising a question the poem does not ask: whose life is in it?

6. the merchant's truck (line 7)

Change of subject; personification; possessive; register shift. Stanza 3 opens on the carpet, and the children vanish for three lines. The carpet is given a verb of travel normally used of people, while the merchant, the one adult who turns the children's work into money, exists only as a possessive attached to a vehicle; truck is hard, modern and commercial after the tree-tops. Intention and effect: the politics are done by grammar — the product gets a route and a destination, the makers stay put — and the merchant's near-absence is how a supply chain looks from the workshop floor.

7. heaped with prayer (line 9)

Polysemy; tactile imagery; metaphor. The line opens on the touch of a fine pile, soft, the language of a hand run over a carpet before buying it. give means both to yield under weight and to bestow, and heaped makes worship physical — the weight of kneeling bodies — in a word used for piled goods. Intention and effect: the carpet's purpose is generous and the poem respects it: the children's work becomes the softness beneath other people's devotion. But heaped measures prayer by bulk, and the poem neither places the children among the worshippers nor excludes them; the silence is the reader's to fill.

8. fly … freeze (lines 11–12)

The only enjambment; hyphenated compounds; paradox; antithesis; f-alliteration. The colours fly across the poem's only open line-end and are caught by the next word. The compounds all-that-will-be and all-that-was turn clauses into nouns, so future and past become materials; frame is the loom, a picture-frame and a film's freeze-frame; fingers, fly, freeze and frame chain the sentence on one sound. Intention and effect: as each knot is tied, the future becomes the past with no lasting present between — the instant the children have lived in all along — and the form allows the flight exactly one line-break before it stops.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Marxist / materialist

What it makes visible. The carpet as a commodity. As it travels, the labour in it disappears: the product takes over the verbs, the garden grows as if by itself, and the merchant is reduced to a possessive — ownership without action. assorted and heaped are market words, and the children's time is converted into a saleable object, all-that-will-be into all-that-was. The poem stages what Marx called the fetishism of commodities: a made thing that seems to have a life of its own while its makers drop out of view.

What it flattens. The faith and the craft. The carpet's destination is a mosque, not a showroom, and give is generous; a materialist reading can turn devotion into mere disguise and miss the poem's respect for both the skill and the prayer.

2. Postcolonial

What it makes visible. The observer's position. A British poet looks at Moroccan children, finds them lovely, and gives them braids, heights and fingers but no thoughts or speech. another world can be an exoticising phrase, like television brings in the West's frame of reference, and the absent 'I' can be read as a gaze that never has to account for itself.

What it flattens. The poem's self-awareness. would marks the aestheticising as the onlooker's, the television simile turns the eye back on the viewer's own culture, and the refusal to speak for the children is arguably more respectful than putting words in their mouths.

3. Feminist

What it makes visible. The weavers are almost certainly girls — the braids and dresses suggest it, and Moroccan carpet weaving has long been women's and girls' work. Textile craft is one of the oldest forms of women's labour to be prized as art in the object and ignored in the maker: once finished, the carpet passes into the public worlds of trade and worship, the merchant and the mosque, and its makers stay inside.

What it flattens. The poem never says 'girls'. Its stated focus is childhood, and a gender reading has to infer what the text leaves implicit.

4. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The reader's position is built in. We watch, as the children watch their knots and as viewers watch television; we may own a carpet like this one; and because the poem never says what to feel, the judgement we form is ours. The discomfort many readers feel is the poem working.

What it flattens. It can make the poem about the reader's feelings, which is exactly what the absent 'I' refuses to do with the observer's.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A protest poem by implication

The poem indicts child labour through grammar instead of statement. Evidence: hard at work in the school of days, where there is no school; the bench raised by no one; the merchant's truck, someone profiting unseen; stanza 3's future tense, which belongs only to the carpet; the children's futures frozen into someone else's object. Weakness: it must ignore what the poem plainly honours — the skill, the care in the oiled braids, the dignity of the mosque, the generosity of give — and cannot explain why there is not one word of complaint.

2. A celebration of craft and devotion

The language resists a quick reading of the poem as a critique of forced child labour: the children's work is a genuine act of religious significance, and Morocco should not be equated with poverty. Evidence: the garden of Islam; the dignity of the servants of the mosque; give as bestowal; the school of days as the proud school of life; the colours that fly. Weakness: it must read hard at work against its grain, and cannot account for the tense pattern — the carpet's journey while the children stay — or for a word like assorted.

3. The poem as a postcolonial problem

The poem itself is complicit: a British poet turns other people's working children into twelve beautiful lines for a British readership. Evidence: the children are given exteriors and no inner lives; the connoisseur's vocabulary of touch and assorted sizes; the phrase another world; no 'I' to account for the looking. Weakness: the poem marks its own aestheticising with would, turns the screen simile back on the viewer's culture and refuses to speak for the children, so the reading accuses it of a blindness it openly displays.

4. A poem about making poems

'Text' and 'textile' share a Latin root, texere, to weave. The poem is twelve tight rows, made one at a time, that freeze a moment of other lives into a frame — and it too will travel, be spread out in classrooms, and outlive the people in it. Evidence: the stanzas as bands of pattern; end-stopped lines as rows; frame as picture-frame and poem-shape; a closing paradox true of all making. Weakness: it can turn the children into a metaphor for the poet, the very appropriation the poem guards against, and the poem never mentions writing.

The working notes, quotation by quotation

  • l.2: b-alliteration; oiled = cared for → real children, not a statistic
  • described, not doing → photographer's eye; children composed
  • l.3: would = only conditional → observer's fancy
  • synaesthesia: heights → bells; instruments struck by someone else
  • assorted = shop word
Effect, style & response
  • prettiest image = the one marked as invented → poem confesses its aestheticising
4

like television

Analysis
  • simile from the reader's world → TV = what children do instead of work
  • irony: viewers consume images; these children produce one
  • flickering = screen + fast fingers → trance of repetition
  • first action = watching, not weaving
  • film words: flickering → television → freeze → frame
5–6

the bench will be raised

Analysis
  • garden grows → design grows 'by itself'
  • first future tense; agentless passive → no employer anywhere
  • bench raised = literal; only advancement = furniture
  • lace = thread delicately + tie tight
  • dark-rose veins → carpet alive; whose life?
  • they will lace = children's only future verb → more work, higher up
7–8

the merchant's truck

Analysis
  • new subject: the carpet → children vanish for all of st.3
  • verb of travel for an object → product moves, makers stay
  • merchant = only a possessive → ownership without action
  • truck = hard, modern; register drop after tree-tops
  • servants of the mosque = only named agent; another link in the chain
  • truck / mosque = same /k/ → trade + worship = one journey
9

heaped with prayer

Analysis
  • tactile; buyer's language; only line starting on a stress
  • give = yield under weight + bestow
  • heaped = bulk-goods word → devotion measured like goods
  • children's work = floor beneath others' devotion
  • children neither among the worshippers nor excluded → silence
10

the school of days

Analysis
  • repeats l.1's opening → nothing has changed for them
  • hard at work = pupil's praise applied to labour → praise + accusation
  • no school, only days ↔ apprenticeship / school of life
  • time = their teacher → sets up the ending
11–12

all-that-will-be → all-that-was

Analysis
  • only enjambment: colours fly → caught by freeze
  • paradox: future → past in the instant of the knot; no lasting present
  • hyphenated compounds → time turned into objects
  • f-chain: fingers, fly, freeze, frame = source, motion, arrest, enclosure
  • frame = loom + picture + freeze-frame
Effect, style & response
  • what freezes? pattern / children's futures / permanence that outlasts them
  • fly = escape? lasts one line-break
  • ends on the past + full stop
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. William Blake, 'The Chimney Sweeper'

Link. Children working for adults' comfort and worship, in two poems of exactly twelve lines: Blake's sweep works while his parents praise ‘God and his priest and king’, Rumens's children weave a carpet that will be heaped with prayer, and both hear children as music (Blake's ‘notes of woe’, Rumens's chime). Difference. Blake gives the poem to the child, who accuses the adults of making ‘a heaven of our misery’; Rumens gives her children no voice, names no one, and lets tense and grammar carry the charge, her end-stopped lines withholding the verdict Blake's rhymes deliver.

2. Charles Mungoshi, 'Before the Sun'

Link. A child at work, things flying from working hands, a stretched instant and a sacred note: Mungoshi's ‘bright chips’ fly from the axe and land ‘eternities later’, and his smoke may be a ‘sacrificial prayer’; Rumens's colours fly and freeze, and her carpet is heaped with prayer. Difference. Mungoshi's boy works for his own day and pleasure, and the poem lives inside his senses; Rumens's children have braids, heights and fingers but no thoughts. His work feels like freedom; theirs is the school of days.

3. Liz Lochhead, 'Storyteller'

Link. Textile craft as an image of art that outlasts its moment, ending on the same verb: Lochhead's storyteller talks while ‘five or forty fingers stitched’ and her stories wait ‘till they flew again’; Rumens's colours fly — and freeze. Difference. Lochhead's craft passes into the children and lives on in them; Rumens's passes out of the children into an object that leaves on the merchant's truck.

4. Seamus Heaney, 'Follower'

Link. Manual skill watched closely, in exact technical detail (the plough's wing and sock; the raised bench and the tree-tops woven last), with an ending that turns on time. Difference. The roles are inverted: Heaney's child longs to work and cannot, beside a father who is ‘An expert’, while Rumens's children are the experts and no adult master appears. Heaney looks back with an ‘I’; Rumens looks on, in the present, with none.

5. Elizabeth Brewster, 'Where I Come From'

Link. How places and work make people: Brewster begins ‘People are made of places’, Rumens's children are made by their place of work, where the loom is their school, and both build a world from calm, concrete detail. Difference. Brewster's speaker knows her place from inside and carries it with her; Rumens's children are seen only from outside, and what they make is carried away while they stay.

Summer only rents its beauty, on a short lease; the sonnet promises the beloved outright possession, then keeps the title itself: in the last line it is this that lives, and he is given life on its terms.
