CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet and the 1609 Sonnets

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an actor and playwright, from 1594 a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men. Sonnet 18 was probably written in the 1590s: by 1598 Francis Meres could praise his "sugred Sonnets among his priuate friends", circulating in manuscript. Thomas Thorpe published all 154 in 1609 as SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS, numbered and untitled, with a dedication wishing "Mr. W. H." "that eternitie promised by our ever-living poet": the boast this sonnet makes was already the book's selling point.

A Young Man, and Seventeen Sonnets about Children

Sonnets 1–126 mostly address or concern a young man, never identified. Sonnet 18 itself never gives the beloved's sex (its only his belong to the sun and death), so the woman many readers picture is their assumption, not the poem's. Sonnets 1–17 urge him to have children so that his beauty survives him, and 18 recycles their vocabulary: in 13 he holds his beauty "in lease"; 14 foresees beauty's "doom and date"; 15 first offers verse ("I engraft you new"); 16 retreats, calling it "my barren rhyme", unable to make him "live yourself in eyes of men"; 17 settles for both: "You should live twice, in it and in my rhyme." Sonnet 18 is the first poem after the group, and the call for children never returns: from here, verse alone will do it.

Praise by Comparison, and the Eternising Boast

Petrarchan love poetry praised by comparison (eyes like suns, lips like coral), a method Shakespeare mocks in Sonnet 130 ("My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun"); Sonnet 18 tests the stock comparison and outbids it. Its second move is older. Horace built "a monument more lasting than bronze" and Ovid ended the Metamorphoses on vivam, "I shall live": classical poets promised immortality to themselves. Elizabethan sonneteers promised it to the beloved, as Spenser does in Amoretti 75 (1595): "My verse your virtues rare shall eternize, / And in the heavens write your glorious name." Sonnet 18 is Shakespeare's first full statement of the boast, and beside Spenser, who writes his lady's name to save it, it is strikingly bare: eternal life for a beloved it never names.

Words the Elizabethans Heard

Humours. In medicine after Galen, body and character depended on a balance of four humours, and temperament was literally a matter of temperature: a person's complexion was their mixture, temperate meant in proportion, and imbalance was distemper. So temperate (2), too hot (5) and complexion (6) belong to one vocabulary: the beloved is in balance where the sun is not.

Leases. A lease let land or a house for a fixed term, after which it returned to the owner; a date was the term's length and end, and owe often meant own. lease, date, possession and ow’st sounded like the language of tenancy and title.

The calendar. England kept the Julian calendar, ten days behind ours, so Shakespeare's May ran to about our 10 June: the darling buds of May could be early summer's own.

THE POEM

The Poem

Line by line, with the analysis alongside

Sonnet 18
TSonnet 18
1Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
2Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
3Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
4And summer’s lease hath all too short a date;
5Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
6And often is his gold complexion dimm’d;
7And every fair from fair sometime declines,
8By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d;
9But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
10Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st;
11Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
12When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st:
13So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
14So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Lines with a marker have analysis — click one, or just scroll.

Title
Sonnet 18
Language & devices

The 1609 Quarto prints the poem as number 18, untitled. 'Sonnet 18', Cambridge's title, is a Genre label plus a place in a sequence; 'Shall I Compare Thee…?', used by many anthologies, turns the opening Rhetorical question into a name and cuts it off with an Ellipsis. Sonnet is Italian sonetto, "little sound".

Meaning & effect

The number is an argument in itself: eighteen is the first sonnet after the seventeen that urge the young man to have children, and the call never returns, so the plain title marks the point where verse takes over the work of a son. The first-line title makes hesitation the poem's identity and leaves the comparison hanging. Neither title names the beloved, and the poem never will; and a "little sound" of fourteen lines, quicker to read than a summer's day is long, is about to claim it will outlast summer.

Line 1
Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Language & devices

Rhetorical question as Dubitatio, feigned hesitation over how to praise. Shall is deliberative (should I?); I is the poem's only first-person pronoun, and thee the intimate singular. a summer’s day puts love poetry's stock method, praise by comparison with nature, on trial, and the Possessive summer’s makes summer an owner.

Meaning & effect

The pretended doubt is the first compliment: the obvious praise may not be good enough. It also makes the act of praising the subject, and gives that act to I, who holds the poem's first main verb; by the last line the main verbs will belong to this. The chosen unit carries its own expiry, a day being summer's briefest holding, and Shall will return in line 9 as prophecy: shall not fade.

Line 2
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Language & devices

Two Comparatives answer at once: more lovely and more temperate. temperate has three senses: mild (weather), with the four humours in balance (medicine, in which temperament was literally a matter of temperature), self-governed (virtue). Thou art is the beloved's only main verb in the poem; the Colon presents what follows as evidence.

Meaning & effect

He compares at once, so the doubt of line 1 was rhetorical. lovely praises a degree of beauty, temperate a kind, and the kind is balance: every fault the octave finds in summer will be an extreme or a lapse. And the beloved is given being, not action: winds, sun, death and finally the poem do things, while he only is.

Line 3
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
Language & devices

Spondee: Rough winds puts two stresses together before the iambs settle. The violent do shake meets darling (dear-ling, little dear), the poem's only endearment, softened by the Alliteration of darling buds. buds are beauty not yet open.

Meaning & effect

The first count against summer is violence, done to beauty from outside. The poem's one endearment goes to the buds, not the beloved: tenderness is spent on what is small and exposed, which is what he would be if he belonged to nature. Because buds are promise, summer is shown wrecking its own future.

Line 4
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date;
Language & devices

Legal metaphor: a lease grants property for a fixed term, after which it returns to its owner, and date is that term: its length and its end. Personification makes summer a tenant, and summer’s repeats line 1's possessive. all too short is a lover's complaint, not a measurement.

Meaning & effect

The second count, brevity, is a matter of contract: the end is written into the terms from the start, so transience is not bad luck but law. Summer's possessive is cut down to size, since all it owns is a tenancy, and the rhyme says the same in sound: date is day with a stop on the end, so the day already contains its deadline. The legal word also sets the question line 10 answers: if summer only rents beauty, can anyone own it?

Line 5
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
Language & devices

Trochaic inversion: Sometime (sometimes) takes the first stress. too hot is excess, the opposite of temperate: in humoural terms, a distemper. Periphrasis and Personification: the eye of heaven is the sun as a watching face.

Meaning & effect

The third count is excess, and the beloved is now set against the sun itself: the hyperbole has climbed from a day to the source of daylight. Two small words carry the verdict, the beloved more, summer too. Sometime keeps the fault occasional, and that is the complaint: summer cannot be relied on. Time, the real enemy, is so far present only inside Sometime, as mere occasion.

Line 6
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d;
Language & devices

often outnumbers Sometime. Inversion puts the verb before the subject, and Personification gives the sun his gold complexion: complexion is both facial colouring and humoural temperament, and gold the colour of wealth and of fair beauty. The passive dimm’d names no agent.

Meaning & effect

The fourth count is the opposite of the third: summer is too much and too little, never temperate. complexion comes from the same medical vocabulary as temperate, so the beloved out-tempers the sun on its own terms, and often against Sometime says the sun is clouded more often than it scorches: an English summer. A golden face losing its colour is also ageing slipped into a weather report.

Line 7
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
Language & devices

Generalisation: every. Antanaclasis, one word in two senses: fair from fair, a beautiful thing from beauty itself. sometime now means in the course of time, stressed on its second syllable, and declines means sinks, as the sun does. Polysyndeton (And… And… And, 4, 6, 7) piles up the counts.

Meaning & effect

The counts become a law: every beautiful thing loses its beauty, and the preposition from splits the word from itself as beauty is split from its owner. The verdict lies in sometime: in line 5 bad days came now and then, here decline comes sooner or later, so occasional misfortune has hardened into certainty. every fair includes the beloved, which makes the turn necessary rather than decorative.

Line 8
By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d;
Language & devices

Two agents: chance (accident) and nature’s changing course (ageing, the seasons), bound by Alliteration (chance… changing course). Polysemy: untrimm’d is stripped of trim (ornament), or out of trim, like a sail not set to the wind. The By phrase supplies the agents that the passive dimm’d withheld.

Meaning & effect

The octave closes by naming who does the damage, and the answer is no one: chance and nature are forces without faces, and in a poem of leases there is nobody to sue. Between them, sudden loss and slow loss, they cover every case, so decay's argument is complete and the turn has something real to defeat. The sailing sense makes beauty a balance that a shifting wind can upset, which suits a poem whose standard is temperate.

Line 9
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Language & devices

Volta: But, where an Italian sonnet turns. Paradox: eternal summer. thy takes a contrastive stress, and summer changes case: possessor in lines 1 and 4 (summer’s), possessed here (thy). The Modal verb shall not is promise or prophecy, and fade is gentle after the octave's violence.

Meaning & effect

The turn exempts the beloved from everything the octave proved, not by refusing the comparison but by conveying it: summer, owner of a day and a lease, now belongs to him, a summer without a lease. Shall returns from line 1 with its meaning reversed, from should I? to it will not: doubt has become decree. The paradox cannot be true in nature, so it raises the question how?, which the poem holds back until line 12.

Line 10
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st;
Language & devices

Legal diction: possession answers lease (4), and that fair (that beauty) answers line 7. Pun: ow’st means ownest, Shakespeare's usual sense, with owe audible. Ellipsis: shall is understood, so the subject of lose is still thy eternal summer, and Anaphora on Nor (10, 11) stacks the denials.

Meaning & effect

The beloved will hold his beauty as owner, not tenant; strictly, the grammar gives the possession to his summer, so the season that held a lease in line 4 now holds title. The pun keeps the debt to nature audible at the moment it is cancelled. His own verb, ow’st, his first since art, is tucked inside a relative clause, and that fair is the poem's only distant demonstrative: the near one, this, is kept for the poem itself.

Line 11
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
Language & devices

Personification: death as a braggart, brag a blunt, almost comic monosyllable. Allusion: his shade recalls Psalm 23's "valley of the shadow of death" and the classical shades, the dead who wander the underworld. his passes from the sun (6) to death.

Meaning & effect

The third denial reaches the last enemy and meets him with contempt. The limit is exact: what is denied is death's brag, not death, so the body will still die but death will not own him. Yet thou wander’st in his shade is the most physical picture of the beloved the poem gives, and it shows him as a ghost, inside a boast that will never be made. The shared his pairs sun and death, gold and shadow, and the beloved slips out from under both.

Line 12
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st:
Language & devices

When means since or as long as: a condition. Pun: lines of verse, and a line of descent: Sonnet 16's "lines of life", the children it set above verse. Metaphor: to time thou grow’st is a gardener's image, you are engrafted into time, as a cutting grows into its stock. time stands alone for the first time, and grow’st contains its rhyme, ow’st.

Meaning & effect

Here is the mechanism: he escapes time by being written into it. lines compresses the sequence's change of plan into one word, verse replacing the bloodline the earlier sonnets demanded, and the graft completes Sonnet 15's promise, "I engraft you new". Time appears by itself only now, at the moment it stops being the enemy and becomes the stock he grows on; owning (ow’st) becomes growing (grow’st). And When makes the promises of lines 9–11 depend on the poem.

Line 13
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
Language & devices

Conditional: So long as is both a duration and a condition, and Anaphora repeats So long (13, 14). men is humankind; Synecdoche: eyes for readers; breathe is to live or to speak aloud, see to read. Ten monosyllables in regular Iambic pentameter.

Meaning & effect

The promise gets its terms: he will live as long as there are readers. So long answers all too short a date, so the poem does not abolish the lease but writes a longer one, with humanity as its term. Human eyes replace the sun's failing eye. The condition is also an admission: when the readers end, so does the life.

Line 14
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
Language & devices

Deixis: this, twice, the poem pointing at itself, both times on the beat. Chiasmus and Polyptoton: lives this… this gives life. Present tense after the sestet's future, and the last word, thee, returns from line 1.

Meaning & effect

The poem names itself as the giver of life. Its verbs complete an arc: Shall (1) deliberates, shall (9, 11) promises, can (13) sets a condition, and lives and gives state a fact, true in the present of every reading. Two sonnets earlier, verse could not make him "live yourself in eyes of men"; this line keeps the men and the eyes but gives lives to this, so he receives a life rather than living his own. The procreation sonnets told him to give life to a child; here the poem gives life to him.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

Sonnet 18 is usually read as the poem that sets its beloved free from time. Its grammar tells a more exact story. The sonnet is a transfer of title: beauty passes from summer, which only rents it, to the beloved, who is promised possession of it, and in the last line to the poem, which takes both of that line's main verbs. The beloved is not freed from tenure; he changes landlords. Two things the poem keeps exact show this: what stands in the possessive case, and who is the subject of the main verbs.

The first main verb belongs to the poet: Shall I compare. The hesitation is a compliment, answered at once by comparing, more lovely and more temperate, and temperate sets the standard the octave will apply: balance. The beloved's own grammar is already telling. Thou art is the only main verb he will ever own. He is; everything else in the poem acts.

For the next six lines he disappears, and summer takes the possessive: a summer’s day, summer’s lease. Summer owns a day, then a lease, which is to say nothing but a tenancy. The main verbs pass to nature (winds shake, the eye of heaven shines, every fair declines), and every count is an extreme or a lapse, summer too where the beloved was more. Time itself enters only by stealth: Sometime (5) means at times, sometime (7) in the course of time, and between them occasional misfortune becomes certainty. every fair, the beloved included, declines, and line 8 names faceless culprits, chance or nature’s changing course.

But thy eternal summer shall not fade changes summer's case. The possessor of lines 1 and 4 is now possessed, thy summer, so the comparison the poem pretended to doubt is not refused but conveyed. The Shall that hesitated in line 1 returns as decree, and an understood shall carries it into line 10, where the strict subject of lose is still thy eternal summer: the season that held a lease now holds possession, and ow’st lets a debt to nature be heard at the moment it is cancelled.

Yet watch the beloved's verbs. ow’st, wander’st and grow’st all sit in subordinate clauses, and the most physical image of him in the poem, thou wander’st in his shade, shows him as a ghost, inside a boast death will not be allowed to make. Even the promise rests on a condition: When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st. time stands alone here for the first time, as it stops being the enemy and becomes the stock he is grafted onto; lines replaces the bloodline the earlier sonnets demanded.

The couplet supplies the terms, and they are the terms of a lease. So long answers all too short a date: summer's short tenancy is replaced by a long one, held So long as men can breathe or eyes can see. The chain of verbs that began with Shall I ends in the plain present, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee. The near demonstrative this is the subject twice; the beloved, whose beauty was that fair, is the one to whom life is given.

The strongest objection is that this turns a love poem into a deed of conveyance. The poem's energy, on this view, is exuberance, not book-keeping: having proved that everything fades, the speaker simply says not you, three times over (shall not… Nor… Nor), and that is what readers and wedding guests have answered to for four centuries.

The objection is right about the feeling and wrong to set it against the grammar, because the grammar is how the feeling is spent. A Petrarchan lover talks about his own suffering; this one says I once and then hands every verb away, first to the beloved's summer and finally to the poem. And the terms are exact because the sequence has already tested them. Two sonnets earlier, verse could not make the young man "live yourself in eyes of men"; the couplet keeps those men and those eyes and changes only the subject. What the poet cannot give is a life of the beloved's own, the life a child would have carried; what he can give is a life held on the poem's terms, and So long as is his honest statement of them, the one condition in a poem of guarantees. That honesty makes the ending moving rather than merely proud: the poem knows that it is the thing that survives, and its last two words still send the life elsewhere, to thee.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

An English (Shakespearean) sonnet: fourteen lines of iambic pentameter in three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. A sonnet of praise that becomes an eternising sonnet, one that promises its subject life through verse.

Metre

Ten syllables in every line (every and wander'st count as two syllables, ow'st and grow'st as one), so regular that the few departures stand out.

Rhyme

Seven rhyme sounds, all full rhymes except temperate/date, where the light last syllable of temperate carries the rhyme (a normal licence of the period).

Punctuation

Every line ends on a mark, so there is no enjambment, though the sense runs on across 7–8, 9–10, 11–12 and 13–14. After the question, lines 2–14 are one sentence, its pointing largely editorial (1609 runs the sestet on commas) but logical: the colon after temperate, also in 1609, opens the case; semicolons divide the counts and denials; the colon after grow’st opens onto the terms.

Words

114 words, 93 of them monosyllables. Sixteen of the 21 longer words are in the octave, five in lines 9–12 and none in the couplet: the claim grows as the language gets plainer.

The argument

The sonnet is built as a case and its answer: a question and its answer (1–2), four counts against summer (violence, brevity, excess, deficiency: 3–6), a law of decline and its faceless agents (7–8), the turn to possession (9–10), the denial of death's brag (11), the means (12) and the terms (13–14). Proportion carries the argument. Eight lines go to summer and decay, four to the beloved, two to the poem, and the four on the beloved are mostly negative (shall not, Nor, Nor), so he is defined by what will not happen to him. The sestet answers the octave term for term: fade for the shaken buds and the dimmed sun, that fair for every fair from fair, possession for lease.

The pronouns track who matters. I appears once, in the first three words. The beloved is addressed seven times, framing the poem but absent from lines 3–8 and from line 13. The tenses move with the argument: the octave's general present (do shake, hath, shines, declines) is the tense of laws, the sestet's future (shall not fade, Nor shall death brag) the tense of promise, and the couplet's present (lives, gives) fulfils the promise whenever the poem is read.

The turn, and the second turn

The But of line 9 gives this English sonnet an Italian shape inside it, eight lines of case and six of answer, while the rhyme scheme still divides the answer into the denials (9–12) and the couplet. The couplet reverses nothing: it changes the subject, from thee to this, and reveals what the promise rests on, so it is better called a second hinge than a second volta.

Scansion

Stresses are in capitals, with feet marked by |.

Line Scansion What it does
1 shall I | com-PARE | thee TO | a SUM- | mer's DAY Regular, with the beat on I, the only first-person pronoun; a reader may lean on thee instead, tilting the line towards the beloved.
3 ROUGH WINDS | do SHAKE | the DAR- | ling BUDS | of MAY Spondee: two stresses collide at the gust, then four smooth iambs carry the buds.
5 SOME-time | too HOT | the EYE | of HEAV- | en SHINES Initial trochee: Sometime leads, so the sun's excess arrives as something occasional and unpredictable.
7 and EV- | 'ry FAIR | from FAIR | some-TIME | de-CLINES Both fairs take beats; sometime is now stressed on its second syllable as its meaning shifts from at times to in time (the 1609 text even prints it "some-time").
9 but THY | e-TER- | nal SUM- | mer SHALL | not FADE Contrastive stress on thy (your summer, not nature's); shall takes the beat, making the promise metrically certain.
11 nor SHALL | death BRAG | thou WAN- | der'st IN | his SHADE death falls on an off-beat, metrically demoted, though spoken naturally shall death brag is three heavy syllables: the swagger the line mocks.
14 so LONG | lives THIS, | and THIS | gives LIFE | to THEE Regular in pattern but heavy in speech: lives and gives are strong verbs on off-beats, so the last line slows to a close, and the beats go to this, twice.

The regularity is expressive. A poem praising the temperate is metrically temperate: every line keeps its five beats without strain, and the few substitutions fall on the moments of violence (3), unpredictability (5) and contrast (9).

Rhyme, pair by pair

  • day / May and temperate / date: the first quatrain's two rhyme sounds almost coincide, and temperate is pulled into the deadline's rhyme on its weakest syllable.
  • shines / declines: the sun's shining rhymed with the decline of every fair, so the sun's setting is handed on to all beauty.
  • dimm’d / untrimm’d: two past participles of damage; only the second names who did it.
  • fade / shade: the two fates the sestet denies, rhymed together.
  • ow’st / grow’st: the only rhyme made of the beloved's own verbs, and grow’st contains ow’st: owning turns into growing.
  • see / thee: reading rhymed with the beloved, and the last rhyme word repeats the poem's first thee.
SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sound patterns

The gust and the buds. Line 3 opens with two heavy stresses, Rough winds, on a rolling /r/ and a breathy /f/. Then the consonants soften into the voiced plosives of darling buds, and the line ends on the open vowel of May: harshness meets tenderness in the mouth as it does in the image.

A short date said slowly. all too short a date lengthens the very phrase that complains of shortness: the long vowels of all, too and short hold the voice, and then the line stops dead on the /t/ of date, as a lease ends.

Heat, then dimming. Line 5 is breathy with /h/ (hot, heaven) and open vowels. Line 6 closes on dimm’d, where the lips shut on /m/ and the /d/ cuts the sound off, and untrimm’d repeats the muffled ending, so the octave closes twice on the sound of something shut off.

fair from fair. The /f/ alliteration and the exact repetition make the ear hear one word returning slightly changed: beauty slipping away from the beautiful thing.

The vowel of day. The poem's first rhyme sound, the long /eɪ/ of day, runs through May and date and returns in fade and shade: the sound that opened on summer comes back in the two words of loss at the very moment the sestet denies them.

Denial and swagger. The nasal /n/ of Nor… Nor gives lines 10–11 a flat, firm sound, like an objection entered twice. death brag packs /d/, /b/ and /g/ into two blunt syllables, so the boast sounds like what it is, before the line softens into the hushed /ʃ/ of his shade.

The couplet's breath. Lines 13–14 are twenty monosyllables, mostly long open vowels (so, long, breathe, eyes, see, life, thee) with few hard clusters: a couplet about breathing that is effortless to breathe. After lovely (2) the only words beginning with /l/ are words of loss, lease and lose, until lines, long, lives and life reclaim the sound. The repeated So long gives the couplet the cadence of an oath, and it ends on an open vowel that could be held indefinitely, the thee of line 1 returning.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs and symbols

1. Summer and its sun

Summer is the poem's measuring-rod, and its grammar changes as the poem goes on. In lines 1 and 4 it stands in the possessive, an owner: a summer’s day, summer’s lease, though what it owns turns out to be a tenancy. In lines 5–6 it becomes the sun, the eye of heaven with his gold complexion, the grandest beauty nature has and still unreliable, too hot or dimm’d. In line 9 it returns as a possession: thy eternal summer. Summer is not discarded but transferred, from nature, where it ends, to the beloved, where it will not.

2. "Fair": beauty as a thing

The word for beauty is used three times, always as a noun: every fair from fair (7) and that fair thou ow’st (10). As a noun, beauty becomes a thing that can be separated from its owner, lost, owned or owed. Around it gather the poem's other words for beauty, lovely, darling, gold and the trim implied by untrimm’d, and none of them describes the beloved's body. Beauty here is a property rather than a picture, which is why it can be moved from nature into verse.

3. Lease, possession and gift

A vocabulary of property runs beneath the imagery and changes the kind of holding at each stage: rented (lease, date, 4), owned or owed (possession, ow’st, 10), claimed (death's brag, 11), grafted (grow’st, 12) and finally given (this gives life to thee, 14). The sequence traces the poem's movement from a world where beauty is borrowed to one where it is bestowed, by a giver who keeps the title.

4. Eyes and lines

Seeing and writing come together at the end. The first eye in the poem is the sun's, the eye of heaven (5), and it fails: too hot, often dimmed. The second belongs to readers: eyes can see (13). Between them stand the eternal lines (12), verse to be seen and a line of descent, the poem in the place of a child. this (14) is what those eyes are looking at, so the motif replaces nature's unreliable eye with human ones and makes reading the light by which the beloved lives.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Poetry against time

The central claim is that verse can do what nature cannot: the octave makes decay as strong as it can, until every fair from fair sometime declines, and the answer is a change of medium, When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st. The scale grows to meet the claim, from a day (1) and a season (4) to eternal (9, 12) and the life of humanity (13). Yet the claim is limited with care: death loses only his brag, and eternity lasts So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, coming true each time the poem is read.

02

Love as praise and gift

A love poem without the word love, without a description of the beloved and without the speaker's feelings: love is two acts, praise that outbids the sun and a guarantee repeated three ways (shall not… Nor… Nor). The speaker says I once and then gives every verb away; what a poet can give is not a body, a marriage or a child, but this.

03

Nature on trial

Summer, love poetry's standard of praise, is convicted of violence, brevity, excess and unreliability. Yet every image of beauty in the poem is natural, and the beloved's immortality is an eternal summer: art does not replace nature so much as perfect it, keeping summer's beauty and cancelling its lease.

04

Ownership and debt

Time works like a contract: summer holds a lease, and the sestet upgrades the beloved from tenant to owner (possession, ow’st). But ow’st also says owe, So long as makes even eternity a term, and the poem, not the beloved, ends holding the verbs: he gains possession and loses agency.

05

Balance and constancy

temperate (mild, balanced in humour, self-governed) is the beloved's virtue, and every fault of summer is a lack of it; eternal is temperateness without end. The form is temperate too, regular, end-stopped and orderly, which helps its claim to last feel earned; the one intemperate thing in it is the praise.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Does the poem compare, or refuse to compare?

The difficulty. Line 1 seems to ask whether summer is a fit comparison, and the usual paraphrase is no: you are better. But line 2 is itself a comparison, the octave carries it out count by count, and line 9 gives the beloved thy eternal summer, as if he were a summer after all.

Competing readings. (a) Rejection: summer is too flawed to be worthy, and the beloved is placed above nature. (b) Outdoing: praise by dispraising the standard (the beloved is like summer, only better), so comparing is the method rather than the problem. (c) Transfer: the possessive grammar shows summer passing from owner (a summer’s day, summer’s lease) to owned (thy eternal summer), and in line 10 it is that summer which will not lose possession: the comparison is kept, and only its lease is removed.

What a strong answer does. It treats Shall I compare…? as a question about method that the poem answers in practice, and uses the three appearances of summer (1, 4, 9) to show that the result is not "unlike summer" but "summer, now yours". That is why the turn needs the word summer at all: the beloved is still measured in the unit the poem began with.

2. ow’st and grow’st: owning, owing or growing?

The difficulty. In Shakespeare's English ow’st means ownest, but owe sits very close in a poem full of leases; and its rhyme partner, grow’st, leaves the law for the garden.

Competing readings. (a) Own: the beloved holds his beauty as property, the exact answer to summer's lease; this is the editors' gloss. (b) Owe: beauty is a loan from nature that must be repaid, as the procreation sonnets said ("Nature's bequest gives nothing but doth lend", Sonnet 4), and they named the repayment, a child. (c) Grow: to time thou grow’st means you are engrafted into time, the gardener's image of Sonnet 15 ("I engraft you new"), and grow’st contains ow’st letter for letter, so the one rhyme made of the beloved's own verbs turns holding into living.

What a strong answer does. It treats the puns as the poem's subject rather than its slips. A title can be lost, reclaimed or contested, as death's brag contests it in the very next line; so the sestet finishes its property argument with a graft, a life joined to another life. Owe need not win, but it explains why the triumph sounds like a settlement of accounts.

3. this and thee: whose eternity, and on what terms?

The difficulty. The sestet promises an eternal summer and eternal lines, but the couplet adds a condition, So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, and gives both its main verbs to this, not to the beloved, who is never described.

Competing readings. (a) Hyperbole: "as long as humanity lasts" simply means for ever. (b) Another lease: So long answers all too short a date, so the poem replaces summer's short tenancy with a long one, held from readers. (c) The poem, not the man: the near demonstrative this is the subject twice, while his beauty was only that fair. Shakespeare draws the line openly in Sonnet 74: "The worth of that is that which it contains, / And that is this, and this with thee remains."

What a strong answer does. It weighs the boast against its terms instead of ignoring either. The ending is confident because the poem has in fact been read for four centuries, and moving because it admits it might not be; and the last two words, to thee, still insist that the life was meant for someone else.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

Eight moments, in the poem's order.

1. Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? / Thou art more lovely and more temperate (1–2) — dubitatio; possessive; comparatives; polysemy. The doubt is both a compliment and a statement of method: before the poem is about whom it praises, it is about how, and the comparison it doubts is made at once. summer’s makes summer an owner, and what it owns is a day, the briefest of its holdings. temperate joins three vocabularies (weather, humours, virtue) and makes balance the standard by which summer will be convicted. Intention and effect: the praise arrives as a verdict reached rather than a compliment recited, and it goes to evenness, the one quality that can plausibly be stretched into eternal; that moderation is praised in hyperbole is part of the charm, since love cannot be temperate about temperance.

2. Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, / And summer’s lease hath all too short a date (3–4) — spondee; displaced endearment; legal metaphor. Two stresses strike (Rough winds) before the iambs recover, and darling, the poem's only endearment, is given to buds, not to the beloved. Then violence gives way to contract: summer holds only a tenancy, and its end is one of the terms. Intention and effect: tenderness is spent on beauty not yet open and already damaged, so the reader feels on the flowers' behalf a fear the poem never states for the beloved, and transience becomes law rather than bad luck, opening the argument about ownership.

3. Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, / And often is his gold complexion dimm’d (5–6) — periphrasis; personification; humoural pun; words of frequency. The beloved is measured against the sun and still wins: too hot Sometime, dimmed often, balanced never. complexion is both face and humoural temperament, and too hot a distemper: the sun is intemperate in the medical sense. Intention and effect: the hyperbole is earned by argument, and a golden face losing its colour smuggles the beloved's own ageing into a weather report.

4. And every fair from fair sometime declines, / By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d (7–8) — generalisation; antanaclasis; shift of sense; polysemy. from splits fair (a beautiful thing) from fair (beauty itself); sometime, at times in line 5, now means in the course of time; the agents named have no faces; untrimm’d is stripped of ornament, or out of balance like an untrimmed sail. Intention and effect: the octave ends on a law that includes the beloved, made as strong as possible so that the reply has a real opponent.

5. But thy eternal summer shall not fade, / Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st (9–10) — volta; paradox; change of case; legal diction; pun. Summer passes from possessor (summer’s) to possessed (thy), and the tenant's lease becomes possession; ow’st means own and lets owe be heard. Intention and effect: the comparison is transformed rather than rejected, and shall, hesitant in line 1, now speaks as decree.

6. Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade (11) — personification; allusion; negated clause. Death is a braggart, his shade both the psalm's shadow and the classical underworld, and his is the sun's pronoun passed on to death. Intention and effect: contempt replaces fear, but only the boast is denied, not the dying; and the poem's one concrete image of the beloved, a ghost wandering, is called up in order to be cancelled.

7. When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st (12) — pun; grafting metaphor; conditional. lines are verse and lineage at once; to grow to is to be engrafted, as a cutting grows into its stock; time appears as itself for the first time. Intention and effect: the procreation argument of seventeen sonnets is replaced in one word, time becomes the stock the beloved grows on rather than the enemy, and When quietly makes every promise depend on the poem.

8. So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee. (13–14) — conditional; anaphora; deixis; chiasmus. So long, said twice like an oath, turns eternity into a duration with a condition attached. The chiasmus lives this… this gives life balances on its comma, and this, on the beat both times, is the subject of both verbs, while thee is only the receiver. Intention and effect: each reading fulfils the promise in the present tense, while the grammar admits what survives most surely: not a face but this, holding its life So long as there are readers.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Materialist: love in the language of property

What it makes visible. A love poem that thinks in tenure: beauty rented, owned, owed and finally given, while the poem keeps the title. If the young man was a nobleman and the poet a writer in need of support, the poem is also an offer: I can give you what no one else can, permanence. The boast was saleable, and by 1609 it was being sold on the book's dedication page.

What it flattens. Nothing in Sonnet 18, or in the record, shows it was written for a patron, and reading every word as money misses the poem's tenderness: darling buds and eternal summer are not only transactions.

2. Queer and gender criticism

What it makes visible. In the sequence the beloved is a young man (Sonnet 20's "master-mistress of my passion"), and the poem is one man's unembarrassed praise of another's beauty, in a form built for praising women: Petrarch's Laura, Spenser's Elizabeth. Because the sonnet never genders its beloved, it has also lived a second life as a wedding reading, its silence filled by whoever recites it.

What it flattens. The poem's own text does not settle the beloved's sex, and reading it only through the sequence can overwrite what makes it so widely usable.

3. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The poem makes its reader the mechanism of its promise: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see describes the very act of reading, so this lives whenever someone breathes its words and sees its lines. The blank beloved invites each reader to supply a thee.

What it flattens. The original address to a particular person: making the poem about us can erase the young man it was written for.

4. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. Nature as a foil to be outdone: summer is rough, brief, excessive and dim, and the poem sides with art against it. Beside Boey's 'Report to Wordsworth' or Clarke's 'Lament', its confidence that nature is merely imperfect, not damaged, belongs to a world that could take the seasons for granted.

What it flattens. The poem uses nature as its standard of praise rather than its subject, and it depends on nature for every image of beauty it has, so its victory over summer is a tribute to summer too.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A love poem of praise and promise

The default reading, and the one that has made the poem a wedding favourite: a lover finds the conventional comparison too weak, outdoes it, and offers a guarantee instead of a compliment.

Evidence: the comparatives of line 2, the exuberant thy eternal summer shall not fade, the three denials (shall not… Nor… Nor), and the gift in the last line, this gives life to thee.

Weakness: it has to explain why a love poem never says love, never describes the beloved and ends by praising itself.

2. A poem about poetry

The real subject is the power of verse: eight lines dismantle nature, four make a claim, and two name the poem as the agent.

Evidence: eternal lines; the doubled this; the vanishing I, as the poet steps aside and the poem takes the subject of the final sentence.

Weakness: the poem's power is put at the beloved's service, and the last word is thee, not this.

3. Verse instead of children

Read in the sequence, Sonnet 18 is the first poem after the seventeen that urge the young man to father children, and it answers them in their own vocabulary.

Evidence: the procreation sonnets' words return (lease, date, lines), and so does their grafting image, in grow’st; lines puns on lineage, and gives life puts the poem in the parent's place.

Weakness: the 1609 order may not be Shakespeare's own, and the poem works fully on its own, as anthologies print it.

4. The vanishing beloved

The poem promises immortality and gives its subject no features at all: what is immortalised is the description, not the young man, and four centuries on nobody knows who he was.

Evidence: no physical detail; thee only a pronoun; the poem as grammatical subject at the end; Sonnet 17's worry that future readers would not believe a description of him.

Weakness: Renaissance praise often idealises rather than describes, and the blankness is also generous, since it lets any reader fill thee.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

'Sonnet 18' / 'Shall I Compare Thee…?'

Analysis
  • 1609 Quarto: numbered, no titles
  • 18 = first after the procreation sonnets (1–17) → children never urged again; verse takes over
  • First-line title → question + ellipsis, comparison left hanging
Effect, style & response
  • "Little sound" (sonetto), 14 lines → claims to outlast summer
1–2

Shall I compare thee… / more temperate

Analysis
  • Dubitatio: feigned doubt → first compliment
  • Shall = deliberating → l.9 shall not = decree
  • Only I in the poem; first main verb → last ones go to this
  • summer’s possessive → summer = owner (of a day: shortest unit)
  • temperate: mild weather / balanced humours / self-control → the standard
  • Thou art = beloved's ONLY main verb → he is, never does
3–4

darling buds / summer’s lease

Analysis
  • Spondee Rough winds → gust in the metre
  • darling = only endearment → buds, not the beloved
  • Buds = beauty unopened → summer wrecks its own future
  • lease / date = fixed term: its length + its end → brevity = contract
  • day → date: + one consonant → deadline inside the day
Effect, style & response
  • Opens the property argument → possession (10), So long (13–14)
5–6

the eye of heaven / gold complexion dimm’d

Analysis
  • too hot (excess) / dimm’d (deficiency) → never temperate
  • Humours: temperament = temperature → too hot = distemper
  • complexion = colouring + humoural temperament → links temperate
  • often > Sometime → more cloud than heat
Effect, style & response
  • Hyperbole climbs: beloved beats the sun itself
  • Ageing hidden in a weather report
7–8

every fair from fair sometime declines

Analysis
  • every → law for all beauty, incl. the beloved
  • fair from fair = antanaclasis: beautiful thing / beauty → word split from itself
  • sometime: l.5 = at times → l.7 = in the course of time
  • Agents: chance + nature → faceless; no one to sue
  • untrimm’d = stripped of ornament / sail out of trim
Effect, style & response
  • Occasional → inevitable: the turn becomes necessary
9–10

thy eternal summer / possession

Analysis
  • Volta But l.9 (Italian position)
  • Summer: possessor (summer’s, 1, 4) → possessed (thy)
  • Comparison conveyed, not refused: summer without a lease
  • possession answers lease; that fair answers l.7
  • ow’st = own (+ owe) → debt heard, then cancelled
  • that fair (far) vs this (near, l.14) → nearness kept for the poem
Effect, style & response
  • Doubt (l.1) → decree
11–12

death brag / eternal lines

Analysis
  • Death = braggart → mocked; only the brag denied, the body still dies
  • shade = Psalm 23 + classical ghosts; his: sun (6) → death (11)
  • Most physical image of the beloved = a ghost, in a denied boast
  • lines = verse / lineage (16's "lines of life" = children)
  • grow’st = engrafted into time (15: "I engraft you new"); contains ow’st
  • When → every promise conditional on the poem
Effect, style & response
  • Time: enemy → stock he grows on; owning → growing
13–14

So long lives this, and this gives life to thee

Analysis
  • So long as = condition → a longer lease, held from readers
  • Deixis this ×2 = subject; thee = receiver
  • Shall → shall → can → lives / gives = doubt → promise → condition → fact
  • 16: verse can't make him "live yourself in eyes of men" → 18: this lives, he receives life
Effect, style & response
  • Beloved in the child's place: the poem gives life to him

Grammar & form

Analysis
  • Main-clause subjects: I → Thou (art) → nature → thy summer → death → this
  • Beloved's verbs ow'st / wander'st / grow'st → all subordinate
  • 8 lines summer + decay, 4 beloved, 2 poem
Effect, style & response
  • Grammar = transfer of title: summer → beloved → poem

Sound & metre

Analysis
  • Spondee l.3; trochee l.5; death demoted l.11; heavy l.14
  • day / May / date → fade / shade: summer's vowel in the denials
  • /l/: lease, lose → lines, long, lives, life
  • Couplet: 20 monosyllables, open vowels → effortless to breathe

Context

Analysis
  • 1609 (Thorpe); 1–126 young man; 1–17 = children
  • Beloved's sex never given in 18 → "she" = reader's assumption
  • Probably 1590s (Meres 1598: "sugred Sonnets")
  • Eternising: Horace, Ovid (vivam); Spenser writes his lady's name → 18 names no one

Ironies

Analysis
  • Doubts comparison → compares throughout (eternal summer)
  • Praises temperance intemperately
  • Beloved never named or described; poet's name survives, the youth's doesn't
  • "Eternal" → on a condition (So long as)
  • Wedding favourite that abandons marriage
Effect, style & response
  • Generosity (any reader fills thee) or the art praising itself?
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. Boey Kim Cheng, 'Report to Wordsworth' (05)

Link: two sonnets about what poetry can do against loss, each ending in a couplet about seeing (eyes can see; "O see the wound widening in the sky").

Shared technique: the Shakespearean rhyme pattern (half-rhymed in Boey) and personified nature and heavens.

Difference: Shakespeare's nature is merely imperfect, and art perfects it; Boey's is destroyed by "insatiate man", and "Poetry and piety have begun to fail".

2. Kevin Halligan, 'The Cockroach' (06)

Link: two sonnets whose last line fuses the subject with something else: the poem becomes the beloved's life (this gives life to thee); Halligan's speaker finds himself in the insect ("I thought I recognised myself").

Shared technique: iambic pentameter, a sonnet's argument, and a last line that changes how the whole poem reads.

Difference: Sonnet 18's couplet is the set's most confident resolution; Halligan withholds a couplet (ABAB CDCD EFGEGF) and ends on "I don't know" and a guess.

3. Aphra Behn, 'Song: Love Armed' (01)

Link: two love lyrics in the Petrarchan tradition of praise by comparison: Behn's beloved has "Bright Eyes" from which Love takes "his fire"; Shakespeare's is set against the sun, the eye of heaven.

Shared technique: an argument organised around pronouns, ending on the long /iː/ of the beloved's pronoun: Behn's "thee… free", Shakespeare's see… thee.

Difference: Behn's love wounds the speaker ("my poor Heart alone is harmed"); Shakespeare's speaker hardly mentions himself: her ending is a complaint, his a guarantee.

4. Katherine Philips, 'A Married State' (11)

Link: both turn from marriage and children as the answer to a life: Sonnet 18 drops the demand for children made in Sonnets 1–17; Philips urges a woman to stay single, spared childbirth's pains that "extort your tears".

Shared technique: rhymed iambic pentameter driving an argument to a decisive close, in couplets throughout (Philips) or in one (Shakespeare).

Difference: Philips argues with dry wit ("A married state affords but little ease"); Shakespeare is rapturous, and his alternative to children is not freedom but poetry.

5. Carol Rumens, 'Carpet-weavers, Morocco' (13)

Link: both are about making what outlasts its makers' moment: Rumens's weavers knot "all-that-will-be" into a pattern that will "freeze" into "all-that-was"; Shakespeare's beloved grow’st into eternal lines.

Shared technique: the made object, a carpet's pattern or a poem's lines, becomes the image of time.

Difference: Shakespeare's art is meant to preserve a person, Rumens's a pattern whose child makers stay in "the school of days"; both keep the art more surely than the people, but Shakespeare calls this a triumph, Rumens leaves it uneasy.

CONTEXT

Context

The world the poem came out of

The Poet: Judith Wright (1915–2000)

Born at Armidale on the New England tableland of northern New South Wales, the eldest child of a grazier, Wright grew up on her family's sheep country. Her activism was not a sideline to the poetry. She was a founding member of the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland (1962) and its president from 1964 to 1976, when the society campaigned against oil drilling on the Great Barrier Reef and sand mining on Fraser Island (K'gari); she was equally committed to Aboriginal land rights, as a founding member of the Aboriginal Treaty Committee (1979) and author of The Cry for the Dead (1981), a history of dispossession in the region her own family had settled. She knew her family's land had been taken from its first owners.

Dated c. 1964, 'Hunting Snake' belongs to the years when Wright was helping to build Queensland's first serious wildlife-preservation campaign: a poem about letting a dangerous animal pass unharmed, by someone organising to stop the killing of wild things.

'The Killer' (1947)

Wright had written this encounter before. In 'The Killer' (1947) a speaker goes down to a creek to rest and drink, is surprised by a black snake, and lashes out and kills it. 'Hunting Snake' returns to the same scene — a sunlit day, a sudden meeting, a great black snake — and reverses the outcome: the walkers freeze, watch and let it go. The titles mirror each other ('The Killer' leaves open who kills, 'Hunting Snake' who hunts), so the later poem can be read as an answer to the earlier one.

The great black snake

Wright names no species, but in eastern Australia a “black snake” usually means the red-bellied black snake (Pseudechis porphyriacus): large and glossy black, common from south-east Queensland through New England, often near water, active by day, eating mainly frogs as well as lizards and small mammals — venomous, but shy rather than aggressive.

Two details are exact. A snake hunts by scent, its forked tongue collecting chemical traces from the ground and carrying them to a sensing organ in the roof of the mouth: hence a tongue flickering on a trail. And snakes take their body heat from their surroundings, so the mild, sunny late season's grace that comforts the walkers may also be the snake's last good hunting weather before winter. The poem never uses the words venom, bite or danger; to an Australian reader none needs saying.

Serpent and sublime

In Genesis the serpent is the tempter, cursed to crawl on its belly, and settlers carried that meaning to a continent full of venomous snakes; in many Aboriginal cultures, by contrast, a great serpent (often called the Rainbow Serpent in English) is a creator being linked to water and life — a reading the poem does not depict, but one present in the country where Wright refused the Genesis reflex. Edmund Burke's Philosophical Enquiry (1757) argued that power and danger, felt at a safe distance, produce “a sort of delightful horror” — the sublime. The closest poem in English is D. H. Lawrence's 'Snake' (1923), in which a man admires a snake drinking at his water-trough, then obeys “my accursed human education” and throws a log at it. Wright's walkers feel the same awe and throw nothing.

THunting Snake
1basking in sunlight, in the kindly lateness of the year
2beneath the mildest heaven of the fall
3the two are strolling, then stop dead mid-stride
4a huge dark serpent swings swiftly past them
5its head held low, its tongue testing the ground for scent
6it hunts onward, the stems opening before it

8the watchers' breathing stops as it goes by
9which path it traced, which little creature
10ran, still alive, from its savage purpose

14among stems that concealed its quarry
15they breathe in the daylight more fully than before
