Hunting Snake
Language & devices

A two-word Noun phrase with no article, like a field-guide label or a painting's caption. Hunting is Ambiguous: a Participial adjective (a snake that hunts) or a Gerund with Snake as its object (the hunting of snakes, as in “duck hunting”).

Meaning & effect

The title puts the snake's purpose first, and the poem keeps faith with it: from first appearance to last the animal is hunting, and it never once attends to the people. The second sense names the outcome the poem refuses — settler Australians killed snakes on sight, and Wright's own 'The Killer' (1947) has a speaker kill a black snake at a creek — so the title holds the violence the poem withholds.

Lines 1–2
Sun-warmed … gentlest sky
Language & devices

The Compound adjective Sun-warmed opens a Periodic sentence: two lines of setting before the subject we arrives in line 3. grace is a Pun: gracefulness, a favour freely given, and a period of grace before winter. The Superlative gentlest goes one step past gentle, a light touch of Pathetic fallacy, and soft sibilance, liquids and nasals leave almost no hard stops.

Meaning & effect

The poem begins in exact comfort: a last mild spell before the cold, felt as a gift, so that what follows feels like a privilege, a sighting the walkers are allowed. Stacking warmth, grace and gentleness makes nature first appear kindly, and the syntax lingers as the walkers do — the last moment in the poem when their world is the subject. Sun-warmed also states, without comment, what walkers and snake share: the people enjoy the sun, and the cold-blooded snake depends on it to move at all.

Line 3
froze half-through a pace
Language & devices

The subject at last is the First-person plural we; the poem never says “I”. Two verbs either side of a Caesura make a Juxtaposition of motion and its stopping. froze is a Metaphor turning temperature into sudden stillness, and half-through a pace is precise Kinaesthetic imagery: a stride interrupted, one foot still lifted.

Meaning & effect

The long, easy sentence ends in an arrest, and the cause is not named until line 4, so the walkers' bodies react before their minds know why: awe and fear arrive as physical events, not thoughts. In a poem so full of warmth, the warm-blooded people turn cold and still while the cold-blooded snake moves fluidly. we makes the reaction shared and simultaneous, two people stopping as one.

Line 4
The great black snake
Language & devices

The snake gets a whole line and a whole sentence. great black snake is three stressed monosyllables, a Spondee of hard Plosives (g, b, k), and the Definite article treats it as a known presence of this country, not “a snake”. reeling is a fluid Present participle: whirling, swaying, a line paying out from a reel.

Meaning & effect

The cause arrives after the effect. Wright names the animal in plain, weighty words for size, colour and kind, then releases it into motion as the hard consonants give way to the liquid r and l of reeling. Most importantly, from its first moment the snake is passing by: it has no interest in the people, and the poem never suggests an attack.

Line 5
Head down, tongue flickering
Language & devices

Two Absolute phrases present head and tongue before the pronoun he, building the snake from close-up details as if through a lens. flickering is quick Kinaesthetic imagery and trail is hunting vocabulary. The poem's most irregular line: four stresses packed at the start, then a rush of light syllables.

Meaning & effect

A naturalist's description: a snake hunts by scent, flicking its forked tongue to gather traces from the ground, so tongue flickering on a trail is exact. Head down shows complete absorption — the snake is reading the ground, not watching the watchers — and the metre flickers like the tongue's rapid touches.

Line 6
quested … the parting grass
Language & devices

The pronoun he gives the snake a gender and a self; the humans never become individuals. quested is elevated diction with the Connotation of a knight's quest, and in older hunting usage hounds “quest” for a scent. In the parting grass the Present participle and a touch of Personification open the grass ahead of him, as a crowd parts for royalty, in perfectly regular Iambic tetrameter.

Meaning & effect

The verb raises the hunt to something heroic while staying technically exact for an animal following a scent. The landscape makes way: the snake moves smoothly through its own domain, while the people are visitors standing still at its edge.

Line 7
diamond scale
Language & devices

glazed is a Metaphor: sunlight as a glassy coating, like glaze on pottery. diamond scale joins the Connotation of gems — brilliant, precious, the hardest stone — to accuracy, since snake scales are diamond-shaped, and the singular scale makes the skin a material, like mail. sun returns from line 1: there it warmed the walkers, here it gilds the snake.

Meaning & effect

The poem's most beautiful image makes the snake precious rather than repellent: the vocabulary of jewellery and craft turns it into an object of value, leaving no room for the serpent as sly tempter. diamond keeps hardness inside the beauty, splendour and danger in one word, and though the same sun touches walkers and snake, only the snake shines.

Line 8
we lost breath to see
Language & devices

lost breath is a compressed Idiom (not “lost our breath”), a bare bodily fact. A small Stress clash: the metre wants “and WE lost BREATH”, speech says “we LOST BREATH”, so two heavy syllables collide where the breath stops. A full stop closes the stanza.

Meaning & effect

Three lines for the snake, one clause for the humans, and that clause is a loss: as with the frozen stride, awe is registered by the body. see names the walkers' only action in the poem — they can only look — and pass repeats that the snake is passing through. The breath lost here is taken back, deeper, in line 15; the poem's emotional arc lies between those two breaths.

Lines 9–10
what small food / fled living
Language & devices

Two fronted Noun clauses (indirect questions, no question marks) come before their verb, which arrives only in line 11 — Hyperbaton — with Anaphora on What… what. Enjambment at small food / fled living holds the prey as mere food at the line-end, then restores it as a living, fleeing creature. Alliteration links fled and fierce intent.

Meaning & effect

The poem turns to the snake's hidden world, its route and prey, which the walkers cannot see. small food is the predator's view of a frog or lizard, fled living insists on the prey's life at the moment it is threatened, and fierce intent is the poem's strongest statement of the snake's will: not drifting but wanting. Because the verb is delayed, the poem thinks what its people did not.

Line 11
we scarcely thought
Language & devices

Paralipsis: the poem raises the prey, then says the walkers hardly considered it; scarcely is Understatement. After the semicolon's Caesura, an Inversion puts still before its verb, and still is Ambiguous: motionless, and “even now”. A Trochaic substitution lands the stress on still, and Consonance on st (still, stood) makes the phrase hard to say quickly.

Meaning & effect

The walkers' minds are suspended with their bodies: thought gives way to pure attention. scarcely is honest, almost a confession — the wonder depends on not thinking about the death the snake pursues — and Wright neither condemns nor excuses this; she records it. The clustered consonants make the line itself stand still.

Line 12
our eyes went
Language & devices

went is repeated in two senses, an Antanaclasis: the eyes “go” figuratively, the snake literally. eyes is Synecdoche, the part of the walkers that leaves while their bodies stay. Soft sounds (w, h, s, n) and almost no hard consonants make the line glide to the stanza's full stop.

Meaning & effect

The stanza's paradox: standing completely still, the walkers are carried off, their attention travelling with the snake — the closest they come to joining it. The repeated verb makes the line follow itself, acting out the watching of something moving away. The people have become pure eyes.

Line 13
Cold, dark and splendid
Language & devices

A Tricolon of adjectives before the pronoun (Inversion), opening on a Spondee slowed by a comma and rising to a Climax. Cold: cold-blooded, unfeeling, deathly; dark: black, mysterious, menacing; splendid: magnificent, from Latin splendere, to shine — so dark and splendid is close to an Oxymoron, exact for a glossy black snake. Enjambment leaves gone alone at the line-end.

Meaning & effect

The poem's one explicit judgement, delivered as the snake disappears. The first two adjectives are the ones a frightened settler might use, and Wright does not deny them; the third changes their moral weight, so coldness and darkness become part of the splendour, not grounds for killing. Described only once it is gone, the snake is defined by its after-image, vanishing before the sentence says where.

Line 14
hid his prey
Language & devices

A Trochaic inversion opens the line. the grass returns from line 6 in Contrast: grass that parted for the snake now hid its prey. hid his prey is Ambiguous: hidden from the snake (no protection from a hunter working by scent), or from the walkers and from us. The full stop ends the snake's part of the poem.

Meaning & effect

The snake leaves through the grass it entered, which now works as a curtain: the kill is never shown, and the hunt continues without witnesses. The snake's last word in the poem is prey — its hunt is its whole story, and its final image is purpose carrying on out of sight.

Line 15
a deeper breath
Language & devices

Echo and Antithesis with line 8: lost breath becomes deeper breath, the Comparative implying “deeper than before”. In breath of day the Metaphor makes the day air to be breathed, and day answers the snake's dark and rhymes with prey. Perfectly regular Iambic tetrameter: the metre steadies as the breathing does.

Meaning & effect

Breathing is restored and deepened: the encounter has enlarged the walkers' sense of being alive, and their first act afterwards is again bodily. The snake goes into darkness, the grass and the kill, while the people breathe the daylight more fully — the death hidden in the grass rhymed with the life breathed in.

Line 16
each other … went on
Language & devices

Lines 15–16 make a Tricolon of verbs (took, looked, went on) answering line 13's three adjectives. The Reciprocal pronoun each other is the first point at which we divides into two people. The plainest diction in the poem — no adjective, image or figure — is a deliberate Anticlimax, and on closes the Envelope rhyme begun by gone.

Meaning & effect

A shared look, and the walk resumes. What passes in that look — relief, wonder, leftover fear — is left unsaid, and the poem trusts the silence. went on rhymes with the snake's gone, two lives going separate ways; against 'The Killer', the plainness carries the moral: nobody strikes, and simply going on is the act that matters.

THE WHOLE POEM

The Whole Poem

Stepping back: what the poem is doing, first line to last

'Hunting Snake' looks like the simplest poem in the set: two people on an autumn walk see a large black snake, stop, watch it pass, and walk on. It states no argument and no lesson, but it is built on a sharp asymmetry: the snake never notices the people, and the people cannot stop noticing the snake. Wright measures, almost entirely through the body, what it does to human beings to meet something magnificent that is not about them at all. Read against her own earlier 'The Killer' (1947) and the settler reflex of killing snakes on sight, the poem's real event is something that does not happen: nobody strikes.

The first stanza sets a trap of comfort. The opening sentence delays its subject through two lines of warmth, a late season's grace and a gentlest sky, so the reader settles as the walkers do; then the sentence and the stride stop together, half-through a pace. The reaction comes before its cause, the first sign of Wright's method. Only in line 4 does the snake arrive, in a line of its own, and from the first moment it goes by: it is passing them, not coming at them.

Stanza 2 is the poem's long look. Wright builds the snake out of close-up detail before naming it he — the lowered head, the tongue on a scent trail, the hunting verb quested, grass parting for it, sun glazing its scales to diamond. The description is both exact natural history and a deliberate act of valuing: the diction of quest and jewellery makes the animal noble and precious rather than sinister, and the serpent-as-tempter never gets a foothold. The grammar agrees. The snake has three full lines and all the active verbs; the humans get one clause, and its verb is a loss: we lost breath.

Stanza 3 turns from what can be seen to what cannot: the snake's route and prey (what small food), with the line-break before fled living holding a living animal for one beat as nothing but food. Then comes the poem's most honest phrase — the walkers scarcely thought about any of it. Because the questions come before the verb that dismisses them, the reader thinks what the walkers did not, and Wright admits that rapture depends on a suspension of moral attention. The stanza ends in a paradox: the walkers stand still, yet our eyes went with the snake.

Stanza 4 delivers the poem's single judgement as the snake disappears. Cold, dark and splendid lets the two adjectives a frightened settler would use stand, then adds a third that changes their weight: coldness and darkness become part of the splendour, not reasons to kill. The snake is already gone when it is described, and the grass that hid his prey takes the kill out of sight. Then the humans return as subjects — a deeper breath of day, a look at each other, the walk resumed — and the breath lost in line 8 comes back deeper while the joint we divides, for the first time, into two people. The rhyme seals the parting of ways: the last stanza turns back on itself, pairing the snake's gone with the humans' went on and its prey with their day.

The strongest objection is that the poem aestheticises a killer. It makes a predator gorgeous, looks away from the victim and buys its sublime moment with inattention, since the grass that conceals the kill hides it from us too. But Wright does not edit the death out; she puts it in. fled living insists on the prey's life, fierce intent names the snake's will to kill, and we scarcely thought records the walkers' looking-away as a fact, almost a confession. The poem does not pretend nature is gentle — its gentlest sky hangs over a hunt. What it refuses is the human urge to intervene, judge or destroy. The speaker of 'The Killer' kills the black snake, and Lawrence's man throws a log at his; Wright's walkers feel the same awe and do nothing, and in a country that killed snakes by reflex, doing nothing is the moral act.

So the poem's plainness is its point. A writer who spent her life campaigning to stop the destruction of wild places wrote a poem whose whole drama is looking properly and letting be. The snake goes on hunting, the people go on walking, and the poem holds the two lives side by side in a single rhyme without letting either one take the other.

FORM & STRUCTURE

Form & Structure

How the poem is built, and why it matters

Form & genre

A short narrative lyric of a single encounter, told in the past tense by a plural we: no argument and no stated lesson, only a sequence of observed events.

Stanzas

Four quatrains, each a stage of the encounter: the walk and the sighting (1–4); the snake seen close (5–8); its unseen hunt and the walkers' absorption (9–12); its disappearance and their recovery (13–16). Every stanza ends with a full stop.

Metre

Iambic tetrameter: four beats and, in fifteen lines, eight syllables (line 5 has nine unless flickering is clipped). Every line ends on a stress, and fifteen of the sixteen end-words are monosyllables.

Rhyme

ABAB CDCD EFEF, then GHHG: twelve lines of cross-rhyme give way to an envelope rhyme as the snake disappears. All full except food / stood, a slant (eye) rhyme.

A form that moves, then closes

The first three stanzas rhyme alternately — grace / pace, sky / by; trail / scale, grass / pass; food / stood, intent / went — and alternating rhyme reaches forward: each sound jumps a line to find its partner, so the ear is pulled on while the snake reels, quests and passes. The last stanza turns back on itself (gone … prey / day … on), and two things make this more than a change of pattern.

Each final pair joins the snake's world to the humans'. Lines 13–14 belong to the snake and 15–16 to the walkers, and the rhymes cross that boundary: the snake's gone with the humans' went on, its prey with their day. The death in the grass and the breath of daylight are bound together by sound, and so are the animal's departure and the people's continuing.

The ending is delayed. In stanzas 1–3 every rhyme returns after one line; in stanza 4 gone waits three lines for its partner, so the poem's final word completes a sound left hanging since the snake vanished, and the stanza clicks shut on the last syllable.

The one imperfect rhyme matters too. food and stood look alike but do not sound alike, and they pair the prey with the motionless watchers in the sentence that admits they scarcely thought about it: the one rhyme that fails to chime falls on the poem's one moral blind spot.

Metre and where it breaks

The tetrameter is very regular, which is why its departures register (/ stressed, x unstressed).

Line Fragment Pattern What the variation does
2 under the… / x x / trochaic first foot: the line eases in rather than striding
3 froze half-through / (/) / a run of heavy syllables after the caesura slows the line as the walkers halt
4 great black snake / / / three stresses in a row: the snake arrives with weight, then reeling releases it
5 Head down, tongue flick- / / / / x x x / the one nine-syllable line: four stresses piled up, then a light rush, like the tongue's flicker
8 we lost breath metre x / x /, speech x / / metre and speech clash on two heavy syllables where breath stops
11 still as we stood / x x / trochaic substitution after the semicolon: the beat lands on stillness
13 Cold, dark / / spondaic opening for the poem's one judgement
15 (whole line) x / x / x / x / perfectly regular: the metre steadies as the breathing does

The most regular lines (6, 15) are the snake's easy movement and the humans' recovered breath. Wright saves metrical disturbance for the moments of greatest intensity: the arrival, the close look, the halt, the verdict.

Sentence shapes

Six sentences tell the story. The first (lines 1–3) is periodic — two lines of setting before we, then a verb of moving and a verb of stopping — and its full stop, the only mid-stanza stop in stanzas 1–3, falls exactly where the walkers stop. Line 4 gives the snake a sentence to itself. Lines 5–8 are cumulative, body details, then he, then sun on his scales, and the humans get only the last clause, a loss of breath. Lines 9–12 are inverted: two indirect questions placed before the verb that dismisses them. Lines 13–14 put three adjectives before the pronoun, defining the snake as it vanishes; lines 15–16 give the humans three verbs in a row, active subjects again. The final stanza divides cleanly, two lines of snake and two of humans: the structural form of the poem's parting of ways.

The plural we and the frozen stride

There is no I anywhere. The walkers are never named, described or told apart, and they do everything together: walk, freeze, lose breath, stand, watch, breathe. The snake is he nine times in nine lines (6–14), with a head, a tongue, curves, scales, a track, an intent and a prey. The animal is the poem's only individual; the humans are a joint reaction, until each other splits the we into two people who can look at one another.

From froze to stood the humans perform no voluntary act, and between walked (3) and went on (16) they essentially stop being agents. Their stillness frames the snake's movement, as the full-stopped quatrains frame lines that run on: continuous motion in four still frames. The two key line-breaks act this out — small food / fled living holds the prey as food for one beat, then restores its life; gone / into lets the snake vanish at the line-end before the next line says where.

The turn and the ending

The volta comes at line 15. Its first word, We, takes the sentence back from the snake, and the rhyme turns at the same moment: day answers prey where the earlier stanzas would have answered gone. The ending is anti-climactic on purpose. After splendid, diamond and fierce intent, the last line is the plainest in the poem — seven words, six of them monosyllables, no adjective and no image — as if the beauty belonged to the encounter rather than to the world. Yet went on supplies the rhyme that closes the whole form: the plainest words do the final structural work.

SOUND

Sound

What the poem does to the ear

Sound palette

Soft at the opening (sibilants, liquids, long open vowels), hard with plosives the moment the snake appears, heaviest in hard consonants in the final stanza — before the last line goes plain.

Rhyme sounds

All masculine and nearly all full. The long “ay” of the first rhyme (grace / pace) returns in stanza 2 (trail / scale) and again in the last stanza (prey / day).

The opening hush. Lines 1–2 are built on s-sounds and open vowels — Sun-warmed, season's grace, gentlest sky — with hardly a hard stop: the acoustic version of gentlest, relaxing the reader so the next sounds can startle.

The snake arrives in plosives. great black snake packs hard g, b and k into three stressed syllables just after the walkers froze, then releases into the liquid r and l of reeling: first the shock of the thing, then its motion.

The flicker and the sheen. In Head down, tongue flickering quick d, t and ck taps between short vowels move like a tongue sampling scent. quested and the parting grass are thick with st, rt and ss, a dry, brushing texture; then sun glazed his curves goes smooth — the buzz of glazed, long vowels, the liquid l of scale — and the sound itself seems to shine.

Breath, flight and stillness. In lost breath the stopped st runs into plosive b, so the reader's mouth checks for a moment. The fricative f of fled living and fierce intent is the breathy sound of escape, linking the prey's flight to the hunter's will. still as we stood packs two st clusters into four words that cannot be said quickly, while our eyes went glides on w, h and vowels: the gaze moves smoothly while the body stays put.

The verdict and the plain close. Cold, dark sets two hard, stressed monosyllables either side of a comma, each landing like a judgement entered, before splendid opens out through l and n. The last line has almost no patterning, the sound of the ordinary world resuming; its one acoustic event is on, answering gone three lines back, so the poem shuts on a sound the ear had almost stopped waiting for.

MOTIFS & SYMBOLS

Motifs & Symbols

Images that recur, and what they accumulate

Motifs & symbols

1. Sun, shine and dark

The poem's first word, Sun-warmed, gives the warmth to the walkers; in line 7 the same sun moves to the snake (sun glazed his curves) and makes it glitter like diamond. Light passes from the people to the animal, and the snake becomes the bright thing in the scene. At the end light and darkness meet in one creature, dark and splendid, where splendid at root means shining, and when it leaves, the humans are left with plain day. Darkness and brilliance, the motif argues, are not opposites in nature, whatever the moral tradition says.

2. Breath

Breath measures the encounter: lost at the poem's centre (we lost breath, line 8), taken back deeper near the end (line 15). Between the two the walkers barely live as agents — they cannot think or move, only watch — so awe is made physiological, the idiom taken literally. The motif also gives the ending its claim: the encounter changes not the world but how fully the walkers inhabit it, in a breath of day the snake has made deeper.

3. Grass

The grass is the snake's element and the poem's curtain. In stanza 2 it is parting, opening ahead of the snake as if for royalty; in stanza 4 it hid his prey, closing over the hunt. Same noun, opposite offices, eight lines apart: the grass reveals the snake to the walkers and then conceals what it is doing. It marks the boundary of human knowledge — we see what shows above it, and the business below (the small food, the fierce intent) stays out of sight.

4. Going and staying still

went occurs four times, and who owns it tells the story. The snake went reeling by (line 4); in line 12 it comes twice, the eyes borrowing it (our eyes went) only to follow him; the humans get it for themselves only in the last line, went on, once the snake has finished using it. Against this stand the walkers' stillness words, froze, still and stood. Motion is the snake's property, and the humans can move again only after the moving thing has gone.

THEMES

Themes

The ideas the poem is arguing about

01

Awe as a bodily event

Awe is rendered as a sequence of physical events, never named: the stride halts (froze half-through a pace), breath stops (we lost breath), thought switches off (we scarcely thought), and breathing comes back deeper. Wright never uses the words fear, wonder or awe.

02

A world not about us

The snake never notices the walkers — Head down, driven by its own fierce intent — and what stops them is not menace but irrelevance. Being ignored by the sublime is stranger than being threatened by it.

03

The hunt, and what goes unthought

Beneath the beauty is a killing: the prey is raised (small food, fled living), left unthought, then hidden as the grass hid his prey. Wright neither condemns the snake nor sentimentalises the prey; she records the suspension of moral attention instead of hiding it.

04

Restraint: the blow not struck

Against 'The Killer' (1947) and the settler habit of killing snakes on sight, the poem's real event is a non-event: the walkers freeze, watch and let the animal go. The restraint carries Wright's conservationist ethic — looking properly is the first step towards not destroying — and the plain went on is the moral act.

05

The inherited serpent, refused

Wright lets two inherited adjectives stand (Cold, dark), then adds splendid, while diamond scale makes a sinister body precious and quested makes a predator a knight. There is no simile anywhere: the animal is described on its own terms, and that refusal to domesticate it is itself an argument about how to see.

DIFFICULT MOMENTS

Difficult Moments

Where the poem is genuinely undecidable — and what to do about it

Cruxes

1. Who is hunting?

The difficulty. The title is grammatically double: Hunting can describe the snake (a snake that hunts) or name an activity of which the snake is the object (the hunting of snakes). The poem never settles which, and a third candidate emerges as it goes on: the watchers themselves.

Competing readings. The snake hunts — the plain sense, supported everywhere: the tongue flickering on the trail, the verb quested, the fierce intent, the small food that flees, the prey in the grass. Snakes are hunted — what settler Australians did by reflex and what Wright's own speaker does in 'The Killer', so the title points to the violence the poem withholds. The humans hunt with their eyes — the walkers track the snake as it tracks its prey (our eyes went with him): a chain of attention running prey, hunter, watchers.

What a strong answer does. It keeps the first sense primary, since that is what happens, then shows how the poem uses the other two. The second gives the restraint its meaning (no one hunts the snake); the third makes human looking a kind of pursuit, which the poem ends by turning away from as the walkers look at each other instead.

2. we scarcely thought: honesty or complicity?

The difficulty. Stanza 3 raises the prey's fate in two careful clauses, then says the walkers hardly considered it, and in stanza 4 the grass hid his prey. Is the poem admitting a moral blind spot, or committing one?

Competing readings. Complicity: the sublime is bought by looking away; the grandest description (Cold, dark and splendid) sits beside the hidden kill, and the grass hides the death from the reader too. Honesty: Wright puts the prey in — fled living insists on its life, fierce intent names the will to kill — and scarcely is an exact admission, recording the suspension of moral attention as part of what awe is. Ecological realism: predation is how the snake lives, not a moral failure to be noticed or judged, and admiring the hunter is not approving cruelty.

What a strong answer does. It notices the paralipsis — the poem raises exactly what it says the walkers did not think about — and argues that the poem is more aware than its people: the reader is made to think what the walkers scarcely thought. It grants the complicity reading its force while showing that Wright exposes the looking-away instead of performing it.

3. Fear or wonder?

The difficulty. The poem never names an emotion. The walkers freeze, lose breath, stop thinking and later breathe deeper, and every one of these can signal terror or rapture.

Competing readings. Fear: froze suggests the freeze response to a predator; Australian black snakes are venomous; Cold and dark carry menace; the deeper breath reads as relief at a danger passed. Wonder: the diction is admiring — grace, quested, glazed, diamond, splendid — the snake goes by without threatening them, and their eyes go with it willingly. Both, which is the sublime: Burke's “delightful horror”, fear felt at a safe distance turning into a kind of delight, with the snake's indifference providing the safety.

What a strong answer does. It shows that the refusal to name the emotion is deliberate: physical reactions come before categories, so the reader feels the mixture instead of being told about it. It locates the fear (the freeze, Cold, dark) and the wonder (diamond, splendid) in particular words, and notices that the one evaluative line places splendid last.

CLOSE ANALYSIS

Close Analysis

The moments that repay pressure, worked through

Quotation analysis

1. froze half-through a pace (line 3)

Techniques. Metaphor, kinaesthetic imagery, caesura, mid-stanza full stop.

The walkers are arrested mid-stride, one foot off the ground, the comma splitting the line between moving and stopping. The verb turns temperature into stillness: in a poem that begins Sun-warmed, warm-blooded people go cold and motionless, while the cold-blooded snake will move fluidly. The cause is not named until the next line, so the body reacts before the mind, or the reader, knows why.

Intention and effect. Awe and fear arrive as physical facts, faster than thought, and the reader's own momentum through the long first sentence halts at the same point.

2. The great black snake (line 4)

Techniques. Spondee, plosives, definite article, present participle.

Size, colour, kind: the animal is named in the plainest, heaviest words, g, b and k packed into three beats, then let loose in the liquid reeling — swaying, whirling, unwinding like a line from a reel. The treats it as a known presence of the country, not a stray “a snake”.

Intention and effect. The sound performs the shock of the sighting and then the fluency of the creature, and from the first moment the snake is passing, not attacking.

3. tongue flickering on the trail (line 5)

Techniques. Absolute phrase, kinaesthetic imagery, hunting vocabulary, metrical irregularity.

Natural history set to rhythm: snakes hunt by scent, collecting traces on the forked tongue, and the line packs four stresses at its start before a run of light syllables, moving like the tongue's quick touches. The lowered head keeps the snake's attention on the ground, not on the people.

Intention and effect. Exactness is a form of respect: Wright looks at the animal as it really is, absorbed in its own work, and the people are already irrelevant to it.

4. sun glazed … diamond scale (line 7)

Techniques. Metaphor, visual imagery, the semantic field of jewellery and craft, repeated sun.

Sunlight becomes glaze, the glassy coat fired onto pottery, and the scales become diamond: brilliant, precious, the hardest stone — and accurate, since snake scales are diamond-shaped. The sun that warmed the walkers in line 1 now gilds the snake.

Intention and effect. Wright re-codes the serpent: the vocabulary of value and art leaves no room for the Genesis tempter, and diamond keeps hardness, and so danger, inside the beauty.

5. what small food / fled living (lines 9–10)

Techniques. Enjambment, fronted noun clause (inversion), alliteration with fierce.

The line-break holds the prey at the line-end as nothing but food, the predator's view of it; the next line begins fled living and restores its life and fear. The clause is one of two indirect questions placed before the verb that dismisses them.

Intention and effect. For one beat the reader shares the snake's view and then the prey's: the poem quietly brings in the death the walkers do not think about.

6. Cold, dark and splendid (line 13)

Techniques. Tricolon with climax, spondaic opening, inversion (adjectives before the pronoun), near-oxymoron.

Cold (cold-blooded, unfeeling) and dark (black, mysterious, menacing) are the inherited settler adjectives, and Wright lets them stand. splendid, whose Latin root means shining, comes last and changes their weight, and dark and splendid is exact for a glossy black body. The description arrives as the snake is already gone.

Intention and effect. The poem's one judgement is a verdict of splendour: coldness and darkness become part of the snake's magnificence, not grounds for killing it.

7. a deeper breath of day … went on (lines 15–16)

Techniques. Echo and antithesis with lost breath (line 8), metaphor, regular metre, reciprocal pronoun, tricolon of verbs, plain diction, closing envelope rhyme.

The breath taken away at the poem's centre returns deeper, the day itself breathed in, its light set against the snake's dark and rhymed with its prey. Then the joint we splits for the first time into two people who look at each other, and the last verb is simply continuing: no adjective, no image, no lesson, only on completing the rhyme left open by the snake's gone.

Intention and effect. The walkers are left not changed in belief but living more fully, and the poem trusts the silence of their look: unlike the speaker of 'The Killer', no one strikes, and two lives go their separate ways.

CRITICAL LENSES

Critical Lenses

What each way of reading makes visible, and what it flattens

Critical lenses

1. Ecocritical

What it makes visible. The poem models the attention ecocriticism values. It looks exactly at a living animal (tongue on the scent trail, head down, scales in the sun), grants it its own purposes (fierce intent) and its own pronoun (he), and lets it go. Nature is not scenery, symbol or threat but a life going on independently of us, and the poem's central act, doing nothing, is the ethic Wright argued for in her public life: see properly, then leave alone. Even predation is accepted as part of the snake's splendour, not edited into a gentler nature.

What it flattens. It can make the poem sound like a manifesto, and it is not one: there is no message about conservation, and the walkers do not reflect, resolve or campaign. It also struggles with the aestheticising language (diamond, glazed), which treats the animal as a precious object to be admired, close to the human-centred gaze the lens criticises.

2. Formalist

What it makes visible. The meaning sits in the mechanics: the rhyme closes into an envelope exactly as the snake disappears, each final pair joining a snake-word to a human-word; one individual he stands against a plural we; the last line drops every adjective the poem has been spending. None of it is stated, and all of it is meaning.

What it flattens. Context — the answer to 'The Killer' and the settler habit of killing snakes — which changes what the restraint means.

3. Psychoanalytic

What it makes visible. Andrew Taylor read Wright's earlier 'The Killer' as guilt at failing to recognise the enemy within and killing the creature outside instead. Through that lens 'Hunting Snake' is the same confrontation resolved differently: the Cold, dark thing is encountered, acknowledged as splendid and allowed to live, a reconciliation with what had been projected outward and destroyed. The suspension of thought (we scarcely thought) fits a state in which the controlling ego gives way to pure perception.

What it flattens. It turns a real animal into a figure of the psyche, the very translation the poem resists with its exact natural history, and it depends heavily on reading the two poems as a pair.

4. Reader-response

What it makes visible. The poem works on the reader's body as well as the walkers'. The long first sentence lulls, the halt at pace stops the reader too, and the clustered sounds of still as we stood are hard to say quickly. Because emotions are never named, the reader must supply them, and the final look between the walkers is left blank, to be filled in.

What it flattens. It can make the poem's indeterminacy sound total, but Wright does steer: the one evaluative line ends on splendid, and grace, quested and diamond tilt the reader firmly towards admiration.

OTHER READINGS

Other Readings

Contested interpretations, and where each is weak

Other readings

1. A precise account of the sublime

The poem records an encounter with something beautiful and dangerous that overwhelms ordinary perception and leaves the observers more alive. Its distinction is accuracy: the sublime rendered as a sequence of bodily events, not an emotion described.

Evidence. The frozen stride, lost breath, we scarcely thought, eyes that follow involuntarily, and finally a deeper breath of day; the snake's indifference supplies the safe distance.

Weakness. The classic sublime is vast — mountains, storms, the sea — and this is a snake in the grass. The poem's after-effect is not exaltation but a quiet return to ordinary life, which the label can overstate.

2. An answer to 'The Killer'

Wright had already written this meeting: in 'The Killer' (1947) a speaker surprised by a black snake at a creek kills it. 'Hunting Snake' revisits the scene and reverses the outcome, a self-correction in which stillness is the achievement.

Evidence. The same animal and the same sunlit setting, an ambiguous title in both (who is the killer, who is hunting), and a final stanza whose plainness makes not striking the event.

Weakness. Wright is not recorded as linking the two poems, which are probably about seventeen years apart. The pairing is the critic's construction, and the later poem stands complete without it.

3. A parable of settler presence

Two people pass through country where a creature is entirely at home, sovereign and indifferent to them, and for once they take nothing. The Genesis serpent and the reflex to kill snakes came with the colonists; Wright refuses that imported reading in the plainest way, by calling the animal splendid.

Evidence. The snake's ease (the parting grass), the humans' stillness and plural anonymity, went on as what visitors do, and Wright's lifelong reckoning with her pastoral family's inheritance of Aboriginal land.

Weakness. The poem contains no reference to history, land ownership or Aboriginal people. The reading is imported from biography, and it risks turning a real snake into a symbol.

4. Just a snake

The plainest reading: there is no symbol at all. The poem is a snake, hunting, in autumn, seen exactly, and its refusal to make the animal mean something is the point.

Evidence. There is no simile, so the snake is never likened to anything; the details are exact natural history (the tongue, the scent trail, basking-season warmth); no moral is drawn, and the ending is plain.

Weakness. Language is never neutral. quested, diamond and splendid are evaluative choices, and the title's double grammar invites more than description.

REVISION NOTES

Revision Notes

The working notes, quotation by quotation

Title

“Hunting Snake”

Analysis
  • ambiguous: snake that hunts (participle) / the hunting of snakes (gerund)
  • snake = hunter, not hunted
  • humans' eyes also track him → chain of attention
Effect, style & response
  • names the act the poem refuses → nobody kills the snake
  • cf. Wright's 'The Killer' (1947): speaker kills a black snake at a creek → opposite outcome

Context

Analysis
  • Judith Wright (1915–2000), grazier's daughter, New England tableland NSW
  • Wildlife Preservation Society of Qld (founded 1962; president 1964–76)
  • Aboriginal land rights: Aboriginal Treaty Committee (1979)
  • poem c. 1964
Effect, style & response
  • settler reflex: kill snakes on sight; Genesis serpent = evil
  • many Aboriginal cultures: great serpent as creator being
  • sublime (Burke 1757): danger at a safe distance → “delightful horror”
1–2

late season's grace

Analysis
  • warm, gentle, peaceful → calm before the encounter
  • grace = gift / elegance / reprieve before winter
  • gentlest sky superlative → nature benign
  • soft sibilance; subject delayed to l.3 (periodic sentence)
Effect, style & response
  • more peaceful the start → sharper the shock
  • Sun-warmed: humans enjoy the sun; cold-blooded snake needs it
3

froze half-through a pace

Analysis
  • arrested mid-step; body reacts before mind
  • caesura: walking | freezing
  • reaction before cause → snake only named in l.4
Effect, style & response
  • warm-blooded humans froze vs cold-blooded snake moves freely
  • we throughout, never I → shared, simultaneous
4

great black snake

Analysis
  • three monosyllables: size, colour, kind → spondee, plosives = weight
  • reeling: swaying, unwinding like a line off a reel
  • passes by → not attacking; indifferent
5–6

tongue flickering · quested

Analysis
  • exact: tongue collects scent → hunting by smell
  • Head down → absorbed; ignores humans
  • l.5 = only 9-syllable line → metre “flickers”
  • quested → knightly quest; also hounds questing for scent
  • the parting grass → nature makes way; snake belongs here
7–8

diamond scale

Analysis
  • glazed, diamond → jewellery/craft vocab → precious, not sinister
  • reverses the Eden serpent
  • lost breath → breathlessness = sublime; body again
  • stanza: 3 lines snake, 1 clause humans
9–12

we scarcely thought

Analysis
  • small food / fled living → enjambment: prey = food, then alive
  • fierce intent → snake's will
  • scarcely thought → prey's death not thought about (paralipsis)
  • bodies still, but our eyes went with him
13

Cold, dark and splendid

Analysis
  • tricolon, climax: cold (ectotherm, unfeeling) · dark (black, mystery) · splendid (magnificent; Latin “shining”)
  • settler adjectives kept → splendid changes their weight
  • gone: already vanished; enjambment
14–16

a deeper breath of day

Analysis
  • grass hid his prey → kill offstage
  • lost breath (8) → deeper breath (15): restored + enlarged
  • each other → we splits into two people
  • plain last line, went on → ordinary life resumes
Effect, style & response
  • nobody strikes → restraint = the moral act

Structure

Analysis
  • 16 lines, 4 quatrains; iambic tetrameter (l.5 = 9 syllables)
  • ABAB CDCD EFEF → GHHG (envelope rhyme) as the snake vanishes
  • gone / on (snake leaves / humans go on); prey / day (death / life)
  • only slant rhyme: food / stood
  • no simile; no I; snake = he ×9 (ll.6–14)

Themes

Analysis
  • sublime: awe as bodily event (freeze → breath lost → thought stops → deeper breath)
  • nature's indifference: snake never notices them
  • predation unthought: prey hidden in the grass
  • restraint: the blow not struck (vs 'The Killer'; Lawrence's 'Snake')
  • inherited serpent symbol refused
CONNECTIONS

Connections

How this poem pairs with the rest of the set

Comparison hooks

1. The Cockroach — Kevin Halligan

Link. The set's other poem built on watching one creature, with the same word for a step: Halligan's cockroach starts to pace, Wright's walkers freeze half-through a pace. Shared technique. Plain past-tense narration of observed movement and an understated ending. Difference. Halligan's creature loses its purpose (uncertain where to go) and the watcher recognises himself in it; Wright's snake is nothing but purpose (fierce intent) — Halligan finds the human in the animal, Wright what is not human, and honours it.

2. Report to Wordsworth — Boey Kim Cheng

Link. Nature intact against nature destroyed: Boey's Nature has been laid waste; Wright's snake is magnificent and in no danger, even from the people who meet it. Shared technique. An implied we set against a natural power (Boey's we dump, Wright's watchers). Difference. In Boey insatiate man is the predator who moves in for the kill; in Wright the only kill is the snake's, and the humans conspicuously do not move in — Wright shows the alternative to appetite.

3. An Essay on Man — Alexander Pope

Link. What kind of creature a human being is: Pope's man hangs in doubt whether to count himself a god or beast, while Wright's walkers meet a creature with no such doubt, wholly itself. Shared technique. Both define the human against the rest of creation — Pope by abstract antithesis, Wright by the asymmetry of an active he and a passive we. Difference. Pope states the paradox in heroic couplets; Wright's quatrains state nothing, and human smallness is produced in the reader.

4. Follower — Seamus Heaney

Link. Admiring observation of something more skilled than the watcher: Heaney's father is An expert at the plough, and Wright's snake works its scent trail with the same competence. Shared technique. Precise technical detail as praise, and a plain, withholding final line. Difference. Heaney's son stumbles in his father's hob-nailed wake, wanting to become him, and the father will not go away; Wright's snake never acknowledges its followers and does go away, and the walkers only want to let it be.

5. Before the Sun — Charles Mungoshi

Link. Two sunlit encounters, each turning an ordinary moment into something like a rite: Mungoshi's boy shares his breakfast with the sun, Wright's walkers take a deeper breath of day. Shared technique. A short episode, observed sensuously, with no stated moral. Difference. Mungoshi's nature is companionable and responsive, Wright's splendid and indifferent: the set's range from nature as intimate to nature as wholly other.

Synthesis

All fifteen at once

The paper sets one poem at a time, but the best answers know what is distinctive about it — and that is easiest to see against the others. Threads that run through several poems first, then the whole set side by side: read along a row.

01

Power, and who pays for it

Each of these poems locates a beneficiary and a bill, and refuses to let them be the same person. The interesting move is always the accounting: who is enriched, who is spent, and whether the poem says so outright.

Song: Love Armedthe lover is spent; the beloved goes free The Chimney-Sweeperthe parents rise to church on the child's labour A Different Historythe conqueror's tongue, paid for in the soul A Married Statethe wife pays in tears; the husband is merely hard to please Carpet-weavers, Moroccochildren knot the carpet that merchant and mosque will use Lamentthe war's bill is presented in turtles and boys
02

Inheritance, not choice

The speakers do not decide who they are. Place, language, family and history have already decided, and the poem is the discovery of that — sometimes as a gift, sometimes as a sentence, often as both.

Where I Come FromPeople are made of places A Different Historythe grandchildren inherit the language, and love it Followerthe son inherits the father — as a figure he cannot shake off Carpet-weavers, Moroccochildren born into a pattern they did not design Storytellerthe stories pass into the sleeping children's heads The Chimney-Sweeperthe child is dressed in the clothes of death
03

Institutions and their alibis

Church, state, empire, marriage and war all arrive with an explanation ready. The poems are interested in the gap between the explanation and the damage — and in how normal the damage looks.

The Chimney-SweeperGod and his priest and king A Different Historycolonial education as cultural cropping A Married Statemarriage itself — even The best of husbands fail Lamentthe gunsmith, the armourer, and the company Song: Love Armedthe lovers set him up a Deity by mutual agreement Carpet-weavers, Moroccocommerce and faith share the same carpet
04

Nature: casualty, mirror or mystery

Nature is never scenery here. It is a casualty, a witness, the thing that formed the speaker, a guest at breakfast, or something wholly indifferent to us — and the poems measure what it costs, or gives, to be near it.

Report to Wordsworththe sea-gods entombed in the waste / we dump Lamentthe scalded ocean and the blazing well Where I Come Fromthe mind keeps the weather of its landscape Hunting Snakean animal that never notices the people it awes Before the Suna boy who shares his breakfast with the sun A Different Historythe tree the paper came from must not be offended
05

Form turned against itself

Several poems adopt a form with an established promise — the love sonnet, the song, the nursery rhyme, the wedding-poem's couplets — then make the form say something it was never built to say.

The Cockroacha sonnet that withholds its own resolving couplet Report to Wordsworththe sonnet as a casualty report The Chimney-Sweepera nursery-rhyme lilt that delivers an indictment Song: Love Armeda stage song whose dance-metre delivers a verdict A Married Statethe heroic couplet, voice of public reason, turned against marriage Sonnet 18a love sonnet that ends by praising itself
06

Watching, and being implicated

Many of these poems begin with a speaker at a safe distance and end with the distance gone. Track the pronouns and you can date the collapse almost to the word.

The CockroachI watched becomes I recognised myself Report to Wordsworththe waste / we dump — the poet is inside the we Song: Love ArmedThus thou and I, the God have armed Hunting Snaketwo watchers frozen mid-step, then let go Followerthe boy who watched his father is now the one being followed The Chimney-Sweeperthe observer's question hands the poem to the child
07

Time, and what outlasts it

Summer fades, mornings end, fathers age, carpets are finished and nights run out. Each poem pits something against time — verse, story, ritual, memory, pattern — and each is honest about what it costs.

Sonnet 18verse against death: So long as men can breathe Carpet-weavers, Moroccothe future knotted into the past as the weaving is done Storytellerstories that outlive the night that told them Followera past that will not go away Before the Sunone ordinary morning made into a rite An Essay on Manman Born but to die, and reasoning but to err
08

Work, craft and skill

A surprising number of these poems are about work done with the hands — and about how a poem can honour, envy, imitate or indict it.

Followerploughing as mastery: An expert Storytellerstory-telling counted as work, alongside stitching and darning Carpet-weavers, Moroccosmall fingers at the loom Before the Sunthe axe, the fire, the roasting maize The Chimney-Sweepera trade advertised by a child's street-cry Where I Come Fromthe city's smell of work
09

What a human being is

Underneath their subjects, several poems ask the oldest question: what kind of creature are we? Their answers range from Pope's balanced paradox to a man finding himself in an insect.

An Essay on ManThe glory, jest, and riddle of the world! The Cockroacha man who recognises himself in vermin Hunting Snakehumans reduced to held breath before an animal Report to Wordsworthinsatiate man moves in for the kill Song: Love Armedlovers who build the god that rules them
10

Women's lives, women's voices

Three centuries apart, these poems are written from inside the lives women were expected to lead — desire, marriage, housework, story — and they argue with the roles as they describe them.

A Married Statethe virgin state as a crown Song: Love Armeda woman's desire Enough to undo the Amorous World Storytellera woman judged sloven or spotless, honoured for her stories Carpet-weavers, Moroccogirls at the loom whose work will travel without them
11

Childhood

Children appear as workers, listeners, followers and celebrants. What each poem lets a child see — and what it sees that the child cannot — is where the meaning lies.

The Chimney-Sweepera child sold into soot, still singing Before the Suna fourteen-year-old's private morning ritual Followera small boy stumbling in his father's wake Carpet-weavers, Moroccochildren at work in the school of days Storytellerchildren listening, then dreaming the stories

Reference

Techniques, by family

The vocabulary the analysis above depends on. Naming a device earns nothing on its own — the marks are in what you say it does.

Basic 6

Metaphor

Directly compares two different things without using like or as.

  • Life is a roller coaster
  • He is a shining star
  • Her heart is gold
  • Her heart of gold was broken

metaphorical, metaphorically

Extended metaphor

A metaphor that extends

  • The Tyger by William Blake is, at its core, an extended metaphor of the industrial revolution.

Simile

Indirectly compares two different things using like or as

  • He ran like the wind
  • His eyes sparkled like stars

Hyperbole

Metaphor to do with exaggeration

  • I will love you for a million years.
  • His abs of steel could not be penetrated.

hyperbolic, hyperbolically

Onomatopoeia

A word that sounds like something

  • Bang
  • Boom
  • Buzz
  • Sizzle

Symbolism

The use of words or images to symbolise specific ideas or feelings

  • He handed her a red rose and she knew at the moment how he felt.
  • The mirror broke and he knew that things would not be good from there on.
  • Jeff saw a crow next to a black cat on a Friday afternoon.

symbolic, symbolise

Personification 5

Personification

Metaphorically giving human qualities to something nonhuman

  • The sun smiled at us
  • The wind whispered secrets
  • Time waits for no one
  • The business ran and of breath and died

personify

Anthropomorphism

Literally attributing human characteristics, emotions and behaviours to non-human things (think Toy Story, Alice in Wonderland, Zootopia, Tom & Jerry)

  • My cat stood up suddenly to lecture me about taxes

anthropomorphic

Pathetic fallacy

Attributing human emotions to nature & weather (specific form of personification)

  • The rain wept
  • The clouds seemed sullen
  • The rocks seemed indifferent 9

Zoomorphism

Personification but for animals - attributes animal characteristics to non-animals

  • Will barked at us after he was stripped naked.
  • She meowed like a furry

Chremamorphism

Objectifying humans or animals

  • Be a rock
  • Iron heart
  • Man of steel
  • He wore a rock-like expression.

Contrast 5

Juxtaposition

A general contrast arising from two words/phrases that are near each other

  • For some people, it's the age of light, while for others, it's the age of darkness.

juxtapose

Oxymoron

A pair of contrasting words right next to each other

  • Deafening silence
  • Organised chaos
  • Boiling ice

oxymoronic

Antithesis

A contrast of ideas - think yin & yang

  • As the antithesis to the introverted and gloomy Batman, the Joker seems friendly and extroverted but is actually evil.
  • Good vs evil
  • Light vs darkness
  • naivety vs scepticism

antithetical

Foil

A contrast of characters

  • Batman vs Joker (also an antithesis)

Mostly interior to an antithesis, given that the contrast between characters is only significant if it represents some contrast in idea

Paradox

Contrasting, contradictory statements (two things that can’t be true simultaneously)

  • All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others

paradoxical

Repetition 14

Repetition

The repetition of a word or phrase

  • In order to improve my writing, I must practice, practice, practice.

repeated

Parallelism

Any case where the construction/structure of a sentence is repeated, even if they are far apart

  • I have a dream speech opens many verses with the titular I have a dream

Anaphora

Repetition of a sentence structure at the start of a sentence or clause

  • Be bold. Be brief. Be gone.
  • We will fight for our rights. We will fight for our freedom. We will fight for our justice.

Epiphora

Anaphora but at the end of a sentence or clause

  • See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil

Rhyme

Repetition of a sound at the end of each word

  • His palms are sweaty, knees weak, arms are heavy. There’s vomit on his sweater already, mom’s spaghetti.

rhyming

Alliteration

Repetition of a letter at the start of each word

  • Tony the Tiger took the train to town.
  • Madam memory is a great and subtle dissembler.

alliterative

Sibilance

The repetition of ‘s’ sounds (pissing -th, sh and z sounds also count)

  • That slithery, suspicious sibling of his.

sibilant

Assonance

The repetition of vowel sounds → euphonic effect

  • It was raining in Spain.
  • The round flower

Consonance

The repetition of consonant sounds → dissonant/cacophonic effect

  • He struck a streak of bad luck.

Diacope

A repetition that is separated by a few words

  • Every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
  • To be or not to be
  • The wheels on the bus goes round and round
  • A penny saved is a penny earned

Polysyndeton

The repetition of conjunctions

  • And I came and I saw and I conquered
  • → confusion / circularity

Asyndeton

The omission of conjunctions → repeated commas/punctuation

  • I came, I saw, I conquered
  • → assertiveness / briskness / out of breath

Motif

A repeated or recurring symbol

  • Bright light is used multiple times in Romeo & Juliet

Theme

A repeated idea

Diction 12

Diction

Word choice

Assign adjective: childlike, formal/informal, lighthearted/solemn, meaningless, passive-aggressive, intimate, distant

Ethos

Appeal to authority

  • Do it because I’m your dad

Pathos

Appeal to emotion

  • Do it because I just want the best for you

Logos

Appeal to logic

  • Do it because, if you don’t, you may regret it later on in life

Modality

Imperative

Command

  • Die D

Monosyllable

One syllable word(s)

  • Go to die
  • Monosyllabic diction

monosyllabic

Dialogue

An exchange of words by one or more characters

Assign adjective: childlike, formal/informal, lighthearted/solemn, meaningless, passive-aggressive, intimate, distant

Dialect

A local/regional expression of language

  • Howdy! G’day sur.
  • You got dat phat bunda still

Assign adjective: local/native, lower/middle/upper class, foreign

Colloquialism

Informal, everyday language/slang

  • Wanna, y’all, gonna, swag, rizz

Ambiguity/omission

The intentional lack of detail to create a greyish atmosphere or a sense of mystery, or some relation to fragmented memory

  • It was on this poignant day - afternoon, to be precise, since I’ve already had lunch - that I met the detective, looked into his eyes, felt his blistered hands.
  • They departed, the gods, on the day of the strange tide.

ambiguous ***intentionally omitted

Aphorism

A pithy statement that contains a general truth

  • A chain is only as strong as its weakest link
  • A penny saved is a penny earned

Novel 14

Climax

The culmination (most intense or exciting part) in a story.

  • In Shakespeare's play Romeo and Juliet, Romeo finds out that Juliet is dead and makes the decision to kill himself in her tomb. Juliet then sees her lover dead and makes the decision to kill herself as well.

climactic, culminate, reaches fever-pitch, reaches a boiling point

Anticlimax

A disappointing end to an exciting or impressive series of events.

  • At the end of the novel, when the two characters are on top of a ferris wheel gazing over their hometown, they don't kiss and, instead, go home and never confess their love for each other.

anticlimactic

Bathos

Anticlimactic effect created by a build up and then collapse in expectations (serious to ridiculous)

  • The answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything is… 42!

bathetic

Narrative stance

First person: personal + opinionated → we feel closer to the narrator

  • I died
  • Second person: direct + commanding → we feel closer to ourselves
  • You died
  • Third person (limited): limited to one character’s perspective - closer to a character

Multiple perspectives

When the perspective of the narrator shifts from one character to another

  • For example, when chapter 1 of book X starts with narrator Bob, but switches to narrator Jess in chapter 5
  • Atonement, Half of a Yellow Sun

Unreliable narrator

A narrator who may be biassed or are unreliable in telling the story objectively

  • A good example of an unreliable narrator is when the narrator is a child
  • Briony in Atonement

Author surrogate

When the characters are subtly/implicitly reflecting the author or the author’s views

  • Charles Dickens wrote only about orphans because he himself was neglected and abused by his parents
  • David Copperfield, whose initials D.C. are just Charles Dickens’ initials C.D. reversed, bears a strong resemblance in both background and personality to his author.

Authorial intrusion

When the author explicitly intrudes into a story by revealing his/her existence or by showcasing his/her own feelings/thoughts/opinions

  • Warning: the dialogue above is for fictional purposes only
  • Certain kinds of narration/commentary may be considered a form of authorial intrusion too

Red Herring

Something to distract the reader/audience from what is really important in the plot

  • The reader was too engrossed in the melodramatic traits of X to realise that Y had been plotting the murder behind the scenes

Characterisation

A character’s experience and development can be an implicit technique to reveal effects/ideas to the audience

  • While all love outside of loving the Big Brother party is disapproved of in Oceania, Winston is depicted uniquely as a hopeful romantic, bravely professing to Julia that the real betrayal would be if they could make me stop loving you. This is what renders the outcome of the torture scene in room 101 all the more heartbreaking, as we, alongside Julia who was watching from a distance, discover that the party has effortlessly succeeded in reintegrating Winston: Tear her face off, strip her to the bones. Not me! Julia! Not me!. Here, not only has Winston betrayed Julia, but he has betrayed himself, and every quality that had made him virtuous - his love for Julia has been demolished and replaced by his refound love for the Party, showing how individual strength pales in the face of collective villainy.

Epiphany

When a character suddenly realises something important

  • In the middle of a typical argument with his wife, a man realises he has been the one causing every single argument, and that in order to keep his marriage, he must stop being such an aggressive person.

Allegory

A story that appears lighthearted, but actually reveals a deep insight into human understanding (esp morality or politics)

  • The Nun and the Priest’s tale is an allegory that depicts the lives of several animals who manifest human behaviour
  • Animal Farm
  • Tom & Jerry → anthropomorphism (furries)

allegorical

Anachronism

Something that feels out of time

  • A novel is set in the 21st century, and suddenly someone walks into a ancient temple
  • A novel is set in the 18th century, and suddenly someone walks into a theme park

Foreshadowing/foreboding

Indicating the soon occurrence of a significant event (something bad in the case of forebode)

  • If a character mentions offhandedly that bad things always happen to them in autumn, then the observant reader will be alert when the leaves in the story begin to fall.

foreshadow/forebode

Sensing 3

Tone / mood / atmosphere

Imagery

The use of visually descriptive and colourful language (usually as a means to an end - the middleman effect)

  • Visual: sight
  • Auditory: hearing
  • Gustatory: taste
  • The sky, at sunset, looked like a carnivorous flower

Semantic field

A group of related diction to create a collective imagery

  • I miss you blindingly like the sun, musically like a song with wings, frankly like the wind, and a sceptre lost at sea. Let us fly and fall together, my darling and rain.
  • ____, which culminates in an alliterative semantic field concerning darkness: gloom, grey, ghastly, establishing ____.
  • ____, where a semantic field of X imagery is established, moving from gloom to grey to ghastly, culminating in gas!, which ____

Sound 9

Rhyme

Couplet

  • Full rhyme:
  • Masculine: harsh stressed rhyme - rat + cat
  • Feminine: soft unstressed rhyme - room + gloom
  • Half (slant) rhyme: forge + orange

Rhythm

Fast vs slow

  • Intense vs lighthearted
  • Light vs heavy
  • Consistent vs inconsistent
  • Examples:

Meters

Iambic pentameter (mostly used by Shakespeare)

  • A line of verse with five metrical feet (10 syllables, 5 stressed, 5 unstressed)
  • Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
  • Two households, both alike in dignity.
  • Now is the winter of our discontent

Euphony

Use of pleasant harmonious sounds (usually soft vowel sounds)

  • A mellow, soothing lullaby
  • row row row the boat

euphonic

Cacophony/dissonance

The use of words with loud, harsh, unpleasant sounds (usually plosive consonant sounds b, d, g, k, p, s, t)

  • Dishes crashing on the floor, horns blaring, f***

Cacophonic + dissonant

Caesura family

Caesura: a pause mid-sentence either using a dash (—) or ellipsis (…)

  • That makes the two of us - don’t tell anyone!
  • Hmm… maybe I should eat
  • → hesitation
  • Aposiopesis: when a writer stops speaking suddenly without finishing a sentence

Ellison

Where the writer omits a letter or letters in part of a word

Arise, awake, or be forever fall’n

Often indicates dialect

Enjambment

Continuation of a sentence from one line to the next in a poem

  • I went out and / lost my way, where the "/" is a line break.
  • → more liquid flow to the poem

The Allusion Family 20

Allusion

Making an indirect reference to something outside the text.

  • Biblical: she was the sacrificial lamb → Abraham & Isaac
  • Historical: the war to end all wars → WWI

allude, allusive

Biblical allusion

She was the sacrificial lamb → Abraham & Isaac

Historical allusion

the war to end all wars → WWI

Psychological allusion

all her problems can be traced back to when her mum beat her with an iron rod → Freudian psychoanalysis

Stoicism

be a rock - resilient & unfazed, unaffected by the outside world

Existentialism

individuals are driven by a pursuit of purpose and meaning in existence - it is the individual’s responsibility to find such.

Absurdism

life is ridiculous, chaotic, purposeless and meaningless

Nihilism

life is meaningless and empty (philosophy of nothing, slightly pessimistic)

Utilitarianism

actions/morality are to be judged on net consequence or utility

Deontology

morality should follow a moral code

Relativism

morality as a whole is relative and culture-dependent

Liberalism

Left-wing

Conservatism

Right-wing

Libertarianism

prioritise individual freedom

Cynicism

a slightly pessimistic, critical outlook on life

Hedonism

life is about maximising pleasure (Hayden’s oyster)

Marxism

society - and life - can be categorised into hierarchical classes and individuals are shaped by their class experience

Myth of Sisyphus

struggling is pleasure (the journey is pleasure) and is indeed the purpose of life

Romanticism/idealism

dreams and ideals can conquer reality/practicalities

Realism

practicality comes first

Drama (General) 13

Staging/stage direction

An instruction in the text of a play indicating the movement, position, or tone of an actor, or the sound effects and lighting.

  • The man deals a deck of cards or Katy enters the room are examples of stage directions.

Euphemism

Sugar-coating

  • Melody is vertically-challenged
  • Bob passed away
  • Ted kicked the bucket

Rhetorical question

A figure of speech in which a question is asked for a reason other than to get an answer

  • I am a Jew. Hath not a jew eyes?
  • Why didn’t you turn off the lights?

Monologue

When a character speaks out loud for a long time in a dramatic way

  • Someone might lecture you with a monologue

Soliloquy

When a character speaks alone to himself/herself or to the audience

  • Now is the winter of our discontent made glorious summer by the sun of York.

Aside

When a fictional character breaks away from the events of the story to talk to themselves or directly to the audience.

  • Hamlet's first line in the play Hamlet is a great example of an aside. His stepfather/uncle addresses Hamlet as such, and Hamlet addresses the audience with, A little more than kin and less than kind, demonstrating his feelings about the situation without revealing this to anyone else onstage.

Apostrophe

When a speaker switches from addressing the audience to directly addressing an absent third party

  • O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?

Comic relief family

Comic relief

Humorous characters or events that intends to offset more serious episodes, lightening the mood to give the audiences a break

  • The archaeologist, who begins as oafish comic relief, exemplifies her gift for character drawing
  • The gravedigger in Shakespeare’s Hamlet is constantly surrounded by death, yet he possesses a humorous and lighthearted aura → comic relief

Sarcasm

Funny, mocking exaggeration

  • Melody, you’re so tall today

Satire

A lighthearted mockery/critique of something important such as politics

  • Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice is a prime example of social satire, questioning and poking fun at the customs and expectations surrounding marriage in 19th century English society

satirical

Irony (verbal, situational, dramatic)

Verbal: when a character says something and means another, especially if they mean the opposite

  • But Brutus says he was ambitious; And Brutus is an honourable man.
  • Situational: an expected outcome does not happen, or if the opposite happens instead (gap between our expectations and reality)
  • A fire station burns down
  • The whole of Romeo & Juliet

Pun

Make a joke exploiting the different possible meanings of a word.

  • Harold and the apple lived apple-y ever after.
  • Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun [or son] of York

Puns are only useful for Shakespearean plays

Tragedy 5

Tragic hero (Aristotle)

Aristotle's mould of a tragic hero is an individual who commits a tragic flaw (hamartia), without evil intent, great wrongs or injuries that ultimately lead to their misfortune, followed by them realising their wrongdoings and the true nature of events that led to this destiny. This means the hero still must be – to some degree – morally grounded.

  • Such tragedies can happen to anyone, yet can be prevented, thus the audience learns from tragic heroes.
  • They fall. We rise.
  • Aristotle claims: A man does not become a hero until he can see the root of his own downfall. - catharsis
  • Macbeth fits the role of a tragic hero because he is born to nobility, and he has good character. But his fatal flaw, his ambition, leads to his death at the end of the play. It also pushes him to commit many atrocities, including murder, as he falls deeper and deeper into darkness.

Hamartia (tragic flaw)

A fatal flaw leading to the downfall of a tragic hero or heroine.

  • Othello's fatal flaw is his jealousy. Fueled by Iago's lies, Othello flies into a jealous rage and murders his wife. Having discovered that she is in truth innocent, he kills himself as well.

Hubris

Possessing too much pride / arrogance (hubris can be an example of hamartia)

  • At the start of Macbeth, Macbeth is not a prideful character. However, by the end of the play, he becomes a prideful tyrant where his hubris ultimately gets the best of him.

Catharsis

When a character is released and relieved from strong or repressed emotions

  • Caesar was betrayed by his comrade, Brutus, and was brutally murdered. Brutus feels an overwhelming amount of guilt due to this action and catharsis occurs when he commits suicide bringing a purge of emotions.

Peripeteia

A sudden reversal of fortune or change in circumstances

  • An example of this is the death of King Creon's son Haemon at his father's hands after he opposes him, and Oedipus' discovery that he killed his own father and married his mother..
